items.title: North Korea Rejects IAEA Resolution, Vows to Keep Nuclear Status
body: North Korea dismissed a recent resolution by the UN nuclear watchdog against Pyongyang’s nuclear program and vowed to maintain its status as a nuclear-armed state.

In a statement carried Saturday by North Korea’s state-run Korean Central News Agency, Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of the North Korean leader, called the International Atomic Energy Agency’s recent resolution “meaningless and inefficient”and said that it would have “no effect” on the nation’s position as a nuclear weapons state.

The IAEA adopted the resolution earlier this week, reaffirming that North Korea cannot have nuclear-weapons-state status under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, according to Yonhap News. It also called on Pyongyang to immediately cease all related activities.

“It is the most important matter for the national security to ensure that the credibility of the nuclear force is not questioned in any case for the DPRK, which is constantly exposed to the nuclear threat of the hostile forces,” Kim said in the KCNA report, referring to the North’s official name.

items.title: Trump to Meet Japan's Takaichi on UN Sidelines Next Week
body: President Donald Trump will meet with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly meeting in New York next week, their first-face-to-face since the US intervened to help prop up Japan’s yen.
US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz shared plans for the two leaders to meet during a call with reporters Friday.

The US and Japan in late July moved to bolster the Japanese yen after the currency dropped to a near four-decade low of 164 per US dollar. It was the first coordinated yen-buying operation from the two countries since 1998.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent earlier this week defended the moves, saying that a stronger yen was better for US exports and meant Tokyo would not have to sell US assets to finance foreign currency intervention.
Read More: Bessent Says US Yen Intervention Was ‘Nominal,’ Backs US Exports
Takaichi arranged a meeting with Trump next week to align views on China before he meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Japanese media reported earlier.

Besides tensions with China, trade and the war in Iran are likely to be on the docket when Trump and Takaichi meet. The US and Japan agreed to a tariff truce last year, including a $550 billion Japanese investment fund. Takaichi has also sought to boost her country’s military to help counter China in the region, and Trump has praised Tokyo’s purchases of US defense equipment.

The Iran war, however, has been an irritant in relations, with Trump earlier this year expressing frustration that allies including Japan have not responded to his call for military help to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

During her meeting with Trump in March, Takaichi highlighted a pledge to purchase more oil from the US as the war in the Middle East squeezed global energy flows. Japan, which relies on imports for nearly all of its oil, is particularly vulnerable to energy price spikes.

Trump and Takaichi enjoy a warm relationship. During the March meeting, Trump referenced the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor that drew the US into World War II when answering a question about the Iran war. Takaichi was seen pursing her lips and glancing at her advisers during the exchange. Still, Takaichi repeatedly thanked the president for his commitment to the US-Japan alliance.

items.title: Nvidia CEO Says There's '0% Chance' That World Will End in 2030
body: Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang renewed his pushback against AI doomsday scenarios, saying that the technology doesn’t pose an extinction risk to humanity.
“However it’s characterized, 2030 is not going to be the end of the world,” Huang said in an interview with CBS News. “There is a 0% chance it’s going to be the end of the world.”

During multiple appearances at events in recent days, the CEO has reiterated his stance that artificial intelligence can be safely managed. Huang, whose company is the leading provider of AI processors, has also argued against the need for new regulations.
Read More: Nvidia CEO Calls for AI Safety Tests at King Charles Summit

Anthropic PBC employee Jacob Coxon kicked off a wave of AI unease with his resignation earlier this month. He warned that the researchers building AI “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
During the CBS interview, which is slated to air in full on Sunday, Huang argued that the industry shouldn’t slow down.
“We should go as fast as we can, irrespective of anyone else,” he said. “But we would never ever, and never should, ship products before they’re ready and deliver products that are unsafe.”

items.title: Paramount in Settlement Talks With States Over Warner Takeover
body: Paramount Skydance Corp. shares rose as much as 8.7% in after-hours trading after the Wall Street Journal reported the company was in advanced talks with California officials about settling litigation surrounding its proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery Inc.
Reuters reported that a settlement could come this weekend or Monday. Warner Bros. shares climbed 8.6%.
California and 11 other states, along with the Writers Guild trade union, have sued to block the $110 billion deal, arguing that it will stifle competition in the cable-TV and film business.

A California judge ordered settlement talks, which have been formally scheduled for Oct. 14-15. But discussions between the parties have been ongoing, according to two people familiar with the talks who asked not to be identified because the deliberations aren’t public.

A spokesperson for Paramount declined to comment. A spokesperson for California Attorney General Rob Bonta said potential settlement talks are confidential and that his office “cannot confirm or deny whether settlement talks are occurring or their alleged substance.”
Paramount has made offers to try and settle the suits, including promises to release 30 films a year in theaters and increase production of TV shows.
Bonta has said he doesn’t favor behavioral remedies like that because they are hard to enforce. The attorney general has said he prefers structural changes, such as a sale of assets.

California’s top law enforcer told Bloomberg TV on Thursday that a sale of some intellectual property “could be a component” of a settlement. The deal would bring well-known Warner Bros. movie franchises such as DC Comics, Harry Potter and The Lord of the Rings into the Paramount fold.
Others have speculated that Paramount might sell some of Warner Bros. cable-TV channels, such as TBS and CNN, to win over the parties who are suing.

Paramount will be required to pay late fees of $7 million a day to Warner Bros. starting at the end of this month. A trial date isn’t scheduled until March. A failed deal would force it to pay $7 billion to Warner Bros.
“Paramount has strong reasons to reach a workable compromise,” Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Geetha Ranganathan wrote in a research note Friday.

items.title: OpenAI Sees Burning Through $278 Billion by 2030: FT
body: OpenAI expects that its negative free cash flow will reach $278 billion from 2026 to the end of 2030, the Financial Times reported, citing a company presentation.

The figures were part of a private company presentation in July related to a computing deal, according to a person with knowledge of the deal, who requested anonymity discussing nonpublic information. This person declined to discuss financial figures.

Though the company projects its revenue will increase from $36 billion this year to $350 billion in 2030, it is investing heavily in computing power and expects expenses to vastly outpace those gains, the FT reported.
OpenAI declined to comment.

On Tuesday, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI has been holding early talks with investors about a fresh funding round that would value the company at more than $1.2 trillion ahead of an initial public offering. The FT first reported those talks.

OpenAI Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman told Fortune earlier that the company’s long-anticipated IPO is still in the works but would not happen this year. The additional funding, if the AI giant takes it, would provide flexibility to potentially push back its IPO further, by one or two quarters, Bloomberg reported.
Another reason OpenAI could consider additional fundraising would be to support more mergers and acquisitions, Bloomberg reported.

items.title: ECP-Backed ProEnergy Seeks Up to $50 Billion Value in IPO
body: ProEnergy, a power generation firm backed by Energy Capital Partners, is seeking a valuation of as much as $50 billion in a US initial public offering, according to people familiar with the matter.

The company, which builds and tests gas turbines and small so-called dispatchable power facilities, is working with Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan Chase & Co. on the IPO process, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private.
Depending on the market, the IPO could value ProEnergy at around $40 billion to $50 billion, one of the people said. ECP could also consider selling ProEnergy, a different person said.

ProEnergy’s PE6000 aeroderivative gas turbine can produce enough energy to power 40,000 homes, according to the company’s website. The company struck a pact with artificial intelligence infrastructure provider Crusoe to power its data center projects with a deal that features 13 of the turbines, according to a statement in April.
ECP paid about $275 million for roughly 60% of the company in 2024, one of the people said.

Deliberations are ongoing, details of the deal may change and more banks could be added to the lineup, the people said. Representatives for ECP, Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan declined to comment. A spokesperson for ProEnergy didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

ProEnergy is among the companies seeking to capture surging demand for power for data centers, and is also seeking to pitch its natural gas-powered equipment to help bridge the gap as coal-fired plants are retired and renewables have yet to come online, its website shows.
Read More: Natural Gas Set to Dethrone Oil as Top US Energy Source by 2030

A listing would build on a string of debuts from companies that will benefit from the push to build out and power artificial intelligence operations. However, performances have mostly been mixed in the aftermarket.

Half of the 10 largest US IPOs this year comprise companies that are benefiting from the boom in AI data center construction. Their share prices have mostly struggled, with Innio NV and Madison Air Solutions Corp. down at least 11% from IPOs that brought in more than $2.5 billion each.

items.title: Google Joins OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta in Disclosing AI Hacks
body: Google’s Gemini artificial intelligence model inadvertently hacked into three company systems in May during cybersecurity testing, adding to a string of breaches by AI agents that have alarmed security experts and developers of the technology alike.

The hacks happened during the same tests run by the AI security vendor Irregular that led to breaches previously disclosed by OpenAI, Anthropic PBC and Meta Platforms Inc. Irregular confirmed on Friday that the breaches were all part of the same issue and that the firm had disclosed them to the relevant AI developers in late July.

One of the Google breaches occurred when Gemini was asked to retrieve information from a fictional company that happened to have the same name as a real company, Google confirmed after an earlier Wall Street Journal report. The model guessed a password to access the real company’s service. A Google spokesperson said the company notified authorities.

A recent series of breaches by agentic AI systems have touched off a worldwide debate over the escalating risks of AI and the measures required to mitigate them. Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei has called for an industrywide slowdown in development of the technology — a proposal endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Elon Musk and others.

US President Donald Trump, Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg are among those who’ve pushed back against the idea of new regulation, however, arguing among other things that companies should be capable of regulating themselves. Some AI upstarts have also warned that more regulations threaten to make it harder for smaller companies to compete against larger rivals.
The Gemini breaches “highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly,” said Heather Adkins, vice president of security engineering at Google.

The other Gemini hacks occurred when the model performed web searches with the name of the company. Adkins said that led the model to public online repositories containing credentials belonging to other companies that it used to access more systems.
“In all three of these instances, the model stopped,” Adkins said. “We ensured the three entities were made aware.”
Irregular spokesperson Josef Laor said the company took “immediate action, and all known issues on our end were remedied and resolved weeks ago.”

items.title: Trump Says Son Will Repay Russian Oligarch for Wedding Party
body: President Donald Trump said his son, Donald Trump Jr., told him he was repaying a Russian oligarch for a wedding party, seeking to tamp down on an incident that has spurred fresh ethical questions.
“I asked about it. He said, ‘No, I’m paying him back, Dad,’ so, and that was a while ago, so I heard he’s paying him,” Trump told reporters Friday in the Oval Office when asked about the controversy.
“I understand that Don’s paid him back,” he said at one point.
Trump sought to downplay the matter, casting the oligarch as a friend of his son’s and saying it was common for those who know a bride or groom to pay for a wedding party.
“A person that he knows, I guess a friend of his, gave him a wedding party. That’s very common. I’ve heard of many people giving wedding parties,” Trump said.

A person familiar with the matter also said the president’s son had made a repayment, though the total sum and timing are not clear. The person spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the transaction.

The president’s daughter-in-law, Bettina Trump, said in an Instagram post earlier this week that the couple had a private marriage ceremony in May, which was followed by a celebration the following weekend in the Bahamas. The second event was hosted by Umar Kremlev, Bettina Trump said.

ProPublica reported this week that Kremlev bankrolled the Bahamas celebration, shelling out hundreds of thousands of dollars to rent a private island and put on a fireworks show, among other expenses. Kremlev is a Russian oligarch with ties to President Vladimir Putin and has been personally sanctioned by Ukraine over those connections.
The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee is probing Kremlev’s role in funding the celebrations.

The wedding party is one of only a number of ethical flashpoints during Trump’s second term as the president’s family has continued to pursue business ventures. Trump has also at times mixed his official and personal duties, drawing scrutiny. Last weekend, he attended the Amgen Irish Open at one of his family’s golf resorts in Ireland.

items.title: Trump to Meet Venezuelan Leader Delcy Rodríguez in New York
body: President Donald Trump will meet with Venezuelan leader Delcy Rodríguez in New York next week on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly meeting, US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz told reporters.

Rodríguez’s visit to the US and her meeting with Trump, planned as a pull-aside conversation, mark a major step in the rapid normalization of relations between Caracas and the Trump administration. She will be the first Venezuelan head of state to attend the gathering in nearly a decade, following Nicolas Maduro’s visit in 2018.
Rodríguez was removed from the US Treasury’s sanctions list on April 1, eliminating a major obstacle to a potential visit.

Her travel would also put Rodríguez in the same city where Maduro remains in federal custody while facing US narco-terrorism and drug-trafficking charges, after a US military raid removed him from power, underscoring the remarkable reversal that has made his former vice president a partner of the government prosecuting him.

items.title: Trump Extends $100,000 H-1B Visa Fee That's Tied Up in Court
body: President Donald Trump extended for another year a $100,000 payment requirement for employers seeking to bring certain H-1B workers into the US, saying the restriction has reduced the reliance on lower-paid foreign labor.

The policy, which has drawn opposition from major firms that rely on skilled foreign workers, will remain in place through Sept. 21, 2027, with limited exceptions for workers, companies or industries deemed to be in the national interest, the White House said in a statement on Friday.

The extension comes as the payment requirement remains tied up in court. A federal judge in Massachusetts struck down the government’s guidance for implementing it in June, and the administration has appealed.

The Department of Homeland Security last month also began pursuing a separate and more far-reaching proposal that would impose a roughly $103,000 fee on all H-1B petitions subject to the annual visa cap. Unlike the earlier initiative, it would apply to almost anyone getting a new visa, not just those who are outside the country.

The White House said on Friday that registrations from the largest information technology staffing and outsourcing firms have fallen 92% since the H-1B payment requirement and a new weighted selection system took effect, while more applications are now for workers with advanced degrees and higher-paying job offers.

But critics say some of the planned changes could hurt US-driven innovation by severely impairing the coveted visa program. More than 700 petitions have included the $100,000 payment, according to Trump’s Friday proclamation.

The White House also issued a separate executive order Friday directing government officials to review would-be H-1B employers for “recent or planned layoffs” of US workers when considering whether to approve H-1B applications. That will include H-1B petitions that have already been filed.
Trump is also asking the agencies reviewing H-1B applications to consider more data on pay, industrial conditions and employment specialization from other parts of the government.

items.title: Protect College Sports Act Gains Steam With Saban, Deion Sanders, Cruz Support
body: A lot of times when something is described as the Wild West, it’s hyperbole. But in the case of all the money pouring into major US college sports, it seems appropriate. Politicians have taken notice and now a push to regulate the system is gaining steam. This week, we catch you up on that and detail more Wrexham effect.

We’d also be remiss, if we didn’t acknowledge that Giles Turner is leaving Business of Sports for a bigger job with Bloomberg. Although, we’ll probably be able to twist his arm to keep writing about the mess at Chelsea and other football matters.
Matt Townsend is taking his place for the meantime, so send any feedback, tips or ideas to him here. And If you aren’t yet signed up to receive this newsletter, you can do so here.

There is bipartisan agreement that the US government should do something about the state of college sports, and over the past week or so sweeping legislation made progress in the Senate and gained more media attention.

Texas Senator Ted Cruz, a sponsor of the Protect College Sports Act, appeared on ESPN’s College GameDay last weekend and made his case for the legislation in Austin ahead of the Texas-Ohio State matchup.
“Right now, college sports is in chaos,” Cruz said amid a rowdy crowd. The Republican said his confidence in the bill becoming a law is “very, very high.”

Nick Saban, one of college football’s winningest coaches, is being featured in an ad supporting the bill, with the former Alabama and LSU coach saying the legislation “ends the chaos.” The same nonprofit, Saving College Sports, is also running a spot with Deion Sanders, the NFL Hall of Famer, in which the current University of Colorado head coach touts how the SCPA strengthens historically Black colleges and universities.
The bill easily passed a procedural hurdle in the Senate Thursday and is nearing a final vote. But there are still many potential roadblocks ahead, and it is Washington, where nothing is ever easy.

Andrew Silverman, an analyst for Bloomberg Intelligence, points out that there is strong support in the Senate and from the White House, the NCAA and several collegiate conferences, including the powerful SEC and Big Ten. But companion legislation in the House of Representatives is still in committee, and a similar bill last year never got to a floor vote. He estimated there’s a 60% chance a law gets enacted before the end of the year.

A lot is likely to change in the bills given all the powerful entities with money on the line, and that could decrease support. OpenSecrets said there’s been a “surge” in lobbying spending from broadcasters, athlete-advocacy groups, schools and athletic conferences, and that’s only for data through the end of June.

There is also a growing partisan divide, even though the Senate bill has sponsors from both sides of the aisle. OpenSecrets, which tracks lobbying spending, noted that Saving College Sports was founded by Cody Campbell, a billionaire who funds Republican causes and has financially backed Texas Tech’s football team. The nonprofit is also led by Republican strategists, including Cruz’s former chief of staff, according to OpenSecrets.

Some Democrats, including Connecticut Senator Chris Murphy, say the bill doesn’t go far enough in protecting the rights of student athletes. Labor unions, including the AFL-CIO, have also opposed the legislation.

“Is it a perfect bill? No,” said Shelley Moore Capito, a Republican senator from West Virginia and one of the PCSA’s sponsors, before this week’s procedural vote. Some of the concerns being raised are a “smokescreen, quite frankly. I don’t think it has much validation.”

The PCSA seeks to rein in the money that flooded college sports in recent years following court decisions that allowed athletes to be paid for their name, image and likeness. The bill would also limit player transfers, while addressing other issues including media rights and fee caps for agents.

Even less publicized parts of the legislation could hold it up. The PCSA would limit the ability of conferences to expand and for schools to change leagues. Per the bill’s original text, a university wanting to move would have to spend five years as an independent, which would likely hurt its finances without the revenue from a conference media deal.

According to Sports Illustrated, there is big pushback to that part of the bill coming from politicians in Florida working on behalf of Florida State and the University of Miami, who have been looking to leave the Atlantic Coast Conference. This week, the Republican senators from Florida (Rick Scott and Ashley Moody) voted against progressing the PCSA.
A 60% chance of this becoming law by year end might be too high. – Matt Townsend
Bath City’s new owner Andrew Stalbow says that when he was looking for a club to buy, he wanted a small team in a beautiful location that owns its own stadium.

Bath, which is a historic Roman City in the west of England, is where Stalbow and his global consortium of about 50 investors have settled. He’s lived in California working as a prominent mobile gaming executive and co-founder of Seriously, known for the hit game Best Fiends.

Stalbow raised a total of $8.5 million and says he could have attracted more. The money will be used to help get Bath City promoted and upgrade infrastructure. It’s in the seventh tier of English football, two below where Wrexham was when it was acquired.

The new owner is also going to do a Wrexham, as it were, by documenting the club’s journey by launching a daily video called Bath Time. “We all know stories of clubs that have had incredible seasons,” he said. One of the backers is Tears For Fears bandmate Curt Smith, who was born near Bath’s city center. Smith is “very community minded,” Stalbow said.
Apart from Wrexham, Stalbow takes some inspiration from the Italian football teams in Como and Venezia. Both are trying to leverage their region’s tourism to bring in more fans.

Investor interest in the lower leagues of English football has been enhanced by the success of Wrexham. A new ownership group at York City has helped take the club into England’s 92-strong football league, and KSI, the influencer, recently bought a minority stake in Dagenham & Redbridge.

Bath City runs a women’s team and an under-18 team, which both add to costs. And there are no big broadcast deals in the seventh tier of the football pyramid. Some would say the only broadcast deal of any size is the one enjoyed by the 20 teams in the Premier League (minimum of £120 million a year compared to around £10 million in the tier below and less beyond that).
For the time being, Stalbow is dreaming of the journey, adding that “we need to prove that we will be great custodians of the club.” — David Hellier

items.title: Carney Pursues EU Partnership, Investment Boom to Reduce US Dependence
body: Welcome back to Canada Daily, the newsletter on business, economics and politics from Vancouver to Montreal and beyond. If this was forwarded to you, sign up.
If the trade wars launched by US President Donald Trump really do cause a global realignment, this past week gave a glimpse of what it may look like — at least for Canada.

At the start of the week, Prime Minister Mark Carney kicked off a much-hyped investment summit in Toronto that drew many of the world’s biggest money managers, who looked through a “deal book” of Canadian projects hungry for global capital.

Carney then flew to France, where he addressed the European Parliament and discussed an ambitious plan to forge a new partnership with the continent. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen pitched that Canada become an “associate member” of the EU, a title that does not yet exist but could include closer alignment on defense, energy, university research, space and artificial intelligence.

For the prime minister, the two events are a demonstration of “the ambition and clarity of his foreign policy,” said Roland Paris, a University of Ottawa professor and former adviser to Carney’s predecessor, Justin Trudeau.

Paris cautioned against overstating the shift, pointing out that the US “is going to continue to be Canada’s principal trading partner, period.” But he said Carney is clearly pursuing twin objectives of stimulating an investment boom in Canada while securing greater market access for its exports — all with the larger goal of reducing economic dependence on the US.

The coming weeks will reveal more about how far Carney is willing and able to go with the EU. He’s scheduled to meet French President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday on the islands of Saint Pierre and Miquelon, just off the coast of Newfoundland. The next day he’ll fly to New York for the United Nations General Assembly. At the end of October, Canada will host an EU summit in Montreal.
In the meantime, Parliament resumes from its summer break on Monday and Carney’s big plans will face the scrutiny of opposition parties.

All signs are that the prime minister has the Canadian public behind him. Walking away from trade talks with Trump last month has resulted in Carney’s strongest polling since he took office in March 2025, despite the damage the economy will suffer from new tariffs on both sides of the border.

“He has a great deal of political latitude at home to be pursuing this agenda,” Paris said. “As the additional US tariffs begin to bite, that could have a political cost for Carney, but at this moment he has so much political momentum that he has room to maneuver,” he added. “You just see the extent to which Canadians are determined to withstand the kind of pressure that Donald Trump has placed on Canada.”

Also in this newsletter: Morgan Stanley and CIBC win a big mandate for airport deals. Brookfield’s CEO says AI development is already slowing down. Mexico says it’s making progress toward a possible US trade deal.
The following was produced with the assistance of Bloomberg Automation.

Morgan Stanley and Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce have been hired by the Canadian government to advise on selling the operating rights to the country’s four largest airports, according to people with knowledge of the discussions. The government expects the deals to raise tens of billions of dollars — a sizable new investment opportunity for pension funds and other infrastructure investors.

Brookfield Corp. CEO Bruce Flatt said the artificial-intelligence race is already slowing because developers can’t build enough infrastructure to keep pace. The leaders of major AI labs have said in recent days that they must slow the pace of the technology to prevent advanced models from slipping beyond human control. But even before then, the sector was already reaching the limitations of how quickly data centers can be put in place, Flatt said.

Industry Minister Melanie Joly urged Stellantis and its unionized workers to return to the negotiating table, as a collective agreement covering thousands of employees in Canada is set to expire Sunday. The parties have been at an impasse since last week, when armored-vehicle maker Roshel said it had signed a memo that outlines steps toward buying the company’s Brampton plant. Unifor opposes the potential sale.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said her government is making progress toward a possible trade deal with the US following a phone conversation with her President Donald Trump. “The call went very well,” Sheinbaum said Friday. “We reached some agreements, but we cannot announce them until the final deal is in place.”

Westinghouse Electric, a provider of reactor technology to nuclear power plants, is seeking a valuation of more than $50 billion in its US initial public offering, according to people familiar with the matter. The company, which is owned by Brookfield and Cameco, is targeting a public filing as soon as in October, they said, though that timing may change.

Macron said he would convene a meeting of the Group of Seven countries in the coming weeks to discuss a potential release from strategic oil-product stockpiles as soaring energy prices sap economic growth. As well, Saudi Aramco told at least two oil refining customers in Europe that they will be allocated no crude next month under long-term agreements after the kingdom’s key pipeline to the Red Sea was attacked, people informed of the decision said.
The S&P/TSX Composite Index fell 0.2% on Friday but still ended the week up 0.3%. That ended a four-week losing skid for the stocks benchmark.

America is in the midst of a “fun shortage,” with people going out less and going home early, delivering a particularly hard blow to nightlife. The US has lost 7,000 bars and nightclubs since 2006, and downtown streets in many cities haven’t fully recovered from the pandemic slump. But this summer’s World Cup offered a glimpse of what might be possible and showcased cities’ potential vibrancy. This success has led some policymakers to push for more permanent changes. Massachusetts passed new “fun agenda” measures to allow towns and cities to offer discounted drinks during happy hour and create public drinking districts.

items.title: Trump Says US Has Security Deal on Greenland With Denmark
body: President Donald Trump said he reached an agreement with Denmark over Greenland that would give the US “permanent control over security” for the Arctic island, but without specifying the terms of any pact.
Trump announced the deal on social media Friday, saying that the arrangement was one that addressed “ALL of our many US concerns” and would be at “NO COST to the United States.”

“At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America,” he wrote.

“This is an ‘Infinite Life’ Agreement, there is no end,” Trump added. He didn’t share the text for the deal, but the Danish government said the pact is expected to be signed on at the United Nations General Assembly.

“I am glad that we are about to make a great agreement for Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, and the United States,” Denmark’s Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said in a statement Friday. “An agreement which strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic Area and therefore is great for NATO and Europe as well.”

The deal touted by the US president appears to be a significant pullback from his previous attempts to take control of the Danish territory. That demand drew pushback from European allies and presented one of the gravest challenges to the NATO alliance since the end of World War II.

Trump had repeatedly ramped up intimidation over Greenland during his second term as US president, including making veiled threats to seize the island by force and raising the prospect of higher tariffs on goods from European nations that do not fall in line.

That pressure campaign came to a dramatic head in January during the World Economic Forum at Davos, where Trump assailed European allies in his address. The president, though, eventually backed down following talks with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, claiming instead that he had reached the parameters of a framework agreement regarding Greenland and the Arctic region.
Earlier: US Seeks Carte Blanche for Military Presence in Greenland

The US had sought to rewrite its defense agreement with Denmark to remove any limits on its military presence in Greenland, even though it has scaled back its presence there for decades. A 1951 deal with Denmark said the US must consult with and inform Copenhagen of its plans but even that was seen as a largely pro forma stipulation that required little more than notification.

Friday’s announcement could signal a resolution to a standoff that was almost entirely of Trump’s own making. Trump’s post suggested the US was getting what it already had, and his claims were impossible to assess without a text of any revised agreement.

“Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defense area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a separate statement.

A US official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the deal, said the agreement would ban any non-NATO bases on the island and adversaries from making investments that could threaten the US.

items.title: Saudi Oil Cuts Tied to War Hit Europe: Evening Briefing Americas
body: Europe is suffering more collateral damage from the Iran war. Saudi Aramco told at least two oil refining customers on the continent that they will be allocated no crude next month under long-term agreements after a key pipeline to the Red Sea was attacked.

The absence of Saudi flows next month will heighten the need for European buyers to secure replacements. Already, Poland’s Orlen SA has been hunting for shipments, helping propel prices of regional oil grades higher. Dated Brent, which is the benchmark for real-world barrels in Europe, topped $130 this week at one point.

Saudi Arabia was forced to shut its East-West pipeline after it was reportedly attacked by drones launched from Iraq. Fighting has intensified across the Middle East in recent weeks amid the stalemated war, with Iran-aligned forces, including the Yemen-based Houthis, targeting US allies.

Westinghouse Electric, a provider of reactor technology to nuclear power plants, is said to seek a valuation of more than $50 billion in its US initial public offering. Westinghouse’s nuclear power technology is used by 57% of the world’s 417 nuclear reactors and the company is said to have a pipeline of as many as 91 opportunities for its latest generation reactor.

The nuclear industry is seeing a revival thanks in part to the power needs of data centers. AI companies and firms building the infrastructure have seen a wave of investment, including blockbuster IPOs like SpaceX’s record-breaking debut, whose pitch focused on its growing AI business. Few of the deals, however, have been standout successes in the aftermarket. Half of the 10 largest US IPOs this year comprise companies benefiting from the AI data center boom. Their share prices have mostly struggled.

Down on the planet’s surface, though, the US is running low. The Trump administration has warned allies to expect delays of as much as five years in key weapons deliveries as it rebuilds its own depleted munitions stocks.

Multiple European nations are expecting deliveries of key missile and air defense capabilities to be pushed back as a result of the US military exhausting its own arsenal in the Iran war. Germany has asked the US to speed up delivery of the long-range Tomahawk cruise missile and the ground-based Typhon launcher, but depleted US stocks means its manufacturer, RTX’s Raytheon, is unlikely to fulfill the order for half a decade.

US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has long criticized the health agencies he now oversees for being captured by corporate influence, has ties to a nonprofit group that solicited payment from companies in exchange for access to top agency officials.

Ahead of the “MAHA Summit” on Sept. 29, a menu of sponsorship options was circulated to companies and consultants with various tiers of support, according to people familiar with the solicitations who weren’t authorized to speak publicly.

The highest level, quoted at $300,000 to some prospective sponsors, guaranteed a speaking slot at the event “with meaningful input on the panel composition and topic” as well as a “private dinner for 30 guests” with Kennedy and Mehmet Oz, head of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.

items.title: Trump Pushes Back at Lawmaker Who Criticized Him on Immigration
body: President Donald Trump said he disagreed with a Republican from Florida who criticized his immigration policies, defending his stance for helping him and other GOP lawmakers win office.

Maria Elvira Salazar, who is fighting to keep her seat in November’s midterm election in a Miami-area district heavily impacted by the administration’s policies, posted an ad this week saying Trump’s approach has gone too far.
“I disagree with her,” Trump told reporters Friday. “She obviously doesn’t have a very strong feeling for the border, but I do, and I understand what she’s saying.”
Trump said that he had won the presidential election because of his policies on the border and credited a past endorsement with helping Salazar win election to Congress.
“I’m very strong on the borders, and she isn’t, and she’s a nice person. I got her elected. Without me, she wouldn’t have gotten elected,” he added. “She got a little bit soft on the border.”

In a 30-second ad that was filmed in front of the White House, Salazar, who has been in Congress since 2021, warned that Trump was alienating many of his own supporters. She urged the president to “be careful” of what his advisers are telling him about immigration policy, saying “the same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”
With the midterms just over six weeks away, some Republicans are showing an increased willingness to push back on or keep their distance from the administration.

Utah Senator John Curtis on Friday put out a social media post criticizing the president’s son, Donald Trump Jr., over reports a Russian oligarch with ties to Vladimir Putin helped pay for a party at his wedding, calling it “corruption.” In Iowa, Senate candidate Ashley Hinson didn’t appear with Vice President JD Vance at a rally for Republicans.

South Florida, where Salazar’s district is, has one of the biggest immigrant populations in the US. The Cook Political report has rated her district as “likely Republican.” Democrats will need to flip just a handful of seats to win control of the House, with Republicans facing headwinds from voter discontent over the high cost of living and the Iran war.

items.title: Anthropic to Embed Accenture Evaluators to Test AI Safety
body: Anthropic PBC is partnering with Accenture Plc, a management and technology consulting company, to test the safety of its advanced artificial intelligence models by embedding evaluators from the consulting firm directly within its operations.

Accenture’s evaluators will red-team the AI lab’s newest models and test their safeguards, as well as conduct assessments to ensure its technology is aligned, or acting in line with human objectives, Anthropic said in a Friday blog post. The evaluators will have similar levels of access inside Anthropic as the startup’s own employees, the company said.
Both Anthropic and Accenture, which have an existing relationship, expect to invest at least $1 billion in building capacity in this area, Anthropic said.

On Saturday, Anthropic chief Amodei addressed growing concerns about the security risks of cutting-edge AI models in a 3,800-word essay, calling for a slowdown in development and saying he would implement new safety steps such as third-party evaluators.
Accenture’s embedded assessors will closely track how AI models evolve in training and observe the behind-the-scenes decision-making on how Anthropic is developing its technology, the company said.

“From this vantage point, embedded evaluators can assess how a company operates, verify that it is keeping its safety commitments, and identify blind spots. They can also report incidents and give the public a more informed account of benefits and risks,” Anthropic said.

Last year, Accenture and Anthropic struck a multiyear partnership to deploy AI at companies, forming a group of 30,000 people to be trained on Claude so they can help scale AI-powered systems for clients. And this March, Accenture announced Cyber.AI, a security solution powered by Anthropic’s Claude AI model.

The “third-party” nature of the partnership stands to draw skepticism given the close ties between Accenture and the large AI startups. Earlier this year, the consulting giant projected that its work with key AI partners such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Palantir would more than double in the coming year.

Anxiety about AI’s existential risks gained momentum last week, driven by the high-profile departure of Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon, who accused AI companies of “gambling with our lives” in a resignation post he shared on social media.

In the past several days, numerous AI company leaders, including Amodei and OpenAI Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman, have urged slowing the pace of the development of the technology to address its increasingly unpredictable risks — though they diverge on exactly how it should be handled. Amodei had suggested that companies open themselves to embedded independent evaluators to oversee the development of the technology.

Anthropic on Thursday issued a report detailing that 26% of its AI research and development work was driven by its Claude chatbot, providing an indication of how AI can help speed up development of future models.

items.title: Trump's Tariff Clout Will Survive a Democratic Blue Wave in the Midterms
body: This is Washington Edition, the newsletter about money, power and politics in the nation’s capital. Every Friday, Bloomberg Intelligence senior analyst Nathan Dean gives his insights into what’s been happening and what’s coming up in the nooks and crannies of government and markets. Sign up here. Email our editors here.

The House is gone – after passing legislation that will allow President Donald Trump to impose new tariffs on countries that buy Russia oil (think China and India). The Senate has failed to pass the crypto bill known as the Clarity Act (for what that means, please see my piece from Aug. 21). And now we’re heading into the thick of election season.
So I figured this week that I’d bring you the two top questions my clients are asking about the midterms.

What is one thing the market is under-appreciating? There seems to be a thought that if a Blue Wave happens, Trump will walk back on tariffs. We don’t think that’s the case. Whether it’s holding off announcing new China tariffs until after next week’s Xi-Trump summit or threatening new European Union tariffs over its relationship with Canada, we are likely heading for two more years of tariff announcements, retreats and implementation. The president wasn’t on firm legal grounds when tried tariffs in 2025; he will be in 2027.

What industries are most exposed to the election? As we write on the Bloomberg Terminal, Trump’s increasing reliance on executive authority and regulation after the midterms highlights consumer, energy, defense and financial services. A good example is this piece from Ari Natter and David Wethe on how Continental Resources Inc. has agreed to explore Venezuela for oil after Trump has pushed companies to do so.

And while it’s easy to say no legislation will happen in a gridlocked Congress, this interview from my colleague Wayne Sanders shows that if you are invested in defense contractors, Democratic control means defense spending debates in Congress will be even more important next year.
What to Know This Weekend

Trump said he would ban the cable news networks CNN and MS NOW as well as the online publication Politico from the White House, a move that strikes at the heart of First Amendment protections for the news media.
California Governor Gavin Newsom issued an executive order yesterday pushing to implement safeguards on artificial intelligence in the state that’s the epicenter of the technology’s boom.

US factory output unexpectedly declined for the first time this year as production of business equipment cooled and manufacturers grappled with higher input costs. Production fell 0.3% in August, according to Federal Reserve data released yesterday.

The crypto industry’s alliance with Trump led to many victories in Washington, but his own crypto business dealings became a factor in the failure of the landmark Clarity Act on the Senate floor this week.

Saudi Aramco told at least two oil refining customers in Europe that they will be allocated no crude next month under long-term agreements after the kingdom’s key pipeline to the Red Sea was attacked, people informed of the decision said.

The US has warned European allies to expect delays of as long as five years in deliveries of key missile and air defense weaponry as a result of the American military exhausting its own arsenal in the Iran war, officials said.

A nonprofit group with ties to US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. solicited payment from companies in exchange for access to top agency officials at an upcoming event, according to documents seen by Bloomberg News.

Warren Buffet, is stepping down as the chairman of Berkshire Hathaway Inc. to be succeeded by his son Howard, effectively ending roughly six decades at the helm of the conglomerate he founded. A federal judge in Vermont ruled that the Justice Department cannot obtain the state’s voter roles, making the 24th such loss for the government in cases around the country.

Supporters of a bill to regulate college sports expressed optimism after the Senate advanced the legislation yesterday in the second procedural vote this week. The measure calls for guidelines, including on name, image and likeness deals.

Missouri urged a federal appeals court to order a GOP-favored congressional map be used in the November election, putting the state in an unusual posture of administratively preparing for one map while its lawyers argue for another.

Today on Bloomberg Television’s Balance of Power early edition at 1 p.m., hosts Joe Mathieu and Kailey Leinz interviewed Charles Booker, the Democratic Senate candidate in Kentucky, who said “we have a real chance to win this race.”
On the program at 5 p.m., they talk with Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys about an accord with the US signed yesterday, Russia’s confrontations with the Baltic States.

On the Big Take podcast, Bloomberg’s host Sarah Holder talks to Bloomberg Opinion columnist Allison Schrager, Bertha Bradley, a labor activist known as Mama Cookie, and Joan C. Williams, a law professor, about what “working class” means today. Listen on iHeart, Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

American manufacturers continue to abandon passenger cars in favor of crossovers, SUVs and pickups. US motor vehicle assemblies were near their lowest on record in August, according to data released yesterday by the Federal Reserve. Just over 1.1 million cars were produced as a seasonally adjusted annual rate. That’s down from close to 10 million in the mid-1970s. As recently as 2015, nearly five million automobiles were produced. Part of the decline is because larger vehicles bring larger profits for auto makers. The margins are generally simply bigger on a pickup truck or SUV. The decline also reflects changing buyer tastes as buyers want more space, higher seating, and a sense of safety that larger vehicles often offer. — Alex Tanzi
The United Nations General Assembly begins its 81st session on Monday in New York.
Trump will host the Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a summit in Washington next week.
The US House is in recess until after the midterm elections. The Senate is still in session.

items.title: Anthropic Sales Near $100 Billion Before November IPO, NYT Says
body: Anthropic PBC is expected to generate more than $100 billion in annualized revenue this year as it continues to prepare for a trading debut as soon as November, according to the New York Times, citing people familiar with the matter.

The company’s run rate, a metric that projects full-year revenue from a shorter period, has surged throughout the year as business customers have embraced using its Claude artificial intelligence software to streamline coding and other workplace tasks.

As the company moves forward with plans for an IPO, it’s also confronting heightened public anxiety about AI’s potential to cause catastrophic harms. On Saturday, Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei kicked off a fresh wave of calls from top AI firms to slow down the progress of future artificial intelligence models.
Anthropic declined to comment.
Anthropic’s revenue run rate hit $65 billion by the end of July, Bloomberg News has previously reported, up from $9 billion at the end of 2025.

The dramatic acceleration in revenue bolsters Anthropic’s plans for a public listing. Anthropic and OpenAI have filed confidential paperwork to go public, with Anthropic expected to make its Wall Street debut in the coming weeks.

Reuters reported earlier this month that Anthropic was expecting to begin marketing its initial public offering in mid-October at ​the earliest and complete the listing days before the US midterm elections in November. The Wall Street Journal similarly reported on Friday that Anthropic planned to stage its IPO in November, citing unidentified people familiar with the matter.

This week, Anthropic hosted a venture capital forum to discuss developments in its AI work, with several investors in attendance, according to social media posts. Questions in the public poll for the event included how to determine whether firms have reached a more powerful form of AI known as artificial general intelligence.

items.title: Greece Wins Highest Rating Since Europe's Sovereign Debt Crisis
body: Greece clinched a double victory for its credit status, with one upgrade to Italy’s level and the hope of shedding its last score at the brink of junk.
The country is now BBB+ at Scope Ratings, on a par with that company’s view of its Mediterranean neighbor, according to a statement. That’s Greece’s highest score at any major assessor.
Separately, rival Moody’s Ratings changed its outlook to positive while keeping the nation at Baa3, its lowest rung of investment grade.

The upgrade reflects “a rapidly declining public debt ratio and strengthening fiscal sustainability, supported by large and sustained primary surpluses, structural improvements in tax administration and compliance, and a track record of prudent fiscal management,” Scope said.

There are increasing signs that the authorities’ continued focus on structural economic and institutional reforms “is bearing fruit in the form of increased economic and fiscal resilience that will exceed our current expectations,” Moody’s said in its statement.

Together, the announcements on Friday mark another milestone in Greece’s rehabilitation as a borrower, turning the page from the dark days when calamitous public finances almost forced it out of the euro.
The country’s fiscal repair has been so determined that it will probably succeed this year in bringing its debt ratio below that of Italy, whose mountain of borrowings will then be Europe’s biggest.
Greece’s central-bank chief Yannis Stournaras said Saturday in an interview that “good policies can change everything,” adding that “there are no structural constraints that cannot be addressed.”

“Many people in the past had forecast Greece would not make it,” he said. But now the country is growing twice as fast as the rest of the euro zone, there’s a rapid decline in the public debt-to-GDP ratio, and it’s undergoing reforms though more is needed, he said.
Speaking in Dublin on the sidelines of a meeting of finance ministers and central bankers, he stressed that this is also “an encouraging conclusion for many countries now.”
“But of course it needs political will and governments that understand the important issues,” he said.

Greece’s bond yields are now lower than those of France, Italy and the US. The country stands out in the region for its budget overperformance at a time when investors worry about such peers. On Friday, one measure of French bond risk rose to a key level for the first time in 14 years.
The Greek economy is growing faster than many others in Europe. The government’s primary surpluses, a budget measure which exclude interest payments, consistently exceed targets.

As a result, Athens keeps reimbursing creditors ahead of schedule. The finance ministry plans to repay some €13 billion ($14.9 billion) of bailout program debt in 2026, and continuing to do so in the future.

One source of potential turbulence for Greece is the upcoming elections, due to the highly fragmented political situation. Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis has repeatedly said that they will take place next spring.
While his center-right New Democracy party is leading the race in polls, the premier, currently in his second term, may fall short of the necessary support to shape an single-party government.
“While current polling suggests government formation could become more complex, the risk of material policy reversals appears limited,” Scope said.

items.title: Nvidia-Backed Data Center Firm Nscale Files Publicly for IPO
body: Nscale, a developer of artificial intelligence data centers that counts Nvidia Corp. and Microsoft Corp. among its partners, filed for an initial public offering in New York to fund the equipment satisfying AI’s insatiable demand for computing power.

The London-based firm had a net loss of $1.02 billion on revenue of $140.6 million for the six months ended June 30, compared with a net loss of $368.9 million on revenue of $10.4 million in the corresponding period a year earlier, according to its filing Friday with the US Securities and Exchange Commission.

Spun off from a cryptocurrency mining operation in early 2024, Nscale quickly became one of the most prominent data center newcomers powering the AI boom as a so-called neocloud operator, renting out computing resources to companies developing AI.
The company was valued in March at about $14.6 billion, in a Series C funding round led by Aker ASA and investment firm 8090 Industries. Nvidia and Nokia Oyj also participated in the round.
Nscale is seeking to raise as much as $3 billion in the IPO, Bloomberg News reported.

The company’s so-called hyperscale AI hubs in Norway, Portugal, Texas and West Virginia each have 200 megawatts of power or more, according to the filing. It agreed in April to add more than 30,000 Nvidia chips to an existing rental agreement with Microsoft at its Narvik, Norway facility.

As of August 2026, Nscale has more than 10 gigawatts of owned and controlled power at its data centers, and about $103 billion of total contract value, the filing shows. A gigawatt of electricity can provide power at any given moment to roughly 750,000 houses.

Anthropic PBC said in August it has agreed to spend $45 billion to rent AI cloud computing power from the Monarch Compute Campus, the company’s flagship data center development in West Virginia. A roughly 2,250 acre site, Monarch is expected to have 2 gigawatts of gross power capacity online by the first half of 2028, and to expand to approximately 8 GWs of gross capacity by 2031, according to the filing.
Nscale’s board includes former Meta Platforms Inc. executives Sheryl Sandberg and Nick Clegg, who previously served as the UK’s deputy prime minister.
Read More: Sandberg Says Nscale and Its CEO Remind Her of Early Facebook
Aker, Sandton Capital Partners and a trust associated with Nscale Founder and Chief Executive Officer Josh Payne are listed as having stakes of 5% in the company or more, the filing shows.

Nscale’s filing cites its close ties with Nvidia among the IPO’s risk factors, saying that the AI cloud company relies on Nvidia for its GPUs. The company issued warrants to Nvidia in 2025 as part of a Series B financing that made the chipmaker a greater than 5% holder of its stock, the filing shows. Any warrants exercised by Nvidia would be fulfilled with non-voting shares.

As part of a subscription agreement, Nscale agreed on Sept. 15 to offer $2.1 billion of unsecured convertible loan notes to investors, as well as $1 billion of unsecured convertible loan notes or non-voting shares to Nvidia, with the Nvidia portion closing on Nov. 16, according to the filing.
Companies offering investors exposure to AI infrastructure have lifted this year’s first-time share sale volume to $161.4 billion, the most since 2021, data compiled by Bloomberg show.

SpaceX raised $86.2 billion in its record IPO, touting revenue from selling AI processing power to companies including Anthropic, while South Korean memory chipmaker SK Hynix Inc.’s $26.5 billion listing came with a data center-focused pitch. Brookfield-backed data center firm Csquare Inc. raised $1.2 billion in an IPO in July.
Nscale agreed in July to buy San Francisco-based software startup Anyscale in a $1.65 billion deal, to help customers use AI computing power more efficiently.

Goldman Sachs Group Inc., JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Morgan Stanley are leading the offering, with 19 other banks working on the deal. The shares are expected to trade on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol NSCL.

items.title: Trump Drops a Legal Bid to Block Funding of Gateway Tunnel
body: The Trump administration ended its latest effort to block federal funding for the $16 billion Gateway tunnel project connecting New York and New Jersey, dropping an appeal of a judge’s ruling that funds couldn’t be suspended even as the US vowed to continue the fight.
The government agreed to dismiss its challenge to a June ruling by a federal judge who said that withholding funds from the project “flagrantly” violates the law, according to court records.

“This is a big victory for millions of New Jersey commuters and for the nearly 100,000 jobs the Gateway Tunnel Project will create,” New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill said Friday. “The Trump Administration has tried, over and over again, to illegally stop the funding for the nation’s most urgent infrastructure project.”

The Gateway project is set to build a new two-track rail tunnel beneath the Hudson River and rehabilitate the existing North River Tunnel, which opened in 1910 and was damaged by Hurricane Sandy. About 200,000 people travel on the two tracks between Newark and New York Penn Station each day. The new tunnel is scheduled to open in 2035.
A US Department of Transportation spokesman said the broader legal fight will continue.

“USDOT’s appeal against the possible use of taxpayer dollars for unconstitutional, discriminatory contracting practices continues,” the spokesman said. “What the Department dropped today was an appeal against the court’s preliminary injunction from earlier this spring which the final judgment settled in June.”

President Donald Trump’s administration froze Gateway funding in September 2025, putting construction at risk and leading New York and New Jersey to sue. Judge Jeannette Vargas temporarily blocked the attempt in February, allowing money to begin flowing again. She extended the ruling in June.
Read More: NY-NJ Gateway Tunnel Funding Freeze Ruled Flagrantly Illegal
“We took them to court and we won for New Jerseyans,” Sherrill said.

In a related lawsuit at the US Court of Federal Claims, the US and the Gateway Development Commission said Thursday that they wanted to halt the case for six months so they can “focus on settlement efforts.”

items.title: NBA Paves Way for Lakers Deal With Private Equity Policy Change
body: The NBA is amending its private equity policy to allow a firm and its executives to invest in a franchise at the same time, according to people familiar with the situation.

The shift will allow Joshua Kushner and Bob Iger to invest their own money alongside capital from Kushner’s Thrive Eternal in their purchase of the Los Angeles Lakers, said the people who weren’t authorized to speak publicly about the change.
The NBA declined to comment. Thrive didn’t respond to requests for comment.

Kushner and Iger reached a deal last month to buy the storied franchise at a record $12.5 billion valuation. But questions arose about how Thrive Eternal would support the sale, since Kushner runs the company and NBA rules previously forbid an institutional investment firm supporting its manager’s purchase.
Read More: Josh Kushner, Bob Iger Buy LA Lakers for $12.5 Billion

The NBA allows funds to acquire minority stakes in several teams. But under this new amendment, if a firm has money in a team with one of its executives, then it can’t have any ownership in another franchise, the people said.
The rule shift might boost the bidders for teams because, with valuations surging in recent years, it’s become harder for a potential owner to come up with the funds to buy a controlling stake.

The change will allow owners like the Atlanta Hawks’ Tony Ressler, who co-founded Apollo Global Management and Ares Management, to sell stakes to both firms since neither private equity group has stakes in an NBA team.

Other private equity billionaires in the NBA include Josh Harris, who also co-founded Apollo and his partner David Blitzer, who comes from Blackstone, and Celtics owner Bill Chisholm, of Symphony Technology Group.
Outside of individuals, the league has seen private equity transactions from firms like Arctos Partners, Blue Owl’s Dyal HomeCourt Partners fund and Sixth Street.

Iger told Bloomberg in August that he and Kushner didn’t make any calls reaching out to potential investors to support the bid because of how quickly it came together. Since then the pair have been in the process of adding limited partners.
The Lakers deal still needs approval from the NBA’s Board of Governors, a sign-off that could come later this year.

items.title: Trump Says He'll Ban CNN, MS NOW, Politico From White House
body: President Donald Trump said he would ban cable news outlets CNN and MS NOW as well as online publication Politico from the White House, a move that strikes at the heart of First Amendment protections for the news media.

Trump posted Friday on social media that the ban would become “effective immediately,” citing what he said was unfavorable coverage of his administration. He also threatened to bar other outlets from the executive mansion, saying “other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”

Asked by a reporter later Friday in the Oval Office why he decided to ban the outlets now, Trump responded, “It’s really just cumulative stories over the last few years. You get sick of it.” Trump mentioned the New York Times and Washington Post as other examples of what he sees as “fake news” and said “we’re probably not going to display the paper anymore in the White House.”
It wasn’t immediately clear how the president would attempt to enforce the ban.
“A very simple ban. I don’t want them in my office. I don’t want them here. I would say the ban would go as far as you can,” Trump said when asked what it would entail.
The president referred to the new policy as “the ban on the free press.”
The move, if it is made, is likely to draw a legal challenge. Federal courts have previously overturned the Trump administration’s efforts to bar reporters entirely from the White House campus.
Trump acknowledged that the ban could be struck down by a judge, saying “I think it’s good to point it out whether it survives or doesn’t.”

“There’s something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories,” he continued. “Now, if they want to write them, that’s fine. But I don’t have to let them into my — into the people’s house.”
The First Amendment of the US Constitution bars the government from making laws that abridge freedom of speech and the press.

“CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting. We have a right under the US Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government. Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally-protected right,” CNN said in a statement.

Politico “will continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones. We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them. The claims that POLITICO received government subsidies are false and have been thoroughly debunked,” the news outlet said in a statement.
MS NOW declined to comment.
The White House Correspondents’ Association, a collection of reporters from news organizations that cover the White House, issued a statement Friday evening supporting the outlets.

“The president said it plainly in the Oval Office, describing his own planned action as a “ban on the free press,” WHCA President Jacqui Heinrich said in the statement, adding that the Constitution protects press freedoms whether or not the president likes or approves an organization’s coverage or journalists’ questions.

“This is about more than the rights of journalists. It is about the right of the American people to receive a full and independent account of the activities, policies and decisions of whoever occupies the nation’s highest office. The WHCA stands in defense of our colleagues at CNN, MS NOW, and Politico who are being singled out for doing their jobs,” WHCA’s Heinrich wrote.
Trump’s announcement is the latest attempt by the administration to curb press access to events that are in the public interest since the president returned to office.

The Associated Press sued Trump administration officials last year when the White House excluded the outlet from presidential events, though its reporters were still allowed to work from the grounds. A district judge initially sided with the AP, saying that the White House cannot punish outlets over the content of their news stories. A higher court largely stayed the injunction issued by a lower court judge, however. The case is awaiting a decision by an appeals court.

The US Treasury Department excluded journalists from several outlets, including Bloomberg News, the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal, from covering the recent Group of 20 finance ministers summit.
The Defense Department separately barred mainstream media organizations last year from keeping offices in the Pentagon after they refused to sign onto new limits on their activities.

And before that, the White House seized control of picking the group of reporters able to cover Trump in smaller environments including Air Force One and the Oval Office. The group, known as the protective pool, had for decades been formed by the WHCA.

“The First Amendment prohibits the president from punishing journalists because he doesn’t like their coverage,” Jameel Jaffer, executive director of Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University, said in a statement.

items.title: Iran War Drives Bigger Diesel Supply Loss Despite Trump's Claims
body: Diesel prices have never been higher. US President Donald Trump contends that’s not because of the war he started nearly seven months ago.
“The World’s Diesel price rise is mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine War, not Iran,” Trump said in a social media post this week. He’s since reiterated the assertion.
But according to estimates compiled by Bloomberg and double-checked with diesel traders, the Iran war has removed more diesel supply from the market than the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

From March to August, estimates from energy analytics companies, Energy Aspects, Kpler and Vortexa, imply an average loss of about 770,000 barrels a day from the Middle East compared to the same period in 2025. That’s more than twice the roughly 350,000-barrel-a-day loss of Russian supplies over the same time-frame.

The global energy market was thrown into disarray this year, with a widely expected oil glut erased by the Iran conflict. Crude prices soared after the US and Israel attacked Tehran at the end of February, with supply squeezed through the Strait of Hormuz. While crude barrels are again making their way through Hormuz, shipments of oil products, including diesel, are more heavily curtailed.

To be sure, the impact on diesel supply from the Ukraine conflict has grown in recent months after a barrage of attacks on Russian oil refineries. In July and August, when Moscow imposed a diesel-exports ban, shipments fell by 615,000 barrels a day compared to the same months in 2025. That’s almost as many barrels as were lost from the Middle East.
Read More: War Brings Winter of Discontent for the World’s Workhorse Fuel
Critically, the loss of Russian supplies occurred months into the Iran war, during which the world’s fuel and crude oil stockpiles drew down — leaving little cushion to absorb the blow.

“In pure volumetric terms Iran is bigger,” Eugene Lindell, head of refined products at consultancy FGE NexantECA, said of the war-driven loss. “But, of course, prices are set at the margin,” he said. Taking hundreds of thousands of further barrels off the market “turned a super tight market into a historically tight one.”

White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in an emailed statement on Friday that “The President is right: the Russia-Ukraine war, which would never have started if President Trump had been in office, has greatly contributed to diesel prices reaching record highs. Thanks to President Trump’s energy dominance agenda, the United States is the world’s leading producer and exporter of oil.”

As a country, Russia is typically the world’s second-largest exporter of diesel, the industrial fuel essential for everything from freight to agriculture. In 2024, it averaged around 930,000 barrels a day of exports of the fuel, according to Vortexa.
But taken as a region, the Middle East is a more prolific shipper, exporting around 1.7 million barrels a day in the same year.

Trump, in his social media post, said Moscow and Kyiv had agreed to stop attacks on energy infrastructure. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said no deal had been finalized and strikes have continued this week. Russia’s diesel export ban may be extended through October.
US and European refiners, meanwhile, have been running near full capacity to try and meet global demand.

European diesel futures rose over 100% in the early months of the Iran war, while US contracts also soared. Those prices cooled as the US and Iran agreed to a temporary ceasefire. But as conflict in the Middle East re-escalated and Russian exports collapsed, prices climbed once more, eclipsing the springtime highs. In the US, diesel futures settled at an all-time record on Tuesday.
Midterm Battlegrounds Hit by Diesel, Heating Oil Price Spikes
Given the scale of the problem, an agreement between Russia and Ukraine to halt strikes might offer some relief, but wouldn’t fully solve the supply shortfall, analysts and traders say.

“Iran conflict-related shortages are the biggest driver of the diesel and product shortage and price spike, though damage to Russian refineries is exacerbating these trends,” said Rachel Ziemba, adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, a Washington-based think tank. “A ceasefire that leads to repair of refineries and return of Russian products would ease some pressure.”

items.title: Judge Floats US Fund Oversight Amid Trump 'Weaponization' Flap
body: A federal judge suggested a court-appointed “neutral” overseer could allay concerns that the Justice Department might use a long-standing US fund to revive plans to compensate supporters of President Donald Trump as victims of government “weaponization.”

US District Judge Leonie Brinkema made clear during a hearing Friday in Virginia that any such court action would depend on whether a lawsuit challenging the special compensation program can go forward.

But her comments suggested that she’s thinking about the court’s ability to intervene, as claims for payouts from what’s called the Judgment Fund have mounted since US officials said they wouldn’t create a separate, dedicated $1.8 billion pool to pay individuals Trump alleged were targets of politicized law enforcement.

The judge made the comments in a lawsuit challenging an agreement this summer to resolve Trump’s $10 billion case against the Internal Revenue Service over a leak of his tax information years ago. That deal between Trump in his personal capacity and the Justice and Treasury Departments — which he controls as head of the executive branch — included the “anti-weaponization” fund as well as immunity from audits for past tax filings by the president, his oldest sons Don Jr. and Eric, and the Trump Organization.
Read More: Jan. 6 Defendants Boost Claims for Million-Dollar US Payouts

Brinkema didn’t rule from the bench on whether the lawsuit could proceed. The case features a coalition of challengers with varying claims for why they were harmed by the Trump deal, including a union representing Treasury Department employees that alleges its members risk being compelled to violate the law by halting audits or face retaliation.

The Justice Department has argued the case is moot, pointing to statements by top officials under oath that the “weaponization” fund is dead. DOJ also said claims related to the audit immunity are too speculative because no Treasury employee has come forward to say they were asked to take action.

The challengers contend the dispute is still live because of comments by Attorney General Todd Blanche and Trump about wanting to find ways to compensate people who would have been eligible for the “anti-weaponization” fund.

The fund was viewed as a way to streamline claims from hundreds of people pardoned by Trump for charges related to the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol as lawmakers met to certify his presidential election loss to Joe Biden. The Justice Department said the program would be nonpartisan, but the settlement terms listed examples of actions by Democratic officials.

Under existing federal law, individuals with claims for damages against the government must go through a monthslong administrative review process and, if that isn’t successful, can sue in federal court. Individuals charged or convicted in connection with Jan. 6 have filed multiple lawsuits seeking millions of dollars in recent months, court records show.

During Friday’s hearing, Justice Department attorney Andrew Block argued another reason the case should be tossed out is because there is no longer a “remedy” the court could impose now that the fund won’t happen. Brinkema pushed back, saying she could envision options such as requiring a “neutral” person to oversee claims related to Jan. 6 and Biden-era prosecutions involving incidents at reproductive healthcare facilities, which the Trump settlement also mentioned.

Brinkema told Block that statements by Trump and other administration officials “undercut” his representations in court and that the underlying issues in the case related to the fund plan are “alive and kicking.” She rejected his argument that a Florida federal judge’s findings that Trump sued the IRS in bad faith and reached a collusive settlement with his administration weren’t relevant to her consideration.
Trump and the Justice Department are appealing the Florida judge’s order.

A lawyer for the challengers said that it would be difficult to present more specific evidence related to the audit immunity claim because IRS auditors are under strict rules about what they can disclose. Brinkema questioned if that would “doom” that part of the lawsuit. The lawyer argued it was still live as long as the government maintained the immunity protection was enforceable.
The case is Floyd v. Department of Justice, 26-cv-1399, US District Court, Eastern District of Virginia (Alexandria).
