items.title: North Sea Oil Premiums Soar to Records as Saudis Cut Sales
body: Europe’s oil refiners are paying eyewatering premiums for cargoes, as the shutdown of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline forces the region’s buyers to scramble for alternatives with fuel prices soaring.

Saudi Aramco has responded to the attack on its pipeline to the Red Sea by seeking to ramp up shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, with buyers in Asia this week snapping up tens of millions of barrels of Saudi oil from just outside the strait. But the shift also means that those cargoes are emerging further away from desperate European refiners, at a time when markets were already tightening as Chinese purchases and disruptions in Hormuz eat away at global stockpiles.

Physical premiums for oil in the North Sea, a key reference for global prices, soared to record levels in recent days. On Friday, Aramco told its customers in Europe that they wouldn’t receive any supplies under their long-term agreements next month. Norway’s Johan Sverdrup, a grade of crude that is closely comparable with Saudi supplies, was offered at a premium of as much as $35 a barrel above the Dated Brent physical benchmark this week, traders involved in the market said. On Sept. 8, the same oil was trading at a 60c premium.

The surge in real-world oil prices is a sign of how the region’s processors are desperate to secure supplies in order to keep refinery rates high enough to alleviate a fuel crunch that has pushed diesel in the region above $200 a barrel.
Read: Saudis Give European Oil Buyers No Supplies for Next Month

Global oil supplies tightened significantly at the end of the summer as disruption to flows through Hormuz persisted, while some of the market’s biggest workarounds in the early days of the conflict began to reverse. Chinese buying picked up, lifting the value of Middle Eastern barrels, while emergency reserve releases slowed. The attack on Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline has been the latest blow.

The kingdom has managed to continue exporting significant volumes of oil since the early days of the war, when it quickly ramped up exports through the cross-country pipeline to the Red Sea. The workaround meant it was less reliant on Hormuz than most of its regional neighbors. However, Saudi Arabia had been raising shipments through Hormuz this month from August levels, Bloomberg reported on Sept. 14, and was seeking to further boost volumes from inside the Persian Gulf in the wake of the pipeline attack.

The East-West pipeline has a capacity of as much as 7 million barrels a day and had been key in keeping supply flowing to global oil markets during the Iran war. The kingdom is seeking to return about half of the capacity on the pipeline within days, a person familiar with the matter said earlier this week.

While oil markets have been tightening around the world, the strain is most apparent in Europe. At one point this week, the Dated Brent benchmark climbed above $130 a barrel for the first time since April as the frenzy of buying propelled prices higher.

Soaring freight costs — moving crude from the US to Asia costs $26 a barrel — also mean that most refiners are looking for cargoes that don’t have to sail very far. That’s adding to the interest in European crudes from local buyers.

The supply situation in Europe appears even worse than in early April when the Iran war caused a spike in oil prices and started a race to secure alternatives among refineries, traders said. There are limited cargoes available in the market, and sellers are leaving no room for negotiation despite the high offer prices, one of them said.

In the clearest example of a rush for replacement cargoes, Poland’s Orlen has issued more than 10 tenders since Sept. 11 as it seeks alternative supplies. The company’s Chief Executive Officer said in an interview that it was aware of four September shipments that wouldn’t arrive and was actively looking for alternative supplies.
Even grades that are less direct replacements for Middle Eastern cargoes are rallying too.

Another Norwegian grade, Johan Castberg, was also being offered at premiums of more than $30, the traders said. CPC Blend — a much lighter crude that isn’t generally considered a close substitute for Middle Eastern grades — was offered at about $9 above Dated Brent, compared with a premium of less than $1 a barrel just a week ago.
Brent futures edged 0.9% lower to settle near $104 a barrel, cementing a narrow loss for the week.

items.title: US Warns Allies of Missile Delivery Delays Due to Shortage
body: The US has warned allies to expect delays of as much as five years in key weapons deliveries as it rebuilds its own depleted munitions stocks.

Multiple European nations are expecting deliveries of key missile and air defense capabilities to be pushed back as a result of the US military exhausting its own arsenal in the Iran war, officials said.

Germany has asked the US to speed up delivery of the long-range Tomahawk cruise missile and the ground-based Typhon launcher, but depleted US stocks of the powerful weapon means its manufacturer, RTX Corp.’s Raytheon, is unlikely to fulfill the order in the next five years.
Two other officials said some Eastern European nations also reliant on US weapons systems have experienced delays since soon after the US and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb. 28.
The Defense Department didn’t immediately return a call seeking comment.

The Pentagon’s decision to prioritize its own stockpiles is also straining Ukraine’s push for the US to send it more Patriot air defense interceptors ahead of what is expected to be a difficult winter for the war-torn nation. The issue of Ukraine’s badly needed air defense will be a key topic at next week’s United Nations meetings in New York.

President Donald Trump earlier this week told reporters that he’s talking to Ukraine about either sending them a “far less sophisticated version” of the Patriot system, or granting licenses for Europeans to build the weapons.
Read More: Iran Blockade’s Rising Price Tag Drains US Global Military Power

The US is estimated to have used more than half of its most advanced Patriot missile variants, a third of its Tomahawk missiles and almost half of its precision strike missiles and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, interceptors in Iran. The Congressional Budget Office said the US had probably used as much as two-thirds of its inventory of missile defense interceptors since June 2025.

The military fired so many munitions at Iranian targets during the first few months of the war that it “has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply,” Pentagon officials acknowledged to its inspector general.
Officials are now working to stockpile critical components and selected munitions, as well as streamline production lead times, the watchdog office said in a report released this week.

Defense firms are ramping up production, with Lockheed Martin Corp working to increase annual capacity from around 600 to 2,000 of the most advanced PAC-3 MSE, or Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement.

The stockpile shortages aren’t just impacting the US and Europe. In April the US told Japan its Tomahawk deliveries would be delayed by as much as two years. Saudi Arabia has also urged allies, including the US, to provide military support to help counter attacks from the Houthis in Yemen. Washington has not said if it will provide extra assistance.
Trump Says Iran-Backed Houthis Asked US Not to Target Them
Still, the US continues to deliver weapons bought by European allies for Ukraine through NATO and European Union initiatives, the people said.
Europe’s main concern is that the US continues to provide Ukraine with battlefield support.

European leaders plan to lobby Trump on providing Ukraine with more Patriots next week as world leaders attend United Nations meetings. EU officials also hope to push the US to grant European nations licenses to build their own Patriots that could eventually be provided to Kyiv.

items.title: Dollar Surges to Best Week Since June on Higher Rate Outlook
body: The dollar staged its biggest weekly advance in more than three months after the US central bank signaled more interest-rate hikes are to come.

The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index climbed 1.1% this week, powered by solid US economic growth and the Federal Reserve’s anti-inflation message after raising interest rates for the first time in more than three years. The decision removed the biggest impediment to a stronger dollar, according to JPMorgan, Standard Chartered Bank and Brown Brothers Harriman.

On Wednesday and Thursday, the dollar gauge consolidated around its 200-day moving average before closing just above the key level on Friday. Historically, a daily close above the moving average has ushered in more gains for the greenback, as seen back in March and June when the index broke above the 200-day.

The index pared a weekly gain that would have been the biggest rally since the outbreak of the Iran War in March, as the yen trimmed its declines amid a report of a Bank of Japan rate check, a step often seen as a precursor to official intervention.

“The quarter-point hike seems to have removed one of the market’s major deterrents to buying the dollar — namely the fear that Chairman Warsh would not raise rates in defiance of President Trump,” said Steve Englander, co-head of FX research ex-China and head of North America macro strategy at Standard Chartered Bank in New York. “In one swoop, Warsh may have removed the biggest impediment to dollar-buying and created the biggest impediment to dollar-selling. We now see a clear path to dollar strength with 10-year Treasury yields rising to 5.5% over the next 12 months.”

Leading up to this week’s Fed decision, speculative currency traders, including asset managers and non-commercial players — have been reducing their bullish greenback wagers for quite some time. Positions were trimmed for a seventh straight week through Sept. 15, according to Commodity Futures Trading Commission data released Friday and compiled by Bloomberg.

Still, some remain cautious. “Tightening by other major central banks limits policy divergence and suggests the dollar is unlikely to make new cyclical highs,” said Elias Haddad, global head of markets strategy at Brown Brothers Harriman in London.

The dollar gauge trades about 1.9% below its 2026 peak reached on June 24. While options traders are expecting a modestly stronger greenback over the coming month, according to risk reversals data, gains implied by options pricing fall well short of what’s needed for the dollar index to reach a new year-to-date high.

Nevertheless, Haddad said the US still enjoys a formidable growth advantage relative to peers. “Next week’s September S&P Global PMI readings will likely show US maintaining its edge over the Eurozone, UK and Japan,” he added.

According to JPMorgan currency analyst Pat Locke, the greenback was undervalued by about 2%-4% prior to this week’s Fed meeting based on several metrics, including interest-rate differentials. Prospects of further hikes are “prompting a catch-up trade, particularly versus low-yielding currencies,” he said.

items.title: Meta-Tied Data Center Prices Junk Bond Amid Blowout Demand
body: The first junk-bond offering for a data center tied to Meta Platforms Inc. attracted demand more than four times the deal’s size, with juicy yields helping to lure investors.
Money managers placed orders of about $10 billion for CleanSpark Inc.’s debt sale, set at almost $2.28 billion, according to people familiar with the matter.

The five-year notes priced at 98.5 cents on the dollar to yield 8.25%, a separate person said, asking not to be identified because they are not authorized to speak publicly. That’s roughly 1.75 percentage points more than the average for debt issued by BB rated firms tracked by Bloomberg.

Investors have demanded higher premiums for data center financings amid a surge in such offerings and growing concerns about excessive capital spending, raising funding costs for the AI infrastructure buildout. Similar financings backed by investment-grade tenants were sold at yields as low as below 6% earlier this year.
The CleanSpark fundraising, led by Morgan Stanley, will help finance construction of a data center in Sandersville, Georgia, according to a regulatory filing.

The facility has been fully leased to Anviran LLC, a Meta subsidiary, under a $6.6 billion, 20-year contract, according to a CleanSpark presentation. The data center is expected to begin operations in the fourth quarter of 2027, and Meta will guarantee rent and operating expenses, the firm said.

Meta’s commitment to CleanSpark gives the junk-rated borrower a predictable revenue stream to support borrowing for a costly project. Data center developers have now sold more than $3 billion of high-yield bonds so far this year, with most of them backed by long-term leases with hyperscalers including Oracle Corp. and Amazon.com Inc., according to Bloomberg-compiled data.
CleanSpark didn’t respond to a request for comment, while Morgan Stanley declined to comment.

Las Vegas-based CleanSpark is among a growing number of public Bitcoin-mining companies that are becoming data-center operators to support artificial intelligence applications. The company has a market value of roughly $3.63 billion.

items.title: Germany Agrees on €2.5 Billion Fuel Relief, Price Cap Plan
body: Germany’s government agreed on a €2.5 billion ($2.9 billion) relief package featuring a three-month fuel-tax cut through year-end and plans for a state-set cap on pump prices to ease the burden of record fuel costs.

The energy tax on gasoline and diesel will be cut by 14 euro cents a liter, reducing the overall tax burden by about 17 cents once value added tax is included and matching a two-month tax cut introduced earlier this year.

The price cap, which still needs to be worked out and would be introduced at a later stage, would set a maximum retail price linked to movements in oil markets, drawing on systems used in Belgium and Luxembourg.

The accord was sealed just days before Sunday’s state elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and caps a week of wrangling within Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government over how to cushion motorists and businesses after renewed fighting in the Middle East drove up energy costs.

“We’re putting a stop to price gouging by oil companies as well, and we’re now making sure fuel prices come down quickly,” Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil told reporters in Dublin, where European Union finance ministers and central bank governors were meeting Friday.
Klingbeil confirmed plans for both measures, adding that the government would continue to pursue ideas of a windfall tax on oil companies.
He didn’t give an exact start date for the fuel-tax cut, saying only that it would run for three months through year-end.
Economy Minister Katherina Reiche said in an emailed statement that the package would cost about €2.5 billion, with Germany’s states covering half the amount.

The federal government will draw on unspent budget funds this year and cover the balance through a “mix of financing measures,” Klingbeil said. He added that he expected a windfall tax to play a key role in funding the package.
The measures still need approval from the Bundestag and the Bundesrat, the upper house representing Germany’s states, and that should happen “quickly,” Klingbeil said.
Diesel averaged a record €2.47 a liter on Sept. 17, while Super E10 gasoline cost €2.30, also a record, according to German auto club ADAC.

The measure revives a two-month fuel-tax cut implemented in May and June. Germany reduced excise duty on gasoline and diesel by 14 cents a liter, equal to about 17 cents of relief once value-added tax was included. The government budgeted €1.6 billion for the program, though the extent to which the reduction was passed on to motorists was disputed.

Germany has also tightened oversight of fuel pricing. Since April 1, filling stations have been allowed to raise prices only once a day, at noon, while price cuts remain permitted at any time. The government also broadened the Federal Cartel Office’s powers to investigate price abuse.

Officials had considered cutting the VAT on motor fuel to 7% from 19%, as well as targeted payments to lower-income households. EU rules, however, prevent Germany from unilaterally applying a reduced VAT rate to gasoline and diesel.

At the EU level, Klingbeil urged the European Commission to present options for a bloc-wide windfall tax on oil companies by the next meeting of finance ministers in October. Germany and five other countries — Austria, Italy, Poland, Portugal and Spain — had asked Ireland’s rotating EU presidency to put the issue on the agenda.
The commission said Friday it wasn’t preparing an EU-wide proposal at this stage, adding that national governments could impose such levies under their own tax systems and in line with EU law.

items.title: California's Economy Has an AI Angle in Everything
body: Hello and welcome to a special Odd Lots meets California Edition newsletter. In this week’s crossover, you’re getting Joe Weisenthal and Tracy Alloway, bringing you their thoughts straight from a live show in Los Angeles. And Felipe Marques, San Francisco bureau chief, on everything else California.
Sign up here for more Odd Lots in your inbox — or check out the Odd Lots Discord channel — and register here for a weekly fix of the Golden State.
If you’ve missed the LA show (how could you?), don’t worry: Joe and Tracy are coming back to California soon — this time trading palm trees for Karl, the Fog.
Hello from Los Angeles, where Joe and I just wrapped up our first ever live show in the city, recorded last night at The Vermont Hollywood.

Since this was our LA debut, we wanted to try to sample as many slices of the California economy as we could in one evening — everything from Hollywood screenwriting, to the property market and real estate development, to new attempts at manufacturing and space tech, and of course, the influencer economy. Perhaps unsurprisingly, every single conversation ended up veering into a discussion of AI. It’s just impossible to get away from nowadays.

Our first guest was Hayes Davenport, who’s written for shows like Eastbound & Down and Family Guy and is now creative director of L.A. Material and the co-host of the fantastic Hollywood Handbook podcast. AI angst is obviously running high in Hollywood, but Hayes pointed out that a lot of the production pain predates the current panic. Shoos hours have been declining for years. And shoots had already been migrating to places like North Carolina, Canada and (interestingly) Ireland as production followed a ‘race to the bottom’ in tax credits. So Tinsel Town was having a tough time even before chatbots showed up to workshop its third act.Setting aside Hollywood studios, one of the most distinctive physical aspects of the LA landscape is its sheer volume of independent shops and small businesses. A single strip mall might have a donut store, a karate studio, a tax accountant, a linoleum emporium, and a place that will gauge your aura for $50. It’s just not something you see much anymore in places like NYC, where the same footprint would probably end up being one bank branch and a Duane Reade. So this was one of the things we asked Zach Lasry, who’s been developing a new neighborhood around Melrose Hill, as well as Bill McBride, veteran real estate analyst and author of Calculated Risk. We also talked about the economics of installing crosswalks (surprisingly tough) and the difficulty of securing construction components like transformers. Even when it comes to the very physical realm of property and construction, there was an AI angle here too. We talked about the rise of self-driving cars and what wide-spread adoption might mean for parking in commercial developments and urban layouts.

The decline of manufacturing in the US has been a long-running story and one of the things you often hear, is that one of the reasons China excels in terms of making stuff is because of the network effects of its manufacturing base and ‘ecosystem’ of developers. So, it was interesting to talk to Chris Power, founder of Hadrian, which is making precision parts for aerospace and defense, as well as Tom Mueller, founder of Impulse Space, which is doing orbital transfers (he was also employee No. 1 at SpaceX). We asked whether the California industrial scene is changing such that the kind of industrial vertical integration made famous by SpaceX — roughly defined as “build everything yourself, because nobody else will,” is no longer needed.

Finally, you can’t go to LA without talking about the influencer economy, and when it comes to marketing and social media, and AI anxieties are running high here too. We spoke with Taylor Lorenz, founder of User Mag and well-known chronicler of internet culture and tech, as well as Rachel Karten, a social media consultant and author of the Link in Bio newsletter. One thing that I keep wondering is why people seem to dislike AI-generated content (or at least, claim they do, even as they sometimes consume it). Rachel’s answer from a marketing perspective is that if customers think AI is being used to cut corners from a marketing perspective, then the concern is where else a company might be skimping out on. In other words, the slop becomes the corporate tell.

So what did we learn from our LA debut? The California economy is a comedy writer (turned podcaster), a developer, a machinist and an influencer all trying, in their own way, to navigate the 101 at the same time. We came out here looking for the industries and economies that make California different, and there are plenty of those! But the underlying throughline of each conversation ended up being an AI angle of some sort. We’re pretty sure there’s even an AI angle on the linoleum emporium and karate dojo and donut shop in the strip mall, we just didn’t have time to get into it, so we’ll have to come back!

A huge thank you to all of our guests and to everyone who came out to the show! Full conversations from the show will be dropping in the Odd Lots feed over the coming days. You can listen for free on Spotify or Apple.

The Tax Reform Act of 1986 transformed how Americans pay taxes, fueling the rise of pass-through business that offered private business owners new ways to lower their tax bills. Decades later, economists Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick set out to determine how much those owners — from auto dealers to contractors — actually owed in taxes and, in the process, uncovered a vast and almost invisible class of ultra-wealthy Americans hiding in plain sight. Today, they join us to discuss their new, The Everywhere Millionaire: Who Is Really Rich in America and How They Got There, and  explain the links between pass-through businesses and the rise of inequality —  and why the collective revenue of the nation’s dentists far exceeds that of the NFL.
Watch: Bloomberg / YouTube
Listen: Apple / Spotify

Hello from San Francisco. I’m Felipe and like fellow Odd Lots aficionados, I love breaking down economic patterns and paradoxes (like the brilliant economics of chickens and mule trading Odd Lots episodes).

Well, California is a place like few others to watch capitalism’s strangest contradictions unfold. My colleague Francesca Maglione recently went on an 11 a.m. Monday hike through the majestic Mount Tamalpais, just across the Golden State bridge, to chronicle the flip side of the AI wealth boom.

She followed a group of more than four dozen laid-off workers who are part of un(PTO), a community for people navigating unemployment as tech layoffs surge in the San Francisco Bay Area. Tech-industry employers filed layoff notices for more than 14,500 Bay Area workers in the 12 months that ended in June, almost double the count for the previous fiscal year.

In a world of trillion-dollar startups, once-unthinkable compensation packages and fears that AI will wipe us all off the face the Earth, un(PTO) represents  people who once helped power San Francisco’s last boom and are now struggling to find their place in this one — to a point they are considering opening flower shops.

You can read her full story here (🎁). And here’s a newsletter-only bonus: A beautiful shot Francesca took from Mt. Tam, your reminder of just how stunning California can be, no matter how brutal its economics.

My frenemy, Kamala. Governor Gavin Newsom told CNN he wouldn’t mount a highly anticipated bid for president in 2028 if his longtime former Vice President Kamala Harris decides that she wants to run too. The statement was a shrewd political calculation that could help his standing with both voters and the Democratic Party, said Erika D. Smith.

So, are the machines coming for us? This week in San Francisco, Dreamforce was all around, Salesforce’s annual conference that inundates the city with even more tech bros and their bosses. One topic stood out: AI doom — and Dario Amodei, Sam Altman and Jensen Huang all weighed in.

Growing pains. Stanford University has long been an academic cornerstone of Silicon Valley. Now, the school is looking to expand — but first it needs to persuade the neighbors, who have helped scotch previous growth plans. Stanford’s strategy? Offering $100 million to the local community.

items.title: Stellantis, Union Urged to Resume Talks by Canada's Joly
body: Jeep parent Stellantis NV and its unionized workers should resume labor talks, Canadian Industry Minister Melanie Joly urged Friday.
“They need to get back to the negotiation table, and they can find a really trustworthy partner in myself and the government to make sure that they get to a deal,” Joly told reporters in Ottawa.

A collective agreement between Stellantis and Unifor, which represents about 9,000 unionized employees at the company’s factories in Canada, expires Sunday. The two parties have been at an impasse since last week, when armored-vehicle maker Roshel Inc. said it had signed a memo that outlines steps toward buying an idled Toronto-area plant from Stellantis.
The defense supplier is trying to get a Canadian military contract to build light utility vehicles, and has said it could bring back workers quickly to the Brampton facility if it’s successful.
Unifor opposes the transaction, which “should be met with fierce resistance from the federal government,” it said in a letter to Joly dated Wednesday.
Joly said Friday that the government “didn’t participate in any form of negotiation or endorsement whatsoever” with regards to talks between Roshel and Stellantis.

As a result of the impasse, “strike action remains a real possibility,” Unifor National President Lana Payne said at a news conference Thursday, though the union hopes to reach a tentative settlement without it. The same morning, Stellantis sent a letter to workers at its plant in Brampton, Ontario, saying it sees “no long-term business case” for making cars there. The facility has not produced vehicles since late 2023.
The Canadian government had given hundreds of millions of dollars in financial help to Stellantis in return for production promises.
“When it comes to the Stellantis plant, my position has always been clear: That plant needs to reopen. We need a new model. If not, we’ll get our money back,” Joly said.

items.title: Westinghouse Targeting Over $50 Billion Valuation in US IPO
body: Westinghouse Electric Co., a provider of reactor technology to nuclear power plants, is seeking a valuation of more than $50 billion in its US initial public offering, according to people familiar with the matter.

The company, which is jointly owned by Brookfield Renewable Partners and Cameco Corp., is targeting a public filing as soon as in October, the people said, asking not to be identified as the information isn’t public. Details of the offering including the timing could still change, they said.
Cameco’s US shares jumped as much as 3.6% on Friday, the most since Sept. 3, according to data compiled by Bloomberg, giving the company a market value of more than $41 billion.
Citigroup Inc. and Goldman Sachs Group Inc. are leading Westinghouse’s IPO, the people said. The company said in July it had filed confidentially for a listing.
Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Royal Bank of Canada are also working on the listing, the people said.
Representatives for Westinghouse, Brookfield, Cameco, Citigroup, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan declined to comment. Spokespeople for CIBC and RBC didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

AI companies and firms making the infrastructure to enable their operations have seen a wave of investment, including blockbuster IPOs like SpaceX’s record-breaking debut, whose pitch focused squarely on its growing AI business. Few of the deals have been standout successes in the aftermarket, however.

Standard Nuclear Inc. went public in July in a downsized US IPO and is 14% below its listing price while X-Energy Inc., which went public in April, has fallen 32% below its IPO price. Holtec Nuclear Corp., a supplier of specialty services to the nuclear power industry, postponed its planned offering earlier this week.
Read More:  Nuclear Power Services Firm Holtec Postpones Planned US IPO

Half of the 10 largest US IPOs this year comprise companies that are benefiting from the boom in AI data center construction. Their share prices have mostly struggled, with Innio NV and Madison Air Solutions Corp. down at least 13% from IPOs that brought in more than $2.5 billion each.
Westinghouse traces its roots back to the 1800s and touts its role as the creator of the world’s first commercial pressurized water reactor in Pennsylvania, according to its website.

The company, which has more than 12,500 employees across 21 countries, is set to benefit from the Trump Administration’s efforts to boost America’s nuclear industry. The US Army tapped Westinghouse and four other firms to build, own and operate its power plants, according to a statement in August.

Westinghouse’s nuclear power technology is used by 57% of the world’s 417 nuclear reactors and the company has a pipeline of as many as 91 opportunities for its latest generation reactor, Cameco said in an earnings release.
Cameco completed a deal in 2023 to buy a 49% stake in Westinghouse at about an $8 billion value.

items.title: Investor Sentiment Plunges to 16-Month Low, AAII Survey Shows
body: Investor sentiment fell to its lowest point since 2025, a weekly survey from the American Association of Individual Investors showed, as oil prices remained elevated while the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time since 2023.
More than half of investors (53.3%) responding to the latest survey from AAII, released Friday, said they were bearish. Just 28.8% of investors are bullish, the lowest reading in a year.

All told, the spread between the number of bulls and bears in the market has fallen to -24.5%, which is “unusually low” and below its historical average of 6.5% for the ninth consecutive week, Charles Rotblut, vice-president of the American Association of Individual Investors, said in a release. The reading is the lowest since May 2025.

Traders sometimes use the sentiment gauge as a contrarian indicator, with a high reading showing complacency and a low one indicating investor fear. The latest result comes with the S&P 500 Index some 2% from its all-time high following a period of late-summer volatility.

The latest survey also showed over half of respondents had larger allocations to cash than normal — a sign of caution. Indeed, 19.1% of respondents said their cash allocations were “much higher than normal.”

items.title: Economía argentina pierde impulso y amenaza reelección de Milei
body: Read story in English
A un año de que el presidente argentino Javier Milei busque la reelección, la recuperación económica que sustentó su popularidad está perdiendo impulso.

El producto interno bruto se contrajo un 0,6% en el segundo trimestre respecto de los tres meses anteriores, la primera caída en dos años y un revés para un gobierno que apuesta por una aceleración del crecimiento de cara a las elecciones de octubre de 2027.

Los argentinos eligieron en 2023 al outsider libertario con la esperanza de que la austeridad y una mayor apertura de los mercados pudieran contener la inflación y estabilizar una economía propensa a las crisis. La “terapia de shock” de Milei logró desacelerar drásticamente las alzas de precios, pero las encuestas muestran una creciente preocupación entre los votantes por la debilidad del mercado laboral.
Suscríbase   aquí   al boletín Morning Briefing Español y conozca nuestro canal de   WhatsApp

La economía creció un 2% interanual, respaldada por el auge de las exportaciones de energía y productos agrícolas, mientras las importaciones disminuyeron. En una publicación en X, el ministro de Economía, Luis Caputo, destacó que 13 de los 16 sectores de actividad que se incluyen en la medición crecieron durante el primer semestre del año.

Sin embargo, las últimas cifras del PIB “están lejos de ser lo suficientemente convincentes como para disipar las preocupaciones políticas, la variable clave que pesa sobre los mercados argentinos”, señaló Jimena Zúñiga, economista para Argentina de Bloomberg Economics.

Los inversores en deuda soberana del país temen que un debilitamiento del respaldo al programa de Milei pueda aumentar las posibilidades de que sus reformas fiscales y de mercado sean revertidas después de las elecciones de 2027.
Los opositores de izquierda de Milei buscan convertir el aumento del desempleo y la debilidad de los ingresos de los hogares en temas centrales de las elecciones de octubre de 2027.
Fernando Marull, socio de la consultora FM&A, ve la posibilidad de una segunda contracción consecutiva en el tercer trimestre, lo que situaría a Argentina en una recesión técnica.
Incluso si la economía evita una recesión, las perspectivas para los hogares siguen siendo sombrías, señaló Carlos Melconian, director de MacroView SA.

“Que sean dos trimestres negativos desde la matemática, te da muy finito que pueda ser negativo o que pueda ser positivo y es irrelevante para la diaria”, sostuvo Melconian. “Porque los componentes ya están muy mal y no hay chance de que construcción, manufactura y comercio repunten”.

La inflación anual fue del 34% el mes pasado, lo que se compara con más del 200% en que se encontraba cuando Milei asumió el cargo. Una encuesta de AtlasIntel del mes pasado mostró que la corrupción y el desempleo han superado a la inflación entre las principales preocupaciones de los votantes.
Milei, sin embargo, sigue concentrado en consolidar su victoria sobre la inflación, que quiere llevar por debajo de una tasa mensual del 1%.

Ello lo ha llevado a respaldar una política de peso fuerte, aunque esté pesando sobre el crecimiento. La moneda se debilitó apenas un 3,7% frente al dólar en el año hasta agosto, mientras los precios al consumidor aumentaron un 21%.
Esa apreciación real se ha visto reforzada en las últimas semanas por intervenciones oficiales en los mercados de bonos y futuros, mientras siguen vigentes los controles cambiarios para las empresas.

Los opositores de Milei se centran cada vez más en este punto. En un evento a comienzos de este mes, su principal contendiente, el gobernador de Buenos Aires, Axel Kicillof, calificó el enfoque del gobierno como una “política criminal y suicida de desindustrialización del país”.

Los legisladores de la oposición también han llevado el argumento al Congreso y recientemente forzaron una sesión sobre el creciente endeudamiento y morosidad de los hogares, aunque ninguna de las propuestas de alivio ha avanzado hasta ahora.
Milei presenta una visión muy diferente y destaca el fuerte crecimiento de la agricultura, la energía y la minería como prueba de que la economía superó la crisis.

Al mismo tiempo, los sectores minorista, construcción e industria manufacturera, que emplean a muchas más personas, están perdiendo puestos de trabajo, mientras los créditos de consumo morosos se disparan.
El consumo se contrajo un 2,4% en el segundo trimestre, ya que el débil crecimiento de los salarios y las restrictivas condiciones crediticias golpearon las finanzas de los hogares.

Estos sectores en dificultades representan aproximadamente la mitad del empleo asalariado privado registrado de Argentina, mientras las industrias que impulsan las exportaciones y la inversión representan solo alrededor de una quinta parte.
En total, el empleo asalariado privado registrado ha disminuido en unos 246.300 puestos de trabajo desde poco antes de que Milei asumiera el cargo, mientras más de 30.000 empresas han cerrado.

Esto deja a Milei vulnerable de cara a las elecciones. Su aprobación fue del 38% en la última encuesta de AtlasIntel, mientras que un 58% desaprobó su gestión y un 70% calificó de malo el mercado laboral.
El gobierno redujo esta semana su proyección de crecimiento para 2026 al 3% desde el 5%, mientras los economistas encuestados por el banco central esperan una expansión más cercana al 2%.

Osvaldo Giordano, presidente del instituto de estudios IERAL de la Fundación Mediterránea, prevé que la economía evite una recesión y que la actividad se mantenga prácticamente estancada este trimestre. Sin embargo, señaló que la brecha entre el escaso crecimiento y lo que esperan los argentinos después de soportar años de turbulencias económicas representa un riesgo para Milei.
“No es lo mismo la tolerancia de una sociedad cuando tenés un mal año”, afirmó Giordano. “Acá es una sucesión de muy malos años. Entonces la paciencia es menor”.Traducción editada por Paulina Munita
Nota Original: Stalling Argentine Recovery Is a Risk for Milei’s Reelection Bid

items.title: US Oilman Who Worked Years in Venezuela Is Shut Out
body: Lea la nota en español
The veteran oil executive who oversaw Chevron Corp.’s strategy to stay in Venezuela through years of political turmoil says Caracas is now freezing him out.

Ali Moshiri, currently chief executive officer of Amos Global Energy, has lined up $2 billion from about 15 investors to plow into Venezuelan oil production and infrastructure as the Trump administration pushes for US companies to revive the nation’s energy sector. Yet state-owned Petróleos de Venezuela SA, or PDVSA, is moving at a glacial place with his proposals, he said in an interview.

“There’s no process — no sense of urgency,” said Moshiri, who is traveling to Caracas this weekend to push for a face-to-face meeting with PDVSA executives. “We are ready to fix something. It’s so critical.”
PDVSA and Venezuela’s oil and information ministries didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Moshiri, who ran Chevron’s Latin American operations until 2017, said he and his fund have been in talks with the Venezuelan government over deals since before US forces captured former President Nicolás Maduro in January.

Moshiri’s team in Caracas is negotiating a memorandum of understanding for one of seven oil fields he’s interested in. Combined, he says the assets have potential to produce about 200,000 barrels a day of oil, or around 20% of the country’s current output.

Moshiri, who sponsors an annual golf tournament in Caracas, is also trying to negotiate for a contract to renovate Venezuela’s main oil exporting port on the Caribbean coast, which he says is only 40% operational. He plans to spend up to $1 billion on repairs at José Antonio Anzoátegui Oil and Petrochemical Industrial Complex.

“I have my anchor investors and $500 million that I can spend tomorrow. You’ve got to recognize I’m different than other companies because we’ve been evaluating Venezuela fields for 10 years,” said Moshiri, who also plans to try to meet with acting President Delcy Rodríguez while in Caracas. “I don’t need a memorandum of understanding.”

Moshiri credited the Trump administration for its initial efforts to stabilize Venezuela and helping create an environment that’s giving foreign corporations confidence to return. But he said the recent push for US companies to sign contracts is overly “opportunistic” and focuses too much on short-term gains instead crafting a broad, long-term plan for a lasting recovery.
Moshiri said rebuilding Venezuela’s economy will be “like lifting the Titanic from the bottom of the ocean” — requiring a tremendous amount of infrastructure, development and planning.

Moshiri, who was born in Iran and graduated from the University of Tulsa, joined Chevron in 1978 and retired from the company in 2017. He was a key figure behind the company’s decision to remain in Venezuela in 2007 when then-President Hugo Chávez took control of major oil projects from foreign operators in the nation’s prolific Orinoco Belt, prompting ExxonMobil Holdings Corp., ConocoPhillips and others to leave.
Chevron is now Venezuela’s leading private-sector producer, poised to double its output there over the next five years.

Moshiri said he doubted North American Blue Energy Partners — the company partnering with the US government to produce crude in Venezuela — has the capability to significantly lift output at the fields it holds.

“I really don’t believe they’ve got the capacity to be able to do what has played out in front of them,” Moshiri said. “This company never had an operational experience” and their 17 fields are “very, very complicated.”
North American Blue Energy Partners didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Moshiri isn’t interested in production-sharing deals like those signed by other producers, saying Venezuela could terminate them. Rather, he wants a joint venture with PDVSA, with contracts approved by lawmakers.
“Any opportunity that is awarded has to be competitive,” he said. “If it’s not competitive — it’s going to be challenging the future.”

items.title: Ryanair CEO O'Leary Apologizes for 'Rapists' Remark in Video
body: Ryanair Holdings Plc Chief Executive Officer Michael O’Leary apologized for using the term “rapists” last week when describing some of his European competitors.

O’Leary came under fire, including from Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin and the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre, after calling rivals such as Aer Lingus, Deutsche Lufthansa AG and British Airways “high-fare rapists” outside Ryanair’s annual general meeting in Dublin.

When questioned by reporters soon after, the CEO steadfastly denied he was trivializing the crime. On Friday, though, he said he consulted with family and friends, and concluded that an apology was in order for his “careless” comment, according to a short video posted by Virgin Media News YT.

“I’ve come to realize, however, that the word I used so carelessly has caused ... considerable upset and offense to a wide number of people, especially to victims and survivors,” he said. “I want to apologize, sincerely and unreservedly, to those people.”
He concluded by saying, “I will try to learn from this mistake and do better in future.”
O’Leary, who became CEO in 1994, is known for giving brusque opinions on a range of aviation and social issues, and for sparring online with Elon Musk earlier this year.

items.title: Fire Flares Up at Damaged Moss Landing Battery Storage Site
body: Fire crews have contained a blaze Friday at Vistra Corp.’s damaged battery storage facility in California.

About 1,200 batteries ignited this morning at the Moss Landing site in Monterey County, Vistra said in a statement late Friday. County officials report that the fire is inactive with crews remaining on site to monitor the situation, according to the statement.

The storage facility was the site of a significant blaze in January 2025, which prompted local evacuations. Less than 5% of the original batteries remain at the site, Vistra said. The modules that caught fire have remained charged and have not been de-energized because they are located in a portion of the building that has not been safely accessible due to damage from the original conflagration, the company said.
Vistra said earlier Friday that personnel identified a “flare-up” on the north side of the building around 6 a.m. local time Friday.

The company said the natural gas plant located at the site has been temporarily shut down “out of an abundance of caution.” Air quality monitors are active along the site perimeter and in the surrounding community, the company added.

items.title: Blackstone Lands Loan for Data Center Cooling Firm Acquisition
body: Blackstone Inc. has secured a first-lien term loan to support its acquisition of a controlling stake in Flow Control Holdings, a provider of components for data center liquid cooling.

UBS Group AG has been mandated to provide the loan, the terms and size of which were not disclosed, according to a person familiar with the matter who asked not to be named discussing private information.

Blackstone agreed to acquire the Flow Control stake from Audax Private Equity, which will retain a minority interest in the firm, on Sept. 10. Flow Control provides components used in liquid cooling systems for data centers, as well as in the food, beverage and pharmaceutical sectors.

Debt financing for data center—related deals across investment grade bonds, high yield notes, and leveraged loans has soared as so-called hyperscalers, such as Amazon.com Inc and Google parent Alphabet Inc., race to build out the infrastructure for artificial intelligence. So far this year, US-dollar debt financing for such deals has totaled more than $350 billion, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.
The Blackstone loan is expected to launch in the coming weeks, according to two other people familiar with the matter. The acquisition is expected to close by year-end.
A representative for UBS declined to comment. Blackstone and Flow Control representatives did not immediately respond to requests for comments.

The transaction adds to a growing pipeline of acquisition financings in the leveraged-loan market, with the floating-rate asset class seeing a pickup in such deals following a summer lull. There’s about $92 billion in leveraged financing pending in the US for M&A activity, according to JPMorgan figures.

items.title: Deluge of Copper Arriving in US Leaves New Orleans With Logjam
body: There’s nothing outwardly remarkable about the journey of the Nord Norfolk, a Liberian-flagged bulk carrier sailing across the Atlantic toward New Orleans.

But the boat is loaded with roughly half a billion dollars of African copper, the highest market value for a single commodity shipment ever recorded by analytics firm Kpler. It’s part of a rush of copper to US shores ahead of potential import tariffs, a deluge that’s key ports are struggling to absorb.

The Port of New Orleans — a key metals gateway and major hub for CME Group’s Comex copper warehouses — is already largely full, according to people familiar with the matter. And that’s before a total of around 100,000 metric tons more of African and South American copper they say is due to arrive in September and October.

“We are seeing serious congestion at marine terminals in the New Orleans area, causing delays for loading copper and other metals and steel to trucks and railcars,” said Anton Posner, chief executive officer of logistics-services provider Mercury Resources. His firm is sending metal up the Mississippi by barge instead.
Port of New Orleans didn’t respond to an emailed request for comment.

The $500 million boatload and the New Orleans logjam are part of a long drama playing out in the global copper market as traders brace for President Donald Trump to decide whether to expand copper import levies to refined metal. He hasn’t done so months after a decision was expected, and the metal is still pouring in for now.

The strength of US copper imports has been the key force behind a record-breaking rally in copper prices, with the global benchmark set on the London Metal Exchange climbing about 50% since Trump first formally proposed tariffs on the metal in February last year. US futures have rallied even more sharply, creating huge arbitrage profits for the traders and producers that have been shipping copper to the US in record volumes.
Read More: How US Tariff Fears Are Driving Record Copper Prices: Explainer

But in recent weeks the gap between US and international prices has narrowed as doubts grow about whether Trump will ultimately push ahead with tariffs. In turn, the question of whether US imports will slow has become a crucial one in all corners of the copper industry — from investors weighing whether copper’s record rally can be sustained, to Chinese manufacturers who’ve seen costs to secure their own imports surge as copper has gravitated toward the US.

One measure puts the arbitrage gap now at $169 a ton, versus $789 at this year’s height, and it has fluctuated a lot since Trump’s return to office. The narrower premium weakens the incentive to keep shipping to the US, and some future shipments could be redirected instead to Asia. But changing course en route can be complicated and expensive.
“I wouldn’t call the arbitrage dead just yet,” said Marcos Carias, North America economist at global trade-credit insurer Coface.

Warehousing companies are seeking approval for additional capacity from Comex as US storage requirements balloon. Since the start of 2025, the exchange said it has added 20 warehouses and nearly 725,000 short tons of copper capacity. That’s equivalent to about 39% of annual US refined-copper consumption. Sites were added in Mobile, Chicago and Atlanta this year.
Shipper BBC Chartering also added Mobile — on the Alabama coast — as another stop for South American copper, according to a person with knowledge of the matter.

“The potential for tariffs alone has essentially had the effect they want from tariffs; that is, bringing lots of supply into the country and increasing domestic premiums to support domestic projects,” said Ryan McKay, senior commodity strategist at TD Securities. The White House will likely continue to delay a decision to keep this the case, he said.

items.title: Cities Eye Reforms to Boost Nightlife, Economy: CityLab Weekly
body: Welcome to CityLab Weekly. I’m Linda Poon, your guide to ideas, reporting and analysis from cities around the world. Sign up here to get the newsletter every Friday in your inbox and send us your feedback.

They say nothing good happens after midnight, and over the last few years, the adage has felt a little more true in cities. The US has lost 7,000 bars and nightclubs since 2006, and many of the ones still standing are struggling to stay open amid rising costs and a tangle of red tape.

America’s fun shortage, which isn’t limited to late nights, is making people unhappy and hurting local economies. Now cities want to reinvigorate their dying social scenes, and as my colleague Annika Inampudi reports, this summer’s World Cup offered a glimpse of what’s possible, as cities saw some of their once-vibrant streets come back to life with nightly revelers. This nightlife success was boosted by policies: Massachusetts, for example, temporarily loosened rules on outdoor drinking and how late bars and restaurants can serve alcohol. Now state lawmakers are advancing proposals to make similar “fun” reforms permanent.

Outside the US, cities from Montreal to Berlin have had more ambitious visions for keeping people out late, with measures like 24-hour zones. In London, Mayor Sadiq Khan wants to simplify a fractured licensing system for nightlife businesses that, in his words, “has been shackled by the whims of joyless NIMBYs.” It’s part of a broader hospitality-boosting measure that also seeks to make al fresco dining “the norm, not the exception,” as one city official told me.

Outdoor “streateries” became a fixture of local dining scenes during the pandemic, but many have since disappeared as new city regulations made them harder and more expensive to operate. As Fola Akinnibi, Jack Trapanick and I reported last week, some cities are trying to tweak their rules to bring them back.

Built to be looked at, remade to be lived inNew York’s iconic Flatiron building sat vacant for years; now it’s being turned into luxury housing, with architects retaining much of the original structure. The office-to-residential conversation likely saved the iconic tower from demolition, preservationists say.

World’s most expensive rideA new car cost $50,000 on average in the US. That’s a steal compared to Singapore, where drivers must cough up $100,000-plus for the right to even buy a vehicle. If the system appears to limit car ownership for only a select few, well, that’s kind of the point, writes David Zipper.

An upgrade for Billy BuffaloThe Buffalo Bills are charging into football season with a sleek $2.2 billion stadium in the team’s home city, putting an end to relocation rumors — at least for few years. The new venue offers a lot more creature comforts for long-suffering fans.

John Wilson’s first feature-length film The History of Concrete hit theaters this week. Much like in his comedy series How To with John Wilson, the documentarian starts out ruminating about the mundane, only to then veer off into a world of modern absurdities — a concrete conference in Las Vegas, a 3D-printed Starbucks, a “gum busting” company. Sprinkled throughout: real concerns about the fragility of the built environment, and revelations about humanity.

“Whenever he’s given the opportunity, he leaps at the chance to digress and turn to something completely different, like, for instance, a very touching and human story of an aspiring rock musician,” Felix Salmon writes.
And in a conversation with CityLab, Wilson tells Mark Byrnes, “Everything is fragile and nothing lasts forever. This movie is me dealing with that.”

items.title: BOJ's Ueda Balances Between Japan's Takaichi and US Treasury's Bessent
body: Nobody likes a back-seat driver. Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda now has two — and they want to move at different speeds.

Ueda on Friday raised interest rates for a second time in three months, giving Scott Bessent — the US Treasury chief who stepped in to bolster the yen — the acceleration of monetary tightening he’s been urging. But Japan’s premier Sanae Takaichi is focused on faster economic growth. Her two BOJ appointees were the only ones to vote against Friday’s hike, a harbinger of what may come next year when she gets to replace the two most hawkish members of the current board.
Follow The Big Take daily podcast wherever you listen.

At a turbulent time for global bond markets, with inflation and borrowing costs on the rise almost everywhere, keeping both camps happy will only get harder. It’s not clear what level of rates would satisfy Bessent, whose priority is to shield US Treasuries from any ructions in Japan — or how that squares with domestic needs as seen by the prime minister. Inflation may be trending above-target but consumer spending and broader economic growth have lagged.

“The balancing act for Ueda is extremely difficult. He is caught between pressures from Takaichi and Bessent,” said Atsushi Takeuchi, a former head of the BOJ’s foreign exchange division. “Japan has the weakest inflationary pressure compared with US and Europe. It's a fact that if the BOJ races toward rate hikes with other central banks, the BOJ will lose.”

Rapid increases would also risk tipping Japan back toward the long economic stagnation it’s only recently emerged from, and raise awkward questions about the BOJ’s independence if it’s perceived to be following a US roadmap. But going too slowly could undo the gains of a currency intervention into which Bessent put American money and prestige — and which succeeded in dragging the yen back from a four-decade low. And with the board changes looming, time may be running short to normalize policy.

At a press conference later Friday, Ueda said policy had entered a “new stage,” and declined to rule out another hike in October or a bigger-than-usual move at some point. Those were hawkish comments, but markets weren’t convinced and the yen fell anyway, dropping 1.3% against the dollar by 7 p.m. in Tokyo. While Ueda said the BOJ doesn’t set rates in order to control the foreign-exchange market, many investors see currency moves as a key driver of decisions.

The governor’s job is “about as hard as it gets,” said Shoki Omori, chief Japan fixed-income strategist at Deutsche Bank. “No single pace will please investors, Washington and the government at once."
Right now there’s just about enough alignment to keep everyone on board.

Local media have portrayed Bessent’s remarks about the BOJ as an unusually direct form of pressure, and in the days leading up to Friday’s decision, the mood at the central bank seemed to be one of quiet defiance. Behind closed doors, officials maintained they would make decisions based on inflation, the economy and financial conditions rather than comments from foreign or government officials, according to people familiar with the matter.

Still, Ueda is likely happy to have Bessent supporting the case for further rate hikes and keeping Takaichi at bay, while the premier has gone along without too much protest. That’s likely the price she had to pay for Bessent’s help with the yen — and it also may leave Washington content before the Japanese leader’s potential meeting with President Donald Trump in New York next week.

That doesn’t mean she’s going to stay quiet. Takaichi has tweaked the country’s main debt metric in a way that gives her room to boost spending. Faster growth accompanied by a bit of inflation helps that cause, while higher rates will drive up debt-servicing costs that are already projected to climb some 30% by 2029. The two dissents on Friday by Takaichi-appointed BOJ officials raised the prospect of stiffer opposition to future hikes.
Nevertheless, the Bessent-backed currency intervention has likely made it harder for the government to oppose BOJ tightening, according to around 80% of economists in a Bloomberg survey.

Bessent’s public advocacy “has made the BOJ free from domestic political pressure, which is a big deal,” said Takahide Kiuchi, a former board member at the central bank and now executive economist at the Nomura Research Institute. “Since the Takaichi administration started last year, it has faced quite blatant political interference. I think they have postponed rate hikes when there was strong opposition from the administration. This time they didn’t do so, thanks to the US.”

Most BOJ-watchers are split between December (the favorite) and January as the month of the next hike. The picture gets cloudier later deeper into 2027. Hawkish board members Hajime Takata and Naoki Tamura are both set to leave in July, and if the two replacements appointed by Takaichi prove as dovish as Friday’s two dissenters, the balance of power on the nine-member board could shift significantly.

The BOJ has been raising rates gradually for a couple of years now. Still, by the time Friday’s widely telegraphed hike arrived, some had come to view it as essentially a quid-pro-quo. After Bessent had the US Treasury join Japan to prop up the yen in late July, Bessent, the former hedge fund manager said his actions were based on “pretty good insight” into what Japan’s central bank would do, and he dared traders to “bet against me if you want.”
Central bankers quite often get told what to do by their own governments, and typically resent it. There are fewer precedents for the pressure coming from abroad.

“There is nothing unusual in having the US Treasury secretary aim to jawbone the market into having a major Asian currency appreciate,” said Kenneth Rogoff, an economics professor at Harvard University. “It is, however, questionable for a foreignpower to impinge on the independence of the Bank of Japan.”

Bessent has been much more concerned about US yield trends than developments in Japan, according to one government official familiar with the matter. The Treasury secretary took office promising to bring borrowing costs down, especially the 10-year yields that are key to pricing things like mortgages. But after a decline in 2025, those rates have soared this year as America’s war on Iran drove inflation up.

Asked this week what was at stake for the US in Japan, Bessent pointed straight at the $32 trillion Treasuries market. “A stronger yen means that the Japanese government will not have to sell US assets to finance foreign currency intervention,” he said. Japan is the largest foreign holder of US public debt, at more than $1 trillion.
As things turned out, this week, the Treasury chief wasn’t the only US official making Ueda’s life difficult.

Ueda is reckoned to be a pioneer of “forward guidance,” central-bank jargon for giving markets a steer about what’s in the pipeline, while Kevin Warsh is a fierce critic of the strategy. Yet on Wednesday the new Fed chairman not only raised borrowing costs — by the same amount as the BOJ did two days later — but left investors convinced that more hikes are on the way.

That raises the stakes for Ueda, whose communications about BOJ intentions have sometimes puzzled markets. A wide interest-rate gap between the US and Japan has been one factor in the yen’s slide, and now the BOJ has a more hawkish Fed to keep pace with.On a broader view, the Bessent Treasury’s close interest in Japanese policy can be read as confirmation of what Takaichi claimed with a fist-pump during a White House dinner this year: “Japan is back.”

While rifts have opened with traditional US allies in Europe and the Middle East during Trump’s second term, Washington and Tokyo appear to be drawing closer. Takaichi has embraced Trump’s call for ramped-up defense spending, in a country that’s key to American strategy in the superpower rivalry with China.

The country is also becoming “a more normal economy,” with financial markets that show signs of renewed dynamism, said Tetsuya Inoue, an economist at Sony Financial Group and former secretary to Ueda when he was a BOJ board member in the early 2000s.

What’s more, some of Japan’s recent increase in inflation and borrowing costs also stems from the war on Iran that Trump’s been waging since February — as is also the case in the US, where higher energy costs have been driving up yields.

That doesn’t have much to do with Japan. But it does mean Japan should expect to remain under the US Treasury secretary’s scrutiny, according to Nobuyasu Atago, chief economist at Rakuten Securities Economic Research Institute and a former BOJ official.

“I believe that no matter what the BOJ says, Bessent will keep repeating the same remarks until the rise in long-term Treasury yields subsides,” Atago said. “Bessent’s remarks are ultimately aimed at addressing his own country’s problems.”

items.title: The New Buffett Chairing Berkshire's Board Knows the Firm Well
body: Howard Buffett, the eldest son of legendary investor Warren, is already well-versed in corporate governance as he takes over for his father as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway Inc.

Warren Buffett, 96, will now be chairman emeritus, ending a roughly six-decade run at the conglomerate. Howard, whose work experience includes law enforcement and philanthropy, has also been a director of several large corporations, including Coca-Cola Co., FirsTier Financial and Conagra Brands when it was known as ConAgra Foods.
He’s also had plenty of time to get acquainted with the inner workings of Berkshire.

“Howard has been a Berkshire director for 33 years,” Buffett said of his 71-year-old son in the letter announcing his move Friday. “That is a longer apprenticeship than I served before taking the reins at the age of 34.”

Howard’s appointment is the culmination of a well-telegraphed transition for the leadership at Berkshire, a onetime textile manufacturer that Buffett turned into a trillion-dollar company. In 2011, Buffett told 60 Minutes that his oldest son was qualified to succeed him as chairman. Last year, Buffett announced he would step down as CEO, later ceding that role to one of his top lieutenants, Greg Abel, 64.

In addition to his many corporate roles, Howard has run the Howard G. Buffett Foundation, which has historically focused on food security and conflict mitigation. Since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, his foundation has provided aid to the war-torn country.
The charity, along with the organizations run by his siblings Susie and Peter and his late mother’s Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation, have received donations from their father’s stake in Berkshire.

Over the past decades, Howard Buffett has published numerous books on a diverse group of topics, including wildlife conservation, as well as border security and the US drug epidemic — two issues he became familiar with when he was running the sheriff’s department in his rural Illinois county in 2017 and 2018.
“We are grateful to Howard for the care, discipline, and deep understanding of Berkshire he will bring to his new role,” Abel said in a statement.

items.title: Mbappe Is Kicking Nike When It Is Already Down
body: Just when it looked like things couldn’t get any more bleak for Nike Inc., it is losing one of its biggest stars.

Kylian Mbappe, who has a claim to being the best footballer on the planet and who’s been tied to the US sportswear giant since childhood, is leaving the brand. Making matters worse, he isn’t jumping over to Adidas AG, the other company in the duopoly that has dominated sportswear for decades. He’s headed instead for On Holding AG, a Swiss firm known for its running shoes.

Nike’s grip at the top end of its industry has never looked so tenuous since its rise as a global force in the 1970s and ‘80s. No wonder its shares are at their lowest for more than a decade, threatening its position in the S&P 100 index.

For many years Nike and Adidas were able to serve all customers for almost any sporting occasion. Men, women and kids; people wanting to run and cycle or shoot hoops; and fashionistas wanting the hottest sneakers. The big two had it covered. Now there are upstart rivals on all fronts.

The assault has been particularly fierce in running — a huge business that’s booming because of people’s desire to stay fit and look sharp while doing it. On, Brooks and Hoka are all grabbing market share.

Now, the attack is broadening. On wants to develop its soccer business, and will outfit Mbappe in newly designed boots to bring the attention of amateur footballers everywhere to its laceless, lightweight shoemaking technology. The company — which is backed by the Swiss former tennis player Roger Federer — has hired Mbappe’s fellow Frenchman Thierry Henry as its director of football. Henry is a senior figure in the game after a long and successful career taking in Arsenal, Barcelona and France’s national team.

And On isn’t the only emerging threat. New Balance has a big soccer business and sponsors England winger Bukayo Saka. Skechers USA Inc. has a deal with Bayern Munich forward Harry Kane. Still, On’s snagging of Mbappe is the clearest sign yet of trouble for the industry’s long-standing mainstays.

Adidas is vulnerable, too, although it looks slightly better placed to navigate the new landscape. Its Chief Executive Officer Bjoern Gulden has a natural flair for desirable gear. In the fashion business, his sneakers dominate — led by the Samba. At the same time, the German company is muscling in on Nike’s territory on performance with Sabastian Sawe breaking the two-hour barrier for a marathon runner while wearing a pair of Adidas’s ultra-light racing shoes. The company sponsored both finalists in the football World Cup this year, Spain and Argentina.

Nike isn’t destined for relegation quite yet. The other footballers on its roster include Brazil’s Vinicius Junior and the breakout star of the World Cup Erling Haaland. Given the likeable Norwegian’s celebrity power — and massive social-media fanbase — he looks best placed to take over from Mbappe. And perhaps Nike has had Mbappe’s best years: He’ll be 31 when the next World Cup arrives.

But to make the most of Haaland, a striker with a penchant for Hermes bags, Nike will have to find inspiration in the design room and come up with boots that capture customers’ imagination if they’re to match the inevitable interest around Mbappe’s new footwear.

And this might be the biggest difficulty for the US company. After two years under the leadership of CEO Elliott Hill, it has yet to develop a truly killer new product, whether that’s for the track, field or street.

Hill doubled down on actual sports gear first, rather than fashion. That was reasonable. With a company that still brings in almost $50 billion a year in sales, he had to start somewhere, and our everyday sneakers often originate in performance wear. But On’s move puts the spotlight back on how well he’s delivering on that sports-first strategy. Nike has clawed back revenue in running, with five quarters in a row of double-digit growth. It will have to resharpen its soccer efforts as well, where Hill aims to develop its business for decades to come.

He can’t ignore what’s going on off the pitch, either. Recently there’s been a return to a “blokecore” aesthetic that has seen women wearing football shirts with skirts, the comeback of footy-loving rock band Oasis and a revival of soccer-fan culture more generally (without the hooligan trappings of past generations). This has been a bright spot as the athleisure trend waned. And whose name is on the back of your shirt matters.

Perhaps Alexandre Arnault of the Louis Vuitton dynasty, who has just joined the Nike board, can inject some excitement. He will at least have a strong sense of fashion and digital commerce, and a natural understanding of Haaland’s mix of rugged sportsman and expensive man-bag afficionado.

More buzz is certainly needed. If Hill can’t get to grips with the rise of rivals like On, and the legacy competitor Adidas, investors may have to accept that sportswear has fundamentally changed, and Nike just didn’t shift with it.

items.title: Immunology Drugmaker Electra Falls 12% After Upsized US IPO
body: Electra Therapeutics Inc., a clinical-stage developer of immunology drugs, dropped 12% in its trading debut Friday after raising $350 million in an upsized US initial public offering.

Shares of the San Francisco-based company closed at $13.25 versus an IPO price of $15. The firm, which is backed by OrbiMed, sold 23.3 million shares after marketing 21.67 million shares for $14 to $16 each.
The trading gives Electra a market value of about $831.7 million, based on the outstanding shares in its filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission.

Electra’s lead drug candidate is designed to treat secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, a severe immune system overreaction. The company is conducting a global mid-stage trial of the drug in newly diagnosed patients, according to its filing. The therapy has received a Breakthrough Therapy designation from the US Food and Drug Administration as well as a Priority Medicine designation from the European Medicines Agency.

The IPO hits the US market at an exuberant time for drug developers. Listings of biotech and pharmaceutical companies have raised $7.2 billion this year, versus $1.3 billion in the corresponding period in 2025, data compiled by Bloomberg show.

The company’s investors include entities affiliated with OrbiMed, Westlake BioPartners and Redmile Group. Electra raised about $182.7 million from a Series C funding round in October, led by a unit of French drugmaker Sanofi SA, OrbiMed and Redmile and carried $97.7 million of cash and equivalents at of June 30 this year, according to the filing.
The firm had a net loss of $58.6 million for the six months ended June 30, compared to a net loss of $25.4 million for the same period a year prior, the filing shows.
Electra’s offering was led by Jefferies Financial Group Inc., Toronto-Dominion Bank, Evercore Inc. and Cantor Fitzgerald. Shares trade on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ETRA.

items.title: Yen Pares BOJ-Fueled Declines as Nikkei Reports a Rate Check
body: The yen pared declines on Friday, with the Nikkei newspaper reporting that the Bank of Japan inquired with market participants about exchange-rate levels, a step often seen as a precursor to official intervention.

Japan’s currency had been down more steeply earlier in the session after the BOJ delivered a widely expected interest-rate increase, but disappointed traders who were hoping for clearer guidance from the central bank indicating plans to raise borrowing costs further.

The Japanese currency was down 0.5% at 156.75 per dollar at about 3:45 p.m. in New York, after losing as much as 1.3% earlier in the session. The Nikkei reported, without saying where it got the information, that the BOJ had conducted what traders dub a “rate check.” The report comes just weeks after a historic joint intervention by US and Japanese authorities aimed at supporting the beleaguered yen, which roughly two months ago touched its weakest level in decades.

“With the yen depreciating sharply in spite of last night’s BOJ hike, today’s rate check is yet another warning shot to the market,” said Alex Cohen, a currency strategist at Bank of America. The Ministry of Finance “has shown a willingness to expend large amounts of reserves to intervene, and this should again have the market on notice.”
The Ministry of Finance couldn’t immediately be reached for comment outside of regular business hours.

Earlier Friday, the yen weakened to about 158 per dollar after BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda sent mixed signals on the path for future hikes following the bank’s increase. While he said the stage for policy setting has shifted, he also said it was difficult to determine the terminal rate for the current tightening cycle. Analysts saw his remarks as falling short of the market’s increasingly hawkish expectations.
The decision also drew dissents from board members Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato, adding to uncertainty over the pace and extent of further tightening.

The yen rallied at the start of this month, fueled by expectations of faster BOJ tightening, an unwind of yen-funded carry trades and speculation that Japanese pension funds could shift more money to domestic assets. But the Federal Reserve’s hawkish hike this week has renewed pressure on the currency, with strategists warning the dollar-yen rate could climb toward 160 if investors conclude the BOJ will struggle to keep pace with the Fed’s tightening.

“This is too little, too late,” said Win Thin, chief economist at Bank of Nassau 1982. “The BOJ had another chance to go big and they missed it, same as July. If they really wanted to boost the yen, they should have hiked more than expected and then intervened massively.”

Japan has entered a holiday period through Wednesday, when thinner liquidity could amplify the impact of any official intervention. Authorities used a similar window around the Golden Week holiday in May, first stepping in after the yen weakened beyond 160 just before the holidays and then apparently intervening again during the thinly traded period.

The yen slumped to about 164 per dollar in July, its weakest in four decades. The slide set the stage for a coordinated US-Japan yen-buying operation, the first since 1998, which raised the stakes for traders betting against the yen. Japan spent a record ¥15.4 trillion on intervention in the month through Aug. 26, according to Finance Ministry data. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has since continued to signal support for a stronger yen.
Read more: Bessent Dares Traders to Bet Against Yen: ‘I Am the House’

Still, some of the fundamental pressures weighing on the yen remain in place, including Japan’s wide interest-rate gap relative to other major economies and concerns over the fiscal outlook under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s expansionary spending plans.

A weaker yen helps the nation’s exporters, but it also makes it harder for the BOJ to stabilize inflation at a time when oil prices are soaring on global markets. The country imports the bulk of its energy needs.

Intervention can squeeze speculative yen shorts, but its ability to produce a lasting reversal may depend on monetary policy. However, hedge funds turned positive on the yen for the first time since mid-2025 in the week ended Sept. 15, according to Commodity Futures Trading Commission data released on Friday. They’d been reducing their bets against the yen.
