items.title: RYE By Martin Auer's $60 Bread Loaf Goes Viral at NYC Bakery
body: Have you heard about the new shop in downtown Manhattan that only sells one type of bread? It’s been written up by Grub Street, The Infatuation, the New York Post, Fox News and more. It’s all over Instagram and TikTok. And if you know one thing about the product, you’ll know this: At RYE by Martin Auer, the bread costs $60 per loaf.

Is it special? Eh. It tastes like rye bread. New York City has many bakeries that serve up perfectly good bread; this is one of them. If you bite into this loaf expecting an experience commensurate with the price, you will be disappointed.

That goes double for locals. If you’re a New Yorker and you’ve lived in the city for a while, it won’t be hard for you to find better bread. (You know a spot, I’m sure.) The RYE loaf’s crust isn’t particularly crusty, the crumb can be a bit gummy, and the sourdough tang can be subtle to the point of undetectability. Still, it’s better than supermarket bread — a notch above the $10 sourdough loaf at Wegman’s, up the street, which is not exactly cheap.

If you’re not a New Yorker — if all you know of the town is what you’ve been seeing on social media — then it’s easy to see why you might want to try this bread. There’s no shortage of stores here that get by fine on tourists alone, and Auer’s bakery has been catnip to influencers, who, on the two times I visited, made up the majority of the customers in store.

Auer attracted those content creators in an elegantly simple way, just by charging a ridiculous price for his product. (See also: Meadow Lane, the absurdly expensive Tribeca grocery store with a strikingly similar interior design philosophy that opened to similar viral hype last year.) It wasn’t enough for his bread to be merely expensive; New Yorkers are used to paying double digits for a loaf, and the days of artisanal bakers taking pride in affordability are definitively over. The first-rate rye loaf from Danish chain Ole & Steen will run you about $12, which is more or less the same price that Auer’s sourdough rye costs in his hometown of Graz, Austria.

Ironically, one of the bakers still taking pride in affordability is Auer himself, back in Austria: He has a store on Mariahilferstrasse in Graz that sells yesterday’s bread at half price and gives all the proceeds to charity. Since the rye lasts for a week or more, that’s a very effective way to feed the price-conscious and to honor the tradition of the Martin Auer bakery, which dates back to when his grandfather, Martin Auer IV, set up the business in 1936. Today there are 43 locations, mostly in and around Graz, including a 70,000-square-foot custom-built headquarters featuring not only a massive bakery but also a grain mill, coffee roaster, office and employee academy.

When planning his New York outpost, Auer decided to charge far, far more than Austrian prices — enough so that the price has become the loaf’s defining feature. In conversation, it’s always “the $60 loaf of bread” rather than “Martin Auer’s sourdough rye” or anything else.

The theory behind his gambit dates back at least as far as 1899, when Thorstein Veblen published The Theory of the Leisure Class and posited the existence of a class of goods for which demand rises as the price goes up. A Ferrari Testarossa or a crocodile Birkin is desirable because it’s expensive: To have one is to communicate to people that you have the wherewithal to spend lots of money.

Can a loaf of bread play that role? It’s a bit of a stretch, but it’s not impossible. Auer’s rye loaf has an idiosyncratic crust: It looks a bit like a massively upsized sugar cookie. If you have one sitting out on your waterfall kitchen island, there’s a decent chance your guests will recognize it. Alternatively, if you’re just buying the bread for your own personal consumption, $60 is almost a reasonable amount to pay for the frisson of splurging on something — roughly the price of a blowout, or a high-end glass of Champagne. To knowingly overspend can counterintuitively provide catharsis when times are tough. And for the many very rich denizens of downtown, including those who inhabit the $18 million apartments in the same building as the bakery, $60 is something they’d barely notice.

If you look at this loaf of bread as a loaf of bread, you’re making a category error. The thing that people are spending their $60 on doesn’t belong under goods, it belongs under services. You’re here for the experience, not the rye, which remains unavailable on DoorDash or Grubhub.

The Martin Auer experience is undeniably high-end, with space and light reminiscent of a $3,000 Aman hotel room. At Wegman’s, you have to hunt for an unsliced loaf and then check yourself out at a machine. At Ole & Steen, you’ll stand in a line and get rung up by a bored shop assistant. At RYE by Martin Auer, you’ll enter an ethereal world of luxury greige and be greeted by an assistant who will give you the whole spiel — where the flour comes from, how much time it takes to bake a single loaf, how many years (57) the same sourdough starter has been going. If you order a half loaf or a quarter loaf it will be cut on the counter in front of you, with a Martin Auer branded bread knife, on a Martin Auer branded bread board. It will be wrapped in lovely paper and sealed with a white-on-white Martin Auer sticker. It will be placed in a gorgeously designed heavyweight brown paper bag. It will be reverently transported to the checkout, where you will be rung up after you decide whether you’d also like to order a glass of Austrian wine, or maybe some kombucha on tap.

The problem is that the model doesn’t really lend itself to repeat business. Lots of influencers come once, thanks to the bakery’s demonstrated ability to drive content views. Few, however, are likely to come twice: they’ve already got what they came for. As for the bread-curious, after they’ve tried it once, they’re unlikely to become devoted. ($60 per loaf makes for an expensive habit.) Besides, everyone seems to be cutting back on carbs.

Perhaps the sourdough rye itself just isn’t special enough to become some kind of international phenomenon. Auer told Grub Street that he came to New York because his grandmother had always dreamed of immigrating here; that may prove to be an insufficient basis for a successful business model.

Outside the store is a set of stanchions holding up the Martin Auer version of a velvet rope — this one’s roughly-hewn, made from raw hemp. The idea is that no one wants the store to get overcrowded, so it’s better for would-be patrons to wait in line. So far, however, that hasn’t been a problem. The stanchions remain purely aspirational.

items.title: European Economies Eye Another Energy Crisis Heading Into Winter
body: European Union officials may convene an emergency meeting to discuss how euro-area economies can cope with another energy crisis. We learned today in Dublin about growing alarm among finance ministers over Middle East war fallout hurting households and governments. French President Emmanuel Macron said he’d convene the Group of Seven to weigh another release of stockpiled oil products.

Concern increased after Saudi Aramco told at least two oil refining customers in Europe that they will be allocated no oil next month. The decision was made after Saudi Arabia’s key East-West pipeline was struck by Iran-backed militias. The conduit had been a key relief valve for the world’s biggest crude exporter, allowing it to bypass the blockage at Hormuz and keep its oil shipments flowing from the Red Sea instead.

The potential energy crisis is spurring companies to diversify away from the Middle East. Eastern Europe’s biggest oil company, Warsaw-listed Orlen, had sought Saudi shipments to replace Russian crude following the Kremlin’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Now, Orlen’s CEO tells us the company needs new suppliers.

Now, with EU economies unable to count on either Russia or the Middle East to cover their fuel needs, the transition to renewable energy isn’t just a matter of climate stewardship but strategic imperative. —Jonathan Tirone

Russians are growing fearful that President Vladimir Putin may soon order a massive new mobilization for the war in Ukraine after this weekend’s parliamentary elections. That fear stretches to officials in the Kremlin and army recruitment centers, who’ve been looking to open foreign bank accounts and move assets abroad while encouraging friends and relatives to leave Russia in recent months, according to documents.

As Ukraine and the Kremlin limp toward a fifth year of conflict in February 2027, Russian farmers plan to plant less winter wheat as flows from the country’s crucial Black Sea ports remain stalled. That’s creating a domestic glut and setting the stage for a smaller 2027 harvest from the world’s top shipper.

Friedrich Merz has been haunted by a past boast that he could cut the support of Germany’s surging far-right party in half. Instead, the German chancellor watched this month as the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany trounced his conservative Christian Democrats in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. A satirical website quipped with a headline: “Merz Accidentally Halves Support for the Wrong Party.”

The fallout has shaken Germany’s political establishment spurred a wider, transatlantic crisis in confidence. Defense Minister Boris Pistorius was forced to defend the country’s purchase of American F-35A fighter jets amid simmering tensions with US President Donald Trump.

Market strategists have given the most bullish September forecast on European stocks since 2018, as strong corporate earnings help offset the impact of high energy prices and rising bond yields, according to our survey.
A group of countries including the US, Brazil, Japan and India have called on the EU to backtrack on a pesticides curb proposal that could lead to tighter restrictions on agricultural imports.

An EU-commissioned study found in August that such import restrictions risk pushing up consumer prices. However, the proposal has strong support in some EU countries where farmers fear unfair competition.

Senior tech executives spent the past few weeks loudly warning of the risks posed by artificial intelligence. Critics have pointed out there are aspects of these warnings — and previous warnings from the AI giants — that are potentially self-serving. For instance, they draw attention from more immediate risks, such as AI-generated scams, the proliferation of AI “slop” and the fact that college students are relying on chatbots. Check out this week’s edition of our Everybody’s Business podcast to learn how real the risks are.

items.title: Jet Fuel Prices Rise to Near Highest Levels Since Iran War
body: The price of jet fuel in parts of the US has climbed back near its most expensive level since the US-Iran war began, once again raising cost concerns for airlines and travelers.
Jet fuel on the Gulf Coast, considered the benchmark region for the US, priced at $4.55 a gallon as of Thursday, just over 20 cents off its wartime highs. In New York, it stood at $4.75 a gallon.

A broad-based fuel supply shock is roiling global energy markets, particularly for diesel. Both diesel and jet fuel are “middle distillate” fuels, meaning their prices are closely tied, and marginal diesel output can occur at the expense of jet fuel, and vice versa.
Jet fuel production last week fell to the lowest since early March. Supplies remain high, but are drawing closer to normal seasonal levels, meaning that prices may yet rise further.

In the first months after the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran in late February, jet fuel supplies were considered the most stressed of any refined oil product in the world. That was due to lost Middle Eastern and Asian supplies, along with the comparatively limited amount of storage for the fuel.

Dire warnings emerged in Europe about shortages and prices rose near or over $5 a gallon in New York, Los Angeles and on the Gulf Coast. The crisis pushed up airfares and caused significant strain on airlines, including being a proximate reason Spirit Airlines permanently shuttered in the US.

Concerns temporarily eased over the summer during a spike in production. In the US, refiners produced more than 2 million barrels a day of jet fuel for 21 consecutive weeks, a rate of output only achieved a handful of times before the war. For long stretches of the summer, US storage tanks held far more jet fuel than they typically do at that time of year while exports also soared.
Read More: US Refiners See Billions in Profits From Global Fuel Crunch

items.title: Specialty Insurer Orion180 Falls 2.8% After $240 Million IPO
body: Orion180 Insurance Group Inc. fell 2.8% in its first day of trading after the company raised $240 million from its initial public offering.

The specialty homeowners insurance company’s shares closed at $11.66 each on Friday, below the IPO price of $12. Orion180 sold 20 million Class A shares after marketing them at $15 to $17 each. The offering finished oversubscribed, Bloomberg reported.
The trading gives the Melbourne, Florida-based company a market value of about $1.15 billion based on the outstanding shares listed in its filings.

Founded in 2018, Orion180 operates as an insurer and a managing general agent for other carriers, providing both excess and surplus and state-regulated lines of home insurance, as well as private flood insurance, through a network of more than 14,000 independent agents.

Excess and surplus lines of insurance, which are generally not subject to regulations on premium rates or policy language, represent a small but fast-growing subset of the $187 billion US homeowners insurance market, according to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence cited in Orion180’s filings. E&S insurance covers properties that traditional insurers perceive as too exposed to the risk of severe weather or other catastrophes.

“We tend to come into areas that are more problematic, but there’s a need for that, and that’s where we can shine,” Kenneth Gregg, Orion180’s founder and controlling shareholder, said in an interview.
“We are not here to take advantage of disconnects or dislocations to take customers’ premiums,” Gregg said. “We are finding solutions for customers long-term that meet their needs and wants.”

Orion180 had net income of $13.2 million on revenue of $80.1 million for the first six months of 2026, compared with a net loss of $3 million on revenue of $50.4 million a year earlier. With a presence in 14 states, the company generated $601 million of premiums written in-house or placed with third-party carriers in the 12 months ended June 30.

Earlier this month, the company paid a $55 million dividend to shareholders including Gregg, according to the filings. The funds raised in the IPO may be used to repay a new credit facility that substantially funded both the September dividend and a separate $151 million payout in May.

Orion180’s IPO comes ahead of next week’s expected listing of another home insurance company, Bamboo Insurance Services Inc., whose existing shareholders including private equity firm CVC Capital Partners are seeking to sell as much as $700 million of shares.
The offering was led by Royal Bank of Canada, UBS Group AG and Raymond James Financial Inc. The company’s shares trade on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol OIG.

items.title: Fed's Schmid Backed Rate Hike, Says Inflation Goes Beyond Energy
body: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City President Jeff Schmid said he supported this week’s interest-rate increase as a necessary step to tame high inflation that’s being driven by more than just rising oil prices.
Schmid said inflation excluding energy has “also been running hot,” adding that a “broad range of goods and services” have also seen price growth inconsistent with the Fed’s price stability mandate.

“The Fed has work to do on inflation and this week’s action was a step in that direction,” Schmid said Friday in remarks prepared for an event in Vail, Colorado. “Higher oil prices have been an important driver of elevated inflation, but it is important to acknowledge that our inflation problem is not just about energy.”
Schmid said the labor market appears in balance and described economic growth as solid.

The Kansas City Fed chief spoke two days after policymakers lifted their benchmark rate for the first time in more than three years to help curb persistent inflation. Officials voted unanimously to raise the benchmark federal funds rate by a quarter percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4%, bucking pressure from President Donald Trump to lower borrowing costs. The median forecast released by policymakers showed they see at least one more hike later this year.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said Wednesday the rate increase “removed a dose of accommodation,” and signaled officials are serious about achieving their 2% inflation target.
Read More: Warsh Defies Trump’s Calls for Rate Cut as War Stokes Inflation
Schmid had previously said he probably would have supported a rate increase back in July, when officials voted 9-3 to leave their benchmark rate unchanged.
Schmid dedicated most of his remarks to real-time payments. He encouraged banks to participate in FedNow, a payments rail provided by the Fed that allows for instant inter-bank transfers.

items.title: Main Street Millionaires, What If Phones Aren't So Bad?: On Books
body: Welcome back to On Books, a newsletter from Bloomberg Weekend that brings you a fresh take on the new (and sometimes old!) books dominating the world’s cultural, social and economic conversations.
This weekend:

In the age of the world’s first trillionaire, mere billionaires aren’t enough to shock. The world’s 500th richest person, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires index, has nearly $8 billion — anything below that doesn’t even get you onto the scoreboard. But the tier below that absolutely should be a topic of conversation, writes Ben Steverman in Bloomberg Weekend.

The Everywhere Millionaire: Who Is Really Rich in America and How They Got There by economists Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick has dragged these merely wealthy into the spotlight, arguing that this demographic is actually the country’s true base of wealth and power.

Pulling together years of tax records and other data, the book shows that beyond the headline-making fortunes derived from tech and finance, most of the country’s rich made their money through more prosaic, tangible avenues: real estate, car dealerships, medical facilities, construction and manufacturing. The American dream, Steverman writes, is alive and well. The only problem, the book shows, is that that dream remains a nightmare for everyone else. Many of the country’s wealthiest amassed fortunes by exploiting workers, cutting costs and creating mini-monopolies by buying up competitors to protect margins, thereby shutting the door on aspirants as they attempted to climb the ladder.

The Power of No: A Celebration by Anna HolmesYou’ve been told about the power of saying “yes!” and now it’s time to hear the reverse. Holmes, a writer and editor, is convinced that a little less equivocation (or capitulation) and a lot more firm resistance will improve the lives of her readers. Using a combination of research, anecdotes and a hefty amount of her own voice, she makes a hard sell to just say no.

Timeless: The Art of Reinvention and Resilience at Any Age by Maye MuskThis isn’t the first memoir-as-self-help book that Musk has written. (Her first, A Woman Makes a Plan: Advice for a Lifetime of Adventure, Beauty, and Success came out in 2020 and sold more than 1 million copies.) This time, the model and mother (of Elon) dispenses further wisdom while going deeper into her own biography.

On the Equality of All Things: Lessons on Physics and Philosophy by Carlo RovelliRovelli, a theoretical physicist, has achieved global recognition with his books that make physics, and the concepts that underpin the field, accessible to a layperson. In his latest book, he urges his readers to question any and all “objective” truths they hold dear.

End Times Fascism And the Fight for the Living World by Naomi Klein and Astra TaylorIf the authors of this book are to be believed, we are marching headlong into anarchic end times, led by an unlikely alliance of plutocrats and religious ideologues. While the average reader might look out their window and see a more placid world, Klein and Taylor, left-wing journalists and documentarians, argue that an existential threat to civilization is upon us.

Psychologist Peter Gray has framed his new book Restoring Childhood: How to Set Kids Free in the Age of Anxiety, out this week, as a rebuttal to Jonathan Haidt’s bestseller, The Anxious Generation. While Haidt links phone-based childhoods to rising rates of anxiety and depression, Gray’s argument is that the harm ascribed to smartphones is overstated. Both men criticize a wider erosion of children’s freedom; but for Gray, freedom online is part of the solution.

Central to his theory is a blip in the suicide data for American teens. Since the 1950s, the numbers had been climbing steadily until the 1990s, when they suddenly dropped. To Gray, what that data reflects is that teenagers started to get online. “We had destroyed the culture of childhood, but the internet brought it back,” he says in an interview with Bloomberg Weekend. “They had a new space to play, to explore, to do things independently of adults.”

Gray, who is in his 80s, argues adults shouldn’t be banning kids from one of the last places they can roam free. Sure, there are some harmful effects, he says, but social media isn’t a total trap. “You’re finding people who have interests similar to yours, you’re expressing yourself, you are being creative,” he says.

He dismisses the manipulative effect of recommendation algorithms and sees compulsive scrolling as a “time-management problem.” Of course going online should never replace being outdoors, he says. But it’s also unclear that outdoor time will rise as screen time falls. “People like Jonathan Haidt and some others say, if we took away their smartphones, then they would play outside more,” says Gray. “I don’t see any evidence for that.”
—Morgan Meaker

In his new book, When America Roared, Pulitzer Prize-winning reporter and author Jonathan Kaufman explores the economic and cultural effects of the 1980s. The Reagan years are traditionally thought of as a disaster for Black Americans, he writes in Bloomberg Weekend, but the truth is more complicated. Even as poverty increased, affirmative action helped expand the Black middle class and created significant wealth.

No one embodies this conflicted legacy more than John Rogers, the investor who built the country’s first major Black-owned mutual fund company, Ariel Investments. Yet the higher he has risen, the more disillusioned Rogers has become. He finds himself at odds with a younger generation of Black voters, whom he says are too invested in identity politics. But he also represents the promise of private Black wealth, Kaufman writes, which can still be used as leverage and converted into broader financial and political power.

Journalist Jacob Weisberg’s new book, Profiles in Cowardice: A Study of Collaboration in the Trump Era, is a reversal of John F. Kennedy’s Profiles in Courage — a 1956 book about politicians taking principled stands.

The eight subjects of Weisberg’s book were also faced with a difficult choice: whether or not to stand up to President Donald Trump. Each subject had earlier, loudly disparaged some of Trump’s actions. In the end, they all caved.

There are top-of-the-mountain national leaders (Mitch McConnell, John Roberts, George W. Bush), businessmen (Blackstone’s Stephen Schwarzman, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos), media star Megyn Kelly, and two people who gained notoriety after a Trump shakedown (Brad Karp, the former chairman of Paul, Weiss; and Sian Beilock, the president of Dartmouth College). The book contains refreshers on familiar stories, like Bezos’s kneecapping of the editorial voice of the Washington Post, and highlights lesser-known cowering, like Bush’s silence as Trump incessantly insulted his family.

What makes Profiles in Cowardice valuable, engrossing and alive is that the profiles in cowardice really are profiles: compressed biographies told with a master’s eye for the radiating detail. Weisberg grants moral sophistication and complex lives to all his subjects, with the comical exception of an acidic portrayal of Schwarzman. We know what they are capable of. We know how the story ends. Yet at moments in the book it’s still possible to believe a different ending is possible.
Which, of course, it was. The book’s ultimate utility is to provide readers with our own moral conditioning when we’re forced to choose between cowardice and courage.
—Gary Sernovitz

With Donald Trump’s approval ratings hovering near record lows just six weeks from the country’s all-important midterm elections, the president is doubling down on some of his most unpopular positions, ranging from the war with Iran to data centers.

That disconnect, New York Times journalist Maggie Haberman tells Mishal Husain, is the direct result of a man who’s been cloistered in the Oval Office and surrounded by aides who filter out any negative information. For an inside look into the administration beyond Haberman’s bestselling book written with Jonathan Swan, Regime Change, tune in to Bloomberg Weekend’s The Mishal Husain Show.

Going Further: The Incomparable Clarence Thomas, Texas Senator Ted Cruz’s biography of Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas is now in its second week on the bestseller lists. Cruz, an ideological conservative and a onetime Supreme Court clerk, is uniquely qualified to tell the justice’s story — further aided by the fact that Thomas and Cruz are reportedly close friends.

As such, the book is unsurprisingly admiring of its subject, and, as the Texas Monthly has reported in an unenthusiastic review, draws heavily from Thomas’ own 2007 autobiography, My Grandfather’s Son. Similarly, Cruz is on the justice’s side as he retells the story of his confirmation hearing, when the law professor Anita Hill accused Thomas of sexual harassment — an accusation Thomas denied.

It might be illuminating, however, to read more on that hearing, not least because it sparked a national conversation about sexual harassment that continues to this day. The best book on the subject is the 1994 volume Strange Justice: The Selling of Clarence Thomas by Jane Mayer and Jill Abramson, both of whom were then journalists at the Wall Street Journal. (Mayer is now a staff writer at the New Yorker; Abramson is the former executive editor of the New York Times.)

The book makes the case that Thomas was chosen for his politics rather than his credentials, and articulates the ways in which the Republican political establishment settled on Thomas’s confirmation well before he had been vetted, let alone had his record examined by the public or any senatorial body.  When Hill’s testimony threatened to throw a wrench in the proceedings, what Mayer and and Abramson describe as a DC old-boys club quickly closed ranks. The book is valuable as a piece of history that goes a long way toward explaining the present, far more than any friendly biography ever could.

The founders of Pangram, Max Spero and Bradley Emi, have known each other since their freshman year at Stanford University (which was not all that long ago). When OpenAI’s ChatGPT was released in 2022, they decided to quit their AI jobs to develop a tool to detect AI-produced writing. There weren’t any good AI detectors out there, so they set out to build one, writes Vauhini Vara in Bloomberg Businessweek. They landed on a method called “synthetic mirroring” to recreate AI-generated text from scratch. But that worked only to a point. Soon they learned that what works for LLMs works for AI detectors: You have to train the model on increasingly more and more difficult cases to make it better.

Fast forward to March this year, when the New York Times reported that three-quarters of a soon-to-be-published horror novel called Shy Girl contained passages characteristic of AI-generated text. Hachette Book Group cancelled publication, and soon the internet lit up with people sniffing out alleged AI use in newspapers, YouTube videos and LinkedIn posts with Pangram’s tool.

In July, Pangram released its latest model, Pangram 4; the company says the false positive rate came down to about 1 in 24,000 — pretty good. Not long after, someone posted online that they’ve created a lab offering better AI-generated writing. They claim Pangram is labeling 86% of their output as human. “There is definitely a cat-and-mouse aspect of it, but that’s part of what we’re signing up for,” Spero says.
Have a good weekend, and happy reading!
—James Tarmy, Bloomberg Pursuits and Silvia Killingsworth, Bloomberg Weekend

items.title: RFK Jr.-Linked Group Offered Access to US Officials for Fee
body: A nonprofit group with ties to US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. solicited payment from companies in exchange for access to top agency officials at an upcoming event, according to documents viewed by Bloomberg News.

Ahead of the MAHA Summit on Sept. 29, a menu of sponsorship options was circulated to companies and consultants with various tiers of support, according to people familiar with the solicitations who weren’t authorized to speak publicly. The highest level, quoted at $300,000 to some prospective sponsors, guaranteed a speaking slot at the event “with meaningful input on the panel composition and topic” as well as a “private dinner for 30 guests” with Kennedy and Mehmet Oz, head of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.

The organization running the event is part of a web of interconnected groups that comprise Kennedy’s external political network. It’s unusual for a Cabinet member to maintain an active political operation.

Lawmakers have raised concerns about fundraising by Kennedy’s allied groups. Federal health officials also frequently appear on Zoom calls with Kennedy’s political supporters. Kennedy has refuted speculation that he plans to run for president in 2028.

HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard said in a written statement that “department officials listed as speakers were not involved in the planning or sponsorship activities for the MAHA Summit and were not aware of the sponsorship arrangements described.”
Kennedy has long criticized the health agencies he now oversees for being captured by corporate influences they are meant to regulate.

Companies that have signed on to sponsor the MAHA Summit include Anthropic, OpenAI, Walmart Inc., Hims & Hers Health Inc., Centene Corp., Tempus AI Inc. and Compass Pathways Plc, according to the event website. It’s unclear how much each contributed, though the most prominently featured logos are sleep apnea devicemaker ResMed Inc., whose chief medical officer is appearing on a panel with National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya, and cancer screening company Grail Inc., whose chief executive officer is speaking in another session.

Grail’s blood-based cancer screening test is facing review by a Food and Drug Administration advisory panel next week. CEO Josh Ofman said in a statement that the company welcomes opportunities to engage with policymakers, patients and advocates. Its participation at the summit “reflects our commitment to improving Americans’ health by creating a healthcare system with greater focus on prediction, prevention and early detection.”

Several panels at the conference feature companies that are regulated by various divisions of HHS. Speakers from the Trump administration include Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, HHS Principal Deputy Chief of Staff Stefanie Spear, HHS senior adviser Calley Means and Bhattacharya. Kennedy isn’t currently on the event agenda, but there is a placeholder for a conversation with “special guests.”
Donald Sherman, president of the nonpartisan watchdog group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, said the situation raised questions about whether officials should participate.

“If they didn’t know, they might have some plausible deniability,” he said. “But now that they do know, it certainly doesn’t seem appropriate for the secretary to attend an event that is being marketed to companies with business before the agency.”

One panel on the agenda features psychedelics companies, including Compass Pathways, and is being moderated by HHS Deputy General Counsel Matt Zorn, who plays a leading role in psychedelics policy at the agency.
“Compass Pathways’ participation in the MAHA Summit reflects our commitment to engaging wherever meaningful conversations about mental health reform are happening,” the company said in a statement.

There are two AI panels, with executives from OpenAI and Anthropic. Another session is called “Affordability First” and features executives from health insurers Elevance Health Inc., UnitedHealth Group Inc. and the industry trade group.

“AHIP welcomes opportunities to engage in dialogue about how to reduce the incidence of chronic disease and make healthcare more affordable and accessible for Americans,” the trade group said in a statement.
Other companies and individuals listed as participants or sponsors of the event declined to comment or didn’t return requests for comment.
The summit is being held in Washington by MAHA Center, one of the nonprofit groups with ties to Kennedy. “MAHA” refers to Kennedy’s trademarked slogan, Make America Healthy Again.

The executive branch is responsible for vetting speaking requests for administration officials, said Richard Painter, a professor of corporate law at the University of Minnesota and a former chief ethics lawyer in former President George W. Bush’s White House. The administration normally seeks to ensure the names of those officials aren’t used to help an outside organization raise funds.
Tony Lyons, the president of MAHA Center and a central figure in Kennedy’s orbit, addressed an inquiry about the event’s solicitations for sponsors during a public speech Thursday.

“They said, ‘Oh, you’re taking money from a bunch of different companies, and we’d like to talk about those companies, and doesn’t it feel like you’re you’re being co-opted by these companies?’ And I was thinking, you know, that’s a reasonable question,” Lyons said.
Lyons didn’t answer the question directly but added that he’d like to see similar scrutiny applied to members of Congress.

items.title: King Charles Has an AI Summit: Britain Already Has the Best Watchdog
body: This is Bloomberg Opinion Today, a crowning collation of Bloomberg Opinion’s opinions. Sign up here.

We’re all still trying to answer the question of whether AI poses a civilizational threat to humanity. And that includes King Charles III, who this week convened a meeting on the technology at the nearly 300-year-old Dumfries House in Scotland (a property held by The King’s Foundation, a charity founded by the monarch). The participants at the summit ranged from Jensen Huang, chief executive officer of Nvidia, to Paolo Benanti, a Franciscan friar who advises Pope Leo XIV on AI ethics. In an official statement, Charles said, “The development of AI — its substance and its pace — are both intriguing and deeply concerning in equal measure.”

Andreas Kluth examines various metaphors that may help us weigh the AI risk for nuclear Armageddon, including Robert Oppenheimer’s scorpions in a bottle and the Prisoner’s Dilemma, a behavioral experiment designed by Merril Flood and Melvin Dresher in 1950 (and named by Canadian mathematician Albert Tucker). “AI doesn’t share, at least not intrinsically, our human instinct to avoid catastrophe,” Andreas concludes. “An out-of-control AI contest, like a nuclear war, cannot be won, and must never be fought.”

Gautam Mukunda gets at my biggest concern. “You might be imagining doom from killer robots with thick Austrian accents,” he writes. “But the greatest risk comes from cells, not steel.” Many national security experts believe “AI meaningfully increases — or soon will — bioweapon risk.” I was already having nightmares over a 2024 warning by scientists in the journal Science about artificially created “mirror life” — organisms that “reverse” the natural order of sugars and amino acids in DNA, and to which we have no immunity. Says Gautam: “One key safeguard is to mandate that any sequence of DNA which is synthesized must be screened for possible use in a pathogen.” But who might be the watchdog for something like this? A first line of defense?

That’s where the UK — where King Charles is head of state — can come in, says Parmy Olson. The British monarch can “point to a source of help in his own backyard.” That would be the UK’s AI Security Institute ,“the world’s best funded agency for testing cutting-edge AI models.” Says Parmy: “AISI already has a track record of testing the latest AI systems. It got early access to Mythos, the Anthropic model that was initially restricted because of its cyber capabilities. The government-backed agency lacks a commercial conflict of interest, and its base in London gives it meaningful distance from the financial and ideological bubble of Silicon Valley.”

Parmy says that the overlords of OpenAI and Anthropic “may have their own ideas about who should oversee their work, but in the spirit of proper oversight, the choice shouldn’t be entirely theirs.” She adds, “It would be a great irony if meeting King Charles, a symbol of Britain’s former empire,helped encourage today’s American tech royalty to think about empowering a sophisticated AI inspector in London.”

Remember the specter of “Grexit” back in 2015? That was amid the country’s cataclysmic debt crisis, when it effectively defaulted on a payment to the International Monetary Fund and cash was so swiftly flying out of the country that Athens imposed a €60-a-day ATM withdrawal limit. For a moment, it looked as if Greek banks would run out of euros and be for all practical purposes — and disastrously — out of the Eurozone.

Eleven years later, Greece (having won a last minute bailout from the European Central Bank) is enjoying GDP growth faster than the rest of the euro area. Its finances aren’t perfectly healthy yet, but they have stabilized. The UK, meanwhile, voted for Brexit in 2016 and last week saw one of its biggest taxpayers flee Britain’s high levies for less punitive Athens. As Paul J. Davies notes, “Billionaire hedge fund manager Chris Rokos departing for Greece, where he’ll pay just €100,000 ($115,000) a year.” British media reported he paid £330 million ($446 million) in 2025. Paul calculates a lower figure: £143 million ($190 million).

Paul says that Britain’s bet on soaking the rich — while it may have led to some big name departures — has “had a minimal effect on people whose permanent home was already elsewhere” (the so-called non-doms or non-domiciled UK residents).

Says Paul: “That’s what encouraged the last Conservative administration to propose scrapping the preferential deal [that] exempted non-UK income and investment gains from taxes, and persuaded the current Labour government to end it from April 2025.” He continues: “Plenty of rich people want to live in the UK or are held here by their jobs and family; reducing tax bills to a fraction of what they currently pay would be an unnecessary freebie that the country can’t afford.”
Still, if I had to choose between $115,000 and $190 million, I wonder where I’d go.

“Europe is restricting imports of Chinese-made electric vehicles, but allowing unrestricted trade in the batteries that power them. The set-up is congenial for the continent’s carmakers, which would rather use cheaper Chinese cells than invest in alternatives. If your aim is to support advanced European manufacturing, however, it’s disastrous. ... Chinese car brands... still make up just 6.6% of sales. Meanwhile, Chinese batteries, whose local market share has almost doubled in two years to more than 50%, are barely discussed. Imagine if Britain had spent the 1930s protecting its aircraft companies, while remaining dependent on Germany for the engines they need to fly.” — David Fickling in “China’s Electric Cars Aren’t Europe’s Real Problem.”

“From the runways to resale, Chanel has been the clear standout. Designer Matthieu Blazy caused a frenzy when the first deliveries of his lines arrived in stores in March. Chanel’s sales rose 16% in the first half of this year excluding currency movements. By comparison, LVMH’s fashion and leather goods sales fell 1% in the same period. ... As Chanel is privately owned by brothers Alain and Gerard Wertheimer, it could afford to be patient. The strategy worked, creating — and then unleashing — pent-up demand for Blazy’s oversized bags, tweed jackets and square-toed shoes. Chanel also cleverly introduced new purses priced below its most expensive classics, which helped even top-end customers feel they were getting more value for money.” — Andrea Felsted in “Gucci and Dior’s Outfit Change is a Work in Progress.”

In a column this week, I wrote about the threat war poses to the architectural legacy of humankind. A lot of you are familiar with the perilous survival of St. Paul’s Cathedral here in London in World War II. Still there are many reminders of buildings that were severely damaged but remain standing — as ruins or reconstructions — in the British capital.

Not far from Bloomberg’s European headquarters are the remains of St. Dunstan-in-the-East. A church has been on the site since about 1100, with renovations and rebuilding taking place intermittently (including a spire by Christopher Wren, architect of St. Paul’s) until the early 19th century. In 1821, a refreshed St. Dustan opened for worship, at the cost of what today would be more than £5 million ($6 million). It would last until 1941, when German bombs left only the north and south walls intact (and Wren’s tower). Today, it is a public park, witnessing the occasional wedding party as well as providing a home for squirrels. It remains a reminder of the wages of war.
Please call it a tie.

items.title: VW Slashes Outlook After China Sales Slump, Costs Weigh
body: Volkswagen AG slashed its profit forecast after a sharp contraction in China and a €6 billion ($6.9 billion) writedown tied to sports-car maker Porsche AG, deepening concerns about the strains facing the global auto industry.

Europe’s biggest carmaker now expects an operating margin of no more than 1%, it said Friday, citing to the accelerating shift to EVs in Europe as another drag on profitability. The shares slumped 7.5%, the most in a year, triggering a broader selloff in automakers including BMW AG, Ford Motor Co. and Stellantis NV.

The manufacturer had previously expected an operating margin of at least 4%. VW pegged total charges weighing on results this year at about €10 billion, which include restructuring costs tied to workforce reductions and writedowns on assets in China.
Excluding those items, Volkswagen said its operating margin would be around 4%.

“But even that is not enough to invest forcefully in the future,” Chief Financial Officer Arno Antlitz said in an internal interview seen by Bloomberg News. “The financial development shows: We have no time to lose.”
The broad pullback highlights concerns about the auto industry. Carmakers in Europe and the US are grappling with weaker pricing, costly EV investment, pressure from Chinese rivals and uneven demand.

That’s raising questions over how much of VW’s deterioration is company-specific and how much reflects a wider squeeze on sector profits. In June, BMW also cut back its expectations for the year, for an operating return of as low as 1%.
Read More: BMW Profit Warning Puts It Rock Bottom Among Europe’s Carmakers

The warning deepens the challenge for Chief Executive Officer Oliver Blume, who is trying to overhaul Europe’s biggest carmaker as its former growth engines falter. Earlier this month, VW struck a hard-fought agreement with labor representatives that could double planned job cuts to 100,000 globally, while management is also under pressure to reduce excess factory capacity and costs in Germany.

The setback goes to the heart of the model that powered Volkswagen’s expansion for much of this century. Rich profits from China and its premium brands helped support a sprawling manufacturing base in Germany and finance investment in new technology. Now those pillars are weakening: Porsche is resetting expectations, China is becoming less lucrative and the shift to electric cars is eroding margins before cost cuts at home have fully taken hold.

Nowhere is the strain more evident than in China. Earnings there have slumped as domestic manufacturers take market share and the broader economy remains weak, turning what was once Volkswagen’s most important growth engine into an increasingly acute challenge.

Antlitz said the world’s largest car market has contracted by about 20% and that there is no stabilization in sight. At the same time, Chinese manufacturers are pushing aggressively into Europe with lower-priced electric cars, intensifying pressure in Volkswagen’s home market even as its business in China deteriorates.

Porsche is another worry. The 911 maker is currently preparing a capital markets day for Oct. 7, where it is expected to set out updated medium-term financial targets and strategy. Volkswagen said its writedown followed updated long-term planning and revised assumptions for Porsche’s valuation, suggesting the adjustment is linked to that process.

Volkswagen also said the faster-than-expected growth of EV sales in Europe is weighing on profitability, particularly at the Volkswagen passenger-car and Audi brands. Battery-powered models generally have lower margins than comparable combustion-engine vehicles, meaning the quicker shift in the sales mix is diluting earnings even as EV demand strengthens.

items.title: Deutsche Bank's DWS to Shut US Property Fund Hit by Redemptions
body: A US real estate investment trust managed by Deutsche Bank’s asset manager DWS plans to sell all of its assets and liquidate, highlighting how challenges in the asset class are persisting.

RREEF Property Trust, which had a net asset value of $203 million at the end of June, experienced “a period of heightened redemption activity” and faced “challenges of attracting new capital,” Chief Executive Officer Todd Henderson said in a statement.
The plan to wind down “is subject to the approval of the company’s stockholders, and the company plans to convene a special meeting of its stockholders for their consideration,” it said.
The company intends to return net proceeds from the sale of its assets to its stockholders “when appropriate.”
The fund had invested in US properties, which have been an ongoing headache for Deutsche Bank.
Read More: Deutsche Bank Takes Hit as It Exits Some US Commercial Property

RREEF Property Trust was an early example of what’s known as a net-asset value REIT, because shares can be bought and redeemed based on the value of their holdings. The vehicle has invested in staples like apartments, retail real estate and warehouses.

The model, which typically caters to individual investors, grew popular in US real estate, with Blackstone Inc., Starwood Capital Group and others raising billions for their non-traded REITs. Fundraising for the DWS vehicle lagged, even before a series of interest rate hikes in 2022 made US real estate a less appealing investment.
RREEF Property Trust has seen net outflows in all but one of the past 15 quarters, according to data compiled by Robert A. Stanger Co., an investment bank that follows non-traded REITs.
“It never got traction,” said Michael Covello, executive managing director at Stanger. “They’re doing the right thing by investors to liquidate and return capital.”

items.title: BofA Warns of Warsh's Fed Hiking Rate Above 5% in 2022 Redux
body: It’s time for investors to prepare for the risk that the Federal Reserve raises its benchmark rate above 5%, according to Bank of America Corp. strategists.

The interest-rate market is still underestimating the endpoint of a Fed hiking cycle that started this week, a team including Mark Cabana and Meghan Swiber said, urging clients to position for higher two-year Treasury yields. Swaps imply three more quarter-point hikes, which would take the effective federal funds rate into a 4.5% to 4.75% range, whereas BofA sees the potential for overnight borrowing costs to revisit the highs from the 2022 to 2023 hiking cycle, when the target rate reached as much as 5.5%.

Their forecast that two-year yields will rise to 5% this year, from around 4.7% on Friday, bucks consensus. The BofA team said comments from Chairman Kevin Warsh that Wednesday’s rate hike removed a “dose of accommodation” suggest officials don’t yet view monetary policy as stymieing the US economy.

“A Fed that does not view policy as restrictive is likely to keep hiking until financial conditions become restrictive, strengthening our conviction in a flatter yield curve,” the strategists wrote in a note. As well as their new forecasts, they are recommending clients short two-year Treasuries, with a yield target of 5.25% — around the 2023 peak.

While Warsh was careful not to commit to any future move, he reaffirmed his dissatisfaction with inflation’s trajectory and drove home the central bank’s commitment to price stability. The US yield curve has flattened in recent sessions, with shorter-maturity yields rising faster than those on longer bonds, as traders added to bets for further Fed hikes.

The strategists, who are responsible for covering the bond market and identifying trade opportunities for clients, are a separate group from BofA’s economists, who focus on the central bank. In a note published Wednesday, BofA’s US economist Aditya Bhave said his team is sticking with their call for two more hikes this year in October and December, with no policy action expected in 2027.
Read More: Bond Traders Signal Warsh Credibility Growing in Inflation Fight

BofA’s strategists pointed to the Fed’s latest Summary of Economic Projections, which showed officials see much greater upside risk to inflation than to unemployment. They also cited a measure of the Taylor rule — a widely used formula that generates a suggested policy rate based on how much inflation and economic output are deviating from target levels — as implying the Fed funds rate should be around 5.3%.

“Simple frameworks suggest Fed funds should be greater than 5%,” they said. “While front-end yields can continue to rise, we expect a more limited pass-through to longer tenors,” with the 10-year seen finishing the year at 5%, close to where it was trading on Monday.

items.title: Newsom Wants AI 'Kill Switch' to Rein in Tech Industry
body: California Governor Gavin Newsom issued an executive order on Friday pushing to implement guardrails on artificial intelligence in the state that’s the epicenter of the technology’s boom.

Newsom is ordering a working group to provide a guide in two months with measures to boost California’s AI safety and security laws, according to a statement from the governor’s office on Friday. The group should consider steps such as having companies develop a “kill switch” for frontier models and requiring independent third parties to draft safety plans for AI companies, according to the statement.

“We’re not waiting to act – we’re going to speed up our work on substantial and responsible AI oversight before it’s too late,” Newsom said. “We’re going to do this thoughtfully but with urgent velocity; the stakes are too high to wait or delay action.”
Newsom’s office did not immediately respond to a request about who would be part of the group.

Warnings over AI safety escalated over the past weeks, as CEOs including OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic PBC’s Dario Amodei pushed for greater oversight following high-profile resignations by employees who raised concerns about the technology’s risks.
Read More: Are We Losing Control of AI? What’s Driving Fears: Explainer

Anthropic and OpenAI are both based in California, and Newsom has been enthusiastic supporter of the technology, which is fueling an economic boom in the state. Earlier this year, he touted a partnership between the California government and Anthropic that aimed to expand the use of Claude in state agencies.
Newsom had previously vetoed major AI legislation, including a sweeping AI-safety 2024 bill.

OpenAI called Newsom’s executive order “an important step,” a spokesperson for the company said in a statement. “We look forward to supporting its implementation and working with Governor Newsom, the California Legislature, and the state’s next governor to advance strong, adaptable safeguards that can contribute to a consistent national framework,” OpenAI said in the statement.
Friday’s executive order will also hasten the state’s carrying out of two new laws on AI oversight passed by the legislature this year, including rules for third-party AI auditing.

Other Democratic governors are pushing for tougher AI safeguards, after President Donald Trump dismissed the warnings. Trump compared the warnings to concerns over the threat of global warming and calling safety fears a “hoax.”
On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro called for tougher safeguards around artificial intelligence during a keynote address at the AI Horizons summit in Pittsburgh.
“I don’t think that the very real concerns of our neighbors that they overwhelmingly express about this technology is a hoax, as our president has called it,” he said.

Lawmakers in Washington have floated similar proposals, including a measure backed by Democratic Congressman Ted Lieu and a Senate proposal by Republican Senator John Kennedy — who’s also calling for a “kill switch.”

Smaller AI companies, however, have warned against the risk of regulation stiffing competition. Startup executives have said this approach may enable the top firms to set the rules and tighten their grip on what’s still a nascent technology sector.
Newsom, who’s considering a presidential run in 2028, is also criticizing Trump and Congress for failing to act on AI safeguards.

In a video posted online Friday morning, he urged House Speaker Mike Johnson to call Congress back from recess to pass a federal AI safety bill, calling it “the minimum thing we should expect that he and his colleagues do.”

items.title: Amsted Said to Weigh $6 Billion Sale of Cooling System Unit BAC
body: Amsted Industries is exploring a sale of cooling system provider Baltimore Aircoil Co., as strong demand for data center components pushes more owners to test the market, according to people familiar with the matter.

The industrial conglomerate is working with financial advisers to solicit acquisition interest in BAC, which could be valued at more than $6 billion in a transaction, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private.
Deliberations are early and Amsted could opt to retain the business, the people added. Representatives for Amsted and BAC didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

The sale process will test whether potential buyers, which could include HVAC as well as other industrial companies, are willing to make fresh bets that the data-center build-out will keep its strong momentum.

Companies, other than private equity firms, have been scooping up these high-growth assets in a wave of deals, with Eaton Corp. acquiring Boyd Thermal for $9.5 billion last year and Ecolab Inc. making a $4.75 billion purchase of CoolIT this year.

Founded in 1924 by a Russian immigrant, BAC serves a wide range of industries in addition to data centers with its cooling towers and other refrigeration technologies, including heavy industry, energy, commercial buildings and the food and beverages sectors, according to the company’s website. BAC has operations in North America, Europe and Asia, its website shows.

items.title: Burnham Faces Increasing Pressure From Budget, AI
body: Two stories have dominated this week—the coming Budget and the debate over AI safety. Both question whether this government is in control.

Before he became prime minister, Andy Burnham infamously said that he wanted to “get beyond this thing of being in hock to the bond market.” As PM, he tried to take a pragmatic approach. Burnham emphasised fiscal restraint and there was much talk of economic heavyweights—Jim O’Neill, Andy Haldane, Richard Hughes—being brought into his inner sanctum.

Yet as Bloomberg’s Joe Mayes puts it - the bond markets are very much calling the shots. Bloomberg Economics estimates that rising borrowing costs have wiped out half the government’s headroom and are threatening their desires for a steady-as-she-goes Budget. Here’s Joe:

None of these options are straightforward. Note how Burnham has in recent days lost the support of the second of those two economists mentioned above, paraded in the early days to reassure the markets - Haldane has now joined O’Neill in warning against tax rises.

The other big story is AI, and again it comes down to what the government can actually do. The sprint to the frontier is being led by American-owned firms, and Donald Trump is resistant to any new regulation. King Charles can hold summits but if the US administration won’t move, what can we do?
Well, Parmy Olsen has a suggestion in her column today. She argues that Britain’s AI Security Institute is ideally placed to evaluate how the labs are developing this technology:

But, again, this relies on the US government being prepared to let American-based labs share their development work with AISI—and there are doubts about that after Anthropic did not provide the agency with its latest model to test. This is the depressing counterpoint raised by the Times headline here - that AISI was once world leading but if even firms gripped by an existential crisis won’t let AISI in, is its influence waning?
One bit of good news for the UK is that its stock market - unloved in recent years - is seen as increasingly good value, as Michael Msika writes, with it up about 8% compared to last year.
Oil price hikes may hurt consumers but they strengthen stocks that call the FTSE 100 home — and the hitherto worrying lack of tech stocks in the UK becomes a positive when that sector wobbles.
To date, Burnham has been effective at portraying himself as a decisive PM with grip. This autumn the greatest threat to him is a loss of control.
Want this in your inbox each weekday? You can sign up here.

Hi, I’m Sam from Markets Today and it has been a busy week for UK assets filled with data drops and central bank decisions, all of which left us with the conclusion that much of the fate of the country’s finances is held by elements beyond its control.

The Bank of England made clear this week that energy prices are king when it comes to what happens next with interest rates. If they remain elevated, then the need for rate hikes to tame inflation will increase. Only a sustainable resolution to the conflict in the Middle East would change that equation, and the bank itself acknowledged that the efforts to achieve this seem to have eased off.

Food prices are going to go up too, due to various supply disruptions and climate change, and the BOE sees headline inflation hitting 4%. That’s an important number that their research has indicated flicks a switch for consumers and makes them more concerned. If that happens, and they really feel those food prices increasing, then they start to ask for bigger pay rises. Et voila, the second-round effects all the policymakers are laser-focused on spotting will emerge.
This, plus the upcoming budget and the speculation that will come along with it, spells more volatility in bond markets to come, both for short- and long-dated debt.

items.title: Amazon in EU Crosshairs Over Suspected Price Curbs on Sellers
body: Amazon.com Inc. is under scrutiny from the European Union for potentially imposing unfair restrictions on firms selling on its platform.

As part of the process, the European Commission has quizzed third-party sellers on whether they have been hampered by so-called price-parity restrictions, which allegedly penalize them for offering products and services at lower prices on competing marketplaces or their own websites, according to people familiar with the matter and documents reviewed by Bloomberg.

One of those contacted was Jack Nekhala, inventor of the Bed Scrunchie, a device that keeps sheets attached to mattresses. He told Bloomberg that should his company offer its product for less on its own website, Amazon could suppress it on its own marketplace, allowing the US e-commerce giant “to influence prices across the internet.”

The EU’s scrutiny — under the bloc’s Digital Markets Act — is currently in its early stages but it could develop into a full-scale investigation should regulators unearth evidence of potential wrongdoing, according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity.
A spokesperson for the Brussels-based EU commission said it’s in “regular dialogue with Amazon and its business customers to monitor compliance with the parity ban requirement” under the DMA.
Amazon is “committed to complying with the DMA and we always engage constructively in the commission’s ongoing regulatory oversight,” according to an emailed statement.

The DMA, which imposes a list of dos and don’ts on Big Tech firms, has already led to a slate of headline-hitting cases since it was set up in 2023. These include multi-million-euro fines for Apple Inc., Meta Platforms Inc., and Alphabet Inc.’s Google. The penalties have irked US President Donald Trump’s White House and added an extra layer of tension to fraught EU-US trade relations.

items.title: Treasuries Fall as Fed Rate-Hike Outlook Dents Sentiment
body: Treasuries fell as anticipation of additional Federal Reserve interest-rate hikes drove investors into wagers on rising yields for short-maturity debt.

The selloff lifted yields on two- to five-year notes by at least eight basis points, while longer-maturity yields rose less. The two-year yield climbed to nearly 4.75% for the first time since July 2024, exceeding the level reached Wednesday after Fed policymakers raised interest rates and investors inferred from comments by Chairman Kevin Warsh that at least one additional increase is likely this year.

The rise in two- and five-year Treasury yields also reflects interest in betting against those tenors in anticipation they will cheapen further. Demand to borrow the most recently issued securities in the sector for short positions is so strong that owners can finance them at below-market interest rates.

“People want to be short because the Fed has entered a tightening cycle and the likelihood that they are one-and-done is almost zero,” said Tony Farren, managing director in rates sales and trading at Mischler Financial Group.

Interest-rate strategists at Bank of America recommended its customers set a short position in two-year notes at a yield of 4.73%, targeting an increase to 5.25%. They also recommended positioning for two-year yields to rise relative to 30-year yields, further narrowing the gap between them. The difference shrank to less than 60 basis points this week, the smallest in more than a year.

“We expect front-end rates to continue moving higher and the curve to flatten until there is clearer evidence that policy has become restrictive,” the strategists led by Mark Cabana wrote in a report.
Yields across maturities reached the highest levels in at least two years this week, with 10- and 30-year yields climbing to levels last seen in 2007.

For much of the time since the US attacked Iran in late February, disrupting the supply of oil from the Middle East, oil prices have guided Treasury yields via their impact on gasoline and consumer prices more broadly. Crude oil benchmarks and the national average retail gasoline price this week rebounded to their highest levels since mid-May. Diesel — a key input price for shipping, heating homes and running farm equipment — rose to a record high.

Friday’s Treasury selloff, however, occurred even as oil prices sold off. One factor was an increase in yields across most European government bond markets: In France, a risk gauge climbed to the highest level in 14 years after the government said it would miss its deficit target.

Rising yields on Treasuries also reflect concerns about growth in the supply of debt globally, both by governments to finance deficits and roll over existing debt and by companies to finance capital expenditures.
Warsh, speaking in a news conference immediately after the Sept. 16 rate decision, attributed rising long-term bond yields to economic strength, competition for capital and rising consumer prices.

US government debt auctions next week include bill, note and bond auctions totaling more than $700 billion, in what Mischler’s Farren said would be the 10th-largest gross weekly supply on record. Meanwhile, investment-grade corporate bond sales set records in four of the past eight months, including the last three, and volume is on pace to exceed the $1.75 trillion record set in 2020.

“Government bonds and Treasuries in particular have had a supply and demand problem,” said Christian Hoffmann, head of fixed income at Thornburg Investment Management. “There’s an abundance of supply and demand has been captured by other markets,” including stocks, he said.
Hoffmann said the Fed is unlikely to meet market expectations for three more rate hikes and that the highest yields since 2007 offer value.
“When something is as attractive as it’s been in 20 years, I think you can’t ignore it,” he said.

items.title: Tata Board Mutiny Leaves Patriarch Little Choice But to Litigate
body: Noel Tata, the Tata Group’s founding-family patriarch, is finding himself increasingly boxed in after the conglomerate’s holding company decided to plan a stock listing and extend the chairman’s tenure — moves he opposed but could not stop.

Despite helming the shareholder that controls 66% of Tata Sons Pvt., Noel’s main recourse now appears to be seeking redressal from India’s National Company Law Tribunal, or NCLT, arguing that there were governance issues at the holding company and that the board’s actions violated the articles of association, according to legal experts Bloomberg News spoke to.

“The mutiny of the board against the controlling shareholder is possibly a first, and not the right precedent for corporate India,” Institutional Investor Advisory Services, a Mumbai-based proxy advisory firm, said in a note Friday. The board directors “agreed to change the structure of a 100+ year old group – all this in a few hours and in one board meeting.”

Legal experts say the episode exposes the limits of Noel’s power inside Tata Sons, even as the Tata Trusts — a group of charities of which he is the chairman — remain the dominant owner of the $185 billion conglomerate. This forced the 69-year-old Tata to relay his position through multiple media statements on Thursday evening.

“The next stage will be about whether Tata Sons can practically implement a decision whose legal validity is being challenged” by the majority shareholder, said Sonam Chandwani, managing partner at KS Legal & Associates. “The board has taken a decision which is being expressly disputed by the majority shareholder on the ground that the company’s governance framework has not been followed.”
Tata Sons and Tata Trusts didn’t immediately respond to requests for comments.

Unless the two sides reach a negotiated position on governance and listing, the dispute is likely to develop along two parallel tracks, according to Bishwajit Dubey, a lawyer practising primarily in New Delhi courts.
“One is an internal corporate-governance challenge before the NCLT and a separate regulatory challenge before the High Court” against the banking regulator’s push toward listing, Dubey said.

The developments have set up a showdown on who really controls the holding company of the nearly 160-year-old Indian conglomerate. Tata Group has over two dozen listed companies and is key to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s high-end technology ambitions.
Tata Trusts have opposed a listing ask, since this will bring greater regulatory and market scrutiny of Tata Sons and risks exposing the group to hostile takeover attempts.

“Tata Trusts may take the view that their shareholding will get diluted and ownership structure will change,” said H. P. Ranina, a lawyer who argues cases before the Supreme Court of India. “Reserve Bank of India has the power to regulate, but not change the ownership of an entity.”

The chain of events at Thursday’s Tata Sons board meeting also underscored the power struggle Noel is facing not just at Tata Sons but within charities he leads. Venu Srinivasan, the other Tata Trusts’ representative on Tata Sons board, voted against Noel, revealing an internal divide.
Any legal confrontation will hinge on whether the board can proceed as though its decisions are final when Tata Trusts says they contradict the company’s Articles of Association.

Chandwani noted that if there is a conflict between an ordinary board majority and a special governance mechanism contained in the Articles, “the special provision cannot simply be ignored,” referring to Noel’s veto powers.
Tata Sons board directors nominated by Tata Trusts — Noel being one of them — can veto some key decisions due to these special powers.

Yet on Thursday, the Tata Sons board approved extending Chairman Natarajan Chandrasekaran’s tenure by another five years — through a 4-1 majority vote. Noel cast the lone dissenting vote. Chandrasekaran had said last month he would step down in February 2027, following months of friction with Noel.

Shortly after Thursday’s meeting, Noel called the decision to reappoint Chandra, as he’s widely known, as “illegal.” In a separate statement, the Trusts said they had not agreed to a listing and that the company’s board had to explore all available options.
Shareholder approval at Tata Sons’ annual general meeting is seen as the next significant step, according to K. C. Jacob, partner at Economic Laws Practice.

“Shareholders hold sovereign power in a company,” said Ramesh Kalpathy Vaidyanathan, co-managing partner at BTG Advaya. “They can, in principle, overturn resolutions passed by the board of directors if due process is found to have been violated.”

While Tata Sons was unable to hold an AGM last month due to quorum issues stemming from regulatory restrictions on Sir Ratan Tata Trust, one of its two main charities that make up Tata Trusts, the NCLT can be petitioned to hold a shareholder meeting bypassing the hurdles.
Tata Sons’ Articles confer affirmative voting rights on nominee directors appointed by Tata Trusts, according to V.K. Unni, a professor at the Indian Institute of Management Calcutta.
All major board decisions — including the appointment, re-appointment, or removal of the chairman — cannot be passed by a simple majority of the directors, he said.

“They require the affirmative vote of the nominee directors representing Tata Trusts,” Unni said, pointing to how the Supreme Court had upheld these clauses in the Tata-Cyrus Mistry case in 2021, referring to the legal outcome of another boardroom war that had engulfed the conglomerate a decade.

items.title: Yahoo Finance and Polymarket End Prediction Market Partnership
body: Yahoo Finance has ended a partnership with Polymarket in which the financial news platform used Polymarket data to create a prediction market hub on its website.

The companies joined forces last November, with Polymarket saying in a social media post at the time that it had become Yahoo Finance’s exclusive prediction market partner. The agreement included a hub to display probability data for “key economic, government, & market outcomes.”
The hub was taken down in April, and the overall agreement has concluded.

“We had a previous partnership with Polymarket to display relevant prediction market data across Yahoo Finance,” a Yahoo spokesperson said in a statement. “That specific agreement ended, but Polymarket continues to be an advertising partner across Yahoo and we’re open to similar types of partnerships.”
Polymarket declined to comment.
Yahoo was one of several media companies that has cut deals with prediction markets to use the forecasts on the platforms in news broadcasts, websites and print publications.

Polymarket struck a partnership in January to feed its prediction data to News Corp.’s Dow Jones, the parent of the Wall Street Journal and other publications. Kalshi, a Polymarket rival, has announced deals with Warner Bros. Discovery Inc.’s CNN, Versant Media Group’s CNBC and Fox Corp. (Bloomberg LP, the parent of Bloomberg News, has no such partnership, but it does provide Polymarket and Kalshi data to clients as part of its broader data offering.)

Consumers can use prediction markets to place wagers on sports, election outcomes and financial markets, as well as other events. The odds on the platform reflect the balance of trading on the platform.

While both Kalshi and Polymarket have argued that prediction markets can help enhance journalism, critics have questioned whether their data accurately captures public sentiment. Cash-strapped media organizations have been criticized for looking to these partnerships as a way to drum up new revenue streams.

The platforms are also embroiled in several other controversies, with many state regulators arguing in court that they violate local gambling laws, and prosecutors pointing to several alleged cases of insider trading. The companies have said that they monitor for illegal trading and should be governed as derivatives exchanges by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

Polymarket and Kalshi have struck numerous other partnerships with major sports teams and entertainment companies, as well as several of the top sports leagues. Just this week, LeBron James announced an endorsement deal with Polymarket that will pay him $15 million a year, according to Front Office Sports. Polymarket also entered into an exclusive partnership with the Golden Globe Awards that allowed probabilities of who would win a particular category to be displayed during the broadcast of the 2026 ceremony.
Read More: NFL Confronts Prediction-Market Bets Embraced by Other Leagues

items.title: BlackRock Set to Win $80 Billion Dutch Pension Fund Mandate
body: BlackRock Inc. has emerged as the preferred manager for a portfolio of Dutch pension assets worth just under €70 billion ($80 billion).

BpfBouw, an Amsterdam-based pensions manager representing Dutch builders, carpenters and other members of the construction industry, said BlackRock was chosen due to its international footprint, execution capacity and “alignment in the field of socially responsible investing.”

A spokesperson for BpfBouw declined to provide further details. In its statement, the pension fund said it was still negotiating the terms of the agreement with BlackRock, and would provide updates in due course.

A spokesperson for BlackRock said the firm feels “privileged by BpfBouw’s decision to choose BlackRock as their preferred candidate and look forward to helping their participants, nearly 750,000 construction workers in the Netherlands, continue building towards a dignified retirement.”

BpfBouw has been looking for an external manager since APG, which handles the investments of ABP, announced in early 2025 that it would stop managing assets for other pension funds. ABP is Europe’s largest pension fund, with about $650 billion under management.

In its statement, BpfBouw said the alignment with BlackRock in the area of socially responsible investing was “partly due to the available ESG data, analytical capacity, and support in the further development of its own policy on socially responsible investing.”

For BlackRock, the announcement from BpfBouw follows a period of some turbulence in the Netherlands. In December last year, Dutch pension fund PME said it had severed ties with BlackRock, based on an assessment that the world’s largest money manager was no longer acting in its best interests on issues such as climate risk. That followed a similar decision by Dutch pension fund PFZW, which cited broader portfolio changes for its move.

BlackRock has described itself as a “global leader” in sustainable and transition investing, and says it offers climate-focused clients in Europe products that deliver performance in line with their preferences.
