items.title: The $40 Million Journey Behind 'The Blood of Dawnwalker'
body: Hi everyone. Today we’re talking to the people behind The Blood of Dawnwalker, but first...
This week’s top gaming news:
In the fall of 2021, shortly after leaving CD Projekt SA, the video-game designer Konrad Tomaszkiewicz began talking to the writer Jakub Szamalek about creating something new.

The pair had worked together on the acclaimed roleplaying game The Witcher 3 and the less-acclaimed Cyberpunk 2077. Tomaszkiewicz, who resigned from CD Projekt after bullying accusations from staff, wanted to make games on a small team where he knew everybody’s name and didn’t have to communicate through layers of producers.

They started off by brainstorming the identity of their main character, Tomaszkiewicz told me in a recent interview. They wanted to make the protagonist a vampire, but then they worried that he might be too overpowered.

So Tomaszkiewicz made a proposal: What if he was also kind of a werewolf — human by day, vampire by night, with different gameplay styles for each mode? “We said it’s crazy, but let’s try it,” said Tomaszkiewicz. “It’s like doing the game twice.”

From there they discussed how to address players who might prefer one style over the other, and they eventually arrived at what would become the key conceit of their debut roleplaying game, The Blood of Dawnwalker: a system in which time is a resource. The half-vampire hero, Coen, has 30 days and 30 nights to save his family, and every quest in the game knocks hours off the clock.
In other words, players can’t do everything the game has to offer. They have to be judicious when choosing side quests and activities.

Tomaszkiewicz suspected this system might prove controversial for some players, but it also solved several problems. It would give players the option of spending most of their time as a human and skipping through the vampire bits or vice versa. It would help build tension and eliminate a classic video-game dilemma: The world is ending, but somehow you have as much time as you want to go help villagers farm their crops.
Along the way, they experimented with various aspects of the game to see which should move the clock, like fast travel, but ultimately they decided to be as forgiving as possible.

“This concept of actions passing time is controversial,” said Mateusz Tomaszkiewicz, the game’s creative director and Konrad’s brother. “We knew we wanted this general feature, and the general shape of it, but which actions specifically would cost time was an open question.”

The unorthodox narrative experiment paid off. The Blood of Dawnwalker came out on Sept. 3 to mostly positive buzz and sold more than 1 million copies in its first week. Rebel Wolves, Tomaszkiewicz’s studio, says it’s “extremely” happy with the results so far.

I’ve played a big chunk of the game, and what I enjoy most about the time system is the structure it offers. It’s very easy to get burned out on big open-world games, in part, because it’s so tempting to do all of the side quests. Having a clear endpoint makes it feel more viable to see this game through.

Back in 2022, after coming up with that initial idea, Tomaszkiewicz and his small but growing team put together a pitch document and began recruiting staff for Rebel Wolves. Tomaszkiewicz funded the studio himself for the first year as they built a prototype and went out hunting for investment.

By the end of the year, they’d signed with NetEase Inc., which bought 26% of the studio and gave them a development budget of $40 million, putting it solidly into the “AA” category — much more than an indie but significantly less than the $300 million games developed by many of their peers.

Throughout 2023 they spent a great deal of time recruiting staff. “It’s not like you just say, ‘I want to work with these people’ and they just appear,” Tomaszkiewicz said. They entered production at the end of the year.

One of Tomaszkiewicz’s goals was to avoid growing Rebel Wolves too much. He told me that back in 2024, as production on Dawnwalker was kicking off, the studio had 90 employees and he wanted to cap it there. But now they’re at 160 — the result of ambitions that were difficult to keep in line.
“We sat in the production room and counted everything,” Tomaszkiewicz said. “When we started to work, the game — like always — grew.”
So they hired contractors. But then they grew to like the contractors and wanted to keep them around. So they brought them in full-time. And the team just kept expanding.

“We decided that the size of the team we have right now is the most fitting for our needs,” Tomaszkiewicz said. “It’s still letting me know everyone. I can speak with everyone every day. I still feel like a creator and not a manager, which is the place I want to be.”
Now, they say they’re putting a cap on their size for real. “We are aware of this growth, and we are tracking it,” added Mateusz. “We don’t want to overdo it.”

They signed a deal with Bandai Namco Entertainment Inc. to publish and market the game. And as they neared the finish line and Rebel Wolves began eyeing a release date for Dawnwalker, they had a tough decision to make: release in June with the risk of exhausting the team on a tight deadline, or push until September and face an extraordinarily crowded window of new games?
Ultimately they decided on September, hoping to avoid some of the rampant overtime that they faced at CD Projekt.

“This production was really weird for us,” said Tomaszkiewicz, noting that they made decisions early in development in hopes of avoiding as much overtime as possible, like building only a single demo of the game — and, most importantly, never changing the vision beyond what they had originally set out to create in 2022. Much like the main character of their game, they had limited time and couldn’t do every single thing they might have wanted.

“We decided we’d do everything to not change the foundations of the game,” he said. “And the foundations right now are the same as they were in the pitch deck. Because we knew if we changed those pillars, it’ll impact the whole game.”

Now, as they look toward creating a sequel to The Blood of Dawnwalker — ideally with more time, Tomaszkiewicz says — they look back on the process as a success. “In the end, we landed in a really good production without a lot of big problems,” he said.

I’ll be jumping into Nintendo Co.’s new Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, which looks like it blends some of the best elements of previous games in the strategy series: the combat of Fire Emblem Engage with the story of Fire Emblem: Three Houses. The game came out this week and has gotten rave reviews.

items.title: Construct Capital Hits $1 Billion in Assets as VC Interest in Industrials Soars
body: To get Industrial Strength delivered directly to your inbox, sign up here.
Pre-pandemic, most industrial companies were fighting for relevance in a tech-obsessed market. Nowadays, they’re one of the hottest investments around.

Money has poured into industrial companies both big and small and from all directions, but they’ve been particularly popular with venture capital firms. The reasons for this are varied, but it largely boils down to industrial companies no longer being considered boring or low growth.

The world has collectively woken up to the fact that extreme outsourcing was a bad idea, requiring new facilities to be built closer to home and technological overhauls to make domestic manufacturing more cost-effective. Meanwhile, data centers’ outsized demand for power, water and other resources is inspiring a hunt for creative solutions — in outer space and on land. At the same time, recent geopolitical shockwaves have underscored the unwieldiness of America’s heavily consolidated defense industry, creating an opening for challengers for the first time in decades.
And with advancements in software, artificial intelligence and automation, the solutions no longer have to be slow-moving and highly capital-intensive.
It’s a good time to be an expert in industrials, and not just because these themes have become a lot more popular at cocktail parties.

To that end, Construct Capital, an early-stage venture firm founded in 2020 that’s focused on manufacturing, supply-chain, energy and defense investments, is announcing today that it’s reached $1 billion in assets under management. Only about 25 of the roughly 2,000 venture firms launched in the same era have reached that milestone, according to Construct Capital, citing data from PitchBook and the National Venture Capital Association. The fund was co-founded by Rachel Holt, a former Uber Technologies Inc. executive who at one time oversaw the company’s North American ride-share business, and Dayna Grayson, who previously helped build the industrial software practice as a partner at New Enterprise Associates.

“We really saw that there was a hole in the venture market, in particular at the early stages for people who understood this concept of tech meets the real world,” Holt said in a recent interview. But when the fund first launched in January 2020, before the Covid-19 pandemic upended everyone’s thinking, investors would say, “‘What’s wrong with our supply chain? It seems like everything kind of works,’” she said. “We’d used to joke it was like rearranging deck chairs on the Titanic as we would change our deck and be like, ‘Does anyone care?’”
Read More: Carlyle Sees Massive Opportunity in Mid-Market Defense Sector

Turns out they do: US later-stage venture investment in companies focused on key parts of the industrial economy including robotics, drones, space technology and advanced manufacturing soared to nearly $29 billion last year — roughly 50% of all such investment, according to PitchBook data supplied by Construct Capital. That’s up from just $641 million, or about 17% of the total, in 2020.
Read More: Private Equity Dealmaking Hits Record in US Industrials

Construct Capital was an early investor in Hadrian Automation Inc., the defense manufacturing startup that secured a $7.87 billion valuation in its latest funding round completed in August. Other investments include e-commerce delivery company Veho Tech Inc.; Cowboy Space, which aims to develop orbital data centers; and Amca, which is seeking to acquire smaller aerospace and defense suppliers and improve their operations through software and other technologies and in May reached a more than $1 billion valuation.

Construct Capital recently closed its newest select fund, which focuses on later-stage rounds for companies already in its existing portfolio. Construct Capital prefers this approach over special purpose vehicles — or the pooling of investor money for one particular startup — because that structure can be overly complicated and difficult to untangle, Grayson said in an interview this week. The firm wanted to give its investors the opportunity to stick around for longer on some of its top-performing startups. But it’s not hunting for new later-stage investments and will continue to establish startup positions at the early stage where it sees better return opportunities.

With so much money now sloshing around in the industrial space and valuations soaring, Construct Capital intentionally wants to keep its core funds relatively small and focused — a contrast to bigger firms that are increasingly throwing around larger and larger checks on a broader swatch of companies in the hopes that at least one will hit it big.

“People are investing at valuations that used to be like series A and B valuations, but they’re seed-stage companies,” Holt said. Grayson added that although she used to vow not to walk away from investments based on price alone, that has changed in the last year.
Read More: Zipline in Talks on About $1 Billion Raise at $20 Billion Value

The flood of new competition in industrial venture funding increases the risk that firms end up simply chasing trends, and Construct Capital doesn’t want to fall into that trap. For example, “now is not the time” to invest in another new company trying to disrupt the large defense manufacturing incumbents, with investments increasingly consolidating around a group of key startups, Holt said.

The 10 largest venture funding rounds in defense tech accounted for 62% of total second-quarter deal value, PitchBook said. Meanwhile in the public markets, the iShares US Aerospace & Defense ETF is on pace for two back-to-back quarters of net outflows for the first time since 2023 amid concerns that Democrats will seek to rein in funding if they win one or both chambers of Congress in the upcoming midterms, as Arvelisse Bonilla Ramos of Bloomberg News reported this week. The slump in defense stocks has European tankmaker KNDS NV and its owners considering pushing back its initial public offering, Bloomberg News reported this week, citing people familiar with the matter.

Construct Capital is instead focused on companies that have ideas on how to use AI to overcome the hurdles that have prevented industrial robots from becoming as prevalent on US factory floors as they are in other high-tech manufacturing strongholds. In energy, it’s looking at companies trying to develop new approaches to building grid infrastructure and power supplies. Construct Capital in June invested in a Series A round for Endurance Energy, which is focused on subsea geothermal power generation.
“It’s incumbent on us to keep finding the new areas within these spaces that maybe others aren’t deeply picking over,” Holt said.

“We talk about $6 diesel, but out here it’s $8 diesel if you noticed on the way in, which is like science fiction... What does that mean for the economy over time?” — Ed Elkins, executive vice president and chief commercial officer at Norfolk Southern Corp.

Elkins made the comments this week at Morgan Stanley’s Annual Laguna Conference. Average US diesel prices soared past $6 a gallon for the first time ever this month as war-driven disruptions in Russia and the Middle East curb supplies. In California, where the Morgan Stanley conference was being held, prices topped $8.

Diesel is the lifeblood of the industrial economy, powering agricultural equipment, trucking networks and generators. Although industrial investors fretted over the threat posed by higher fuel costs in the wake of the US’ initial attack on Iran, prices then pulled back as Gulf nations found other lanes to export fuel and China slowed purchases from international suppliers. But China has reversed course, stepping up imports, while a spate of recent drone attacks forced Saudi Arabia to temporarily shutter the East-West pipeline it had been increasingly relying on to circumvent the Strait of Hormuz.

“I wish I could tell you that I saw some reason why things would ease, but it’s difficult right now to see that happen,” Chevron Corp. Chief Executive Officer Mike Wirth told an industry conference last week, the Wall Street Journal reported.
Read More: Midterm Battlegrounds Hit by Diesel, Heating Oil Price Spikes

The higher prices are helping drive shipping traffic off of the roads and onto the railroads, which are more fuel-efficient because they can carry significantly more goods in a single trip, Elkins said. But ultimately this fresh round of energy inflation is going to be a drag on the consumer, he said, as companies look to pass on higher costs and bills rise at the pump. Gasoline prices were already averaging more than $4.40 a barrel across the US on Thursday, according to the American Automobile Association.
Read More: Goldman Says Go for Gasoline as Global Fuel Crunch Morphs

“Gas prices are up, interest rates are up, the consumer remains cautious,” 3M Co. CEO Bill Brown said at the Morgan Stanley conference. “And because of that, some of the retailers are also expressing caution. They’re waiting to place orders to replenish their shelves.”

As of now, CEOs say they see no sign of industrial demand pulling back. With the AI buildout driving so much of the growth in the manufacturing sector, it’s an open question as to whether that momentum can be sustained in the face of a more substantial consumer pullback. Historically speaking, however, where the consumer goes, so goes the rest of the economy.

Generac Holdings Inc. this week agreed to issue Amazon.com Inc. a warrant to acquire as much as 1.69 million shares of the company as part of an agreement to provide up to $8 billion of backup generators for the technology giant’s data centers. A portion of the warrant vested immediately and the remainder is contingent on payments for the generators. Around $2.4 billion of initial deliveries are expected next year and in 2028. The deal helps firm up the longer-term supply outlook for Generac’s data center business, sending the stock up 18% on the announcement. It also underscores the growing interconnectedness of the data center ecosystem as companies seek to lock up key supplies. Oracle Corp. received a similar warrant to purchase shares in Bloom Energy Corp. as part of an agreement for the fuel cell company to provide it with as much as 2.8 gigawatts of power.

items.title: LNG Tanker With US Cargo Reported to Be Victim of Cyberattack
body: A liquefied natural gas tanker bringing fuel from the US to Europe suffered a systems failure that the crew reported as a suspected cyber attack, according to people familiar with the matter.

In the latest of a number of potential cybersecurity incidents on tankers, the Vivit Africa LNG was sailing east in the Mediterranean and Adriatic Seas toward Italy early this month when the crew were suddenly unable to access some of the internal control systems, the people said, asking not be identified because the information was not public.
Trading giant Vitol Group confirmed that it has the ship under a long-term lease known as a time charter, without commenting further.

After idling off the coast of Italy without discharging its cargo, the vessel on Wednesday began sailing away from its intended destination of Rovigo, heading back toward the Spanish port of Algeciras near the entrance to the Mediterranean, according to shipping data compiled by Bloomberg.

The crew reported the incident early last week to Korean Register, the organization that acts as the technical and safety adviser to the South Korean-owned vessel, and investigations are ongoing, the people said. There are no indications of who the perpetrator of the suspected attack may be, they said.
Korean Register and the owner of the Vivit Africa LNG, South Korea’s H-Line Shipping Co. Ltd., didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

The suspected hacking of the Vivit Africa LNG follows other incidents in late August, when two oil and gas tankers off the US coast were boarded by the Coast Guard and Federal Bureau of Investigation due to potential cyberattacks. American officials are monitoring nearly 20 ships around the world for such threats.

The tanker was carrying a cargo loaded at Louisiana’s Cameron LNG terminal, ship-tracking data show. It had sailed across the Atlantic and was nearing its destination in early September, when the crew encountered the technical issues that stalled their voyage.

The Italian Coast Guard assisted the vessel “after the master reported a malfunction in the systems used to monitor cargo parameters, requiring intervention by the company’s technicians,” Captain Roberto D’Arrigo said in an emailed statement. The cause of the problem couldn’t be identified and “the Chioggia Coast Guard intervened solely for navigation safety purposes, issuing an urgent notice to mariners to keep their distance.”

The Vivit Africa LNG used some equipment from Kongsberg Maritime, which provides positioning, navigation and propulsion technology for ships. The company is aware of reports of the incident but “it is too early to draw conclusions regarding the cause or any potential security implications,” said spokesman Jon Berge.

items.title: Mbappé cambia Nike por On para convertir la marca suiza en líder en fútbol
body: On Holding AG incorporó al astro francés Kylian Mbappé como socio para desarrollar productos de fútbol y representar a la marca, desafiando el dominio de Nike Inc. y Adidas AG en este deporte.

La compañía suiza equipará a Mbappé, el delantero de 27 años que ya es el máximo goleador histórico de los Mundiales, con nuevos botines mientras amplía el uso de su tecnología de fabricación de calzado Lightspray, según un comunicado. Mbappé, figura central del poderoso Real Madrid, representaba anteriormente a Nike Inc.
Suscríbase       aquí     al boletín Morning Briefing Español y conozca nuestro canal de       WhatsApp

Las acciones de On se dispararon hasta un 7,4% tras la noticia en las operaciones previas a la apertura del mercado estadounidense. Nike cayó un 0,6%, mientras Adidas registró un descenso similar en Fráncfort.

On también contrató a Thierry Henry, exestrella de la selección francesa y del Arsenal de la Premier League inglesa, como director de la división de fútbol. No se divulgaron los detalles financieros de los acuerdos.

La compañía respaldada por Roger Federer ha crecido rápidamente desde su fundación en 2010, comenzando con zapatillas para correr y expandiéndose al tenis, el entrenamiento y los deportes al aire libre. También busca aumentar los ingresos procedentes de la indumentaria, tanto deportiva como de estilo de vida. On tiene previsto celebrar el martes un día del inversionista, en el que se espera que presente sus objetivos financieros para los próximos años.

Aunque el fútbol ha sido durante mucho tiempo el deporte más popular del mundo, en los últimos años ha cobrado aún más importancia como fuente de productos de moda y estilo de vida para competidores como Adidas y Nike, además de Puma SE. Las marcas registraron un fuerte aumento de las ventas este verano gracias a las camisetas de los equipos que patrocinaron en el Mundial.

El fútbol ha sufrido menos disrupción por parte de las denominadas marcas desafiantes en los últimos años que el running, donde empresas emergentes como On y Hoka han ganado participación de mercado con propuestas innovadoras de calzado. New Balance y Skechers han logrado algunos avances en el fútbol, y esta última patrocina a la estrella inglesa Harry Kane, que también juega en el FC Bayern Munich.
On busca “repensar los productos para las exigencias del juego y, al mismo tiempo, aportar una nueva energía a la cultura que lo rodea”, señaló la empresa en el comunicado.

Mbappé trabajará estrechamente con el personal de On en el desarrollo y las pruebas de botines e indumentaria de fútbol, además de representar a la marca fuera de la cancha, indicó la compañía. Además de ser uno de los mayores talentos del fútbol, Mbappé también ha ganado seguidores por su estilo, apareciendo en campañas de Dior.
“Lo que me atrajo de On fue la oportunidad de construir juntos algo completamente nuevo que ayude a dar forma al fútbol del futuro”, señaló Mbappé en el comunicado.

On considera que su tecnología LightSpray —mediante la cual robots pulverizan en cuestión de minutos la parte superior de un calzado a partir de un filamento— le dará una ventaja en el fútbol. El objetivo es crear productos “excepcionalmente livianos, precisos y ajustados al atleta como una segunda piel”, señaló la compañía.

On presentó la tecnología en 2024 y ha ampliado su uso desde zapatillas de alta gama para maratón hasta productos dirigidos a un mercado más amplio. A comienzos de este año inauguró en Corea del Sur una fábrica dedicada a LightSpray y prevé abrir pronto otra planta en Vietnam, con posibles instalaciones futuras en Estados Unidos y Europa, señaló Caspar Coppetti, codirector ejecutivo, en una entrevista en junio.

La incursión inicial de On en el fútbol se produjo en diciembre, cuando fichó a la joven estrella suiza Sydney Schertenleib, que juega en el equipo femenino del FC Barcelona, para colaborar en productos orientados al entrenamiento y el estilo de vida. Ahora también representará a la marca en el fútbol y ayudará a desarrollar productos diseñados para el fútbol femenino, según el comunicado.Nota Original: Mbappé Signs Up for On’s Push Into Football in Blow to Nike (1)

items.title: Boston, Seattle Pitch Reforms to Keep Nightlife Going After the World Cup
body: On June 19, revelers were packed shoulder to shoulder on Temple Place, a short street near the head of Boston’s Freedom Trail. With their backs to the green lawn of the Boston Common, some had their gazes fixed on a large screen playing one of the debut World Cup matches. Others were conversing with friends, beer sloshing in their plastic cups.

“Everyone was just elated by how the energy felt,” said Babak Bina, the owner of JM Curley, a bar and restaurant on Temple Place. Bina said he hadn’t seen the downtown district so vibrant in the 15 years since his restaurant opened. The data backed up the vibe: That day, JM Curley broke its single-day sales record, and Temple Place saw the most pedestrian traffic on record.

That banner day was boosted by several temporary policy changes Massachusetts enacted during the World Cup: Open alcohol containers were permitted outside, the street was closed to cars, and bars and restaurants were able to stay open later. Now, some Massachusetts lawmakers want to make such policies permanent, in a bid to improve nightlife and retain young professional residents.

America is in the midst of a “fun shortage,” with people going out less and going home early, delivering a particularly hard blow to nightlife. The US has lost 7,000 bars and nightclubs since 2006, and downtown streets in many cities haven’t fully recovered from the pandemic slump. But this summer offered a glimpse of what might be possible and showcased host cities’ potential vibrancy.

A number of states piloted looser nightlife and alcohol policies during the tournament: Many allowed bars and restaurants to stay open later, and a few authorized public drinking zones, relaxing “open container” restrictions.

“There are seldom opportunities to conduct these kinds of experiments,” said Michael Fichman, an associate professor at the University of Pennsylvania’s Weitzman School of Design who specializes in nighttime policy. “The moment was not lost on people that you could try different things and see whether or not the arguments on the pro or con side really would bear out.”

Boston has been notorious for its strict restrictions on alcohol consumption, including being in one of the few states in the US to ban happy hour discounts on drinks. This summer, the state extended its last call from 2 a.m. to 3 a.m. and also enacted social districts with public drinking zones for the duration of the tournament.
Read more: Tartan Army’s Boston Invasion Revives Push to Change State’s Strict Booze Rules

The pilot program was a “shot in the arm” to the Boston restaurant community, which is already dealing with small margins and rising costs, said Michael Nichols, president of the Downtown Boston Alliance. Early data revealed that bar spending during first two weeks of the tournament was up 28% compared to last year. Bar tabs were even higher around the two social districts, up 166% by City Hall and about 86% in the greater downtown area.

Other cities seized the World Cup's opportunity to pilot social initiatives. Washington state relaxed some of its outdoor drinking restrictions this summer and decided to keep the pilot running for more than a year the tournament ends, through December 2027, to see how the policy fares in other scenarios.

In June, Pike Place Market in Seattle launched a “Sip and Savor” program, which allowed guests to purchase alcoholic beverages and walk around the market on the weekends during the summer months. The pilot was designed to encourage people to explore the different areas of the market and lengthen the average stay for a visitor, according to the market’s Chief Executive Officer Rachel Ligtenberg. Pike Place’s June  18 night market saw more than 25,000 visitors between 5 p.m. and 10 p.m., a record crowd, Ligtenberg said.

Washington state has a lot of old rules about liquor which can be difficult to navigate as an event planner, said Gretchen Lenihan, who manages events and contract booking at the Seattle Center, a large government-run event space by the Space Needle. Over Labor Day Weekend, the city organization explored how relaxed liquor laws would work without a World Cup, during the Bumbershoot music festival, with attendees able to carry their drinks throughout the festival grounds rather than having to discard them.

These successes have led some policymakers to push for more permanent changes. The Massachusetts state senate has passed new “fun agenda” measures that would allow towns and cities to offer discounted drinks during happy hour and create public drinking districts. The bill is now waiting for approval from a joint committee and the governor.

The Massachusetts Restaurant Association opposes lifting the state’s ban on happy hours, but is supportive of extending last call and enacting social drinking zones if those programs can be coordinated with public safety officials, said President Stephen Clark. The Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association  opposes a later last call, citing concerns about public safety. The organization didn’t respond to a request for comment.

In Washington, an ongoing pilot program recognizes that not all days will be like the World Cup summer. That law relaxes liquor restrictions until December 2027, which state representative Julia Reed says will give lawmakers plenty of time to see if they want to make a permanent change – something advocates are already calling for. It also gives hospitality businesses more time to see the economic benefits, especially because many businesses had to invest upfront costs for things like security and special license approval. “We thought people would be more likely to use it if they could use it for more than one event,” Reed said.
Read more: Can Cities Save the ‘Streatery’?

Boston lawmakers are particularly focused on retaining young professionals after they graduate from one of the city’s many higher education institutions. “We want to make sure that we are keeping our young people here by merging the great industries we have” with “a level of responsible fun,” said Boston city council member Brian Worrell.

State senator Julian Cyr, whose district includes Cape Cod and Nantucket, has spearheaded multiple efforts over his tenure to relax Massachusetts’ liquor laws. This new generation of young adults spent their most formative years during the Covid-19 lockdown, and might have missed out on some seminal coming of age experiences, Cyr said. “I think we really owe it to these kids to provide opportunity for experiences and fun and joy.”

Fichman, the professor, said a big draw of extending last call is promoting social vibrancy. “We saw during Covid that one of the things that makes it great to live in a city is that there are social and experiential opportunities that you have to spend time with other people,” he said. The creative industry — which includes DJs, live musicians, comedians and other performers — could also benefit economically by selling tickets and drinks for late-night performances.

On public health, the evidence is mixed. On the one hand, extending alcohol service hours can help relieve crowding by staggering the times people travel home and reduce pressure to drink quickly before alcohol sales stop, mitigating binge-drinking, Fichman said. But longer hours can also mean people drink more. One recent study found that reducing the hours of alcohol sales in Baltimore, Maryland, was associated with a 14% immediate decrease in violent crime. Another consideration is the availability of safe public transportation options for both patrons and employees as they get home after closing.

Other cities have opted to keep their World Cup policies temporary. “Kansas City's extended hours during the World Cup were a targeted measure built for a unique moment, and by and large they operated as intended,” Mayor Quinton Lucas said in a statement, noting that any conversation about making those laws permanent would be after hearing feedback from the community.

Nichols, of the Downtown Boston Alliance, doesn’t expect the scale of impact going forward to be the same as this summer even if the state enacts reforms. But he’s ready to see what’s possible. “The World Cup showed us why the change made sense, but the World Cup's not the point.”

items.title: What John Rogers' Success Shows about America's Black Wealth Gap
body: Many Americans worry about the wealth gap between Black and White America. Less noticed is a divide that has grown even faster: the one within Black America. The top 10% of Black earners now make almost 10 times what the bottom 10% make, a wider gap than among Whites or Hispanics. That statistic is the starting point for understanding the paradox of  John Rogers, one of the wealthiest Black money managers on Wall Street.

In the fall of 1983, the 25-year-old Princeton graduate walked into his boss’s office at William Blair, one of Chicago’s most prestigious investment firms, and announced he was leaving to start his own company. The stock market was beginning what would become one of the great bull runs in American history. Chicago had just elected its first Black mayor,  Harold Washington, who had pledged to spread the city’s wealth and power more broadly among Black residents and entrepreneurs. “It’s our turn,” Washington declared.
Rogers’s White boss told him to wait. “Why don’t you make a few more mistakes on our nickel,” he said.
“No,” Rogers answered. “I think now is the time.”

He was right. Within a decade, Rogers had built  Ariel Investments into the country’s first major Black-owned mutual fund company, with nearly $1 billion under management. Today Ariel manages more than $14 billion, and Rogers serves on the boards of Nike, the New York Times and the Obama Foundation — the latter reflecting a 35-year friendship with the former president that began in Chicago in the 1980s.

Yet the higher Rogers has risen, the more disillusioned he has become. Even Black graduates of Ivy League schools and elite business and law programs aren’t doing as well as their White peers, he believes. “I really did think there would be more opportunities,” he says. “You know, hospitals, universities, museums, foundations would want to work with Black money managers. And it ended up being a false hope — very rare that those doors were open and stayed open permanently. Corporations talk about good games. But most of the time it’s just talk.”

When I first met Rogers in the 1980s, he had voted twice for Reagan and once for Bush. He believed Republican free-market policies and efforts to reduce government regulation were good for the economy. Today he is a staunch Democrat and a major fundraiser for Democratic candidates. Yet he also finds himself at odds with a younger generation of Black voters, many of whom he says are too invested in identity politics and attracted to left-wing figures like  Zohran Mamdani. Rogers remains a centrist. “I am a capitalist,” he says, “a middle-of-the-road capitalist.”

Rogers embodies the conflicted legacy of one of America’s most misunderstood decades, the 1980s. As I’ve gone back to explore how that decade reshaped the country, I’ve found a reality more complex than the standard narrative — and one that still shapes debates over race, class and economic opportunity.

The Reagan years are traditionally viewed as a disaster for Black Americans, marked by deep cuts to social programs and a conservative backlash against Black advancement. There was a 49% increase in the number of Black Americans living in poverty during the decade, and episodes of shocking racial violence punctuated the news.

But the big picture was more complicated. Affirmative action across education, employment and investment helped expand the Black middle class. Even as poverty increased, the number of Black families earning $50,000 or more — about $120,000 in today’s money — doubled. By the end of the decade, the average income of a college-educated, married Black couple reached 93% of that of a comparable White couple. White Americans were also more likely than ever to encounter Black Americans at work, in restaurants, in college, at stores and on television.

Popular culture reflected that shift. The Cosby Show put an affluent Black family at the center of the country’s most popular television program. In 1982, Bryant Gumbel became co-host of Today and Michael Jackson released Thriller. The following year, Vanessa Williams became the first Black woman crowned Miss America. Oprah Winfrey arrived in Chicago in 1984 and took her talk show national in 1986.

This marked a dramatic shift from the Civil Rights Movement of the 1960s, with its marches and soaring rhetoric. The 1980s produced a generation of Black entrepreneurs and professionals who believed capitalism, wielded correctly, could help close the racial wealth gap. The hope was that a prosperous Black professional class would create opportunities that ultimately lifted poor and working-class Black Americans as well.

That strategy gained momentum from a wave of newly elected Black mayors — including Harold Washington in Chicago, Maynard Jackson in Atlanta, Tom Bradley in Los Angeles and Coleman Young in Detroit — who used their political muscle to steer municipal pension money and lucrative city contracts toward minority entrepreneurs. In Atlanta, for instance, Jackson insisted that 25% of contracts for the new airport go to minority- or women-owned firms.

Few people embodied that shift more clearly than Rogers. The son of a well-connected Chicago family, he launched Ariel Investments in 1983 with seed money from successful Black businessmen who were family friends, along with investments from municipal pension funds and White-led university endowments seeking to diversify.

Yet even as some Black Americans moved up, many poorer Black Americans fell further behind. As critics warned at the time, affirmative action often benefited people who were already middle class or well positioned for college. Rogers himself grew up in Chicago’s close-knit Black elite. His grandfather, J. B. Stradford, owned a 54-room hotel — then the largest Black-owned hotel in the country — along with a savings and loan firm and other real estate in Tulsa, Oklahoma, part of a thriving community known as Black Wall Street.

During the Tulsa race massacre of 1921, a White mob looted and burned much of that community. Stradford fled north and eventually settled in Chicago. Rogers’s mother, Jewel Lafontant, became the first Black woman to graduate from the University of Chicago Law School, where she met her husband. She later served in senior positions in Republican administrations. His father, a Democrat, became a prominent Chicago lawyer and judge.

Meanwhile, deindustrialization — the loss of manufacturing jobs across the country — hit less-educated Black workers especially hard in cities. Concentrated poverty and mass incarceration created further barriers to employment and wealth-building. And as Black politicians, including Barack Obama, rose to higher office, they also had to appeal to broader constituencies rather than Black voters alone. At the same time, the technology, finance and private equity firms generating enormous new fortunes had few Black investors and employed few Black executives.

Many Black Americans, Democrats and liberals remain invested in the affirmative-action and diversity, equity and inclusion strategies that took shape in the 1980s. But those approaches face a much more hostile legal environment today, with a conservative Supreme Court   sharply limiting race-conscious policies. One response is to shift more attention toward class — targeting first-generation college students and low-income Americans across racial groups — in ways that may preserve some of the goals of those programs while surviving legal scrutiny.
Read more:   ‘They’ve Stolen the Narrative’: Black Business Leaders on the DEI Backlash

There is another legacy of the 1980s to build on: private Black wealth. The decade helped created a larger Black middle and upper class, and the fortunes accumulated since then by athletes, entertainers, executives and entrepreneurs dwarf what existed at the time. High-net-worth Black individuals, working with banks and Wall Street firms, can pool capital into investment syndicates and private equity funds, gaining ownership stakes and seats at the table. That leverage can then be used to direct university endowments, foundations and corporate treasuries toward high-performing minority asset managers, Black-owned law firms, technology firms and marketing companies in ways designed to withstand legal challenge.

items.title: Switzerland Criticizes Russia's Nestle Grab, Seeks Reversal
body: Switzerland said Vladimir Putin’s seizure of Russian assets belonging to Nestle SA is a worrying development and it’s working with the company to get the actions reversed.
The Russian president on Thursday ordered stakes in businesses of Nestle and French supermarket chain Auchan to be placed under temporary administration by a local company.

The Kremlin linked the actions to European military support for Ukraine. For Switzerland, it comes at a particularly sensitive time. The country is less than two weeks away from a national vote on its neutrality, where the result could affect Swiss sanctions on Russia.

Switzerland’s State Secretariat for Economic Affairs, speaking on behalf of the government, said in a statement that it’s “worried” about the seizure of Nestle’s assets. It’s working with Nestle “toward the reversal of the compulsory administration,” it said.
Eric Nussbaumer, a former senior lawmaker of the Social Democrats, called Russia’s move “unjustified.”
“Apparently there’s resentment against Switzerland in high places in Russia,” he said. “I advise extreme caution when dealing with this regime.”

Nussbaumer, who was a foreign policy expert in Switzerland’s parliament for almost 20 years before he retired in April, doesn’t think that Moscow is trying to sway Switzerland’s neutrality vote later this month. Polls indicate that the proposal is likely to fail.

But the timing of the move will add to tensions between Switzerland and Russia. The Swiss initiative proposes imposing stricter rules on how the country applies its longstanding policy of neutrality. It would remove the current flexibility that enabled the government to mirror European Union sanctions on Russia in 2022 after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The Kremlin recently weighed in on the vote, trying to sway voters by saying Switzerland abandoned neutrality with the sanctions move. Switzerland is on a list of countries that Russia deems “unfriendly.”
Read more: Swiss Vote on Neutrality Revives Debate Over National Identity
Swiss neutrality was enshrined at the Treaty of Paris in 1815, and has been a core element of the country’s foreign policy since the founding of the modern Swiss Confederation in 1848.

While neutrality is a strongly held tradition, the Swiss have adapted it as times have changed, including after the end of the Cold War. A government website on the history of neutrality says that the upheaval from the fall of the Berlin Wall and the collapse of the Soviet Union “fundamentally changed Switzerland’s foreign and security policy environment.”
“It is evident that neutrality has never been a rigid institution,” Switzerland said in a white paper in 1993 on neutrality.

The seizure of the Nestle and Auchan units is the largest takeover of foreign corporate assets in Russia since at least 2024. It comes amid deep tensions with Europe, which has been hit with multiple so-called hybrid attacks that have been blamed on Moscow. Among the incidents have been multiple drone attacks, including an attempted one at Leipzig airport in Germany.

Nestle said in a statement Friday that it took note of Putin’s decree and was assessing the situation and its options. “Nestle is committed to taking all necessary steps to protect its rights and ensure continuity of business operations in the interests of all stakeholders, particularly its employees,” it said.

items.title: Options Triple Witching Sees $7 Trillion Expiring on Friday
body: Around $7 trillion of US options notional value rolls off the books Friday, accounting for around a quarter of the market, according to data from Citadel Securities.
The so-called ‘triple witching,’ where monthly S&P 500 Index options and single stock options all expire at the same time, is set to be the second-largest on record, according to the market maker.
The expiry, 60% of which takes place at the open, creates a “potential reset in the market’s technical backdrop,” wrote Citadel Securities’ market intelligence team, led by Scott Rubner.
“As these positions expire or roll forward, the positioning that has helped dampen realized moves can change materially, potentially leaving the market more sensitive to underlying flows afterward.”

items.title: Screwworm Reappears in New Mexico Ahead of Port Reopening
body: The New World screwworm resurfaced in New Mexico just as a major gateway for Mexican cattle imports is poised to open in the state.

The parasite, which infests the wounds of livestock, was confirmed Thursday in a horse in New Mexico’s Grant County, according to the US Department of Agriculture. Earlier that same day, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins had announced plans to reopen the country’s largest port for Mexican cattle — situated roughly 150 miles from the new case.
Read More: US to Reopen Largest Port for Mexican Cattle Shipments

The decision to open the port in Santa Teresa is part of the US’s effort to amp up a trade that had been paused to prevent the spread of the screwworm, and comes as cases of the deadly parasite have been largely contained since the outbreak began in early June. There have been 50 cases of the screwworm in the US, almost all in Texas, with only three currently active. Nearly 2,000 cases remain active in Mexico.

Rollins acknowledged that screwworm has not yet been eradicated, but was confident in the protocols that the USDA has put in place. She said Thursday at a press conference announcing the port reopening that the agency will delay the move if “we’re not 100% sure in the safety and the protocols.”

But that’s unlikely to happen based on the new case, the Santa Fe New Mexican reported, citing state veterinarian Samantha Holeck. She said the source of the infestation is still under investigation, as the horse hadn’t moved from the region recently.

The Santa Teresa port is scheduled to open on Sept. 24. It is the second port-of-entry in the US to accept Mexican live cattle. Nearly 500,000 cattle were shipped through Santa Teresa in 2024, amounting to about 40% of the US’s total imports from Mexico, according to the USDA.
Rollins also said the agency is also looking at reopening a port in Columbus, New Mexico, assuming “that we can continue to show that we have contained” the pest.

The case is the second in New Mexico, the only state outside of Texas where the screwworm has been found. A dog in Lea County was among the first confirmed cases in June. The pet recovered, but questions remained at the time as to whether it had contracted the parasite locally or in Mexico.

items.title: Weil Gotshal Eyes Merger Options as Rainmakers Exit Law Firm
body: Weil Gotshal & Manges, which has been hit by an exodus of top talent in recent weeks, is considering options for its future including a potential merger with a competitor, people with knowledge of the matter said.

Top leaders at the US law firm have become more open to the idea of a combination with a rival, and some have held informal discussions to gauge interest in a deal, according to the people. The moves come as Weil evaluates ways to rebuild its business after a slate of departures including Michael Aiello, chair of the firm’s corporate department and one of its most powerful partners.

Weil has been canvassing its partners in recent days as it seeks to stem the tide of defections, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private. It has also been studying other ways to shore up its business through strategic hires and promotions, and it could still remain independent, the people said.
“Weil is not engaged in merger discussions with any firm,” a spokesperson said in an emailed statement. “Like every leading firm, we continually evaluate opportunities to strengthen our platform.“

Cravath Swaine & Moore is bringing on Aiello along with five other top Weil partners, including Matthew Gilroy, co-head of the firm’s mergers and acquisitions practice. Sullivan & Cromwell then said Thursday it’s hiring David Avery-Gee, Weil’s co-managing partner in London, and Sarah Flaherty, a partner in Weil’s corporate group in the UK capital.

Weil, which was founded in New York in 1931, has long been one of the US’s premier law firms. It is especially renowned for its bankruptcy practice; it acted as lead debtors counsel to Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc after its financial crisis collapse and also represented Enron Corporation in its Chapter 11 bankruptcy.

The firm has also had a track record as an M&A powerhouse, with recent deals including representing Fox Corp. on its $22 billion acquisition of Roku Inc and acting for Orange on its joint bid for €20 billion-valued French telecommunications operator SFR from Altice France.

items.title: US Factory Output Unexpectedly Fell for First Time This Year
body: US factory output unexpectedly declined for the first time this year as production of business equipment cooled and manufacturers grappled with higher input costs.
Production at manufacturers fell 0.3% in August, according to Federal Reserve data out Friday. The median forecast in a Bloomberg survey of economists called for a 0.3% advance.
Total industrial output, which also includes mines and utilities, stagnated. Utility production climbed 1.8%, fueled by a pickup in electricity demand. Mining output edged up.

The cooling in August factory output represents a pause in the upswing in manufacturing this year, largely fueled by solid capital spending and healthy consumer demand. Yet, producers are facing higher costs for oil and other materials as well as supply-chain disruptions tied to wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.

“We have been noting downside risks to the manufacturing sector from higher energy prices and geopolitical risks, and the August IP report could be the first sign that these risks are materializing,” Morgan Stanley economists led by Michael Gapen said in a note.

The Fed’s report showed a 0.5% drop in output of business equipment and a 1.2% decline in defense and space equipment after strength in prior months. Production of construction supplies as well as home electronics and information processing equipment also declined.
Still, output of business equipment and defense and space equipment remained notably higher from a year earlier.
Among industry groups, output of computer and electronic products, furniture and primary metals declined last month. Machinery, apparel and textiles increased.
Auto production fell 1.2% from the prior month. Excluding motor vehicles, manufacturing output dropped 0.2%.
Capacity utilization at factories, a measure of potential output being used, fell to a five-month low of 75.7%. The overall industrial utilization rate was unchanged.

items.title: Next Africa: Chinese Robot Wolves and a Western Withdrawal at Defense Expo
body: Welcome to Next Africa, a daily newsletter on where the continent stands now — and where it’s headed. Sign up here. In today’s edition, we look at:
Africa’s biggest aerospace and defense show this week is as much a window into South Africa’s current place in the world as a demonstration of military prowess.

The exhibits at the main air force base outside Pretoria were dominated by companies from the BRICS political alliance — notably China, India and Brazil — as well as other members of the Global South, Turkey and even Uzbekistan.
Companies from the US, the largest contingent as recently as eight years ago, were virtually absent, while European representation had also dwindled.

Chinese-made robot wolves, one armed with a rocket backpack, were on display alongside drones, planes, naval ships and guns from the world’s emerging powers. South African and Indian companies launched a jointly built armored vehicle.

One notable BRICS exception was Russia, cash-strapped by its war against Ukraine. Its stands were sparsely manned and Roscosmos, the space agency, only had pamphlets in Russian, a language barely spoken in South Africa.

US representation was confined to makers of aircraft parts, optics companies and a helicopter maintenance outfit. In the past, industry titans such as Lockheed Martin and General Atomics, the maker of the Reaper drone, have been present.
That’s likely in some way due to the strained relations between Washington and Pretoria.

Donald Trump’s administration this week announced visa restrictions on South Africans it alleges have engaged in “government sponsored discrimination” against Afrikaners and other minority groups — just the latest in a series of steps taken against the government.
But it’s largely a reflection of the growing power of Asia’s economic giants and how South Africa, as a member of BRICS and China’s biggest trade partner in Africa, is moving into their orbit.
In military parlance, it can be likened to a changing of the guard.

Uganda is debating whether to shift its capital from Kampala to a largely undeveloped town north of the city as gridlock and difficulties in upgrading infrastructure hinder expansion. Congestion has made living in the current capital “unbearable and untenable,” says Margaret Muhanga Mugisa, the minister of state for lands, housing and urban development.

Ivory Coast plans to start operating a gold refinery in the first half of next year as the West African nation seeks to boost local processing and become the continent’s largest producer of the precious metal by 2035. The world’s top cocoa grower currently mines about 60 tons of gold annually and expects output to reach 100 tons by 2030.

Petrobras signed production-sharing contracts for eight exploratory offshore blocks in Ivory Coast, its latest move to expand its footprint in Africa. The state-controlled Brazilian company has already partnered with TotalEnergies to buy a 42.5% stake in an offshore block in Namibia and joined the Deep Western Orange Basin project in South Africa.

Senegalese football star Sadio Mané is betting $20 million of his own money that the West African nation’s mangoes can become a crop that spurs economic development in the country of his birth. Senegal ships tens of thousands of tons of fresh mangoes, mainly to Europe, but processes only about 2% of its crop locally.

Botswana won’t be reckless and risk its financial wellbeing when it increases its investment in De Beers, the biggest diamond company, Vice President Ndaba Gaolathe says. The country wants to boost its involvement in the industry as Anglo American seeks to dispose of its 85% stake in the gems giant. The southern African nation currently owns 15% of the firm.

Mozambique and Senegal’s eurobonds are topping returns across emerging markets, spurred by progress in talks with the IMF over new loans. The gains buck a wider dip in EMs, driven by a sharp rise in developed-market yields from the US to Japan, as investors fret over ballooning fiscal deficits and higher inflation.
Next Africa Quiz — Which African country lured Chinese Bitcoin miners to invest there by offering them some of the world’s cheapest power? Send your answers to nextafrica@bloomberg.net.

Zaria, a firm backed by Dallas Mavericks President Masai Ujiri and Helios Sports & Entertainment, plans to build a 10,000-seater multipurpose indoor arena in Nairobi, Kenya’s capital. With growing and mostly youthful populations, African countries are banking on sporting opportunities to create jobs and spur economic growth. Kenya is already building new stadiums and refurbishing existing facilities ahead of co-hosting the Africa Cup of Nations football tournament next year, alongside Uganda and Tanzania.
We’ll be back in your inbox with another edition on Monday. Send any feedback to nextafrica@bloomberg.net.

items.title: ECB Officials Pave Way for More Tightening as Inflation Worsens
body: European Central Bank officials are preparing the ground for further monetary tightening, signaling another move is possible as soon as October to tackle intensifying inflation pressures.

With prices gains in the 21-nation euro zone barrelling toward 4% and the economy holding up better than anticipated, policymakers are making the case that interest rates need to continue rising. The ECB is already the most hawkish central bank within the Group of Seven following two hikes since the Iran war sent energy costs soaring.

Data released Friday underlined the challenge: Household inflation expectations shifted higher in August across all horizons tracked by the ECB. And while things like wage demands haven’t responded much to rising oil and natural gas prices, officials are making the case for pre-emptive steps to prevent inflation from taking root.

The clearest sign that borrowing costs will be lifted further came Friday from Latvian central-bank Governor Martins Kazaks in Dublin, where he and several of his euro-area peers joined an informal meeting of the region’s finance chiefs and spoke exclusively to Bloomberg Television.

Croatia’s Ante Zigman also emphasized expansion, arguing that a failure to quell price gains would imperil an economy that grew by 0.6% in the second quarter, albeit in part thanks to volatile data from Ireland.
Discussing how inflation is playing out, Estonia’s Ulo Kaasik concurred with President Christine Lagarde that knock-on effects of elevated energy costs aren’t yet visible.

The issue, a particular focus for the ECB, has been used by some to urge caution on additional tightening. Lagarde stressed at a press conference on Friday that upswings on energy markets alone won’t necessarily translate into higher interest rates.
Kaasik struck a more hawkish tone.
On the timing of the next ECB move, which would lift the deposit rate beyond its current level of 2.5% and into so-called restrictive territory for the economy, officials remained tight-lipped.

The two 25 basis-point hikes to date have come at the quarterly policy meetings that feature updated economic projections, the next of which will take place in December and is seen by many as the best juncture for a re-assessment.

But people familiar with the discussions told Bloomberg this month that October is also an option. Markets are split on the likelihood of a hike next month, but have placed aggressive bets on at least three more moves this cycle.
For Ireland’s Gabriel Makhlouf, the high level of uncertainty over the Iran was and its consequences for Europe mean every meeting can result in action, a sentiment that Kazaks echoed on Friday.

items.title: The O-Ring Risk to the Global Economy
body: It’s not comforting when a leading economist draws a parallel between today’s global economy and the disaster of the space shuttle Challenger. Unfortunately Peter Orszag, once in charge of the US budget under President Barack Obama and these days chief executive of the investment bank Lazard, did a very persuasive job this week of doing just that in a speech at the London School of Economics. He doesn’t, to be clear, suggest that the world is bound for a fate as tragic and catastrophic as the spacecraft’s. But the lessons are all too clear.

Richard Feynman, Challenger, and the O-RingThe principal problem was set out by Richard Feynman, the Nobel prize-winning physicist, in his contribution to the official report on how the shuttle came to explode a minute after takeoff in January 1986, killing seven crew members, including the schoolteacher Christa McAuliffe. Challenger was an extraordinary piece of engineering with many important parts. The problem was that they were all interdependent. Failure in any one could mean failure of the whole.

It turned out that Challenger was doomed by an O-ring — a simple circular rubber seal used by engineers and plumbers to stop leakage of different fluids and gases. It shouldn’t have needed a Nobelist to point this out, but in a famous piece of theater, Feynman took a piece of an O-ring from a scale model of the shuttle that he’d dipped in cold water, and showed that it became too rigid to do its job reliably.

On an unusually cold Florida morning, the temperature had barely risen above freezing when the shuttle took off. The launch was not postponed despite plainly elevated risks, and the O-ring failed within seconds.In his last major contribution to public debate before he died of cancer in 1988, Feynman belittled the National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s muddled thinking about risk and probability that allowed this to happen. Many engineers, he discovered, had been concerned about what might happen to O-rings at low temperatures, but NASA’s authorities gained confidence from their ongoing success in avoiding major accidents. Managers told Feynman that the odds of a catastrophic shuttle accident were one in 100,000. Engineers, asked the same question, said one in 200. In What Do You Care What Other People Think?, Feynman said:
The O-Ring Economy

This week, Orszag diagnosed “the O-Ring Economy.” As the world globalized, so trade grew more complex and more vulnerable to the failure of one chokepoint, just as the brilliantly engineered Challenger failed due to an oversight about a rubber O-ring.

Orszag found the same flaw in contemporary economic thinking that Feynman found in NASA. The output of a complex process, he pointed out, is the product of the quality of each of its stages or parts, not the sum: “In a multiplicative production function, one weak link can reduce the value of everything else to nearly nothing.”

In such circumstances, small differences in reliability compound — a company or government that has the best inputs stands to lose the most from having a single weak link. And complexity itself becomes a problem: “As the number of stages rises, the probability that at least one fails rises with it.” The implication is that as supply chains lengthen, as during the era of globalization, they inevitably grow more fragile.

Orszag borrowed his concept from “The O-Ring Theory of Economic Development,” a 1993 paper by Michael Kremer, who applied Feynman’s critique for labor economics. As processes became more complex and more vulnerable to mistakes in their weakest link, he found, so the premium that skilled workers could command would increase. That way led to deeper income inequalities as the economy developed.

Once the O-ring logic is applied to this decade’s supply shocks — from the pandemic and the wars in Ukraine and Iran, to tariff brinkmanship and China’s block on exporting rare earths — they no longer look like a succession of unconnected geopolitically driven events. Rather, they appear more as inevitable consequences of O-ring logic. Add supply chains only as strong as their weakest part to a deglobalizing trend in which countries aim for self-sufficiency and exploit any chokepoints at their disposal, and shocks become a feature, not a bug.

That has huge implications for the conduct of monetary policy. For decades, Orszag notes, supply seemed almost perfectly flexible thanks largely to the phenomenal growth of China. Safe in the knowledge that supply would adjust, finance ministers could focus on demand, much as Keynes might have told them to do. Milton Friedman’s famous comment that “we are all Keynesians now” had in this sense some truth to it.

Now, it appears, we all have to be supply-siders. Monetary policy cannot simply look through a supply shock, as the textbooks dictate, if such shocks become regular events. As people treat these events as a fact of life, so they will adjust their inflation expectations upward. This can become self-fulfilling. To quote Orszag:

Central bankers are getting this message. Asked about the Federal Reserve’s surprisingly aggressive launch this week of a new cycle of raising rates, the chairman, Kevin Warsh, candidly admitted that its judgment of the geopolitical situation had changed. With oil shocks continuing to reverberate, the Fed now appears to be agreeing with Orszag’s logic. As markets have taken the change of direction with surprising equanimity, it appears that others agree.
A Lesson From Finance

These lessons don’t only apply to the physical realm. They also matter, in spades, to finance. In April 2007, Richard Bookstaber published A Demon of Our Own Design, one of the more prophetic books on the then-coming financial crisis. Markets, he argued, were too complex for their own good, creating the risk of disaster. He identified connectedness as a critical issue. The more tightly that different financial securities and markets were tied together, perhaps due to debt contracts or derivatives, the more fragile they all became. Without some give, closely linked systems could crash. Bookstaber was soon proved all too right.

The stakes, thankfully, aren’t as high as they were for the seven brave astronauts on the Challenger, who were doomed the moment the O-ring failed. When economic chokepoints break down (or someone deliberately closes them), the consequences are bad but there is room for adjustment. Indeed, Orszag uses another famous economic dictate to demonstrate that they’re bound to lose their effectiveness once used.
Goodhart’s Law, named for the LSE economist Charles Goodhart, who turns 90 this year, holds that when a measure becomes a target of economic policy, it ceases to be useful. Orszag argues:

Examples include Europe’s survival of the 2022 crisis caused by reliance on Russian natural gas, or the way 2014 sanctions over the annexation of Crimea prompted Moscow to build a new payments infrastructure that allowed it to weather the far broader penalties that followed its invasion of the rest of Ukraine. Currently, the Strait of Hormuz is the key chokepoint, and efforts to find alternative routes for Middle Eastern oil are redoubling.

This doesn’t get central bankers out of their supply-driven bind. Deglobalization, and the process of finding a way around existing chokepoints, involves adding more give to complex systems. That makes them less risky, but also more expensive. It’s not good; but the horrible example of the Challenger shows why it might be best to accept it.

items.title: ECB's Lagarde Preaches Calm Amid European Bond Market Turmoil
body: Welcome to the Brussels Edition. I’m Suzanne Lynch, Bloomberg’s Brussels bureau chief, bringing you the latest from the EU each weekday. Make sure you’re signed up.

“Concerned but not anxious.” That was the response of Eurogroup chief Kyriakos Pierrakakis when asked about the turmoil in European bond markets following a spike in yields on government debt in recent weeks.
Pierrakakis was speaking today following a meeting of euro-area finance ministers in Dublin at which Europe’s fiscal woes and intensifying inflationary pressures dominated the agenda.

In a psychologically significant development, a measure of French bond risk rose to one percentage point for the first time in 14 years, a sign of growing caution among investors given the country’s gaping budget deficit and political instability.

Pierrakakis’ message of relative calm was echoed by ECB President Christine Lagarde. “We monitor markets. We don’t see any disorderly movement, we don’t see any tension,” she told reporters in the Irish capital. “This is a global movement that affects all bonds, particularly at the longer end of the curve.”
With Europe’s soaring oil and gas prices also high on the agenda of the two-day meeting, Lagarde noted that gains in energy costs don’t automatically translate into decisions on monetary policy.
“Because obviously the price of energy and its impact on prices has also an impact on other factors, including notably growth and consumption,” she said. “And we factor in all these elements.”

Nonetheless, several European finance ministers, including German Social Democrat Lars Klingbeil, urged the European Commission to present a proposal for a windfall tax on energy companies by next month, an idea so far resisted by Brussels.
A special Eurogroup meeting to discuss the energy-price shock has not been ruled out before next month’s regular gathering, as countries across Europe try to cushion their citizens and businesses.

Separately, Lagarde brushed off questions about her career plans. She told Irish national broadcaster RTE that she intends to leave in 2027, but declined to say whether she’ll remain until her term ends in October of next year.
Spain’s economy minister, Carlos Cuerpo, weighed in, saying it was time to discuss the ECB succession — a reminder that Lagarde may be forced to provide clarity on her future at some point soon.
“These discussions need to take place or to start taking place,” Cuerpo told Bloomberg TV.

The ECB may have to raise borrowing costs to levels that curb economic activity as it seeks to get inflation under control, according to Governing Council member Martins Kazaks. “With the economy forecasted to close the output gap next year, you know, wading into restrictive territory, in my view, would be appropriate,” the Latvian central bank governor told Bloomberg TV.

The far-right AfD’s crushing election victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt last Sunday has shaken Germany’s political establishment and stoked calls for conservative Chancellor Friedrich Merz to step aside after only 16 months in office. This weekend voters go to the polls again. Further losses loom for Merz’s CDU, in the Baltic coast state of Mecklenburg Western-Pomerania, where the party could even miss the 5% threshold for getting into parliament, and the capital Berlin, where it risks falling behind the anti-capitalist Left party.

If you’re one of the 6 million-plus people heading to Munich’s Oktoberfest, prepare to spend money. The famed festival, which opens this weekend, is making headlines for record prices, with liters of beer set to cost as much as €15.90 in the more popular tents. Munich’s food scene has more going on than traditional fare for the lederhosen and dirndl set though. While the city loves its Bavarian heritage, it’s also home to 1.6 million people, about half of whom have international roots.

items.title: Lawmakers Call for Investigation Into Comments on 401(k) Rule
body: Members of both chambers of Congress called on the Trump administration to investigate thousands of public comments supporting a proposal to encourage more private equity, crypto and other “alternative” investment options in 401(k) retirement plans, based on concerns about their authenticity.

Representatives Bobby Scott and Jamie Raskin, Democrats from Virginia and Maryland who serve as the ranking members of committees overseeing the labor and justice departments, along with Senator Bernie Sanders, requested an “immediate investigation” into the comments, according to a letter sent to US Attorney General Todd Blanche and Federal Bureau of Investigation Director Kash Patel.

Scott and Sanders separately wrote to the inspector general at the US Department of Labor, which put forth the proposal, demanding he conduct an audit. In a third letter, Scott urged the Labor Department’s acting secretary, Keith Sonderling, to investigate.

The letters, dated Sept. 17, cited   recent reporting from Bloomberg News that identified nearly 12,000 public submissions in favor of the proposed rule that showed signs they may have been manufactured to resemble grassroots support. At least two of the comments appear to have been made in the names of dead people.

“This is incredibly concerning,” Scott, Raskin and Sanders wrote. “It is imperative to find out whether federal law was violated in this case and, if it was, ensure that those who broke the law are held accountable.”

The Labor Department declined to comment on the letter sent to Sonderling. Its inspector general’s office and the Department of Justice didn’t respond to requests for comment. A spokesperson for the FBI declined to comment.

It’s difficult for federal agencies to police fake comments on their proposals, and perpetrators are rarely punished. But efforts to manufacture grassroots support — known as “astroturfing” — have spurred political backlash and can lead to government investigations.

The Labor Department published its proposed rule at the end of March, arguing that Americans with 401(k) plans are missing out on the returns and portfolio diversification that have made private equity and hedge funds mainstays of public pensions. The alternative asset management industry has lobbied for the rule as it seeks to manage more of the roughly $10 trillion in the retirement accounts.

To ease its path, the proposed rule would give employers a “safe harbor” from lawsuits alleging they violated fiduciary duties by offering such investments, which can be riskier, more expensive and less liquid.

Roughly 47,000 comments on the proposal poured into the government during a two-month comment period. Bloomberg analyzed these and found that nearly 12,000 lacked any personalization, such as signatures or the commenter’s location, and had no variation in the text.

These submissions followed five templates and were received by the Labor Department in nearly equal numbers each day over the course of a week this spring, then ceased. Reporters contacted more than two dozen organizations in favor of the proposal and none were able to say who was behind the language used in the campaign.

Using public records, reporters identified three dozen of the people whose names were attached to one of the nearly 12,000 comments and attempted to contact them. In five cases, people vehemently denied that they — or their family members — had anything to do with the submissions.
There was no evidence of astroturfing in the main comment campaign against the rule.

A spokesperson for the Labor Department last month declined to say whether it would investigate after Bloomberg contacted it about its findings. The department’s “focus when reviewing a comment is on the substance of the comment and not on the identity of the commenter or the number of commenters making the same point,” the spokesperson said at the time.

Scott and Sanders — a Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats and is the ranking member of a Senate committee overseeing the Labor Department — along with Senator Elizabeth Warren, had  previously urged the Trump administration to scrap the proposal, saying it would erode investor protections.
In their letter to Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito, Scott and Sanders said Bloomberg’s reporting warranted a review of the department's public comment process.
“We hope that the concerns outlined in the article will prompt you to begin an audit immediately,” they wrote.

In his letter to Sonderling, Scott also requested answers to several questions, including whether officials were “aware of any outside parties that had any knowledge of, or involvement with, the public comments utilizing unverifiable or stolen identities.”
