items.title: Value-Conscious Consumers Look for Options as Iran War Drives Up Costs
body: Welcome to Bloomberg’s Retail Monitor. Every Friday we’ll deliver you clear insights on industry trends, headwinds and emerging opportunities. Sign up now if you’re not already on the list.
Clothes are getting more expensive.
Heatwaves are changing eating habits in the UK.
Starbucks merch is very popular.
You’re already here, so check out the rest of this week’s newsletter.
— Tonya Garcia

High oil prices and a fertilizer shortage tied to disruptions from the war in Iran are impacting polyester and cotton. As a result, the cost of clothing is going to rise, adding apparel to a list of things that shoppers across the globe will be paying more for.

While manufacturers have grown accustomed to a range of hurdles — tariffs, supply chain challenges and more — this situation presents a unique problem, according to an expert at McKinsey. Usually companies can switch between the two fibers when one is under cost pressure.

Time and again over recent months, we’ve heard about the resiliency of consumers. But there’s also been talk about their growing value consciousness. Deloitte, in its holiday shopping forecast, called out the dual consumer desire to save money and enjoy the coming season, for example.

Businesses have said that they’re looking for ways to keep costs down. But as companies run out of alternatives, shoppers will also be hard-pressed to find options to stretch a dollar. And it’s not just the US. As you’ll see in this week’s edition, businesses around the world are warning that shoppers are getting more cautious.

Now food companies are saying that prices will go up, which will leave less for things like clothes and other items that can be seen as extras. As the issues mount, everyone is feeling the financial squeeze.
The following was produced with the assistance of Bloomberg Automation.

Walmart and nonprofit insurer Scan Health Plan are partnering to offer co-branded Medicare Advantage plans to seniors, aiming to use Walmart’s consumer data to reduce healthcare costs. The plan will be available in two undisclosed states and, pending regulatory approval, will be offered during the annual enrollment period beginning Oct. 15, with coverage starting Jan. 1. Financial details and expected enrollment figures were not disclosed.

The S&P 500 Consumer Discretionary Index, which includes companies like McDonald’s and Nike, has dropped 5.2% in 2026 while the broader market has gained 11%. Inflationary pressures, subdued real wage growth, and rising shipping and production costs are squeezing consumer-facing companies, with more than a quarter of stocks in the index trading at 52-week lows — a level last seen in April 2025 during the Trump tariff shock.

McDonald’s is revamping its value strategy after posting a 0.8% US same-store sales gain last quarter, its weakest result since early 2025. The company plans to work with franchisees on a longer-term affordability approach while implementing a near-term plan of temporary items and digital offers. The shift marks the first strategic move under new US head Skye Anderson and comes ahead of the company’s investor day.

Users of GLP-1 pills for weight loss curbed their snacking less than those taking the treatment through injections, according to new Bloomberg Intelligence research based on a July survey of 1,001 US respondents. Among oral users, 74% reported eating fewer salty snacks versus 80% for injection users, while 76% of pill takers ate fewer baked goods compared to 82% of those on shots. BI analysts Jennifer Bartashus and Keana Bloomfield noted that while oral GLP-1s still pose a challenge for food makers such as Mondelez, Hershey, Kraft Heinz and General Mills, growth in pill use could reduce the negative impact on product sales.

Giorgio Armani named Dario Vitale creative director of Emporio Armani and Giorgio Armani accessories, making him the first designer outside the Armani family to hold the role. Vitale, whose appointment is effective immediately, previously served briefly as artistic director of Versace before Prada acquired the label. Prior to that, he worked at Prada’s Miu Miu brand. The appointment also gives Vitale oversight of accessories, a category that has not traditionally been a major revenue driver for Armani but one that carries high profit margins.

US retail sales rose 1.2% in August, the largest monthly gain in five months and well above the 0.8% median economist estimate, as consumers continued spending despite rising gasoline prices, according to Census Bureau data. Twelve of 13 retail categories posted increases. Nonstore retailers — primarily online shopping — climbed 2.6%, the most since February 2025. Back-to-school shopping likely boosted general merchandise, clothing and electronics.

Authentic Brands CEO Matthew Maddox said the company could pursue an IPO as early as the first half of 2027. The licensor, which manages brands including Reebok and Elvis Presley’s image, generates $1.8 billion in EBITDA on $2.2 billion in revenue and an 81% profit margin.

Next trimmed its UK sales forecast for the second half to 2% from 2.8%, as CEO Simon Wolfson warned that rising energy bills and mortgage costs will weigh on consumer spending heading into the Christmas season. Despite the downward revision, the British fashion and homewares retailer raised its full-year profit forecast for the fourth time this fiscal year, buoyed by stronger-than-expected demand during the first six months. Wolfson said inflationary pressures — particularly on energy stemming from the conflict in the Middle East — combined with higher interest rates and a weak employment market would pressure consumers, though he predicted any spending decline would be gradual rather than “precipitous.”

LuxExperience, owner of luxury e-commerce platform Mytheresa, posted a 7.6% rise in net sales excluding currency changes in its fiscal fourth quarter, driven by Mytheresa’s focus on ultra-wealthy shoppers. CEO Michael Kliger credited the platform’s nimble model for enabling strong growth, including 39% growth in the US last quarter, even as luxury peers such as LVMH, Hermès and Kering have faced weakening demand.

Pepkor Holdings shares fell after the South African discount clothing retailer forecast earnings excluding certain one-off gains and losses between a 1% decline and a 9% increase for the year through September 30. The muted outlook reflects a subdued retail environment and investment costs tied to its new PlusB banking business.

Britain’s record-breaking summer, with temperatures reaching 38C and an unprecedented 40 days above 30C, has significantly altered UK consumer behavior and retail sales. Associated British Foods, owner of Twinings and Ovaltine, reported weakened demand for hot beverages as shoppers avoided the High Street during extreme heat. British retailers are increasingly treating adaptation to hotter conditions as both a commercial and operational priority, according to Barclays UK.

Starbucks’ limited-edition Snoopy glass cup, retailing for $39.95, is reselling for as much as $200 on StockX — roughly five times its retail price — after launching at select stores as part of a Peanuts merchandise collaboration. The exclusive merchandise strategy is central to CEO Brian Niccol’s turnaround plan, which aims to rebuild the brand’s cultural appeal and drive store traffic without relying on discounts.

items.title: CFTC Seeks White House Review on Crypto Rules After Bill Fails
body: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is delivering on its promise to swiftly move forward with crypto rules after a landmark digital asset bill failed to advance in the Senate this week.

The futures and swaps regulator, which would have become the primary regulator under the so-called Clarity Act, sent a new proposal to regulate crypto transactions and markets to the White House for review. The proposal was received on Thursday, according to a post published Friday by the Office of Management and Budget.

The move is a key initial step in the rulemaking process under the Trump administration, which has required independent agencies like the CFTC and the Securities and Exchange Commission to send significant rulemakings to the OMB for review and edits.
Read More: Crypto Stocks and Tokens Drop After Senate Blocks Landmark Bill

While the details of the proposal won’t be known until it’s made public, CFTC Chairman Michael Selig said at an Aug. 20 agency event that he’d asked staff to find ways to codify market structure for digital assets within the agency’s existing authorities.

“This could enable current registrants as well as non-registrant crypto exchanges to be designated by the CFTC” as a type of exchange known as a crypto asset market and offer crypto asset trading on a leveraged or margin basis, Selig said at the event.

Once the OMB is done reviewing the measure and potentially making edits, it will send it back to the commission for a vote. With Selig as the single commissioner at the five-member board, the proposal will likely be quick to appear once it’s sent back.
The agency will take public comment on the proposal, which will ultimately be incorporated into a final version. That must also be voted on by the commission before it can go into effect.
A spokesperson for the CFTC didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

items.title: Turkish Fund's Goldman Dreams Collapse in 'Ponzi-Like Scheme'
body: The “Goldman Sachs of Turkey” is how they described their ambitions at the investment bank and brokerage Tera Group.

And with a stock price that racked up an improbable 2,000% gain last year, those pronouncements from Tera executives managed to convince some in Istanbul, if not the more sober set, that business was indeed booming. They were, they liked to tell the media, on the cusp of greatness.

It all came crashing down in spectacular fashion this month, with Turkey’s justice minister promising a crackdown on “Ponzi-like schemes.” Some 680 billion lira ($14 billion) in funds at the asset management arm have been forced to liquidate and Turkish authorities arrested one of the firm’s top executives.
This in turn has sent shockwaves through Turkey’s financial system, triggering stock index circuit breakers and forcing regulators into action to stem a liquidity crunch.

In the words of the company’s founder Emre Tezmen, Tera has been the victim of a “speculative attack by the notorious malevolent forces.” Critics have a simpler explanation: pumping illiquid stocks is a strategy destined to fail.
Read More: Turkey Fund Rout Erases $4 Billion From a Rapidly-Won Fortune

“It will probably be a cautionary tale,” said Kamil Dimmich, who helps oversee more than $9 billion as a partner at London-based North of South Capital LLP. “Its funds and associated stocks will have made a lot of paper money for their investors, which have evaporated overnight.”

Tera has long been the subject of scrutiny for how it managed to achieve massive returns at its fund management business. At the heart of the business was its flagship fund with a cult following on social media for returning more than 17,000% since the start of 2025.

Its strategy was to pour billions of lira into a tight circle of related companies and amplify the bets with borrowed cash. The fund amassed stakes in the parent company, Tera, as well as Tera subsidiaries and companies that Tera’s brokerage has helped take public. Filings show that at one point in 2023 the fund had 99% of its assets in shares of Tera Yatirim.

For months, the company seemed to defy gravity, even as suspicions within the industry grew about how it could keep going. Tera’s rise was fueled, in part, by an almost unshakeable faith in its own strategy, embodied by Tezmen, its brash and outspoken founder, who claimed to be the architect of its investment techniques.

In one interview with Bloomberg, he laid out his vision for becoming the “Goldman Sachs of Turkey.” Tezmen and his executives also often boasted in conversations about his close ties to senior government officials in Ankara, including Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek, and claimed he could easily arrange meetings with the minister because of their long-standing relationship, according to people familiar with the matter.
The Turkish president and ministries declined to comment, as did representatives for Tera.
“I make money, the investor makes money. And what does the state lose?” Tezmen said in another interview. “There is no problem here.”

But the rapid unraveling of Tera has become a big problem for Turkish finance. On Friday, officials turned to two of the country’s biggest banks to oversee the liquidation of more than 100 funds from Tera Portfoy and other firms that hold more than $18 billion and have around 350,000 investors.
Read More: Behind the 40,000% Stock Surge That’s Mystifying Traders in Turkey

It’s a “major watershed moment” for Turkish financial markets, according to Defne Arslan, senior director of the Atlantic Council in Turkey. She says the crisis shows how industry loopholes and fund leverage, along with rapid regulatory shifts, have wreaked havoc.
“It exposes how rapidly domestic retail and domestic institutional money can panic when leverage breaks down in a concentrated equity ecosystem,” she said.

In Turkey’s stock market, where stocks can fall no more than 10% a day, losses are deepening. Tera Yatirim shares have plunged 27% in the span of three days, and the wider stock index is on track for its worst week in more than a year. On Friday, one in every six companies in the Borsa Istanbul All Share Index was limit down.
“We have quarantined the problematic area,” Simsek said, speaking in an interview on NTV news channel. “There’s no systemic risk.”

While suspicions about Tera started in Turkey, international investors also started to ring alarm bells this year, with investment groups urging authorities to crack down on unusual trading activity. MSCI Inc. warned that without changes, Turkey could be ejected from its equity benchmarks tracking emerging markets.

Then in August, regulators stepped in, setting off a chain of events that’s pushed Tera to the brink. It first began when regulators tightened rules on stock funds holding concentrated bets in illiquid stocks. That forced funds to sell some of their positions and triggered a rush to exit. Funds at Tera said that they couldn’t meet client demands. As a result, many Turkish savers are now left waiting to learn what their holdings are worth.
“This is a regulatory failure,” said Ramazan Basak, former deputy president of Turkey’s financial crime watchdog Masak. “People were recklessly left at the mercy of these individuals.”
He said he’d been detained twice by authorities for making complaints about Tera. Among Istanbul’s fund managers and analysts, a quiet rule took hold: nobody talked about Tera on the record.

For most of its existence, Tera was a little-known brokerage in Turkey. Only within the past two years, when its funds started earning returns of 1,000% and more did it attract notoriety and grow into one of the country’s biggest asset managers, with all the trappings of success.

Tera Portfoy, the asset management unit, also expanded into a conglomerate, buying companies in technology and cybersecurity, as well as adding a bank, a factoring arm, and a real estate firm to its holdings. Just a few months ago, Tera Yatirim Holding announced a back-of-shirt sponsorship deal with Besiktas, one of Turkey’s most popular football clubs.

As local media noted that Besiktas played their Europa League match against Marseille without the Tera logo, investors ditched shares of the company. The stock, Besiktas Futbol Yatirimlari Sanayi ve Ticaret AS, has erased a third of its value this week.

“There was a clear dereliction of duty on the part of the regulator,” said Murat Gulkan, chief executive officer of OMG Capital Advisors. “Ponzi schemes are like bicycles. They either keep moving, or growing in this case, or they crash.”

items.title: Macron Calls for G7 Meeting to Mull Release of Oil Reserves
body: French President Emmanuel Macron said he would convene a meeting of the Group of Seven countries in the coming weeks to discuss a potential release from strategic oil-product stockpiles as soaring energy prices sap economic growth.

“I will convene a G7 to move forward on improving coordination on the level of stockpiles, with greater cooperation on exports and production capacity,” Macron said at a press conference in Paris on Friday.

The meeting will come as fuel prices in Europe surge, with the Middle East conflict and Russia’s war in Ukraine disrupting supply. This week, the region’s diesel benchmark moved above $200 a barrel for the first time since April. With taxes, retail prices are north of $300.

Earlier this year, the International Energy Agency agreed to release a record amount of supply from emergency reserves onto global markets. In Europe, those stockpiles are mostly made up of fuels like gasoline and diesel, which could make a release more effective at taming fuel prices.

The G7 meeting will be devoted “to increasing cooperation and avoiding unnecessary tensions between G7 countries and our main partners, and to considering options for a potential release of strategic stockpiles,” following similar coordination with the IEA a few months ago, Macron said.

France is working to secure supplies of products such as diesel, jet fuel and natural gas for the coming months, and the government will meet on Monday to consider fresh steps to ease high energy costs, Macron said.

items.title: Trump's $1.4 Billion Haul Comes Back to Haunt Crypto Industry
body: The crypto industry watched with a grim foreboding as its landmark bill detonated on the Senate floor Tuesday. Blame first fell on Democrats, none of whom voted to advance it. But some of the industry’s own supporters pointed elsewhere: at President Donald Trump and the roughly $1.4 billion in income he generated from crypto ventures last year.

Now the industry is confronting the other side of its embrace of Trump: The alliance brought major wins in Washington, only for the president’s own crypto dealings to become an obstacle to locking some of those gains into law.

Crypto spent hundreds of millions of dollars trying to reshape Washington, betting that a friendlier White House and Congress would finally give the industry the legal footing it had sought for a decade. In many ways, the bet worked. The Trump administration dismantled much of the enforcement regime crypto companies had fought under President Joe Biden, regulators began writing friendlier rules and Trump signed landmark stablecoin legislation.

The Clarity Act was supposed to be the bigger prize. At its core, the bill was meant to settle a question that has hung over crypto for years: who regulates what. It would have divided responsibility between the Securities and Exchange Commission and Commodity Futures Trading Commission and set rules for exchanges, brokers and other firms operating in the market. For digital-asset companies, that meant a clearer legal path for doing business in the US, rather than working it out case by case with regulators.

Then Trump’s business dealings became part of the perceived problem. Several people in the industry now say his financial ties to crypto helped turn an already difficult bill into an even harder sell.

“The failure of Clarity begins and ends with Donald Trump,” said Justin Slaughter, senior adviser at crypto and financial technology investment firm Paradigm. The memecoin that launched days before his inauguration “was the first brick in the road to this failing,” he said.

Since the collapse of FTX, crypto has spent years trying to move Washington’s attention beyond the industry’s controversies and toward the technology and the rules governing it. But after its most powerful political ally launched a lucrative memecoin and became one of crypto’s biggest beneficiaries while championing the laws and regulations governing the industry, his opponents in Washington seized on those ties.
A vote for Clarity is a vote “to bless Donald Trump’s corruption,” Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren said before Tuesday’s vote in comments to reporters.

Trump has consistently denied that his family’s business interests conflict with his duties as president. He has cast his support for crypto as part of a broader push to make the US the world leader in digital assets and keep the industry from ceding ground to China.
“The only blame here belongs to Democrats, who continue to put stupid political games over doing what’s best for American technology and innovation,” a White House spokesperson said in a statement.

Crypto executives became familiar faces at Trump’s White House, posing alongside the president at meetings and industry events. The industry kept courting Democrats too, but those encounters rarely came with the same White House backdrop or visibility.
“This has become a partisan issue when it didn’t need to be,” said Carlos Domingo, CEO of Securitize.
Cory Klippsten, CEO of Swan Bitcoin, said the squabble over Trump’s ethics issues “helped turn crypto’s biggest legislative priority into a political fight they couldn’t win.”
Nic Carter, a partner at crypto investment firm Castle Island Ventures, had a similar view.

“Trump needlessly complicated this whole process by entwining himself and his family in crypto, which many of us saw from the start, including me,” he said. Carter has described himself as a Trump voter and supporter but has also been a vocal critic of World Liberty Financial, the crypto firm co-founded by Trump and his family.

While much of the early discussion of the bill focused on key technical points, such as whether companies like exchanges can pay yield on users’ stablecoin holdings, the ethics discussions ultimately drove the conversation away from such questions altogether. Republicans made a last-minute attempt to break the impasse with tougher restrictions on elected officials’ crypto holdings, including provisions that could require Trump to divest significant interests or put them in a blind trust, but Democrats remained unconvinced.

“My personal perspective is the bill became about ethics and had nothing to do with market structure,” said Arjun Sethi, co-CEO of Payward, the parent company of crypto exchange Kraken. “It’s not about safeguarding American people or American assets.”

There were plenty of other disagreements. Banks objected to stablecoin rewards, saying they risked drawing deposits out of the banking system. Another fight involved protections for software developers when their code is used for criminal activity. Those issues were still contentious when the bill came to the floor.
Austin Campbell, who runs consultancy Zero Knowledge Group, said the stablecoin-yield fight and some residual concerns from law enforcement groups “were enough to kill the bill” as well.
Cryptocurrencies rose on Friday as investors moved on from the Clarity Act’s struggles.

Some Republicans insist the bill isn’t dead yet, though its path back to the Senate floor is narrow. Regulators, meanwhile, aren’t waiting around. The SEC on Thursday cleared a path for qualifying venues to trade tokenized versions of US stocks, moving forward with a plan that could reshape traditional market structure. But regulatory actions like these are less durable than legislation and can be revisited by future administrations.

There is plenty left to spend. Since 2024, Fairshake and its affiliates have spent $206 million to influence federal elections, Federal Election Commission records show. They had $123 million cash on hand through the end of July. The question now is where the industry puts it — into trying to win back Democrats or defeating lawmakers it blames for Clarity’s failure.

Voting down the industry’s cherished legislation weeks before the election “is a dangerous game to play given the effectiveness of the crypto lobbyists and donors in past elections,” warned Anthony Pompliano, CEO of ProCap Acquisition Corp.

items.title: Indian Refinery Builder Sees Mideast Orders Slow as War Drags On
body: Engineers India Ltd. is seeing a slowdown in new orders for Middle East energy projects as continued US-Iran hostilities heighten security risks, forcing clients to delay investments and contracts.

The war has impacted new and ongoing projects and is affecting order flow, Chairman Atul Gupta said. He expects contracts to pick up as Middle Eastern producers start investing in infrastructure to bypass disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz that have roiled global energy markets.
“There has been slowdown in orders from the Gulf region as those countries are busy securing and restoring their installations,” Gupta told reporters in New Delhi.

The slowdown is threatening an important growth market for the state-owned construction and project consultancy firm, which has been expanding overseas as Middle Eastern energy producers invested in oil and gas infrastructure. Engineers India builds pipelines, refineries and provides technical services for energy projects.
Read More: Why One Saudi Pipeline Is Key for Global Oil Market: Explainer
Overseas projects account for more than 40% of the company’s 170 billion-rupee ($1.8 billion) order book, and a big chunk of those are from the Middle East, Gupta said.
International markets are becoming increasingly important as almost two-thirds of its new business in the year ended March 2026 came from overseas, including projects in the Middle East and Africa.

The firm’s orders in the region include projects in Abu Dhabi and Kuwait’s Mina Al-Ahmadi refinery, according to its latest annual report. Engineers India opened an office in Saudi Arabia this year to deepen ties with energy companies including Saudi Aramco and compete for contracts requiring local registration.

Opportunities will accelerate after the conflict ends as Middle Eastern energy majors will be spending billions of dollars to build pipelines, storage terminals and other infrastructure to reduce their reliance on the Strait of Hormuz, he said.

items.title: Germany's M&A Boom Is Gathering Strength
body: Hi, it’s Eyk Henning in Frankfurt, where the deals just keep coming after a hot summer for M&A, fueled in part by the AI data center boom. Also today, a number of infrastructure deals move forward.
Today’s top stories
German defense companies, big banks, industrial firms and even schnapps producers are in play as a summer dealmaking surge extends into autumn.

M&A volumes in Europe’s largest economy are running about 80% above last year, according to data compiled by Bloomberg, fueled by multibillion-dollar transactions and a growing pipeline of potential sales.

Among the recent action: UniCredit continues to push for control of Commerzbank, and Frasers Group is strengthening its hold over Hugo Boss. The Wegmann family, which owns half of tankmaker KNDS, is focused on selling shares to the German government, we scooped this week.

Should talks between the Wegmann family and the government break down, big private equity firms and other defense companies are preparing to enter the fray and a bidding war could break out. It’s the latest signal that more and more families that built companies over generations think now is the time to sell. In a sign of which way the wind is blowing, banks mandated to advise on the KNDS IPO are already scouting for buyside mandates with private equity firms. That suggests that M&A is the most likely exit route.

Most activity in Germany is coming from global players who want to gain scale or adapt their business model, according to Thomas Meurer, a partner at law firm Hengeler Mueller. “Strategic M&A is high up on the agenda of many boards we’re speaking with,” he said.
Meurer added that private equity is playing a growing role, too, and providing more capital for Germany, Inc., pointing to energy company RWE’s deals with Apollo Global Management and KKR.

Deals still in the pipeline include the separation of Siemens Energy’s compressor and steam turbine unit, as well as potential take privates of molecular testing company Qiagen and media group Stroeer. Bloomberg reported this week that US spirits maker Sazerac is in talks to buy Berentzen-Gruppe.

Meanwhile, German industrial companies are coming back into focus as elevated geopolitical risk becomes the new normal. That’s especially true for companies playing a role in the global data center boom. Deals include Madison Air Solutions’ purchase of fan maker EBM-Papst and the sale of cooling equipment maker Kelvion to SLB. Güntner, a family-owned manufacturer of cooling systems, is also weighing a sale.

“In Germany, industrial companies catering to the data center industry are benefiting the most from the AI boom, making it an appealing time to consider a sale,” said Lukas Poensgen, co-head of M&A EMEA at Bank of America.

Even software companies, which have been battered this year by fears that AI will disrupt their business models, are seeing interest. Pending acquisitions of IT services firms like Nagarro and All for One “highlight the rising interest of strategic buyers in software assets now trading at lower valuations,” said Christoph Seibt, a partner at law firm Freshfields. —Eyk Henning

Private equity firms previously circling Evergrande Property Services Group are considering making fresh offers for the Hong Kong-listed real estate management business. PAG, Warburg Pincus and Trustar Capital are among those preparing bids.
PT Indesso Aroma’s founding Gunawan family and private equity firm EQT are considering selling the company in a deal that could fetch as much as $1 billion.

The Canadian government has hired Morgan Stanley and Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce to advise on selling the operating rights to the country’s four largest airports, in Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver and Calgary.
PSA International is considering selling a minority stake in its container terminal operations in Jawaharlal Nehru Port in Mumbai. It may seek a valuation of $2 billion including debt for the assets.

Spanish copper manufacturer Cunext Copper Industries is considering holding an IPO. The company, which makes power and data cables, is hiring advisers to work on the potential offering.Also in Spain, the renewable energy company Ignis Energia expects to unveil its stock listing plans on Sept. 28 as it seeks to capitalize on growing demand for data center projects in the country.Airtel Africa is expected to cut the size of a London IPO for its Airtel Money division to at least $800 million. That is substantially lower than the previously targeted deal size of $1.5 billion to $2 billion.

Tata Sons said it would pursue a stock listing and give its chairman another five-year term despite strong — and public — opposition from the founding-family patriarch, setting up a showdown at one of India’s oldest conglomerates.
The company behind GCash, the biggest mobile wallet app in the Philippines, received approval from the country’s stock exchange operator of an IPO of as much as 92.3 billion pesos ($1.47 billion).
Centrum Holding, Uzbekistan’s largest private logistics group, is in talks with Citigroup and JPMorgan Chase to work on its IPO in London.

Matt Holt’s new firm Thoreau is part of a $100 million investment in insurance automation platform Penelope Health. It’s the second investment for Thoreau, which Holt started after a storied exit from New Mountain Capital.
Morgan Stanley has hired Alexander Mejia and Jeremy Duksin as co-heads of private capital advisory solutions in the bank’s financial sponsors group. The two previously worked at Baird.

items.title: Turkey's Wealth Fund Bought Blue-Chip Stocks to Stem Market Rout
body: Turkey’s sovereign wealth fund bought stocks on Thursday to prop up the nation’s equity market, according to people with knowledge of the matter, the latest move to contain fallout from a crash in the country’s fund management industry.

The Turkish Wealth Fund bought shares through an exchange-traded vehicle run by state-owned brokerage Ziraat Portfoy to lift the Borsa Istanbul 30 Index, which tracks the country’s 30 biggest public companies, said the people, asking not to be named because the information wasn’t public. The fund will continue to intervene if it sees extreme volatility in the coming days, one of the people said.
A spokesperson for the wealth fund did not immediately return a request for comment.

Ziraat’s exchange-traded funds tracking Turkish banks and the BIST 30 Index drew 4.05 billion liras ($83 million) of inflows on Thursday. That was the most since April 2025 and helped fuel an 8.9% advance in banking shares.

The move follows a week of turmoil after some high-profile investment funds said they were unable to meet investor redemption requests. The strains had been building since August, when regulators took action against unusual stock moves by tightening rules on funds with concentrated holdings in companies with limited free floats, forcing some managers to unwind positions.
Read more: How Turkey’s High-Flying Funds Came Crashing Down: Explainer

Authorities have moved on several fronts to restore confidence. The capital markets regulator ordered 131 investment funds liquidated and blocked trading in funds run by seven asset managers after investors pulled as much as $1 billion from Turkish funds in a single day. The central bank raised repo funding to 300 billion liras and lifted banks’ interbank borrowing limits 10-fold.

items.title: Lilly's Newest Bull Says Near 300% Rally Is Only the Beginning
body: Eli Lilly & Co. has surged about 300% since its first GLP-1 was approved over four years ago, propelling it past $1 trillion in market value and making it the world’s most valuable pharmaceutical company.
The stock’s newest bull on Wall Street, Berenberg’s Kerry Holford, says the rally is just getting started.

“With solid growth from marketed assets and a significant pipeline contribution, Lilly offers sales growth through to 2030 significantly ahead of peers,” the bank’s head of global pharmaceutical equity research wrote in a report this week.

Throw in “best-in-class R&D productivity,” and that’s why the drugmaker, already trading at a hefty premium to its peers, deserves an even richer valuation, she said while upgrading the stock to buy from hold.

Lilly trades at about 26 times forward earnings, higher than peers in the S&P 500 Pharmaceuticals Index as well as five of the so-called Magnificent Seven stocks. Holford’s new price target of $1,400 implies a 21% increase from Thursday’s close.
“Investor expectations for Lilly to maintain its lead in the fast-growing obesity market are undoubtedly high,” she wrote. “We are confident in this and see” further upside.

Lilly’s stock has been on a tear since its blockbuster GLP-1 drug Mounjaro was first approved as a treatment for diabetes in 2022. Later cleared for obesity under the Zepbound brand, it has since surpassed Novo Nordisk A/S’s Wegovy as the most-prescribed weight-management drug in the US.
Read More: Eli Lilly Ripe for Stock Split After Obesity Drug-Fueled Rally
Yet, there’s still more room to run, according to Holford.
The pending approval of Foundayo, Lilly’s GLP-1 pill, to treat diabetes is likely “to unlock significant demand,” she wrote.

What’s more, the success of Zepbound and Mounjaro have allowed Lilly to invest heavily beyond obesity, bringing “multiple new opportunities to the Lilly pipeline, many of which have megabuster peak sales potential.”

Lilly has committed roughly $60 billion on more than 25 business development deals year-to-date, according to Holford’s calculations. That include the acquisitions of sleep drugmaker Centessa Pharmaceuticals for as much as $7.8 billion and cancer drug developer Kelonia Therapeutics for up to $7 billion. It also bought psychedelic drugmaker AtaiBeckley for $3.8 billion.
“We believe this non-obesity pipeline is underappreciated by investors,” Holford wrote.

items.title: Tata Sons Listing Bets Drive Big Moves in Group Stocks, Tata Chemicals Soars
body: Welcome to India Edition, Bloomberg’s daily dive into what’s moving the worlds of business, markets and politics in this dynamic, fast-paced economy. I’m Samie Modak, Bloomberg’s Asia Equities Reporter in Mumbai, filling in for Menaka. If you didn’t receive this directly in your inbox, you can subscribe here, and share feedback with us here.
The battle over Tata Sons’ future is far from settled, but stock market investors are already trying to trade the outcome, causing group companies’ shares to whipsaw this week.

Tata Sons, the unlisted holding company at the heart of the group, is facing a push to go public even as a boardroom power struggle leaves little clarity over whether a listing will eventually happen or how.

At least seven listed Tata Group companies directly own shares in Tata Sons, giving investors indirect exposure to the closely held parent. The big moves have come in Tata Chemicals, Tata Investment Corp. and Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles, which are seen as among the big gainers from a potential listing.

The latest bout of the so-called “Tata Sons trade” began Tuesday after India’s banking regulator refused to exempt the company from rules requiring it to pursue a listing. Select Tata stocks rose even as the broader market fell.

They rallied again Thursday after the Tata Sons board backed a listing and a five-year extension for Chairman Natarajan Chandrasekaran. But the trade swung the other way on Friday after Tata Trusts, the controlling shareholder, said it had not agreed to a listing and that the board should explore all available options rather than an IPO alone.

Even if Tata Sons does eventually list, shareholders in these companies are unlikely to benefit to the full extent of their Tata Sons holdings, given the steep discounts at which holding companies in India typically trade.
Much would also depend on the route Tata Sons takes to market, how much of the company is sold and the valuation it commands.
And while developments around Tata Sons may drive sharp moves in the short term, investors still have to reckon with the challenges facing the underlying businesses.

“The Tata Group’s business problems are bigger than the leadership problem,” said Chokkalingam G., founder of Equinomics Research. Tata Motors’ European operations face challenges, while Tata Consultancy Services is contending with growth headwinds.

Tata Chemicals captures that contrast well. It could be the “single largest beneficiary” of any value unlocking, according to DRChoksey FinServ, which estimates the value of its Tata Sons holding at about twice Tata Chemicals’ own market capitalization. That said, Tata Chemicals warned in its latest earnings call that the near-term outlook for soda ash remains tough, with Chinese oversupply and higher raw-material and trade costs adding pressure.

The last time investors piled into the Tata Sons trade, it ended badly. In March 2024, speculation over a potential listing sent Tata Chemicals and Tata Investment Corp. surging about 40% each. The rally quickly unwound after reports that Tata Sons was looking for ways to avoid going public, sending both stocks sharply lower.
But hope springs eternal, especially among stock market traders. Investors are at it again, even though there is still no clear path to a listing and no certainty that it will happen at all.

Next up in this edition, my colleague and Asia Agriculture Reporter Pratik Parija explains how rising food prices are squeezing household budgets and complicating the job for policymakers. But first, the stories you need to read, watch or listen to from us today.
Japan raised its benchmark interest rate in a split decision as it confronts mounting inflation risks.
At least two liquefied natural gas shipments transited the Strait of Hormuz this week as producers look for ways to increase flows.
India’s economy may be enjoying a “sugar high” from earlier stimulus, causing markets to price in too many interest-rate increases, says JPMorgan’s Aziz.
Don’t Miss
Want more? Sign up for Markets Daily India, a subscriber-only newsletter featuring key insights before the trading day starts.

Shivam Fauzdar runs a small restaurant in the New Delhi suburb of Noida, where keeping a plate of flatbread and vegetables affordable has become a daily balancing act. He has already raised prices after a surge in cooking-gas costs, but now ingredients are getting more expensive too. Raising menu prices again risks driving customers to the half-dozen food carts nearby that sell similar meals for less. “We can’t raise our rates because customers will stop coming,” he says.

Fauzdar’s dilemma captures a broader problem emerging across India. Food is getting more expensive from several directions at once. Poor weather is hurting crops, higher energy costs are feeding into transport and fertilizer prices, and biofuel demand is pulling some crops away from the food chain. That is making everyday meals more expensive, especially for lower-income households that already spend a large part of their budgets on food.

The shock begins with the weather. India is on course for its driest monsoon in 17 years as a strengthening El Niño curbs rainfall. Cumulative rainfall during the June to September monsoon season is 15% below the long-term average so far, according to the India Meteorological Department.

Rice and corn plantings are behind last season, while concerns over sugar supplies have pushed prices higher and prompted India to allow duty-free imports. Unseasonal rain has damaged the onion crop in Maharashtra, while transport costs are adding to retail prices.

Food is also competing with fuel. India’s push for 20% ethanol blending has increased demand for corn, rice and sugar cane, giving farmers another buyer for crops that would otherwise go into food or animal feed. Because ethanol producers can at times pay more, more of those crops can get pulled toward fuel, leaving less for food and animal feed. That, in turn, can raise costs for businesses such as poultry producers.

For markets, the question is whether this remains a temporary food shock or starts feeding into broader inflation. Already, inflation hit a 20-month high in August, narrowing the RBI’s room to keep interest rates on hold for much longer.

There is also a global angle. India’s return as a sugar buyer could tighten an already strained market, leaving less supply available elsewhere just as El Niño threatens harvests in other major producing regions.

items.title: Hyperscalers invest in ultra-long storage for data centers
body: Power-hungry data centers have led tech giants to invest in large batteries that can store energy for dozens of hours.

Today’s newsletter brings you the latest research from BloombergNEF showing that most      new demand for long-duration storage   comes from the likes of Google and Meta. We also bring you a long read on why Trump is pardoning people convicted of      disabling diesel truck pollution controls  .
And the latest      warning   on how burning coal is accelerating planetary warming comes from... ExxonMobil.
Subscribe to     Bloomberg.com   for     unlimited access   to all our coverage.
By  Coco Liu

Soaring energy demand for artificial intelligence has spurred   billions of dollars in clean energy investments, such as in next-generation geothermal and advanced nuclear reactors. Now, hyperscalers are boosting yet another clean technology: long-lasting batteries.

Developers are starting to add these batteries, known as long-duration energy storage, to data centers. As they do that, there’s a real chance to scale them and unlock more renewable energy, experts say.

“Long-duration storage is an important addition to a growing toolkit that can help us build AI infrastructure at unprecedented scale,” said Cully Cavness, cofounder and president at Crusoe, which builds and operates AI data centers for tech giants.

Long-duration energy storage is an umbrella term for technologies capable of storing and releasing electricity for many hours or even days. Conventional lithium-ion batteries, in contrast, only hold power for a few hours.

Historically, facilities have relied on a mix of diesel generators, natural gas turbines and conventional batteries to keep operations running during grid failures or when renewable power lulls. But adding new fossil-fuel capacity threatens tech companies’ pledges to cut carbon emissions at a time when AI’s   climate toll is growing. The installation of gas turbines is also bogged down by persistent supply chain bottlenecks, leaving developers with multiyear wait times for new orders.
By  Leslie Kaufman

Matthew Geouge built a lucrative business selling technology that, among other things, allowed owners of Ford diesel pickups to boost their horsepower while disabling the pollution controls required under the Clean Air Act. The federal government pursued his company, Spartan Diesel Technologies, in a civil action, ultimately winning a $4.15 million default judgment in 2018. But it didn’t stop there.

US prosecutors later accused Geouge of continuing to tune engines illegally at another company. He pleaded guilty in 2021 to conspiring to violate the Clean Air Act and defraud the US, as well as to tax evasion, and was sentenced to a year and a day in prison. He served four-and-a-half months in 2022.
On July 3, President Donald   Trump pardoned him.

Geouge was among nine people granted clemency that day for Clean Air Act convictions involving vehicle emissions. Trump pardoned additional defendants in similar cases in September, marking a sharp reversal in the federal government’s treatment of an aftermarket industry built around disabling pollution controls. Months earlier, Trump’s Department of Justice had told prosecutors to stop bringing criminal cases involving so-called “defeat devices.” The president cast the pardons as relief for people prosecuted for simply “fixing their car.”

As US air pollution rules have gotten stricter, automakers have installed equipment in diesel trucks to stifle their emissions. But an illegal aftermarket to undo these alterations quickly sprung up and spread. Software developers wrote new engine calibrations, and manufacturers produced hardware. Online distributors sold defeat devices, and repair shops installed them.

Some truck owners wanted more horsepower; others were looking for a way around early pollution-control systems that could be unreliable and expensive to repair; still others felt government regulation infringed on their personal freedoms. Regardless of the motivation, the upshot is dirtier air: The Environmental Protection Agency estimated in 2020 that emissions controls had been fully removed from more than 550,000 diesel pickups since 2009 — about 15% of the trucks originally certified with the equipment.

Defeat devices sold between 2009 and 2020 for certain vehicle models would lead to them releasing an estimated 570,000 additional tons of nitrogen oxides and 5,000 more tons of particulate matter over the vehicles’ lifetimes, the EPA calculated — the pollution equivalent of adding 9 million compliant diesel trucks to US roads. Nitrogen oxides contribute to smog and can aggravate asthma and other respiratory illnesses, while fine particulate pollution is linked to cardiovascular and respiratory disease and premature death.

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis, in response to a request for comment, pointed to a social media post by Trump describing the pardonees as having been “persecuted” by the Biden administration. “I AM SETTING THEM ALL FREE, RIGHT NOW!” Trump wrote.

Iowa, long a renewable-energy paragon, has   cranked up its coal consumption to keep pace with the data-center boom, Inside Climate News reported. The Hawkeye State generated 58.5% of its electricity from wind last year, the highest in the nation. But coal’s share ticked up to 26% from 20.5% in 2024, according to Energy Information Administration data.

When it comes to green tech, China is a list of superlatives. It produces more solar panels, wind turbines, electric vehicles and batteries than anywhere else in the world. But is finance the real climate hero? This week on Zero,  Akshat Rathi is joined by Ma Jun, chairman of the Hong Kong Green Finance Association and former chief economist of China’s central bank. They discuss how the country became a green-finance superpower and how other nations can speed up their own transitions.

items.title: Dutch Aim to Convince Belgium to Deploy Frozen Russian Assets
body: Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen is working to allay Belgium’s concerns about using Russian assets frozen in the European Union to support Ukraine.

There are approximately €210 billion ($241 billion) in immobilized Russian central-bank assets held on EU soil. Most of the bloc’s leaders see these funds as the most feasible way to get Ukraine the billions it needs as Russia’s full-scale invasion approaches its fifth year. But Belgium has so far resisted.
Prime Minister Bart de Wever’s government is worried about the legal ramifications for Belgium, given most of the funds are housed at Brussels-based Euroclear.
“We hear the Belgian concerns and we understand them,” Heinen said on Friday in Dublin. “We’re looking for ways how we can address those concerns.”

Speaking in an interview on the sidelines of the informal meeting of European Union finance ministers, Heinen also sounded upbeat on the prospect of the bloc securing a deal on a capital markets union by year-end.
“I’m optimistic,” he said. “Let’s get it done on this specific matter in order to increase productivity, entrepreneurship and boosting our growth.”

The EU has been trying for more than a decade to create a single, bloc-wide market for capital. That would help local companies secure financing, encourage cross-border investment, and centralize financial oversight. Officials have repeatedly said this is essential to boosting Europe’s long-term growth potential.

items.title: Brookfield's Flatt Says AI 'Slowing Down Anyway' as Builders Can't Keep Up
body: Brookfield Corp. Chief Executive Officer Bruce Flatt said the artificial-intelligence race is already slowing because developers can’t build enough infrastructure to keep pace with what AI companies are demanding.

The leaders of major AI companies, including Anthropic PBC Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, have said in recent days that AI labs must slow the pace of the technology to address unpredictable risks and prevent advanced AI models from slipping beyond human control.
Even before then, the sector was running up against the limitations of how quickly data centers and other infrastructure can be put in place, Flatt said.

“We as an industry can’t build enough. We can’t even build a fraction of what everyone thinks they need,” he said at Brookfield’s annual investor day on Thursday. “So when they say they’re going to slow it down, it’s slowing down anyway because there is not enough compute to be able to deliver what everyone thinks they need.”
Brookfield has estimated that AI infrastructure will require more than $7 trillion in capital investment over the next decade.
Flatt said the slowdown is good because it “will bring more discipline into the system.”

items.title: Singapore Air Wins Best-Airline Award as Qatar Cedes Top Spot
body: Singapore Airlines Ltd. was awarded the title of world’s best airline in the annual rankings by Skytrax, taking the top spot from Qatar Airways in a year that saw Middle Eastern carriers come under significant pressure from the ongoing war in Iran.

The award, which is based on a survey of almost 25 million travelers, was announced in London on Friday, with a list dominated by Asian carriers. Only one European airline — Air France-KLM — made the Top 10, and not a single US company, despite their efforts to upgrade their passenger experience and premium cabins.

The Skytrax recognition gives airlines bragging rights with the flying public, at a time when premium travel is rising in popularity around the world. Besides the overall ranking, Air France was also awarded with the top prize for its La Premiere first class, which the French airline is expanding amid booming demand.
Read More: Air France Expands First-Class ‘La Premiere’ Routes on US Demand

The conflict in the Middle East has proved a major challenge for airlines worldwide, with soaring oil prices and dampened consumer demand. Ultimately, the Gulf carriers were the worst hit in the immediate aftermath forcing Qatar Airways and Emirates to temporarily suspend their service after the conflict erupted.
Last year, Qatar Airways won the best-airline title, a position for which it has dueled with Singapore Airlines over for the past decade.

items.title: Sadio Mané Bets $20 Million of Own Money on Senegalese Mangoes
body: Senegalese football star Sadio Mané is betting millions of dollars of his own money that the West African nation’s mangoes can become a crop that spurs economic development in the country of his birth.

The forward, who now plays for Saudi pro-league club Al-Nassr FC after a storied career with Liverpool, is putting 11.7 billion CFA francs ($20.4 million) into an agro-industrial complex in his hometown of Bambali that will sort and export fresh mangoes and produce pulp, dried fruit and mango butter.
“I want the wealth of our land to stay here, at home,” Mané told reporters in Dakar, Senegal’s capital, on Thursday evening ahead of the project’s opening ceremony.
The goal is to tackle one of the biggest constraints facing Senegal’s mango growers: Turning a highly perishable crop into something that can be stored, processed and sold abroad.

Senegal exports tens of thousands of tons of fresh mangoes, mainly to Europe, but processes only about 2% locally. The project plans to process 8,500 tons a year and includes a 500-hectare (1,236 acres) plantation to secure supply.

The project’s financial model calls for returns of more than 100% on the investment, with the operation turning profitable in its second year, the project’s promoters said. Plans are to sell into Senegal as well as African, European and Middle Eastern markets.

For Mané, the investment is part of a broader portfolio beyond football. He owns a majority stake in French club Bourges FC and has invested in property and hospitality projects there, while also building a real estate portfolio in Senegal including a shopping mall in Dakar’s upscale Almadies neighborhood.

items.title: ECB Rate Hikes Don't Solve Inflation Problem, Giorgetti Says
body: European Central Bank interest-rate increases don’t address soaring consumer prices across the euro area, according to Italian Finance Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti.

“Inflation stems from a supply shock, not so much from an overheated economy and excessive demand, which would need to be tempered by restrictive monetary policy,” he said Friday. “Certainly this can help, but by itself it doesn’t solve the problem.”

This isn’t the first time Italian politicians have voiced discontent with ECB policy, though criticism has typically been more vocal. Deputy Prime Ministers Antonio Tajani and Matteo Salvini have repeatedly chastised the central bank over rate hikes.
“Inflation, if the two wars continue in this manner, is inevitably destined to rise, and this is another serious problem for families and businesses,” Giorgetti said.
The Italian finance minister is in Dublin for informal meetings with European Union peers and monetary policy chiefs, including ECB President Christine Lagarde.

On Friday, Lagarde wouldn’t be drawn on what the ECB — which already has increased interest rates twice — will do next, though she stressed that “interest rates do not move in lockstep with the price of energy.”

In Italy, the government is shielding consumers from spiraling energy prices by implementing a tax cut on diesel fuel. While it describes this measure as “temporary,” it has repeatedly been renewed, most recently this week.
Lagarde on Friday again repeated the ECB’s stance — also shared by EU officials — that support measures for households and companies “should be targeted, temporary and tailored.”

That way “you really hit the nail of this inflation cost, but it’s also sufficiently targeted and temporary that when it becomes smoother, better, cheaper, it’s removed instantly,” she told Irish radio RTE.

items.title: CSN Asset Sales Gain Momentum as New CEO Fuels Bond Rally
body: Bonds issued by Cia. Siderúrgica Nacional SA are among the best performers in emerging markets following the appointment of its new CEO, as investors bet the company’s ambitious asset-sale program will finally move forward and allow the steelmaker to reduce its heavy debt load.
Leia em português.

Former Vale SA boss Fabio Schvartsman was announced as new CEO on Sept. 2 — a move seen by investors and bank creditors as emblematic of a new phase for the steel giant, which has been led by Benjamin Steinbruch for two decades. The naming of a person outside the controlling family was seen as a win, giving power to someone that will finalize deals that have been in the works for years.

“It’s a positive ‘symbolic’ move,” said Nicolas Giannone, an analyst at Balanz. While Steinbruch will still be Chairman, “it does put a new face to a ‘new’ CSN, and reaffirms their intention to delever and streamline the business.”
Bonds issued by the company have returned in the period since the announcement about 5% on average, while a broader gauge of emerging-market corporate debt handed a 0.5% loss.

The sale of the cement unit is more advanced, and a deal could be announced in the coming weeks, according to people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified discussing private information. Huaxin, Votorantim and Polimix each made binding offers of about 11 billion reais, the people said — that’s below the 15 billion reais CSN sought for the asset, though the company may accept the lower price, they added.
The unit is pledged as a collateral to banks in a loan of at least $1.2 billion provided in March, people familiar said earlier this year.

CSN is also selling Stahlwerk Thuringen, or SWT, a steel unit in Germany it bought in 2012 for $634 million, the people said, asking not to be named because negotiations are private. CSN is also receiving bids for some infrastructure assets and may sell them piecemeal instead of the minority stake in the infrastructure business combined it had sought to unload, the people added.

Shareholders of CSN Mineração are also mulling increasing their stake given depressed valuations, buying more from the controlling holding, the people said without specifying which holders. Itochu Corporation is the company’s second biggest shareholder, with a 10.85% bought in 2024 for 4.42 billion reais, while Japão Brasil Minério de Ferro Participações Ltda is the third biggest, with a 9.35% stake, according to the company. Japão Brasil is an Itochu subsidiary.

Votorantim declined to comment. Representatives for CSN, CSN Mineração, Embu SA, Huaxin’s unit in Brazil, and Polimix didn’t reply to a request for comment. Itochu, the owner of Japão Brasil, said in a message that it doesn’t comment on market rumors, speculation, or matters relating to potential changes in its investment holdings unless and until disclosure is required.

Steinbruch is seen as a tough negotiator in asset sales, known to ask for better conditions. The last time CSN sold the control of a business was in 2018, when it received $400 million for its CSN LLC US steel operation.

Investors are largely bullish his replacement will be able to push the divestment forward given Schvartsman’s decades of experience leading some of Brazil’s largest industrial and natural-resource companies, including Vale and paper maker Klabin SA.
Cesar Fernandez, a partner at Alpha Credit Advisors Ltd., said the new CEO has the ability to accelerate CSN’s asset sale program and rein in “a leverage path that has gone the wrong way for years.”

He will be expected to deliver quickly. Even after their recent surge, CSN’s dollar bonds are still nursing an average loss of about 11.2% in 2026. Earlier this year, investors dumped the steelmaker’s notes on fears it could become the next Brazilian company pushed to the brink by the nation’s double-digit interest rates.
Read More: Fears Flare in Brazil as Deep Downgrade Rattles the Bond Market

It also continues to bleed cash. Last quarter CSN posted an adjusted net loss of 773 million reais ($151.7 million), its 10th straight deficit and one that was six times wider than the year-ago period.

CSN borrowed heavily to make investments in its various units, and high interest rates and foreign competition that weighed on growth have battered its balance sheet. Its net debt climbed to 42.1 billion reais as of June 30, pushing the net leverage ratio to 3.5 times earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization.

Schvartsman’s experience could also help during negotiations with creditors, according to Itaú BBA analyst Daniel Sasson. He also pointed to the CEO’s achievements, like approval of the Puma 1 project at Klabin, which doubled the company’s Ebitda.

“The new guy has a strong track record and also managed through uncertain times when he was at Klabin and Vale,” said Manuel Mondia, a portfolio manager at Aquila Asset Management. “The management news brought back bonds from the lows, and further upside is now dependent on the execution of the company’s plans.”

items.title: John Wilson's Documentary 'The History of Concrete' Goes Hard
body: The History of Concrete isn’t quite what its title suggests. In his first feature documentary, out in theaters Sept. 18, filmmaker John Wilson attends a workshop on how to write a Hallmark holiday movie, befriends a musician handing out samples at his neighborhood liquor store, and ends up at a banquet table with Kim Kardashian, all while trying to learn about the ancient and ubiquitous building material.

Fans of his HBO comedy series How To with John Wilson will recognize these unpredictable side-quests. Known for capturing the mundane strangeness of everyday life in his signature, deadpan way, Wilson typically traced a circuitous path over that show’s three seasons, roaming New York City and beyond exploring urban fixtures like scaffolding and public restrooms. His feature-length journey into concrete is similarly singular, but Wilson does provide an unforgettable perspective on the material’s role in the built environment, as well as its enormous environmental impact.

This isn’t an exploration of concrete architecture or a defense of the material’s aesthetic virtues; instead, Wilson is concerned with the modern world’s short-sighted pursuit of growth and profit while humanity inches closer to a catastrophic future. Accordingly, the film’s absurdities are laced with anxieties. A deep-dive into the huge amounts of sand used in the production of concrete and glass will make you fearful of a resource-deprived tomorrow. Wilson’s attempts at home repairs, including mixing his own concrete, will make you want to rent for life. “Everything is fragile and nothing lasts forever,” says the director. “This movie is me dealing with that.”

The History of Concrete is also a portrait of New York City under former Mayor Eric Adams, which was not unlike life in New York before Eric Adams. (Wilson created a video for current Mayor Zohran Mamdani about scaffolding reform earlier this year.) While the mayor promises to unleash a wave of new home construction, public resources like city pools and the triple-cantilevered Brooklyn-Queens Expressway are pushed to their limits. Municipal workers pave over a makeshift goldfish pond Bed-Stuy residents built beneath a leaking fire hydrant, while Nolita residents fight off an affordable housing development proposal.

Wilson’s trips outside the city add tremendous color, especially a visit to Ohio to find America’s oldest concrete street, which leads to meeting people who preserve the tattoos of dead loved ones. At a concrete conference in Las Vegas, the filmmaker learns about 3D printing construction technology and is so turned off by its gloppy look that he declines to visit the much-publicized Starbucks built by it. As in his HBO show, the 39-year-old filmmaker offers voiceover commentary and occasional on-screen presence, often glimpsed behind the camera or Zoom screen as he pursues his latest narrative detour.

Wilson was raised on Long Island but is now fully invested in Ridgewood, Queens, as a homeowner and neighborhood movie theater impresario. He recently spoke with Bloomberg CityLab about his experiences learning about concrete and what he thinks about life in New York after the Adams administration.
What’s with the horrific backgrounds you have in your Zoom meetings throughout the documentary?

I spend a lot of time on Zillow just casually surfing, and I often take screenshots of the most punished interiors that I encounter and then cycle through them as Zoom backgrounds. It’s aspirational. I like to picture myself in these rooms even if I can’t do an open house.

You mentioned at one point in the documentary how you used to live in all sorts of conditions when you were younger. How has homeownership changed your relationship with New York or your perception of city government?

I like owning a house. But it also just feels weird. It’s like I’m still renting, but my security deposit is way bigger. I used to live in a loft with six or seven other people and built a room for myself the size of a mattress. When I got a TV show all of a sudden my value had changed through a bunch of zeros and ones in the air, which meant I was able to buy a house. The only thing that has physically changed in my life is that I have a key to a place that no one else does if society were to collapse.

When you pointed out in the documentary that the sidewalk in front of your house was historically inaccurate and had to be removed — that seemed like something that a homeowner would get wind of. How did you learn about that rule?

I found out only because I asked the contractor why. They were replacing all of the sidewalk nonstop for an entire summer, and just when I had thought they had finally finished, they went and tore up every sidewalk square all over again just because of a historical inaccuracy. I found that so ludicrous because there were so many other strange historical inaccuracies within Ridgewood. It was so funny to pry apart the idea of historical accuracy, and that’s what this movie does.
Your side trip to Bellefontaine, Ohio, was quick but really added a lot. What made you decide to go there?

I initially just wanted to go there because I knew that the oldest concrete street in America was there and it looked like it was in pretty bad shape. I ended up doing a lot more than I thought one could in Bellefontaine. I also went to the highest point in Ohio and the shortest street in America. Those are three very big tourist attractions within one small town. And the tattoo preservation people were nearby, too, which turned out to be maybe my favorite part of the whole experience.
It seemed like you came away from the concrete conference horrified when everyone else there was having a good time. What did you learn from the experience that changed how you see the material?

There’s so many strange environmental factors that go into what makes concrete, which I hadn’t really thought about before. Seeing how the student competition worked was really interesting. You had drastically different mixtures from different parts of the world competing against each other. The mortar workability competition was cool because they brought sand from their home countries; sometimes the sand would be way too wet, and they would have to dry it.

But the 3D-printed concrete demonstration was horrifying to me. Looking at a finished building designed with a machine like that is so inelegant; it just looks like a gray layer cake. It seems like this is what the industry wants the future to look like though. Aesthetic critiques don’t usually age very well, but it just doesn’t seem right to me.

The 3D-printed Starbucks in Texas received a lot of press when it opened, but I hadn’t seen any follow-ups until your documentary. The concrete looked like it was in rough shape. You didn’t even want to visit. What was your takeaway from the footage you received?

I didn’t wanna even be near it. People were using it like any other Starbucks — it doesn’t seem like people seem to care where they get their slop a lot of the time — and for a business like that, let ’em have it. But I don’t like the interchangeability of architecture these days. I don’t like how any building could be any other building. A structure should be built with pride and intent. You should know what’s going in there and it should ideally stay that way.
I found the part about sand to be really anxiety inducing.

The first version of this movie was very gloom and doom, and I think that’s why I had such a hard time getting it financed. I had read all of these books about concrete. There’s a really great book about sand called The World In a Grain. It’s really shocking. I had no idea that everything around us is made from sand. I didn’t want to be too pedantic about it, but it’s really scary what’s happening with sand. The fact that we’re dedicating so much of it to concrete production is alarming.
Read more:     A New Movie Reveals the Most Disliked Substance on Earth

We’re not gonna be able to make concrete as we know it for much longer. That’s just an environmental fact. We take sand from places that need it, and then we try to replenish our shorelines periodically to make up for the fact that we’re taking sand from just offshore. Wealthy beach communities have the tax revenue to replenish their shorelines for vacation communities, but a lot of other places don’t. And then there’s the amount of water needed to make it.

I’m not an engineer or an architect. All I know is what I read and what I see, and I think that not questioning this material has done more harm than good. One of the books I read explained that this all goes back to the San Francisco earthquake of 1906. It was a defining moment for the concrete industry because one or two of the big storage facilities that were made of concrete survived, so they’d say, “Look at how amazing this stuff is! It survived the earthquake and the fires while everything else perished.” But it wasn’t really true because, structurally, it’s heavily compromised by fire. And as I understand it from what I’ve read, the industry has been using that as a way to promote itself for a long time. It feels like people are only thinking with a 40-year timeline, which is really destructive.

This was filmed when Eric Adams was mayor and it seemed like you found that administration to reflect an uninspiring type of city government. Does anything seem meaningfully different in New York since Mamdani came in?

It seems like there’s a lot more attention being paid to issues that affect people during their everyday lives, like Mamdani responding to TikToks about a pothole or when he fixed the Williamsburg Bridge bike lane bump on day one. It’s hard to tell. There are a lot of superficial things that happen within city government and I have a lot of friends that are either within the administration or even nominated for state senate.

I’m invested in whoever is trying to improve the lives of New Yorkers. It’s tough to put politics in a movie; it’s something I was afraid of for a while. But Eric Adams is such a funny character to throw in there, and I’m glad I caught him at the end of his administration, because he is goofy and villainous in certain ways. That’s cool to have as the political figurehead in the movie, because people have such mixed reactions to him. But he also ushered in the City of Yes stuff, which is very much in line with Mamdani’s push to build more affordable housing. You could say that they’re not too dissimilar in that way, but they’re coming at it from different directions.

And then caught in the middle of them, you have the concrete industry that’s obviously happy as a pig in s--t to have the opportunity to build at this scale. But there’s a real blind spot in there somewhere. People get really caught up in political messaging, whether it’s about affordable housing or having a livable city. It seems there’s a party line and I try not to get too close to any party in that way just so that I can try to figure out what’s happening somewhere in the middle, because someone is benefiting from this somewhere.

I just wanted to make a film that took NIMBY politics at surface level in certain ways and critique it. There are a lot of NIMBY voices in the movie, like [New York City Council member] Vickie Paladino, who has said some awful, awful stuff. But I also think there is some truth in the conservative angle about our infrastructure being at a breaking point. What do we plan to do with all of this extra housing that we’re just throwing into the mix? We’ve all seen that the sewers can’t handle the deluges that we get so frequently now. And then you see the Pfizer building falling apart when contractors are building extra layers onto a top of a city that maybe isn’t ready for it.

A lot of the time affordable housing is a third-rail issue because while conservatives might say they’re opposing it because of infrastructure, it might be because of racism. So you have to just look at what they’re voting for to see if they actually care about this thing that they’re complaining about or if they just don’t want their wealthy constituents to have to live near affordable housing.
Is there a type of city storytelling that you haven’t done yet or are really hoping to do next?

I have a couple of big ideas. I’m not gonna say what they are, but I have a project that’s been percolating that has to do with what’s happening at eye level in the city and how our sight lines are being transformed.
