items.title: AI Panic Takes a Page From Medieval Millenarianism
body: The Mainstream Media has finally caught up with The Watchtower, the Jehovah’s Witnesses signature publication, and turned the spotlight on the end of the world. Jacob Coxon quit his job at the AI giant Anthropic in despair, tweeting that people in the industry believe that there is a more than 10% chance of the technology destroying humanity in the next decade; Evan Hubinger, a serving Anthropic executive, tweeted that “Jacob is correct here”; and, lo and behold, columns and editorials on the end of the world rained down like manna from heaven.

I’m not qualified to judge whether the 10% figure makes any sense. Some AI scientists think that it is hysterical nonsense; others that, even if it is on the high side, there is still a chance of Armageddon. It strikes me, as a mere scribbler, that, even if there is only a 1% chance of the total destruction of mankind, we ought to put on the brakes. Donald Trump’s assurance that “the only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT” is not reassuring enough.

The question of whether the world is about to end is only one of two Armageddon-related problems we have. The other is what might be called the “Armageddon mindset.” By the “Armageddon mindset” I mean more than just an undue focus on the end-of-times. (If you really believe that the end of the world is nigh, who is to say what degree of focus is undue.) I mean a style of thinking that sees a cosmic disaster lurking behind every problem and that almost relishes the prospect of a final reckoning.

The best way to understand the apocalypse mindset is to read Norman Cohn’s classic history of medieval religious fervor, The Pursuit of the Millennium (1957). Cohn shows that throughout the Middle Ages European societies were repeatedly convulsed by millenarian frenzies, frenzies that drew in part from Christian texts, particularly the Book of Revelation, and in part from social discontent and alienation, and that were led by a succession of weird prophets.

These prophets did not present the end of the world as a great full stop. They presented it rather as a great reckoning — the world would be convulsed by a final struggle between Good and Evil, with God and his angels on one side and the Antichrist and other horned beasts on the other, and the human species would be divided between the saved and the damned, with the saved living in eternal bliss, free of the curses of work, illness and death, and the damned writhing in hellfire. Having fired up their followers with holy visions, these prophets regularly led them to disaster, either in the form of violent conflicts with the authorities or short-lived communes that collapsed in disaster.

Cohn argues that the great totalitarian movements of the 20th century, Nazism and Communism, have a lot in common with medieval millenarianism. Both Nazis and Communists thought in terms of an existential struggle between good and evil. Both put their faith in prophets who could interpret the hidden meaning of history and lead their followers to the promised land — the Thousand-Year Reich in Hitler’s formulation or the classless society in Lenin’s. “What has set these latter-day movements so utterly apart from the ordinary run of political parties in Europe,” says Cohn, “is precisely their way of endowing social conflicts and aspirations with a transcendental significance — in fact with all the mystery and majesty of the final, eschatological drama.”

It’s hard to read this sentence and not shudder. For the world’s two greatest centers of economic and political power — Silicon Valley and Washington — are full of people who endow “social conflicts and aspirations with a transcendental significance.” Cohn’s millenarians almost always came from the socially marginal groups — the poor, displaced or marginally educated, the wanderers at the edges of medieval society. This was equally true in the 18th and 19th centuries when prominent millenarians included Joanna Southcott, an elderly rural spinster who claimed in 1814 that she was the Woman of the Apocalypse, pregnant with a savior who would usher in the end of times, and attracted 100,000 followers. But many of today’s great prophets of the millennium in Silicon Valley or Washington are among the richest and best educated people on the planet.

The leading merchant of Armageddon is Peter Thiel, a Stanford University graduate, chess prodigy, and a venture capitalist with a fortune of some $35 billion. No Joanna Southcott he. Thiel has taken to giving closed-door (but extensively leaked) lectures on the anti-Christ. There is a lot of trolling going on here — he even suggests that Greta Thunberg is the Antichrist — but there is also a serious point. Thiel appears to believe that the world is currently in a state of unprecedented turmoil because of the technological revolution. Progressives such as Thunberg are determined to preserve the old power structure by playing on people’s fears of the future (“talking constantly about Armageddon, about rumors of wars”); the job of tech revolutionaries is to push ahead, worries be damned, and usher in a new age of abundance. Thiel has a well-stocked compound in New Zealand in case this worries-be-damned strategy goes wrong.

This habit of dividing the world into the saved and the damned pervades everything Thiel does. He invests heavily in building up defenses from external threats (Palantir Technologies); in providing the chosen few with escape routes from failing public services (including funding students to drop out of university); and in extending people’s lifespans, ideally by abolishing death. All this recalls Cohn’s world in which God and the Devil fight their final battle and the Saints emerge from the chaos to live a life of perpetual fruitfulness.

Raised in a conservative Lutheran Christian family, Thiel is unusually vocal on Armageddon. But he is far from alone in his thinking. A surprising number of Silicon Valley residents share his disposition to think about technology, particularly AI, in messianic terms. Their world is divided, if not between saints and sinners, then between high-IQ types who understand the power of technology and regular people who don’t. Nor is Thiel the most extreme of the prophets.

Almost every crazy idea that you can find in the history of millenarianism can be found in the Valley: that a new age of abundance is at hand, ending the need to work; that we can live forever by uploading our mind into machines; that we are creating God in the form of superintelligence; that we can acquire superhuman powers by enhancing our bodies with machines; and, on the negative side, that our only chance of escaping the coming Flood is to build latter-day Arks in the form of spaceships. Elon Musk’s insistence that we must become an inter-planetary species reeks of Star Trek crossed with the Book of Revelation.

You can hear similar arguments in Washington, sometimes dressed up in the language of science (Thiel has more than 16 allies in the Trump administration), sometimes in their original religious idiom. Paula White-Cain, who leads the White House Faith Office and is Trump’s closest spiritual advisor, is a member of the Seven Mountain Mandate, a California-based millenarian sect. Pete Hegseth, the secretary of war, has a tattoo on his biceps that reads “deus vult (“God wills it”) and another one on his chest that depicts a Jerusalem Cross. JD Vance, who made a fortune in Silicon Valley under Thiel’s guidance and has recently converted to Roman Catholicism, bestrides the gap between the religious and scientific wings of Trump’s millenarian army.

A surfeit of millenarianism is hardly conducive to solving ordinary problems. How can politicians focus on fixing potholes when they are trembling at the thought of the end of the world? And how can they strike deals with the other side when they think that it bears the mark of the beast? But there are plenty of extraordinary problems that an addiction to the apocalyptic style of thinking could render terminal: the stand-off between Iran and Israel, in a part of the world that millenarianism has made its home; Vladimir Putin’s increasingly desperate attempt to hold onto power, conflated into a civilizational struggle; and AI’s staggering advance. The worst that Cohn’s millennium-obsessed subjects could do was to put a few thousand people to the flames. Today’s Apocalypse peddlers can bring about the very thing that they are constantly talking about.

items.title: Stalling Argentine Recovery Is a Risk for Milei's Reelection Bid
body: A year out from Argentine President Javier Milei’s reelection bid, the economic recovery that underpinned his popularity is stalling.

Gross domestic product shrank 0.6% in the second quarter from the previous three months, the first contraction in two years and a setback for a government counting on stronger growth ahead of the October 2027 election.

Argentines elected the libertarian outsider in 2023 hoping austerity and freer markets could tame inflation and stabilize the crisis-prone economy. Milei’s “shock therapy” succeeded in sharply slowing price increases, but polls show voters are increasingly concerned about the weak jobs market.

Output rose 2% from a year earlier, supported by booming exports of energy and agricultural products, while imports fell. In a post on X, Economy Minister Luis Caputo boasted that 13 of 16 sectors grew in the first half of the year.

Even so, the latest GDP figures are “not nearly compelling enough to dispel political concerns — the key variable weighing on Argentina’s markets,” said Jimena Zuniga, an Argentina economist at Bloomberg Economics.
Investors in the nation’s sovereign debt worry that weakening support for Milei’s program could increase the chances of a reversal of his fiscal and market reforms after the 2027 election.
Milei’s leftist opponents are seeking to turn rising unemployment and weak household incomes into the central issues of the October 2027 election.
Fernando Marull, partner at consulting firm FM&A, sees a possible second consecutive contraction in the third quarter, which would technically put Argentina in a recession.
Even if the economy escapes a recession, the outlook for households is still bleak, said Carlos Melconian, director of MacroView SA.
“Whether or not you get two negative quarters, it’s going to be extremely close,” Melconian said. “The components people actually feel are already getting crushed.”

Annual inflation slowed to 34% last month, from more than 200% when Milei took office. An AtlasIntel poll last month found that corruption and unemployment have overtaken inflation among voters’ top concerns.
Milei, however, remains focused on consolidating his victory over inflation, which he wants to push below a monthly rate of 1%.
That’s led him to back a strong peso policy, even though it’s weighing on growth. The currency weakened just 3.7% against the dollar in the year through August, while consumer prices rose 21%.
That real appreciation has been bolstered in recent weeks by official intervention in bond and futures markets, while currency controls on companies remain in place.

Milei’s opponents are increasingly focused on this point. At an event earlier this month, the clearest contender, Buenos Aires Governor Axel Kicillof, called the government’s approach a “criminal, suicidal policy of deindustrializing the country.”

Opposition lawmakers have also taken the argument to Congress, recently forcing a session on rising household indebtedness and loan delinquencies, though none of the proposals for relief have moved forward yet.
Milei tells a different story, pointing to strong growth in agriculture, energy and mining as evidence of an economy that has turned the corner.
At the same time, retail, construction and manufacturing, which employ far more people, are shedding jobs, while defaults on consumer loans are soaring.
Consumption contracted 2.4% in the second quarter as sluggish wage growth and tight credit hit household finances.
Those struggling sectors account for roughly half of Argentina’s registered private salaried employment, while the industries powering exports and investment account for only about a fifth.
Overall, registered private salaried employment has shrunk by about 246,300 jobs since just before Milei took office, while the number of companies has fallen by more than 30,000.
That leaves Milei vulnerable heading into the election. His approval stood at 38% in the latest AtlasIntel survey, with 58% disapproving and 70% describing the job market as bad.
The government this week lowered its 2026 growth forecast to 3% from 5%, while economists surveyed by the central bank expect something closer to 2%.

Osvaldo Giordano, president of the IERAL economic institute at Fundación Mediterránea, expects the economy to dodge recession, with output approximately flat this quarter. But the gap between meager growth and what Argentines expect after enduring years of economic turmoil is a risk for Milei, he said.
“A society’s tolerance is not the same when you have a single bad year,” Giordano said. “Here, it’s a succession of very bad years. So patience is lower.”

items.title: Mbappé Signs Up for On's Push Into Football in Blow to Nike
body: On Holding AG has signed French superstar Kylian Mbappé to lead its push into football, mounting a bold challenge to Nike Inc. and Adidas AG’s dominance of the sport.

The Swiss company will outfit Mbappé, the 27-year-old striker who’s already the World Cup’s all-time goal leader, in newly designed boots as it expands the use of its Lightspray shoemaking technology, according to a statement. Mbappé, centerpiece of club powerhouse Real Madrid, previously represented Nike.
The partnership agreement is set to last for 10 years, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named discussing confidential matters.
On shares rose as much as 3.8% on the news, before paring some of those gains. Nike and Adidas edged lower.

On has also hired Thierry Henry, a former star player on the French national team and for Arsenal in the English Premier League, as its director of football. Financial details of the partnerships weren’t disclosed.

The Roger Federer-backed company has grown rapidly since its 2010 founding, starting with running shoes and expanding into tennis, training and outdoor sports. It’s also pushing to increase its revenue from apparel, both from sports and also as lifestyle offerings. On plans to host an investor day on Tuesday where it’s expected to lay out financial targets for the next few years.

The splashy entrance into football helps build the case for long-term revenue growth at On, even as some investors worry about a slowdown in lifestyle products, Kelly Crago, an analyst at BMO Capital Markets, said in a note. It’s possible to imagine football bringing in as much as $400 million in annual revenue by 2031, the analyst estimated.

While football has long been the world’s most popular sport, it’s grown even more as a source of lifestyle and fashion items in recent years for competitors like Adidas and Nike, as well as Puma SE. The brands experienced a spike in sales this summer with football shirts from teams they sponsored in the World Cup.

Football has faced less disruption from so-called challenger brands in recent years than running, where upstarts like On and Hoka have gained market share with innovative footwear offerings. New Balance and Skechers have made some inroads in football, with the latter sponsoring England star Harry Kane, who also plays for FC Bayern Munich.
On is looking to “rethink product for the demands of the game while bringing a new energy to the culture that surrounds it,” it said in the statement.
Earlier: Swiss Brand On Eyes Football Market Dominated by Adidas and Nike

Mbappé will work closely with On’s staff to develop and test football shoes and apparel, while also representing the brand off the pitch, it said. Aside from being one of football’s top talents, Mbappé has also gained fans for his fashion sense, appearing in campaigns for Dior.
“What drew me to On was the opportunity to build something entirely new together that will help shape tomorrow’s game,” Mbappé said in the statement.
A Nike spokesperson didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

On believes that its LightSpray technology — in which robots spray the upper part of a shoe from a filament within minutes — will be an advantage in football. The goal is to create products that are “exceptionally lightweight, precise and close to the athlete like a second skin,” it said.

On introduced the technology in 2024 and has expanded its use from high-end marathon shoes to more mass-market products. It opened a dedicated LightSpray factory in South Korea earlier this year and plans to start another plant soon in Vietnam, with future sites potentially coming in the US and Europe, Caspar Coppetti, co-chief executive officer, said in an interview in June.

On’s initial foray into football came in December when it signed Swiss teenage star Sydney Schertenleib, who plays for the FC Barcelona women’s team, to collaborate on products geared toward training and lifestyle. She will now represent the brand in football, too, helping develop products designed for the women’s game, the statement said.

items.title: EU Trade Partners Call for Retreat From Pesticide Curbs Plan
body: A group of countries including the US, Brazil, Japan and India have called on the European Union to backtrack on a pesticides curb proposal that could lead to tighter restrictions on agricultural imports.

Ahead of a key decision by EU member states next week, ambassadors from 19 nations warned of a “shared and growing concern” over the impact that the proposed rules could have on “international trade, sustainable agricultural practices and a science and rules-based trading system,” according to a letter seen by Bloomberg and addressed to the EU’s agriculture, trade and food safety chiefs on Friday morning.

The countries call for “meaningful consultations” with trade partners and for the EU to stick to international rules for setting setting the levels of pesticide residues allowed in agricultural imports. Most signatories also raised their concerns through the World Trade Organization.

The European Commission, the EU’s executive arm, proposed the measures in December as part of efforts to streamline and simplify food and feed safety legislation, while also aiming to “ensure a level playing field” for the bloc’s producers. The proposal would give the EU the power to ban imports with traces of pesticides that aren’t authorized in the bloc by setting their so-called Maximum Residue Levels, or MRLs, to zero.

An EU-commissioned study found in August that such import restrictions risk pushing up consumer prices. However, the proposal has strong support in some EU countries where farmers fear unfair competition.

EU member states are due to discuss the latest compromise proposal from Ireland, which holds the EU’s rotating presidency, on Wednesday, though it’s unclear whether it will get sufficient support, in part due to concerns over the impact of the MRL plans for global trade. Increasing permitting limits for pesticides in the bloc has also proved a controversial part of the package.

While the proposal is going through a separate process in the European Parliament, an agreement at the EU’s Council, made up of the 27 member countries, would remove a major roadblock for the proposal.
Spokespeople for the European Commission and Ireland’s EU presidency didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

items.title: Shakira vuelve a España con 12 conciertos y disputa fiscal
body: Read the story in English

Shakira vuelve a los escenarios españoles por primera vez en ocho años, en un momento en que el Tribunal Supremo del país examina un recurso que podría reabrir uno de los capítulos de su larga batalla con las autoridades fiscales.

La estrella del pop colombiana, de 49 años, ofrecerá 12 conciertos en Madrid a partir del viernes en un estadio temporal construido para la ocasión, ante una asistencia prevista de más de 600.000 personas. Las presentaciones marcan una suerte de regreso a casa tras años de disputas fiscales centradas en si residía en España a comienzos de la década de 2010.

Shakira obtuvo un fallo favorable que anuló casi €55 millones (US$63 millones) en impuestos y multas correspondientes a 2011. El caso es independiente de los cargos por el período 2012-2014, que resolvió en 2023 al declararse culpable de seis delitos de fraude fiscal y recibir una pena de prisión suspendida. El Tribunal Supremo examina ahora un recurso de las autoridades fiscales para revocar su victoria más reciente.
Shakira criticó duramente a las autoridades fiscales españolas tras el acuerdo de 2023 y se mudó a Miami ese mismo año. Ahora, su tono hacia España es mucho más cordial.

“Elegí Madrid para esta celebración”, escribió el mes pasado en el diario El País. “Aquí sucede algo que el mundo debería ver: la inmigración latina no solo se tolera, sino que se celebra. España la ha acogido con los brazos abiertos”.
En 2024, menos de un año después de declararse culpable, hablaba del país en términos muy distintos.

“Para mí, la década española fue una década financieramente perdida”, dijo Shakira en periódico El Mundo. “Hoy mi patrimonio consiste en lo que gané antes de llegar a España y lo que gané después de salir de ella. Todo lo que gané en esos años se lo quedó el Estado español”.
Un representante de Shakira declinó hacer comentarios.

Después de más de ocho años de batallas con las autoridades fiscales españolas, el caso de Shakira también ha alimentado entre algunos críticos el debate sobre si la autoridad fiscal española se excede en determinadas investigaciones.

Tras su victoria previamente este año, Shakira emitió un duro comunicado en el que dedicó el resultado a los “ciudadanos comunes que son maltratados y oprimidos cada día” por un sistema que, según dijo, parte de una presunción de culpabilidad.
“Nunca hubo fraude, y las autoridades fiscales jamás podrían demostrar lo contrario”, afirmó.

Shakira ha dicho que su residencia de conciertos será la mayor jamás realizada en Europa. La producción en Madrid también pondrá a prueba hasta qué punto un gran espectáculo puede generar ingresos más allá de las pocas horas que los asistentes pasan dentro del estadio.

Live Nation Entertainment Inc. construyó un estadio temporal con capacidad para 55.000 personas al sur de Madrid para acoger los espectáculos. Se estima que el impacto económico para la ciudad rondará los €150 millones, o unos €250 por cada asistente previsto.

Junto al estadio se encuentra el Parque Macondo, una feria bautizada en honor al pueblo imaginario creado por el escritor colombiano Gabriel García Márquez en Cien años de soledad. El espacio reúne decenas de negocios y actividades pensadas para que los fans permanezcan allí durante horas antes de que Shakira suba al escenario.
La residencia de Shakira pondrá fin a la gira mundial de su álbum Las Mujeres Ya No Lloran.
“Quiero que la gente sepa que mi amor por España y por mis queridos amigos y familiares españoles sigue intacto”, escribió Shakira en 2024. “Pero no todo es igual”.
Traducción editada por Malu Poveda.

items.title: Fitch Says Junk Rating Looms for Romania if Political Crisis Persists
body: Romania is running out of time to avoid a credit rating downgrade to junk as the prolonged political crisis puts fiscal credibility in jeopardy, according to an analyst from Fitch Ratings Inc.

Malgorzata Krzywicka said the government’s ability to narrow the budget deficit further and present a credible fiscal plan will be key for the assessment of its creditworthiness in the near term. Fitch is slated to next review Romania’s credit rating in January 2027.

The Black Sea country narrowly avoided the downgrade about two months ago. Since then, attempts to appoint a new prime minister with a stable parliamentary majority have failed, rasing the prospect of an early election.

“The longer the crisis persists without a functioning government, the more it raises questions about fiscal predictability and the capacity to deliver the needed adjustment,” Krzywicka said in an interview.

President Nicusor Dan on Thursday nominated a European lawmaker, Siegfried Muresan, as the country’s next prime minister. But his chances of winning a confidence vote in a highly fragmented parliament appear slim after the biggest party, the Social Democrats, signaled they are unlikely to support him.
Read more: Romania President Nominates Muresan as Premier to End Crisis
Romania’s dollar bonds, which were already underperforming all emerging- and frontier-market peers in a Bloomberg index on Friday, extended losses after the Fitch comments.

Another failed attempt to approve a government would bring Romania closer to early elections, prolonging the uncertainty and increasing the risks for the budget and the sovereign’s credit rating. Muresan has 10 days to form a government and ask for lawmakers’ approval.

Fitch left Romania’s rating at the lowest investment grade of BBB- with a negative outlook at the end of July. The decision came only after the government appealed the rating company’s initial assessment.

Krzywicka signaled the bar for maintaining the rating is rising with every week of the political crisis, which began after the government of Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan collapsed in May. He has stayed in charge with limited powers until his successor is found.

“Something that was supposed to be a relatively short-lived reshuffle of the government back when the government collapsed in the spring has extended well into the summer,” she said. “And now we are sort of past the middle of September and we still don’t have a resolution.”

Other rating companies have also taken note. S&P Global Ratings is scheduled to review Romania early next month. Moody’s Ratings affirmed Romania’s Baa3 score with a negative outlook earlier this year.

Krzywicka said Romania needs an an additional correction of about 1.5 percentage points of gross domestic product in the deficit to help stabilize the surge in the public debt over the medium term. Fitch currently estimates Romania’s 2026 budget deficit at 5.9% of economic output, below the government’s 6.2% target.

While the government has narrowed the gap from 9.3% of GDP in 2024, drafting the 2027 budget and presenting a credible path toward reaching the 3% shortfall are paramount to avoiding a downgrade, she said.

Krzywicka said the improvement in tax collection was one of the key methods to reducing the deficit in the coming years as the “room is limited on the expenditure side” after the austerity measures already implemented.

Romania’s current weak economic growth is also a concern for Fitch as the $430 billion economy struggles to shake off a recession and tame the European Union’s highest inflation rate. Krzywicka pushed back on arguments that stimulating growth could be a substitute for fiscal consolidation.
“Those are marginal gains,” she said. “They are nowhere near the scale of adjustment Romania needs to deliver. Stronger growth alone will not resolve the problem of large deficits.”
Romania’s economy is expected to contract modestly in 2026, with recovery projected for 2027 but still well below pre-pandemic growth rates.
Read more: Investors Look Past Romania Risk to Pocket Junk-Like Yields

Traders are already treating Romanian bonds as the EU’s only junk-rated sovereign debt, forcing the country to pay the highest borrowing costs in the block. The yield on dollar notes due in 2036 traded at 6.84%, higher than the yield on similar securities issued by South Africa that has non-investment credit rating.

Krzywicka described the broader market response to the current crisis as “relatively benign,” saying it was partly due to Romania’s good deficit numbers this year and to the inflow of EU funds. Those provide a backstop that allowed the country to continue accessing markets under pressure, she said.

items.title: Heat Sears Central US This Weekend as Hawaii on Flood Watch
body: Heat will continue to sear the Great Plains and central Mississippi Valley this weekend, as well as pushing into Texas, Oklahoma and even the eastern US, prompting the nation’s largest grid operator to call on customers to conserve energy.

Dallas Fort Worth International Airport is forecast to reach 100F (37.8C) Friday, after tying a daily record of 99F on Thursday. That was 11F warmer than normal, the US Weather Prediction Center said.

In addition to testing daily highs in 82 places, overnight low temperatures are expected to be near or at record warm levels at 122 sites around the US through Monday, the center said. That includes a forecast 71F in New York’s Central Park late Friday, which would come within a degree of toppling a 1972 record for a warm night.

The combination of high daytime temperatures and warm nights will lead to moderate to extreme heat risk — levels 2 to 4 on a 4-step scale — across large parts of the central US this weekend, the weather center said.
Power grids serving more than 100 million North Americans are bracing for a demand surge as the unseasonable heat strains electrical equipment scheduled for repairs.
Read More: Intense Heat Strains Power Grids for 100 Million North Americans

PJM Interconnection LLC issued a level 2 energy emergency alert for three mid-Atlantic utility zones in Maryland, Virginia and Washington DC, according to a website notice. PJM simultaneously asked consumers — mainly industrial and commercial — enrolled in demand-response programs to curtail usage.
Turning to the Pacific, flood watches are up across the Hawaiian Islands through Friday as the remnants of Tropical Storm Norbert move west across the chain, the National Weather Service said.
Norbert broke up about 780 miles (1,255 kilometers) east of Hilo, Hawaii Tuesday, but it’s still pumping heavy rain into the region. Flooding may close roads and cause damage in urban areas.

The US National Hurricane Center is also watching three other potential storms in the eastern and central Pacific. Two off Mexico’s southwest coast have a 80% chance of becoming a tropical system in the next seven days, while a third, east of the Hawaiian Islands, has a 30% chance.

items.title: Tata Sons IPO Tension: How Listing Pressure, Succession Row Is Causing Division
body: India’s largest conglomerate, Tata Group, is headed for an internal showdown as it wrestles with the question of who will lead its holding company Tata Sons Pvt., which is under regulatory pressure to go public.

What began as a succession battle, centered around the future of Natarajan Chandrasekaran as chairman, has escalated into a broader confrontation over who ultimately controls Tata Sons. It’s a dispute that has pitted the board against the patriarch of the founding family.

The crisis comes at a pivotal moment for the sprawling business empire, whose brands range from Taj hotels to Tetley tea. Tata Sons is undertaking a multibillion-push into semiconductor manufacturing — a key part of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s high-end technology ambitions.

Tata Sons is the holding company for all of the businesses of Tata Group. The group was founded nearly 160 years ago by Jamsetji Tata and its firms are among the country’s most influential, spanning cars, steel, software, airlines and hotels.
Of the 32 companies under the Tata Group umbrella, 26 are publicly listed, including industrial heavyweight Tata Steel Ltd., IT firm Tata Consultancy Services Ltd. and automaker Tata Motors Ltd.
The ownership structure of Tata Sons is at the heart of the fight over Chandrasekaran’s tenure and whether the holding company should go public.

Around 66% of Tata Sons is controlled by Tata Trusts, a collective of 13 charities that’s headed by Noel Tata, who took over in October 2024 after the death of his half-brother, Ratan Tata, the group’s longtime patriarch. Noel is also a director of Tata Sons, giving him a seat on both sides of the governance divide.

The Shapoorji Pallonji (SP) Group — chaired by Shapoorji Pallonji Mistry, the brother-in-law of Noel Tata — has an 18.4% stake in Tata Sons, while seven listed Tata companies together hold about 11.94%.

Chandrasekaran, or Chandra as he is commonly known, was the first non-Tata family member to lead Tata Sons. Mentored by Ratan Tata, he spent 30 years at Tata Consultancy Services, eight of them as chief executive officer.

Over the past decade, his biggest success was steering Tata Group into advanced technologies, including the manufacture of iPhones and electric vehicles. More recently, he’s been under pressure to lift the fortunes of the business, which has contended with a deadly Air India crash, a cyberattack on Jaguar Land Rover severe enough to dent the UK’s gross domestic product, and the growing threat that AI poses to Tata Consultancy Services.

Chandra announced in August that he would step down when his current term ends in February. This followed a months-long board impasse over his reappointment and disagreement about whether Tata Sons should pursue a public listing.

But after India’s banking regulator rejected Tata Sons’ request for an exemption from rules requiring it to go public, the company’s board voted 4-1 to pursue a listing and asked Chandra to remain for another five years. He agreed to stay on.

Tata Trusts called the reappointment “illegal” and said that Noel Tata has a special veto power that makes the board’s extension of Chandra’s term a “legal nullity.” It added that it was opposed to a listing and that Tata Sons should explore all available alternatives.
The dispute centers on two linked questions: who has the ultimate authority to choose Tata Sons’ leader, and whether Tata Sons’ century-old ownership structure can survive a public listing.
Ultimately, this is a battle over where the power resides inside the Tata empire, with the Tata Sons board and Noel Tata on opposite sides.

Noel Tata has argued that going public would undermine Tata Sons’ ownership structure. As SP Group has pushed for a listing and proposed monetizing part of its holdings for at least 250 billion rupees ($2.6 billion), Noel Tata has suggested that Tata Sons buy back part of that stake, funding the transaction through internal cash and the sale of listed shares or stakes in newer businesses.
After an Indian shadow lender defaulted on its debts in 2018, the Reserve Bank of India established new rules to try to ensure that such crises don’t endanger the country’s wider financial system.

It classified Tata Sons as an “upper-layer” non-bank finance company (NBFC) under the rules in 2022. This meant the company, whose balance sheet exceeds 1.5 trillion rupees, was deemed big enough by the RBI to pose a systemic risk, and is subject to tighter regulations.
The RBI’s rules require such businesses to list their shares on the stock market within three years as a way to force them to be more transparent about their activities and financial performance.

Since then, Tata Sons’ owners have taken various steps to convince the RBI that it should not be categorized as a shadow lender so that it can avoid going public. In 2024, Tata Sons applied to surrender its NBFC license and cleared its outstanding debts. The RBI rejected this application, signaling that it expects the company to adhere to the rules.
A separate RBI circular stipulated that a shadow lender can’t de-register if it deals directly with customers in its day-to-day business, which Tata Sons doesn’t but Tata Capital does.

Tata Sons sits at the center of the Tata empire. Its status as a private company controlled by Tata Trusts has helped to cement the family’s authority over the group’s array of businesses. Going public could substantially loosen Tata Trusts’ grip on Tata Sons and make it harder for Tata Sons’ directors to block unwanted takeover attempts.

Tata Sons has plowed billions of dollars into Tata Group businesses including its digital services arm and a venture into semiconductors. It has also helped to prop up the unprofitable national flag carrier Air India, which reported record losses for the year to March following a plane crash last year and airspace closures due to the Iran war.

A listing of the holding company would force it to make regular disclosures on its operations and financial dealings, showing how money is channeled through the Tata empire and ultimately forcing its owners to be more accountable for how its capital is spent.

SP Group has been trying for years to monetize its illiquid stake in Tata Sons and would likely be able to get a better price if the shares were listed. The proceeds could help it to pay down a pile of costly private debt.
Mistry welcomed the RBI’s decision not to exempt Tata Sons from the listing rules. He said that he looks forward to working “closely and constructively” with Tata Sons on the pathway to going public.

SP Group has previously locked horns with the Tatas. Ratan Tata and Tata Sons’ then-chairman Cyrus Mistry, a scion of the founding family that runs SP Group, were entangled in a yearlong feud in 2016.

items.title: Air France Expands 'La Premiere' Routes on Rising US Demand
body: Air France is expanding its first-class “La Première” offering to more US cities, including Boston, as the carrier bets on the continued strength of premium international travel.

The flagship airline will add destinations in the coming 18 months while also putting more capacity on existing routes, such as New York and Los Angeles, where demand for first-class seats keeps rising, Air France-KLM Chief Executive Officer Ben Smith said in an interview in Paris.
“We’re having more repeat business in the premium cabins,” Smith said. “It’s better than I would have thought, considering the situation.”

La Première is proving critical for the airline at a time of higher jet-fuel costs in the aftermath of the Iran war and a rising cost of living that’s pushing more Europeans to travel less. Its profile was raised even higher Friday when Air France was cited as having the world’s best first class in the annual airline rankings by Skytrax.

The carrier also won the top spots for first-class lounge dining and first-class comfort amenities, and it was named the best Western European airline for the six consecutive year. Skytrax recognition gives airlines bragging rights with the flying public.

Air France unveiled its redesigned first-class cabin last year, seeking to attract well-heeled customers with a travel experience the airline says is akin to stepping onto a private jet. It also offers spacious private suites at Charles de Gaulle airport for holders of “La Première” tickets.
Read More: Look Inside Air France’s Exclusive New Airport Lounge at CDG

Flights to New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport were the first to feature the redesigned cabin, where suites stretch across five windows and include an armchair and a chaise lounge that converts into a bed.

The largest airline lounge at the new international terminal there will be home to Air France starting next year. Air France will boost the number of New York flights with the new cabin to five daily from the current four, Smith said.
The number of flights on the profitable route between Paris and Miami also is growing.
Smith said the new first-class cabin required heavy investments and represented “a risk” at a time when the group wasn’t profitable.
“It was not a consensual decision,” he said.
Read More: A $5,000 Lounge With BMW Tarmac Drop-off Is New Airport Luxury

The luxury upgrades made with La Première “disproportionately added equity to our brand” and enabled Air France to expand its customer base, Smith said. European rivals Deutsche Lufthansa AG and IAG SA also are putting more emphasis on first-class and business travel.

In the US, Delta Air Lines Inc., American Airlines Group Inc. and United Airlines Holdings Inc. have said they’re generating more revenue from the front of their cabins, helping cushion the blow from soaring oil prices.

items.title: 'Not a Smart Move': Leno Slams Supercar Tax Avoiders as California Cracks Down
body: Jay Leno has amassed a legendary car collection and lent his name to a recent California law easing smog-check rules for some classics. But there’s one break for wealthy car owners he has little sympathy for: Montana license plates.

The comedian, whose Big Dog Garage in Burbank houses everything from century-old vehicles powered by steam to Bugattis and a McLaren F1 car, is siding with California tax authorities as they tighten the rules on luxury-car enthusiasts who use Big Sky tags to cut their bills.
“If you can afford the car, you probably can afford the tax,” Leno said in an interview. “California is ridiculously expensive to live in, but we want to live here.”

Leno is lending a prominent voice to a crackdown spreading across the US. States from Utah to Maryland are getting tough with residents who register vehicles elsewhere to avoid taxes and fees at home. Now California is joining the push and setting its sights on the “Montana loophole,” which lawmakers say is costing the state $20 million a year in lost revenue.

Evidence of what Leno is talking about was on display last month at Monterey Car Week, when some of the world’s rarest and most expensive cars descended on the California coast. Montana plates adorned Koenigsegg supercars, old Land Rover Defenders and Lamborghini Countachs.
Connor Wohl spotted one on a Ferrari 288 GTO, the limited-production 1980s car that now can command prices of more than $6 million.
“Given how rare and valuable those cars are, it certainly stood out,” said Wohl, co-founder of Manhattan Beach Cars and Coffee in El Segundo, California.

Montana, a state with about 1.1 million people, had more than 2.4 million registered vehicles for just 879,000 licensed drivers in 2024. That works out to almost three vehicles per driver — the highest in the country and more than twice the US average, according to a Bloomberg analysis of Federal Highway Administration data.

Lawmakers in California, with a population of around 39.5 million, argue that some residents are improperly putting legal ownership of a vehicle in the hands of out-of-state entities often based in Montana. The California legislature passed a bill in late August to bolster tax collection by making certain shell companies state residents.

Avoiding the state’s base sales and use tax rate of 7.25% would translate into savings of $435,000 on a $6 million car. Montana doesn’t have a general-use sales tax and registration fees are substantially lower than California’s.

“It’s a scam in my mind,” said California State Senator Jerry McNerney, the author of the bill, which has now gone to Governor Gavin Newsom’s desk. “Let’s close this loophole and make people pay their share.”

The practice is legal under certain circumstances. But with tax authorities bearing down, few owners of collectible cars are keen to discuss their use of Montana plates. Luxury-automobile clubs from Los Angeles to Monterey to Napa Valley didn’t respond to requests for comment.

At AutoTalent in Los Angeles County, which sells specialty parts for Ferraris, Lamborghinis, Porsches and other makes, Golan Haiem said the sales tax can make a real difference for those frequently flipping collectible cars.

“These cars are like stocks, going up and down like crazy,” Haiem said, adding that many owners buy and sell several cars a year. “The difference maker to break even or even make a little profit is that sales tax.”
That rankles gearheads like Leno. The former host of The Tonight Show will often take great expense to restore vehicles and keep them operational, a process displayed on Jay Leno’s Garage.

“It just seems like a real short-term solution, and I find a lot of the real car enthusiasts don’t really do it,” he said. “It’s guys that want to have something fancy, some high-powered car, and they don’t use it that much.”

The legislation approved last month expands the definition of who counts as a state resident to include a shell company in which at least one member of the business lives in California. It also authorizes the state to impose tax liabilities on the members of such a company.

Other states are making similar moves. In Utah, State Senator Brady Brammer authored legislation targeting Montana plates, saying his state misses out on millions of dollars a year because of such registrations.

On the East Coast, Maryland is targeting vehicles with Virginia tags, giving residents until Oct. 1 to register their cars under a “Plate Where You Live” campaign before new fines and enforcement measures kick in.

In California, Montana-plated vehicles aren’t automatically breaking the rules. Residents can generally avoid California tax on vehicles purchased for use elsewhere, including by keeping them outside the state for at least 12 months.
“It really ties our hands,” said Dennis David, a technical adviser at the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration.

Montana has a cottage industry for helping out-of-staters form companies to buy vehicles. One such firm, Montana Corporate, has 5,000 active clients, and Chief Executive Officer Jennifer McCluskey estimates that 60% are from California. Some customers register as many as 20 luxury cars at a time, she said.

Only two clients have been audited by their home state’s tax authorities during the 13 years since McCluskey took the business over from her parents, she said, emphasizing the company’s care with the legal details. Even with potential new restrictions, she said she sees little risk for car owners who follow the rules to the letter.

“We’ve had a lot of clients for a lot of years that have been driving around without any sort of problems,” McCluskey said. “I don’t want to sound cavalier, but I don’t take a lot of those threats super seriously.”
California has already been investigating luxury cars with plates from Montana, whose state capital of Helena is more than 16 hours by car from San Francisco or Los Angeles.
David’s team recently assessed more than $600,000 in unpaid taxes and fees after probing a Montana company with nine high-end vehicles including eight Ferraris valued at a combined $8 million.
“No one’s driving a Ferrari or Lamborghini in Montana on those roads, especially when half the year is snow,” said Robert Wellman, an investigator at California’s Department of Motor Vehicles.

Paying back taxes isn’t the only penalty. In March, California brought criminal charges against 14 people they claimed dodged almost $2 million in taxes, accusing them of using luxury vehicles plated in Montana to evade taxes and registration costs.
Leno, whose collection spans more than 300 vehicles, offered some advice for fellow collectors tempted by the savings.
“It’s not a smart move,” the comedian said. “Sooner or later you’re going to get caught.”

items.title: Donald Trump Just Made India's Oil Balancing Act Even Trickier
body: Welcome to our guide to the commodities driving the global economy. Today, New Delhi-based oil reporter Rakesh Sharma looks at the repercussions of shifting US energy policy for India.

For the world’s third-largest oil importer, buying barrels was once boringly predictable. During the past two years, it has been anything but, as India contorts itself to balance supply, price and a fickle White House.
That juggling act has just become even harder.
Indian refiners, once heavily dependent on the Middle East, reworked supply chains to snap up cheap Russian crude after the invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Then last year, the Trump administration publicly pressured New Delhi to cut back those purchases, an effort to resolve the war in Ukraine and its own trade headache.
All that was thrown out when the US began strikes on Iran in February, forcing Washington to relax restrictions in order to maintain the flow of supplies and keep a lid on price gains.
Now, the US has changed course again. Under legislation approved on Wednesday, President Donald Trump can impose tariffs of as much as 100% on major buyers of Russian oil, including India.

India needs the US, its biggest export market and, increasingly, an important energy supplier. At the same time, New Delhi can’t fold — both for domestic political reasons and because of the strategic autonomy it has long defended.

In a forthright statement yesterday, the government said it was “firmly committed to ensuring energy security” for its population, warning the US that there would be implications for the bilateral relationship.
Translated, this means an interim trade pact risks becoming void if punitive levies are applied — a development which serves neither side.
India has two points of leverage. One is fuel exports. The country ships more than 1 million barrels a day of oil products overseas. If kept at home, that could worsen a global crunch.

The more important one is scale. The current market squeeze is less severe for crude than for oil products, yet if India has to search for non-Russian barrels for more than 40% of its purchases — the amount Moscow’s deliveries currently cover — prices will rise.
That’s a worry for India’s government, which shields households, but it’s also a problem for US voters, just ahead of midterm elections.
That may give Trump pause, at least for now.
—Rakesh Sharma, Bloomberg News

India is on course for its driest monsoon in 17 years as a strengthening El Niño curbs rainfall, threatening crop yields and raising the risk of higher food prices. Cumulative rainfall during the June to September wet season is 15% below the long-term average so far, and if the deficit persists, it would be the weakest monsoon since 2009.
At least two liquefied natural gas shipments transited the Strait of Hormuz this week as producers look for ways to increase flows to a market struggling with a lack of supply and surging prices.
Oil dropped for a third day, with traders looking to the next round of diplomacy that’ll shape the US-Iran war as supply concerns start to ease.
Indonesian tycoon Andi Syamsuddin Arsyad agreed to acquire a major stake in miner PT Bayan Resources, setting the stage for him to become one of the biggest players in the global coal industry.

Japan’s nuclear revival is facing fresh setbacks after a summer of scandals and regulatory hurdles delayed reactor restarts, threatening the country’s plans to expand atomic power as electricity demand and energy costs rise.

Plansee Group is building one of the West’s most formidable critical minerals operations outside China, selling tungsten, a metal vital to modern industry. The company’s advantage is that much of its output requires no new mining at all.

More than 150,000 medium- and heavy-duty electric trucks were sold globally in the first half of 2026, up 75% year-on-year, according to BloombergNEF. China continues to lead on volumes, with battery-electric models accounting for 20% of its total truck sales. While the US market remains small, it has become home to some of the more ambitious electrification projects — and their financing.

Bloomberg Green returns to New York on Sept. 23 during Climate Week, convening industry leaders, policymakers and climate innovators to explore what’s next in the transition to a more resilient and future-ready world.

items.title: Democratic Momentum Builds as Early Voting Begins in Several States
body: I’m Jonathan Tamari, senior Washington reporter for Bloomberg Government, and each weekday I’ll be coming to you with inside-the-room reporting and insights that reveal what’s really happening in Washington—and how it impacts you. Email me with feedback and comments here. If this newsletter was forwarded to you sign up here.
Today: Democrats build momentum, Warren Buffett steps aside, and draft fears surge in Russia.
The wheels might not be coming off for Republicans quite yet — but they’re starting to look pretty loose.
A slew of indicators are moving Democrats’ way, while some GOP candidates are scrambling to distance themselves from Donald Trump.

One significant data point — which party voters want to control Congress — has surged for Democrats and roughly matches the advantage they saw at the same point before the 2018 blue wave, according to an average of public polls.
As early voting begins today in Minnesota, Virginia, and South Dakota, Bloomberg’s Gregory Korte shows the jump in recent weeks:

Of course, things can shift between now and Election Day. Republicans have a substantial financial advantage, Democrats have worries in some top Senate races, and new events could still alter the landscape.
While we’ve seen plenty of polling misses (and this could turn out to be a momentary spike for Democrats), right now there are signs the party could be building an electoral monsoon.

They lead on nearly every major issue, according to a New York Times survey, and voters see the GOP as more elitist and corrupt. Other polls show Democrats ahead in Senate races in Texas and Alaska, two reach states Trump won by double digits.
Nearly two-thirds of voters say the Trump administration has made the economy worse, per a Fox News poll released this week.

That’s the biggest difference between this year and 2018, said J.J. Balaban, a Democratic strategist based in Philadelphia. Some voters were furious at Trump that year, but others shrugged off criticisms.
The latest economic news suggests it could get worse for the GOP.

Diesel prices are at record highs, a sharp pain point in states hosting some of the year’s most competitive Senate races, my colleagues Mark Niquette and Steven T. Dennis reported. (In Maine heating fuel prices are up 74%, a state agency said Thursday.)
And this week’s Fed rate hike aims to tame inflation but will raise borrowing costs.
Don’t trust the numbers? Republicans’ actions tell a story, too.

JD Vance just campaigned in Kansas, a red state where the GOP wouldn’t typically devote a major resource. He’s also headed to usually red Iowa, but Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson won’t join him, and two of the state’s GOP House members voted this week to end the Iran war.
In Florida, Republican Representative Maria Elvira Salazar released an ad Thursday saying some of Trump’s deportations have gone “too far.”
She’s the most prominent example of Republicans trying to get distance from one of Trump’s signature policies (after voting to fund it), BGOV’s Mica Soellner and Greg Giroux report.
Even some longtime prominent conservatives (Karl Rove and George Will) are backing Democrats in some races.
Republicans, however, still have a huge edge in campaign cash, and the money flood is just starting to hit the airwaves.
Polls in Michigan and New Hampshire suggest Republicans have a shot to score Senate upsets that would virtually guarantee they hold the chamber. And far-left nominees are fueling Republican attacks.
He predicted Republicans would defy the polls and grow their majority.
Still, just in case, he might want to check the lug nuts on the GOP party bus.
The US is expected to hold off announcing new tariffs on China and other trading partners until after next week’s summit between Trump and Xi Jinping.
Russia took control of the local businesses of Swiss food giant Nestle and French supermarket chain Auchan in the Kremlin’s largest takeover of foreign corporate assets since at least 2024.
Russians are growing fearful that Vladimir Putin may soon order a massive new mobilization for the war in Ukraine after this weekend’s parliamentary elections.
Warren Buffett is stepping down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway and will be replaced by his son Howard.
Trump’s inner circle is “counting on their pardons,” journalist Maggie Haberman tells Bloomberg’s Mishal Husain.
Trump’s pardons of individuals convicted of disabling diesel truck pollution controls mark a sharp reversal in the federal government’s treatment of an aftermarket industry.
Oil dropped for a third day with the focus on the next round of diplomacy that’ll shape the US-Iran war.
At least two liquefied natural gas shipments transited the Strait of Hormuz this week as producers look for ways to increase flows.
Several career Justice Department prosecutors recently confronted Todd Blanche about politically motivated firings and low morale, Bloomberg Law’s Ben Penn reports.

OpenAI and Microsoft executives admitted their AI tools were substitutes for articles published by The New York Times and other outlets, acknowledging the threat their tech posed to the industry, according to court documents.
The data center debate highlights an increasingly visible split heading into the midterms: Trump wants faster buildout, while candidates are urging caution.
“Consequential” is one of Trump’s favorite words to describe his own presidency. That quest is putting the entire world at risk, Brad Stone writes.
Restaurants contending with surging beef prices are re-engineering their menus, experimenting with smaller portions and less expensive cuts of meat.
Senators supporting a bill to regulate college sports are optimistic after the Senate advanced the legislation Thursday.
Sports team values have surged over the past decade. Meet the banker whose firm has advised on 15 deals representing roughly $50 billion in value.
A final pre-election run at passing cryptocurrency regulations fizzled in the Senate this week despite new language aimed at appeasing skeptical Democrats, BGOV’s Galen Bacharier writes.

The latest version of the Clarity Act failed to reach the 60 votes needed to advance after Democrats and several Republicans blocked it, effectively tabling the bill until after the November midterms.

Opponents of the bill weren’t swayed by final tweaks, including ethics guardrails for public officials’ crypto holdings, which have surged to the forefront of debate amid Trump and his family’s personal involvement in the industry.
Early voting begins today in Virginia, Minnesota, and South Dakota.

items.title: Texas Stock Exchange Lures $10 Billion Retailer in New Move
body: Dillard’s Inc. announced plans to shift its primary securities listing to the Texas Stock Exchange, leaving the New York Stock Exchange to become the first retailer to join the startup marketplace.

“The move aligns Dillard’s deep roots and strong retail presence in Texas with TXSE’s technology-driven platform,” the department-store chain said in a statement Friday. Dillard’s, which has a market value of about $10 billion, said its shares would start trading on the Texas exchange on Oct. 5.

The move by the Little Rock, Arkansas-based company bolsters the TXSE’s goal of recruiting corporate listings from around the southeastern US as well as its home state. Since last week, a half-dozen companies have announced plans to switch to the exchange, including pipeline operator Energy Transfer LP and Texas Capital Bancshares Inc.

Most of TXSE’s early joiners have close ties to the exchange. Billionaire Kelcy Warren, the chairman of Energy Transfer, is a major backer of TXSE Group Inc., the marketplace’s parent company. Texas Capital Chief Executive Officer Rob Holmes sits on a TXSE advisory board, and is also a member of the Dillard’s board.
Read more: Texas Challenger to Nasdaq, NYSE Lands Fifth Company in a Week

Founded by James Lee, the Dallas-based TXSE — pronounced “TEX-ee” — has raised over $300 million from investors including JPMorgan Chase & Co., BlackRock Inc. and Ken Griffin’s Citadel Securities. It faces stepped-up competition from Nasdaq and the NYSE, which have launched Texas-based venues.

“The movement of primary listings out of New York and into Texas is just getting started,” Lee said in a post on LinkedIn about the Dillard’s shift. “Companies are recognizing TXSE’s ownership and engagement by the largest financial institutions in the world is already creating better liquidity and improved market quality.”

The decision by Dillard’s came after almost a year of consideration, Lee said. The retailer shifted its incorporation to Texas from Delaware last year following similar moves by companies including Elon Musk’s Tesla Inc. and Space Exploration Technologies Corp. Texas has been establishing new business courts that are designed to ease the legal burden on companies.
Dillard’s has posted a multiyear stock surge coming out of the pandemic. The shares’ tenfold advance since the end of 2020 is about nine times the gain of the S&P 500 over the same period.

The company operates about 270 stores in more than two dozen states, selling apparel, shoes and cosmetics, according to its latest annual report with federal regulators. Texas is its largest market, with more than 50 stores, and it also has a significant footprint in states such as Florida, Louisiana and Arizona.

items.title: Blackstone Alumni Forge Hybrid Capital Challenger
body: Welcome to     Going Private  , I’m     Sinead Cruise   and this is Bloomberg’s twice-weekly newsletter about private markets and the forces moving capital away from the public eye. Today, we explore an intoxicating bet from       Michael Burry    , the latest troubles facing Russia’s richest woman and some striking new data that could draw more US private credit investors to Europe. But first we take a look at how a team of       Blackstone     alums are rewriting the special situations playbook at their UK-based boutique. If you’re not already on our list,     sign up here  . Have feedback? Email us at       goingprivate@bloomberg.net
After years at the heart of the world’s largest alternative asset manager, the founding team behind Trimontium had to make a choice.

As billions of dollars rolled into Blackstone’s Strategic Opportunities business, Vlado Spasov and Yaroslav Syzonov worked round the clock to identify and grow companies through creative capital solutions.Eventually, Spasov chose to walk away from scale and start over at his own company, where the focus is finding alpha without pressure to deploy.
“We apprenticed at some of the best firms in the business and took the best of what we learned there, adapted to our own philosophy,” founder and CIO Spasov told Going Private.
“Our singular aim is to maximize investor returns. We will always size the platform to protect the opportunity set for our investors, not to gather assets.”
Several Blackstone investors followed Spasov to the new firm, whose name derives from the Latin for Plovdiv, the southern Bulgarian “city of three hills” where Spasov was born.

Former Blackstone credit and insurance managing director Bally Sangar serves as chief operating officer and former King Street Capital Management veteran Graham Morrison has also come on board as general counsel.

The London-based firm follows the same unconstrained strategy pursued by the US giant, only now they have the space to craft a bigger crop of ideas for clients before putting dollars to work, according to Syzonov.
Today’s environment poses several simultaneous challenges for companies, the pair said, citing liquidity gaps, geopolitical instability and tech disruption.

“Demand for capital flexible enough to ride that out has risen sharply,” Spasov said, and providing it well demands “first principles thinking, structural creativity, calmness under imperfect information and disciplined underwriting”.

Trimontium raised an initial $1.5 billion of evergreen capital it felt it could invest without compromising those core values. As it grows and sees other opportunities, it will seek new investors. It has a presence in Luxembourg and is also keen to expand in New York.

Earlier this month, Trimontium struck a $325 million deal comprising hybrid, debt and equity financing in a single package with Authentic Restaurant Brands, to support its M&A ambitions and the expansion of existing assets including Pollo Tropical and Tavern in the Square.

The Austin, Texas-based group is backed by Garnett Station Partners and generates over $1 billion in annual revenue and over $150 million in EBITDA. The company will tap capital when opportunities arise, Trimontium said.

Some banks are unenthusiastic about committing super-flexible capital, and for many midsized businesses, finding cash may mean turning to opportunity funds or ‘loan-to-own’ investors with strategies of extraction rather than expansion.
“Our mantra is grow the whole pie, not take a bigger slice of a fixed one”, Syzonov said.

“You have hedge fund-types offering liquidity at the shorter end of the spectrum, and five, seven, 10-year money at the other end. But do people always need money for either one month or seven years? The answer is no.”

Trimontium tests every deal on relative value and resists chasing “the next big thing”, which is why the firm is wary of the hype around AI infrastructure financing, and in particular, the risk-return equation being presented to investors, according to Syzonov.

“This is a market full of unproven operators, unbuilt projects and political noise and that’s before we know what’s going to happen with AI,” he said. “If you put all of this together, is 8% really an attractive return?”
Searching for new private lending opportunities in the wake of   this week’s Fed rate hike? KBRA is offering several reasons why investors might want to train their sights on Europe.

In its first-ever head-to-head comparison of its US mid-market assessment portfolio and its EU/UK equivalent, the ratings firm said the latter showed stronger credit quality on a point-in-time basis, according to the study reported first by Going Private.

KBRA’s Middle Market Default Monitor — a forward-looking gauge of borrowers in default, poised to default or where default has been averted by sponsor or lender intervention — is 2.8% across the US portfolio versus 0.3% on the EU/UK assessed debt.

KBRA says the variation is primarily driven by the volume of older vintages in the US portfolio, which is reflected in a larger number of firms showing at least one hallmark of questionable credit quality, such as elevated leverage, sub- 1.0x interest coverage ratios, or near-term debt maturities.

Median ICR was 1.9x among EU/UK borrowers and 1.6x in the US, while the median implied EBITDA margin is 19% in the EU/UK versus 16% in the US. The median all-in borrowing cost is approximately 110 bps higher in the US versus 9% in the EU/UK.

The median EU/UK loan was originated in 2024, compared with 2023 in the US. Though just one year apart, those 12 months saw stronger earnings growth and marked optimism for lower base rates, KBRA said.
What is more, the spreads on b- rated EU/UK loans are roughly 50 basis points wider than US credits, despite the fact that 82% of the EU/UK debt was assigned a rating of b- or higher.

KBRA largely attributes the wider spreads to lower competition from banks or other direct lenders in Europe, alongside the added complexity premium associated with the region’s myriad jurisdictions and bankruptcy regimes.

That relative risk-return profile might draw new entrants to the European market, but managers lacking local underwriting or portfolio management capabilities remain at risk of weaker credit outcomes compared to seasoned players, KBRA said.

“These comparisons are not perfectly like-for-like, but they reinforce an important point: newer portfolios have had less time for weaker-performing companies to emerge,” the firm said, adding that it expects some of this credit quality advantage to narrow over time.

The year-on-year Q2 2026 comparison includes 2,226 U.S. borrowers and 465 EU/UK borrowers, representing $961 billion and $236 billion of assessed debt, respectively. Average assessed debt is higher in the EU/UK at approximately $507 million per borrower, compared with $432 million in the US.

“Higher for longer rates, inflation and other macro-headwinds on both sides of the Atlantic create more pressure than any other factors for the typical leveraged middle-market borrowers,” said Chief Rating Officer William Cox.

“Given the vintage of related transactions, and our years of experience talking with relevant lenders, the results were not a surprise. But it is great to see the power of a such a large data set confirm what we anecdotally suspected.”
No match for Ukrainian drones,   the critical infrastructure underpinning the e-commerce empire of Russia’s richest woman is in a fragile state.

Tatyana Kim founded Wildberries, Russia’s answer to Amazon.com, while on maternity leave more than 20 years ago. Her brainchild gave time-poor moms a place to shop, and the site chalked up gross stock turnover of about 6.1 trillion rubles in 2025, equivalent to nearly 3% of the country’s gross domestic product.

The firm’s fortunes have shifted dramatically since July when Ukraine started targeting its vast warehouses, destroying about a third of its storage capacity and goods worth at least 550 billion rubles ($6.4 billion) as at August 31.
Rebuilding those units — some roughly the size of 35 standard soccer pitches — will cost more than 200 billion rubles ($2.3 billion), Data Insight estimated.

Ukraine’s tactics echo President Vladimir Putin’s repeated strikes on facilities operated by Nova Poshta, a critical part of Ukraine’s wartime logistics network that moves goods, supports e-commerce and delivers humanitarian aid.
Ozon, Russia’s second-largest e-commerce company co-owned by billionaire Vladimir Evtushenkov has also come under attack.

In an emailed statement, Wildberries parent RWB group said it was “taking all necessary measures to minimize the impact and restore normal operations” despite “the extraordinary nature” of the situation.

Kim’s net worth has plunged by $1.6 billion this year to $6.3 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, but the losses felt by the million or so third-party sellers who rely on its platform are much tougher to compute.
Burned inventories, slower deliveries, and increased logistics costs have all fed into higher consumer prices across Putin’s wartime Russia, already stretched by four years of war.
“This is a direct blow to small entrepreneurs,” said Alexandra Prokopenko, a fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
“Next, we’ll see businesses close, bankruptcies rise and investment activity decline. Many people have now felt the impact of war and realized how it affects their own lives.”

Wildberries is now building a network of partner storage centers, with smaller facilities starting at about 100 square meters. These are more expensive to run than larger sites and it’s unclear how the costs are affecting its financial health.
Wildberries doesn’t report full results under international standards although it described its group debt level as comfortable in a statement earlier this year.
“The only thing we, the Russian business community, can do now is keep a cool head, plan for the near future, adapt and transform,” Kim said in a video posted on Telegram in late July.
“Entrepreneurs know how to do that better than anyone.”
The investor most famous for calling a US housing crash on the eve of the 2008 financial crisis has doled out another tip that has got the market talking.

Michael Burry says unchecked advances in artificial intelligence, quantum computing and digital assets could hasten the decline of the greenback as the world’s preferred reserve currency, pushing up demand for real assets instead.

And while some like-minded bears are making a case for gold, Burry argues that Europe’s bonded fine wine market is a smarter place to play.“Right now, just about every single case of fine wine sitting in a London bonded warehouse can be a short position on the US dollar, a global hedge against fiat currency, and a ward against global financial systems’ vulnerability to the various hellscapes possibly wrought by future iterations of AI and quantum computing,” Burry wrote in on his Cassandra Unchained blog on Substack.

Burry described the European bonded fine wine market as diverse, liquid and therefore “analyzable and investable” much like stocks and bonds. Yet market-makers are few and far between and investors are largely unaware of the opportunities presented, he added.

“What got me here was I heard that wine is in a bit of a depression. My eyes, ears, and every hair on the back of my neck perk up when I hear of formerly highly valued assets beset by a case of the doldrums,” he said.The finest names, the likes of Pétrus, Domaine Romanée-Conti, Mouton Rothschild and Margaux from France and Sassicaia, Ornellaia, and Solaia from Italy remain in demand in good and bad times, he said, advocating for a 10% allocation, or “probably five figures” to bonded fine wine.
“In practice, there are few hard thresholds, few limits. Dealers will take the money. The key is to know when to hand it over or, better, when not to.”

Strategic Value Partners has appointed Goldman Sachs’ partner Matt Gibson as President, effective February 2027. Matt joins SVP after more than 25 years at GS, and will lead SVP’s non-investment activities, including client relations. He will also participate in deal sourcing in the power and infrastructure sectors and join SVP’s management and investment committees.

Adams Street Partners has welcomed   Alec Kersman as partner and global head of client solutions. Based in New York, Kersman will oversee institutional investor relations, wealth management, marketing and product strategy groups and will serve on the firm’s executive, pricing, and new product committees.

Cambridge Associates has opened a new office in Milan and made two senior appointments as it continues its European expansion. Riccardo Pianeti has joined as managing director and head of the Milan office, while Raphael Heynold has also joined as head of EMEA and APAC client solutions.

items.title: Air India CEO Weighs Folding Budget Unit Into Group to Cut Costs
body: Air India Ltd.’s incoming Chief Executive Officer Tewolde Gebremariam is considering folding the no-frills Air India Express unit into the group as he tries to cut costs to counter record losses, according to people familiar with the matter.

In multiple meetings across departments, Tewolde quizzed managers about the need to run two airline companies with separate operating permits, said the people, who asked not to be identified as the talks were private. The CEO-designate argues that having a single airline group would lower regulatory requirements and reduce the need for two sets of managers, engineers, and administrative staff, the people said.

The idea of combining Air India and its budget carrier is at an early stage, and realizing it would require approval from the supervisory board, the people said. Air India Express would keep its brand name in a combination, they added.
An Air India spokesperson did not respond to an email seeking comments.

The deliberations show Tewolde’s eagerness to weed out inefficiencies after Air India posted a loss of 220 billion rupees ($2.3 billion) in the year through March. Reducing losses is also key for the carrier as its parent, Tata Sons Pvt. battles a power struggle over Tata chairman’s tenure extension and a regulatory push to list.
The 61-year-old was chosen largely due to his track record of turning the Ethiopian Airlines Group into Africa’s largest and most profitable carriers.
Read More: Air India’s CEO Pick Cemented by Crash Response, Pandemic Profit

Tewolde needs to tackle a myriad of challenges, including the closing of Pakistani airspace to Indian carriers and the Middle East conflict that’s disrupted travel and driven up fuel costs. Air India is also facing a probe after a pilot of a flight involved in a sudden altitude drop tested positive for illegal drugs.

Air India is not new to mergers, having gone through one with Indian Airlines in 2007. It then went through more portfolio changes after the Tata Group bought the airline in 2022, with four brands combining into two, resulting in the current structure of Air India and Air India Express.

In his earlier meetings, the CEO-designate had raised concerns over Air India’s low cargo load use, a sector that bolstered business at Ethiopian Airlines. He also urged staff to work on a plan to reduce maintenance issues. While Tewolde officially joined the company this month, he still needs to be approved by local regulators as CEO because he’s a foreign national.

The new executive streamlining Air India would be welcome news for Tata Group and its equity partner Singapore Airlines Ltd., which is facing political backlash for backstopping Air India’s loss-making operations.
Read More: Air India Closes in on $1.1 Billion Financial Aid From Owners
