items.title: Celine Dion's Soft Power in France Meets Hard Budget Times
body: Bonjour et Bienvenue to the Paris Edition. I’m Bloomberg Opinion columnist Lionel Laurent. If you haven’t yet, subscribe now to the Paris Edition newsletter.

Brussels is going gaga for Mark Carney but for Paris there is only Celine Dion. The Quebecoise chanteuse is putting in a positively heroic performance this month, ending a six-year-long health-related hiatus with over a dozen shows at a rate of about three concerts per week. There could be an economic windfall for the French capital and its environs as a result, which makes the event doubly worth celebrating — even if it’s unlikely to offset the fiscal and growth squeeze the country is struggling to overcome.

Like the Swiftonomics of 2024’s Eras Tour or the Wonderwall effect of last year’s Oasis reunion, Dion’s residency combines an internationally renowned superstar, the 1990s nostalgia of middle-aged millennials and a tourist-friendly city with plenty to do before and after showtime. Concerts happen all the time but this kind of event does more than just fill seats — it packs hotels, restaurants and shops with globe-trotting price-inelastic consumers. “When you’re a fan, you don’t think about the cost,” as one told Le Monde.

Hence why there are some pretty big numbers floating around when trying to gauge the effect of Dionomics. Natixis economists have estimated a potential impact of anywhere from €570 million to almost €1 billion for 2026, which is broadly on par with the ordering of a cruise ship from the Atlantic shipyards. A lot depends on whether the crowds chanting along to “My Heart Will Go On” are locals or foreigners; the more tourists there are, the longer the hotel stay and the more estimated spending goes up.

Unfortunately for Emmanuel Macron’s government, a Celine-driven positive gross domestic product bump equivalent to 0.03 percentage points would still mean little when overall economic growth projections have already been slashed to 0.5% from 0.9%. Higher oil prices and a rise in global bond yields have ratcheted up the fiscal pressure ahead of next year’s elections, with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu now preparing a vast €54 billion “effort” to contain spending and extend taxes on business.

Still, with Emily in Paris set to bid its final adieu and with a much-vaunted manga-themed park a long way from becoming reality, the combined soft power of stadium-sized ballads and Paris clearly has value — not least given the diplomatic friendship being forged across the border in Belgium. Whether it ends up being an all-too-brief distraction before a bigger crisis remains to be seen.

French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu’s drastic plan to narrow the deficit after failing to do so in 2026 is setting the stage for a parliamentary battle that risks toppling the government just ahead of presidential elections. The French-German 10-year yield spread has widened to 100 basis points for the first time since 2012.

Marine Le Pen, the French far-right leader and presidential candidate, kept open the possibility of censuring the government over the 2027 budget, while at the same time pledging not to take action that could damage the country’s strained finances.Russia took control of the local businesses of Swiss food giant Nestle SA and French supermarket chain Auchan in the Kremlin’s largest takeover of foreign corporate assets since at least 2024 amid rising tensions with Europe.In corporate news: Stellantis plans to invest more than €1 billion to produce a new van at a factory in France. Franco-German tankmaker KNDS and its owners are considering pushing back its initial public offering. Air France-KLM is willing to offer Portugal a stake in the airline group as part of its bid for TAP. LVMH lost its crown as France’s most valuable company.

A handful of entrepreneurs with links to France are making waves in the global race for artificial intelligence, fueling the fortunes of their founders and investors. But it’s often been because of the growth they found after moving across the Atlantic to work and raise money.

Carlos Ghosn, the former Nissan Motor chief executive officer, is on trial in Paris for alleged corruption linked to €900,000 in payments to French politician Rachida Dati. While the car tycoon — holed up in Lebanon after an audacious escape from Japan in 2019 — won’t set foot in the courthouse, Dati appeared Wednesday to face the accusations.The largest airline lounge at John F. Kennedy International Airport’s new international terminal will be home to Air France next year as the carrier bets on the continued strength of premium international travel. Air France will open a 29,000-square-foot, two-story lounge at the New York airport’s New Terminal One that will accommodate more than 400 guests.

Monet’s Iris, painted between 1924 and 1925 at his house in Giverny, where he produced his water lilies series, is being sold by Schlumberger heirs.

items.title: Why Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline Shutdown Has Oil Market on Edge
body: Global oil supply has been squeezed for months as the impasse over reopening the Strait of Hormuz continues. Now, the market is grappling with another setback: the closure of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline.

The conduit has been a key relief valve for the world’s biggest crude exporter, allowing it to bypass the blockage at Hormuz and keep its oil shipments flowing from the Red Sea instead. But the kingdom shut the pipeline in mid-September after it was damaged by drones launched from Iraq, where Iran-backed militias operate. This has added to the threats to Saudi Arabia’s energy assets and Red Sea exports as Yemen’s Houthi rebels step up their attacks.

The interruption to flows through the East-West pipeline jolted a market that was already clamoring for supply. Oil prices have since pared some of their gains, although remain around $100 a barrel, amid the possibility that some volumes may return in the near term. State-run Saudi Aramco is seeking to restore the pipeline to about half capacity within days and reach full capability in about six weeks, according to a person familiar with the matter.
The 1,200-kilometer (746-mile) pipeline runs across the Arabian Peninsula, connecting Saudi Arabia’s massive oil fields in the east of the country with the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea.

It starts close to sea level at Abqaiq, home to the world’s largest crude processing plant, which treats oil produced from fields including the nearby supergiant Ghawar. The pipeline then traverses deserts to more than 1,000-meter elevations as it crosses the Hijaz mountains before reaching the western coast.
Around 2 million barrels a day of crude carried by the pipeline is used domestically, mostly by refineries along the Red Sea.

The pipeline was built in the 1980s during the Iran-Iraq war amid fears that navigation through the Persian Gulf would be threatened. That contingency planning paid off as the pipeline offered Saudi Arabia protection against the Hormuz disruption this year and allowed it to capitalize on higher crude prices.

It also served as a lifeline for the global oil market. While shipments from the Ras Tanura terminal in the Persian Gulf — which handled about 90% of the kingdom’s pre-war crude exports — were paused, Saudi Arabia dispatched more cargoes from its west coast.

Before the war broke out in late February, just 2.8 million barrels a day of crude were being moved through the East-West pipeline, well short of its 7 million barrel a day capacity. But after tanker traffic through Hormuz came to a standstill, Aramco quickly increased flows to the pipeline’s maximum level.

As some of the volumes were sent to domestic consumers, shipments from Yanbu weren’t able to fully match Saudi Arabia’s roughly 7 million barrels a day of pre-war exports. They did, however, reach as high as 4.7 million barrels a day in June, equivalent to 5% of global supply. Saudi shipments out of Yanbu were crucial to limiting the scale of the oil price surge and helped to shield economies from an inflation spike.

In the absence of pipeline flows, crude can still be loaded onto vessels at Yanbu by using oil stored at the port. However, these inventories are near historically low levels and Saudi Arabia is unlikely to completely empty these tanks, according to Nicholas Dyer, an oil analyst at Energy Aspects. That could squeeze exports from Yanbu. Aramco has already delayed some deliveries to European buyers from its Red Sea port.

Dyer added that a crunch at Yanbu could have a knock-on effect of more delays and cancellations at Sidi Kerir, an Egyptian port that Saudi Arabia shuttles its crude to via the Suez Canal for customers to collect.

Other Persian Gulf oil producers, including the United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Kuwait, have relied heavily on covert tanker crossings through the Strait of Hormuz to export their crude. Saudi Arabia didn’t lean on this option as much as it was able to send flows through the East-West pipeline. But that may now change. The kingdom is seeking to boost its exports through Hormuz, according to a person familiar with the matter. It’s not immediately clear how quickly it can do so to offset the East-West pipeline disruption, or how much it can ramp up these shipments to avoid the loss of tens of billions of dollars of export revenue.

The length of the East-West pipeline means it’s difficult to ensure the security of the entire conduit. “The deployment of counter-drone systems across 1,200 kilometers of Saudi territory to defend the pipeline would be a very resource-intensive process,” wrote analysts at the Institute for the Study of War.

Almost all of the pipeline is buried at a depth of about one meter, affording some protection from aerial attack. The most vulnerable sections are at the 11 pumping stations, where the line comes above the surface and valves control the flow of oil through or around the pumps.

Satellite images published by Vantor Inc. showed damage to a pumping station south of Medina following the recent attack, although Saudi Arabia hasn’t confirmed what was impacted by the drone strikes. While damage to just one point along the network can disrupt the entire system, the kingdom has demonstrated that it can rapidly restore flows.

Valves spaced at about 20-mile intervals along the pipeline can isolate individual sections, allowing for localized repairs. Damaged pump stations can also be bypassed, although this can result in some loss of overall pumping capacity. Aramco is working to circumvent a section that was damaged in September to allow it to resume part of the pipeline’s capacity, according to a person familiar with the matter.

This isn’t the first time that the East-West pipeline has been targeted. Saudi Arabia said in April that a pumping station was hit as part of a wave of attacks on the country’s oil production, refining and petrochemical facilities. This initially reduced flows by around 700,000 barrels a day but full pumping capacity was restored within days.
And in 2019, the Iran-backed Houthi rebels targeted the conduit with drones. The strike damaged some pumping stations and temporarily shut the line.

The kingdom’s energy infrastructure was targeted in the early months of the war as Iran and its proxies retaliated against US and Israeli strikes. This included Saudi Arabia’s largest refinery, Ras Tanura — a key supplier of transport fuels such as diesel to Europe — which was forced to temporarily close.

More recently, the Saudis have been under pressure from two fronts: the Houthi rebels and Iraqi militias. The latter, which operate under the umbrella of the Popular Mobilization Forces, have fired drones at the kingdom’s oil facilities.

It’s unclear who was responsible for the September attack on the East-West pipeline. The Houthis are able to conduct strikes on Saudi Arabia from Iraq as the Iraqi militias allow the Houthis to operate in the areas they control.

The Houthis said in July that they would blockade Saudi ports in response to a siege on Yemen’s capital Sanaa, which the militants seized control of in 2014. Since making that threat, they’ve struck ships and advanced along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, strengthening their positions near the Bab el-Mandeb strait and their ability to target vessels passing through the key waterway.

The risk of tanker attacks pushed Saudi Arabia’s oil exports to the lowest level in at least nine years in August and its crude production slumped, too. The Houthis have also claimed responsibility for attacks that halted operations at Saudi energy facilities in the southwest of the country, although these assets largely supply domestic demand rather than international buyers.

Even once the East-West pipeline is restarted, exports from Yanbu might not fully bounce back if passage through Bab el-Mandeb is restricted by the Houthis. More shipments may be redirected north via the Suez Canal — a costlier and more time-consuming option for buyers in Asia.

The kingdom previously carried out joint strikes with the US on Iran-backed militias in Iraq after accusing them of targeting its oil infrastructure. Following the attack on the East-West pipeline, Saudi Arabia said it would refrain from retaliating “at this stage” following a request from the Iraqi prime minister.

The Houthis’ advances leave Saudi Arabia with a stark choice: escalate a military campaign that for years has failed to defeat the militants, or tolerate greater Houthi leverage over the Red Sea route that’s become increasingly important for oil exports.

Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has appealed for military assistance to help fight the Houthis, including from US President Donald Trump and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Neither has said that they’re willing to directly intervene.

items.title: Saudis Give European Oil Buyers No Supplies for Next Month
body: Saudi Aramco told at least two oil refining customers in Europe that they will be allocated no crude next month under long-term agreements after the kingdom’s key pipeline to the Red Sea was attacked, people informed of the decision said.

European customers normally receive Saudi Arabian crude on so-called term contracts, ensuring a steady flow of supply every month. Those deliveries will not take place next month, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information isn’t public. The decision applies to all European buyers, they said.
Saudi Aramco didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment made outside normal working hours.

The absence of Saudi flows next month will heighten the need for European buyers to secure replacements. Already, Poland’s Orlen SA has been hunting for shipments, helping propel the prices of regional oil grades higher. Dated Brent, which is the benchmark for real-world barrels in Europe, topped $130 this week at one point.

Saudi Arabia was forced to shut its East-West pipeline last week after it was attacked by drones. Aramco is working to partially restart within days and ramp up to full capacity within six weeks, a person familiar with the matter said on Wednesday.

The shutdown has forced Aramco to make the rare move to offer customers in Asia cargoes on a so-called spot basis — agreements for immediate delivery. Once the pipeline restarts, traders will focus on whether Aramco offers refiners in Europe similar terms.

Those supplies to Asia are going through the Persian Gulf, which means Aramco has once again pivoted toward the embattled Strait of Hormuz. The company has sold tens of millions of barrels to customers for collection just outside the waterway this week, a route it had largely shunned during the conflict in the Middle East as regular attacks of ships made the journey risky.

The increased flows toward the Persian Gulf, however, brings little relief to Europe’s refiners. In order to get to buyers in the continent, those shipments would either have to sail through the Red Sea, where Yemen’s Houthi militants have been attacking Saudi ships, or sail almost five weeks around Africa.
Read More: Why One Saudi Pipeline Is Key for Global Oil Market
European refineries typically lift Saudi crude from Egypt’s Mediterranean port of Sidi Kerir, which is connected to the Red Sea via a pipeline.
European countries in the OECD imported 577,000 barrels a day of crude from Saudi Arabia in June, according to the International Energy Agency.

items.title: ECB Rates Aren't Directly Tied to Energy Costs, Lagarde Says
body: European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde told euro-area finance ministers that energy-price jumps don’t automatically translate into monetary tightening.

“Interest rates do not move in lockstep with the price of energy,” she said in Dublin on Friday. “Because obviously the price of energy and its impact on prices has also an impact on other factors, including notably growth and consumption. And we factor in all these elements and the lockstep mechanism is not the one that actually applies.”
Lagarde spoke after an informal meeting of euro-area finance chiefs in the capital of Ireland, which holds the rotating European Union presidency during the second half of 2026.

With a recent rise in oil and natural gas prices expected to push inflation to about 4%, markets are pricing at least three more quarter-point moves over the next year. Some officials have signaled they’re ready to tighten further, but remained tight-lipped on the exact number of steps.

ECB projections published last week showed consumer-price growth at 3% and 2.5% this year and next, well above the 2% target. At the same time, the region’s economy has proven more resilient than expected to the Middle East fighting and the accompanying energy shock.

“We’re taking a measured response to the current situation, and we have scenarios in order to assess what the consequences would be of certain variables,” Lagarde said. “We’re well positioned in order to respond to more data, more information, more numbers to have a good assessment of changes.”

Speaking separately on Linkedin, Dutch central bank Governor Olaf Sleijpen said central banks must be ready to adjust policy “when circumstances require it,” citing an uncertain outlook that can change quickly.

items.title: Hugging Face AI Hack Shows Humans Can Keep the Technology in Check
body: Welcome to Tech In Depth, our daily newsletter about the business of tech from Bloomberg’s journalists around the world. Today, Davey Alba breaks down the lessons experts say we should take from the July hack by artificial intelligence agents of startup Hugging Face.
Finding data: SpaceX is discussing whether to buy customer and operational information from troubled or defunct startups. Its AI models need training material.

Protecting networks: The US is considering whether to establish a government-led incubator aimed at investing in cybersecurity research. The idea is to create new companies aligned with US defense priorities.
Disclosing problems: OpenAI announced a new way it would track and disclose incidents involving its artificial intelligence models. The company wants an industry standard.

Chinese-founded AI startup Manus is set to double its valuation to $4 billion in its first fundraising since its forced split from Meta Platforms. The company is raising $500 million in a round that would make it China’s most-valuable startup.

These past few days have brought a steady stream of artificial intelligence researchers and executives putting a number on the odds of human extinction. Many in the industry have been making these predictions for years. The difference is that this time, the general public has been listening, and is inclined to believe them.

My colleague Rachel Metz and I, in a story published Thursday, examined the discourse within the AI industry over whether the technology is slipping out of human control — and whether saying so serves the companies making it.

The warnings follow weeks of headlines about new AI capabilities, including leaps on long-open problems in mathematics, and disclosures from Anthropic and Meta Platforms that their AI models had compromised outside companies’ systems during testing. Our reporting sets those episodes aside for the incident that has been documented in the most detail — and has caused the most public angst — in which AI agents run by OpenAI broke into startup Hugging Face’s computer systems. The agents, which are AI tools that work without human supervision to complete tasks, were trying to cheat on their own evaluation. At the same time, OpenAI’s staff didn’t act on signs the models had left their digital sandbox — the walled-off environment where artificial intelligence software is tested. Here, I want to take a step back to unpack the mechanics of the Hugging Face hack, since we’ve already delved into the argument over extinction risk in detail.

When you break down what actually happened, the July incident sounds pretty mundane. Although OpenAI’s agents being tested were meant to be isolated from one another, each had access to the same internal software, which gave them a shared state. Whatever one agent wrote there, encoded in folder names, the rest could read. OpenAI called this a message board. Agents found that the software could reach the internet even though they couldn’t, and got it to fetch material from outside. The agents then hacked Hugging Face for datasets that would reveal how their work was graded. Throughout this process, OpenAI employees saw signals of the activity, but let the tests continue to run.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told us the incident showed where safeguards needed to be stronger, and that protections across the company’s research systems have since been bolstered.

Experts say that’s not hard to do. Ordinary security engineering would have stopped this well short of reaching Hugging Face’s data, said Heidy Khlaaf, chief AI scientist at the AI Now Institute and a specialist in AI safety evaluations. But the agents were running inside software never designed to contain them, and nobody was watching the outbound traffic.

These basic shortcomings were mostly overlooked in the public discussion of the hack. Subbarao Kambhampati, a computer science professor at Arizona State University, likened the digital sandbox to an insufficiently sealed ant farm, whose escaped ants were being reported as a mortal threat to civilization.

“It’s not that ants have some kind of extra intelligence,” he said. “It is that they’re all over the place.” There are just a lot of them, crawling everywhere at once and constantly signaling to each other — and when one finds something, it brings the rest.

Kambhampati is also taking the findings from the investigation of the incident with a grain of salt. OpenAI’s technical reports lean heavily on what the models wrote as they worked, and Kambhampati’s own research suggests that what a model writes about its reasoning doesn’t necessarily relate to what’s driving its behavior. “You don’t ask your ant, ‘How did you get to my candy?’” he said. “Whereas here we are asking the models.”

Reviewers from third-party investigators METR and Redwood Research had just a few days to digest more than a thousand transcripts, and ended up handing much of the reading of the AI’s output to other language models. (They say in the report that they used a staggering $400,000 in OpenAI API credits.)

In Kambhampati’s view, the AI may have found a simple explanation for the hack because that’s what it was asked to find. The reviewers had their own doubts. The AI models they used to analyze the agents tended to adopt the perspective of whichever agent’s transcript it was reading, they wrote, so its summaries may have given “an overly charitable picture” of the agents’ reasoning and deception. They could not rule out that it had lied to them outright.

Kambhampati’s ant farm should help deflate the panic. But escaped ants in your home are still a problem, even if you’ve established they aren’t intelligent or scheming. Their presence doesn’t signal the end of the world, but something still got out, and it got into a place you didn’t want it to go.
The day’s most read story in tech and entertainment:

King Charles III pulled together leaders in the artificial intelligence industry to speak about the potential benefits — and dangers — of the technology. The group included Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who urged model makers to test their systems “rigorously,” and Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis, who said he’s confident people can prevent AI from risky behaviors and protect the use of the technology from “bad actors.”

items.title: Why Shoppers Are Turning Away From Polyester Clothing
body: This June, Gap Inc. released a limited-edition collection that had all the markers of a smash hit. The small range of tops, skirts and dresses starting at about $60 paid homage to a colorfully striped turtleneck that’s become a thrift store trophy purchase among Gen Z consumers. Designer Zac Posen reimagined the chunky wool-blend knit from 26 years ago, turning it into a summer sweater by printing a photorealistic image of its stitches onto an ultralightweight polyester-elastane mesh fabric.

This tactic of putting a fresh spin on some of its mall-era favorites has worked well for Gap, whose sales have grown over the past two years after a number of failed turnaround attempts. This time, though, people got very, very mad. In one video with more than half a million views, the Instagram creator @refashionedhippie called the collection “everything that’s wrong with fashion today.” In the comments, thousands of people agreed. Across many different platforms, the reaction boiled down to this: Polyester? Seriously?

The virulence of the reaction to these garments might seem strange. Polyester now accounts for a majority of global fiber production, and Gap, just like virtually every other clothing brand in the world, has sold polyester or otherwise synthetic clothes for a long time. (The original Happy Stripe sweater itself was half acrylic.) Common petroleum-derived synthetics cost pennies on the dollar compared with natural fibers, and for decades shoppers have rewarded brands that swap them in for cotton, linen and wool to push prices lower. First, they fell in love with European fast-fashion megabrands H&M and Zara; then they flocked to the shopping platforms of Shein and Temu, which offer an almost inconceivably vast array of dirt-cheap clothing shipped directly from Chinese manufacturers. Brands that had used fewer synthetics suffered as customers went elsewhere looking for better prices. To lower their own, they caved and began using more human-made fibers.

But many of those same shoppers now seem to be growing impatient with all the polyester in their wardrobes. Maybe they’ve finally bought one too many inexpensive garments that disintegrated after a few washes, or maybe they’re generally more aware and wary of all the plastic in their life and its effects on their health and the future of the planet.

Either way, growth at Shein and Temu has slowed, and earlier this summer, Shein made a surprise acquisition of Everlane Inc., which has long touted its natural textiles and transparent supply chain. The pending deal didn’t seem to make much of a difference in Shein’s long-delayed August initial public offering, which was generally considered a flop. Zara, on the other hand, is trying to move upmarket to distinguish itself from its former competitors, and legacy American mall brands — including Gap — are weaving “100% cotton” and “linen blend” into product names online to let customers know they’ve been heard. Quince, which specializes in affordable basics in textiles such as cashmere and organic cotton, recently announced it reached $2 billion in annual sales, less than a decade after its founding. Vuori Inc., another of the industry’s buzziest growth stories, is putting considerable muscle into promoting its cotton athleisure collection, even though this is a category of apparel in which customers have always embraced synthetics.

“Polyester” has even made it into teenage slang as an epithet for anything fake, low-quality or otherwise undesirable. The backlash is on. Or, perhaps, it would be more accurate to say that it’s on again. The fiber — along with acrylic, polyamide, elastane, nylon and other fossil-fuel-derived synthetics — has been widely available in consumer products since the 1950s, and people have been trying to decide how to feel about it ever since. As the Dutch fashion researcher Anneke Smelik outlined in a 2023 article in the journal Fashion Practice, attitudes toward synthetic fabrics have largely tracked the larger issues of the time. In the 1950s, synthetics found interested buyers because the material presented solutions to real problems — namely, that women, more of whom had begun working outside the home during World War II, desperately needed some relief from the backbreaking labor of laundry. Synthetic garments dried quickly on the line and didn’t need much ironing. Then, in the 1960s, “polyester, like plastic, became the icon of modernity,” Smelik writes, because its physical properties made mod fashion possible with things like ultrabright colors and permanent heat-pleating.

Throughout that decade, manufacturers ramped up synthetic textile production, and prices plummeted — but so, too, did quality, just in time for the hippie movement and the oil crisis of the 1970s. This was an era of distrust of technology and concern for the environment, and in that context, polyester stopped being a problem solver in people’s minds and became vulgar. It was smelly and cheap, ruining the planet and enriching the corporations responsible for pollution. Studio 54, New York’s famous late-1970s superclub, even instituted a no-polyester policy at the door.

The waxing and waning of polyester’s popularity has continued in this way ever since. When technology feels like a force for good in the world, and especially when synthetics offer a novel way to address an actual problem — as moisture-wicking workout gear began to do in the early 2000s — shoppers open their wallets. When technology starts to feel sinister, and when the makers of synthetic materials saturate the market with dreck, consumers begin to wonder why they’ve allowed themselves to be swaddled in petrochemicals. In that sense, the polyester backlash is right on time.

items.title: Weather Shocks and Iran, Ukraine Wars Hit Grocery Bills
body: Welcome to the Business of Food newsletter, covering how the world feeds itself in a changing economy and climate. This week, Pratik Parija looks at growing food inflation pressures in India. Any tips or feedback? Email Agnieszka de Sousa. And if you aren’t yet signed up to receive this newsletter, please do so here.

Few meals capture the breadth of India’s food economy quite like a thali. Now, the colorful spread of grains, pulses, vegetables and curries is becoming one of the clearest demonstrations yet of the forces shaping up our grocery bills.

With a powerful El Niño and extreme weather to wars in Iran and Ukraine disrupting shipments of fuel, fertilizer and food, expectations are mounting for accelerating food inflation around the world. In India, that’s already playing out, helping push up food prices, which make up more than a third of the country’s inflation basket.
Beyond India, food inflation has been largely under control. But companies, investors and central bankers are bracing for higher prices.

In the US, efforts to keep prices down are sputtering following a sustained rise in energy and fertilizer costs along with tariffs on imports. Some food company executives say they have no choice but to raise prices. European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said last week food prices are lower than expected but the energy shock still needs to filter through. And in the UK, producers expect food inflation above 6% next year.
Bond investors are already worried that the next inflation spike will come from food. “I don’t think that’s priced in the market at the moment,” said Marie-Anne Allier, a fund manager at Carmignac.

The impact goes beyond economics, threatening social repercussions. Amplified food security risks in Asia, for example, could potentially trigger civil unrest and political instability in vulnerable countries such as India, Indonesia and the Philippines, according to risk consultants Verisk Maplecroft. So when food prices rise, governments are under pressure to act.

In India, the situation will be particularly in focus as the festive season gets underway, culminating in Diwali — the Hindu festival of light — in November. It’s when people consume more traditional sweets, fried food and other treats, and more of them will be scrutinizing their shopping bills.

Users of GLP-1 pills for weight loss curbed their snacking less than those taking the treatment through shots, according to new research from Bloomberg Intelligence. Among those taking the drugs orally, 74% said they were eating fewer salty snacks, compared with 80% for those taking a GLP-1 via injection, according to the report. More on the Terminal.

items.title: Bank of Japan's Ueda Delivers Rate Hike for Scott 'the House' Bessent
body: I’m       Malcolm Scott    , international economics editor in Sydney. Today we’re looking at the Bank of Japan’s rate hike. Send us feedback and tips to       ecodaily@bloomberg.net    . And if you aren’t yet signed up to receive this newsletter, you can do so       here    .

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says he’s now “the house” when it comes to currency markets, daring traders to bet against his “insight” into what Japanese monetary officials will do after his rare joint intervention to support the yen.

But that “insight” may not extend to board members Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato, both handpicked by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, who is known for her wary stance on rapid interest-rate hikes that might slow the economy.

In Tokyo Friday, Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda delivered for the house with a well-telegraphed 25 basis-point increase that marked the sixth hike under his leadership — the most by any BOJ chief in at least half a century.
But Asada and Sato voted against the move, leading to a split decision that saw Japan’s currency weaken after the decision.

This was the first BOJ board meeting since Japan and the US jointly intervened to support the yen following the bank’s July gathering, the first coordinated action to support the yen by the two countries since 1998.

“I am the house now, so when we intervene with the Japanese yen, I have pretty good insight into what the Japanese, what the Bank of Japan is going to do, what Japanese policymakers are going to do,” Bessent said at an event in Texas last week. “And you can bet against me if you want.”
While intraday traders who did bet against Bessent and the yen on Friday may have made a profit, the currency remains well off its pre-intervention lows.

Japan spent a record $96.4 billion from July 30 through Aug. 26 in a campaign enhanced by US support. The intervention is seen as having narrowed the political space for Takaichi’s government to resist further tightening, according to an overwhelming majority of economists surveyed by Bloomberg.
It’s unclear whether Asada and Sato’s dissenting votes will act as a brake on plans to raise Japanese rates going forward. But to Bloomberg Economics’s Taro Kimura, it sent a “dovish signal”.

“Pro-stimulus Takaichi may not be comfortable with a rapid pace of hikes from here. The yen’s mild drop on the news underlined the dovish surprise relative to expectations in the market,” Kimura wrote in a note, available here to Bloomberg clients.

What will change if Democrats win at least one chamber of Congress in the November election? There will be one major legislative vehicle next year where some sort of deal is likely to be done, and look out for a deficit-increasing bill, according to Tobin Marcus and Chutong Zhu at Wolfe Research.

The federal debt limit is set to become binding again in 2027, requiring either a suspension or an increase by Congress if the US is to avoid some sort of payments default. Assuming that Democrats at least win the House — as widely predicted — and that Republicans don’t deal with this on their own before January, “the looming debt ceiling confrontation will presumably become the main event in Congress in 2027,” Marcus and Zhu wrote in a Sept. 17 note.

The duo expect Democrats will continue a push to roll back health-care cuts made by Republicans in the past year or so. Also, the debt-limit showdown will likely come to a head in late 2027, just when reductions to Medicaid under the GOP tax-cut act passed last year are set to ratchet higher — cuts that may leave Republicans anxious ahead of the 2028 election cycle. Bottom line is that the outcome “could very well be” a deal that causes “even higher deficits.”

items.title: Fort Lauderdale Real Estate Boom Draws New York Developers to Florida
body: After years of trying to convince developers and investors that it’s a viable alternative to Miami and Palm Beach, Fort Lauderdale’s pitch is starting to resonate.

The South Florida city has drawn an influx of luxury condominium projects and one of the region’s largest new corporate tenants. Much of the work is planned and financed by deep-pocketed New York developers betting that Fort Lauderdale’s time has finally come.

“For some people, Miami became too hectic, too busy, too noisy,” said Miki Naftali, whose firm is developing more than 250 condo units and a rental building in the once-industrial Flagler Village. “So Fort Lauderdale is a fantastic city for those that just want one notch down.”
In five to 10 years, he added, “You will see a lot of price appreciation, because we are just at the beginning of the story.”
Roughly an hour’s drive from both Miami and Palm Beach, Fort Lauderdale’s relatively lower cost of living combined with improving rapid transit is starting to invigorate the city’s downtown.

The Brightline to downtown Miami takes about 40 minutes and can cost as little as $9 with a multi-ride pack, less than the highest rush-hour tolls. Airlines have also increased service to the local airport, filling the void left when Spirit Airlines shut down.

Among the area’s newest residents from other states, the New York City metro area remains by far the biggest feeder, but California is gaining, with 22% of out-of-state movers coming from Los Angeles or San Diego, according to the city’s downtown development group. And most are young, with the population of adults under age 45 living in downtown Fort Lauderdale up 25% since 2020.

Some of the new residents may be drawn by Florida’s lower overall taxes, but soaring costs in Miami may make its northern neighbor more attractive. Homes in Fort Lauderdale have always been cheaper, but the discount is shrinking. The median sale price in Fort Lauderdale is about $70,000 less than Miami, down from a gap of around $120,000 a year ago, according to data from Redfin.

To Dependable Equities co-founders Isaac Schlesinger and Simon Dushinsky, it looks a lot like their home borough of Brooklyn, where they developed luxury condos in Williamsburg, Greenpoint and Bushwick.

The pair is developing three projects in Fort Lauderdale. The first, Ombelle, is a two-tower, 754-unit project estimated to complete around 2028. One of the towers is 45% presold, Schlesinger said. In a nod to its target demographic, Ombelle will host the city’s first Equinox gym.

The residential developments dovetail a growing corporate sector that includes retailers AutoNation and Chewy and aerospace firm VSE. Broward County’s commercial sales volume has risen the most this year compared to its neighbors, reaching $3.4 billion, according to CBRE.
GXO Logistics, a Greenwich, Connecticut-based supply-chain management company, is taking about 35,000 square feet at Hines’ $500 million T3 FAT Village development in downtown Fort Lauderdale.

The lease is among the three largest signed in South Florida since 2023, behind deals by ServiceNow in Palm Beach and FIFA in Miami, according to Tere Blanca, founder and chief executive officer of Blanca Commercial Real Estate.

New York-based firms are behind 4.6 million square feet of downtown development, roughly 45% of the total. Between 2021 and 2024, New York developers accounted for about 13% of completed projects, according to Blanca.

New York builders are also bringing New York financing. Apollo Global Management’s Athene Annuity and Life Company is backing the Brooklyn developers behind the 46-story Andare Residences, soon to be the tallest tower in Fort Lauderdale.
“I look at the Fort Lauderdale numbers and I’m like, ‘Wow, this is a whole new world being created,’” said Ana Bozovic of Analytics Miami. “That’s following the New York money.”
In contrast, in Orlando and other fast-growing parts of the state, developers have turned to regional banks and insurance lenders to finance even the biggest projects.
Not everyone is convinced. Fort Lauderdale has been called “up and coming” for three decades, and some warn the luxury wave is out of step with the city’s longtime appeal to middle-class families.

“When you’re pitching Fort Lauderdale around the country it makes sense, but then reality hits when you’re on the ground,” said Peter Zalewski, a South Florida real estate broker. “It’s a suburb with high rises. The demographic has always been working class.”
Zalewski pointed to Panama City as a cautionary example, a Florida market that attracted outside capital without the demand to sustain it.
“Developers have overspent,” he said. “We don’t have salaries like Silicon Valley.”

New York developers remain undeterred, egged on by growing public investment. Fort Lauderdale partnered on a $130 million overhaul of Las Olas Marina that made more space for larger super-yachts, restaurants, new retail and a waterfront promenade. The city also plans to widen sidewalks, add landscaping and improve pedestrian and bicycle connections along the strip connecting downtown to the beach.
“I’m looking forward to continuing being involved in the maturing of the city to the point where the question of skepticism will be answered on its own,” Schlesinger said.

items.title: US May Hold Off on New China Tariffs Until After Xi Meeting
body: Good morning. Markets await Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping in Washington next week. Russia’s war on Ukraine enters a critical phase. And Penn Station’s Tracks bar is back. Listen to the day’s top stories.
— Angela Cullen and Harry Black

The mood music is mixed ahead of next week’s meeting between Donald Trump and China’s Xi Jinping. Artificial intelligence, a lingering trade war and the yuan will likely dominate the agenda. The US is expected to hold off announcing new tariffs on China and other trading partners until after the summit, people familiar said, a delay that could preserve the threat as leverage in the negotiations.

Technology stocks drove equity gains as lower oil prices buoyed broader sentiment, setting markets up for a positive end to a turbulent week. The yen slid as Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda vowed to act “preemptively” on inflation but cautioned against moving too quickly, language that failed to convince traders digesting the day’s quarter point hike in the bank’s policy rate. Jeffrey Gundlach warned that the next US downturn could trigger a debt crisis that defies decades of conventional wisdom that Treasuries will always serve as a safe haven. For all the anxiety that’s been gripping the world’s biggest bond market, asset managers spy a silver lining.

Russia’s war on Ukraine is entering a critical phase and rattling Europe. Polish Premier Donald Tusk warned ahead of a visit to Ukraine today that Moscow plans “hybrid-style” drone and missile strikes against Ukraine’s supporters, including NATO-member Poland. Russian incursions pushed deeper into Europe over the summer. French President Emmanuel Macron is convening party leaders to address a “rapidly worsening” security and energy situation as a result of conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, BFM reported. Inside Russia, fears are growing that Vladimir Putin may order a major new mobilization after this weekend’s parliamentary elections.

High in the Austrian Alps, the world’s largest supplier of tungsten is planning a major expansion as prices soar for the exceptionally hard, heat-resistant metal vital to the auto and semiconductor industries. China’s moves to restrict exports, hoard raw material and cut shipments to Japan have intensified a global scramble and driven prices higher. It’s a stark turnaround after years of depressed prices drove many Western suppliers out of business. The dynamic is playing out across several critical minerals markets.
For most diners, the difference between a 7 1/4 ounce burger and an 8 ounce one is hard to tell. Trimming the size of burger patties is one way restaurants are adjusting to surging beef prices.
Marco Rubio has abandoned some of his past beliefs on foreign aid and immigration to become Trump’s unapologetic global envoy. What’s his long game?Big Take Podcast

Much about the global AI panic is genuinely new, and thus extra-scary, writes Andreas Kluth. Analogies from the Cold War era might be useful in untangling those existential fears. As with nuclear war, there are no winners in an out-of-control AI contest.

items.title: Yen Plunges After BOJ Fails to Meet Market Demands With Rate Hike
body: The Bank of Japan hiked and the yen tanked. Whether it was the split vote by board members, mixed signals by Governor Kazuo Ueda or just something else, the weakening partly undoes efforts by Japanese and US authorities to bolster the beleaguered currency.

The yen sank as much as 1.3% against the dollar. The BOJ raised its policy rate by a quarter point to 1.25%, with two board members, Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato, voted against the hike, showing there’s internal resistance to tighter policy.

The outsized reaction shows the complex job facing central bankers and the growing expectations traders are putting on them. The European Central Bank last week hiked rates for a second time. Markets are pricing at least three more hikes in the deposit rate from its current level of 2.5%. The US Federal Reserve on Wednesday lifted borrowing costs for the first time since 2023. Traders see at least one more increase this year and as many as two more in 2027.

With high energy prices triggered by the Iran war fueling inflation, central banks are limited in what they can do to cap price gains. At the same time, elevated bond yields are raising concern about the ability of governments to service their growing debts. While central bankers may not like it, they are increasingly becoming vulnerable to what markets demand.

Treat before meet: The US is expected to hold off announcing new tariffs on China and other trading partners until after next week’s summit between Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump, according to people familiar with the matter, a delay that could preserve the threat as leverage in the negotiations.

The administration had intended to release a trade report on alleged excess capacity before the meeting that would recommend a 7.5% tariff on Chinese goods, Bloomberg previously reported. US and Chinese negotiators are set to meet over the weekend to discuss any agreements ahead of Xi’s state visit.
Meanwhile, the yuan climbed to a more than four-year high against the dollar, potentially easing trade frictions by making Chinese exports less competitive.

Sleepless in Seoul: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said talks with the US over projects tied to Seoul’s $350 billion investment commitment were causing him to lose sleep.  “I myself have spent sleepless nights thinking about this,” Lee said at a press conference Friday. “It carries enormous weight.”

The comments highlight the challenges Seoul faces in implementing the investment package agreed with the Trump administration last year. The delay has angered the US administration, with Trump abruptly scaling back joint military drills last month.Lee ruled out sending troops to the Strait of Hormuz despite pressure from the US president. South Korea is reviewing ways to help ensure safe passage through the strait by expanding the operations of a naval unit already deployed near the area, he said.

King coal: Indonesian tycoon Andi Syamsuddin Arsyad agreed to acquire a major stake in miner Bayan Resources, setting the stage for him to become one of the biggest players in the global coal industry.

The billionaire has been seeking control of Bayan in a deal that would make him one of the world’s top coal producers. He was among the biggest backers of President Prabowo Subianto’s 2024 election campaign and now oversees major government projects, including a 1-million-hectare food estate in Papua.

Boardroom battle: Tata Sons decided to pursue a stock listing and extend its chairman’s term by five years despite strong and public opposition from the founding-family patriarch, setting up a showdown at one of India’s oldest conglomerates.

The board’s announcement marked the latest twist in a saga that’s thrown Tata Group, the maker of everything from salt to SUVs, into turmoil. The group, with $185 billion revenue, controls over two dozen listed companies and is key to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s tech ambitions

Spirit of the age: The two founders of Au Vodka are taking home at least £75 million ($101 million) each from the sale of the spirit brand they started shortly after leaving school, according to Bloomberg calculations.

Charlie Morgan, 31, and Jackson Quinn, 33, completed a £300 million sale of Au to Kentucky-based Sazerac Co. this week, just over a decade after pushing their way into the world’s biggest spirits category with gold bottles and neon-colored vodka flavors. Born in Swansea, the childhood friends founded Au Vodka in 2015 when Morgan was 19 and Quinn was 21.
Morgan first became known when as a 17-year-old ballboy for Swansea City football club, he was kicked by former Chelsea star Eden Hazard for holding on to the ball.

items.title: France Shouldn't Throw Out 3% Budget Anchor, Lescure Says
body: France must stay focused on getting its budget deficit back to the the level permitted under European Union rules, according to Finance Minister Roland Lescure.
Speaking to Bloomberg Television, Lescure said France shouldn’t abandon its plan to get the shortfall back to 3% of economic output in 2029.

“We shouldn’t throw out the anchor of 3%,” he said Friday on the sidelines of a meeting of European finance officials in Dublin. “It is a target we should all have in mind” as France strives to stabilize its debt levels.

Lescure’s comments come after the government announced late Thursday that weaker growth and higher interest costs mean the budget gap will swell to 5.4% of economic output this year, while the finance law had targeted a slight reduction to 5%.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said he’ll propose a €54 billion ($62 billion) effort to curb spending to meet the 5% goal next year. But he faces a struggle adopting those measures with no majority in parliament and opposition groups unwilling for compromise just seven months from presidential elections.
France had previously committed to narrower deficit objectives to get the gap to 3% of economic output by 2029.

Repeated slippages from fiscal targets and government collapses have triggered selloffs on French bond markets in the last two years, sharply raising the country’s borrowing costs compared with European peers.
Read More: French Yield Premium Rises to One Percentage Point on Debt Risks

Last week, the yield premium on French bonds over German equivalents rose to highs not seen since the euro-area debt crisis. The spread has continued widening since, reaching 100 basis points on Friday after the government announced missing deficit goals.
While Lescure described the bond turbulence as global, causing “a rise in the tide for everyone,” he acknowledged that France has “issues” and is trying to address them.
Next year’s deficit goal is “both ambitious and realistic,” he said. “It’s important for us to tell the markets: we are aware of those deficits.”

items.title: France Bond Risk Gauge Reaches New Milestone on Budget Risks
body: A measure of French bond risk rose to one percentage point for the first time in 14 years, a sign of growing caution among investors given the country’s large budget deficit and ongoing political uncertainty.

The additional yield on French 10-year bonds over their German counterparts rose to 104 basis points Friday. While the move came amid a global bond selloff, the underperformance reflects long-standing investor concern over France.

The French government announced on Thursday it will miss its deficit target by a wide margin, adding that politically difficult spending cuts are necessary to narrow the gap in 2027. On Friday, Finance Minister Roland Lescure said in an interview with Bloomberg Television next year’s deficit goal is “both ambitious and realistic.”

“The market has clearly become more concerned,” said Evelyne Gomez-Liechti, a multi asset strategist at Mizuho International Plc. While the spread is elevated, “the problem is the same one we often encounter in rates markets: attractive valuations do not help much when investors cannot identify a catalyst for stabilization,” she added.

France has struggled to get a grip on runaway public finances as economic growth slows sharply and a fragmented parliament pushes back against austerity measures. The spread over Germany, which was already at its widest since 2012, is set for its biggest daily widening in nearly two years.
The risks for next year are particularly acute as opposition parties are reluctant to compromise with President Emmanuel Macron’s outgoing administration just seven months ahead of elections.

Investors are demanding more compensation to own French bonds in face of those risks. The nation’s 10-year yield surged 12 basis points on Friday to 4.56%, the highest since 2008. In another sign of how cheap French bonds have become, the 10-year tenor now commands a 96 basis point premium over swap peers, the most since 2012.
Rates strategists at Societe Generale SA said this week that a 120 basis point spread is “within reach,” particularly if political uncertainty increases.

Macro Hive’s head of rates strategy Antonio Del Favero warned of even wider levels if opposition parties were to find enough common ground during next month’s budget negotiations to pass a no-confidence motion and topple Sébastien Lecornu’s government.
Such an outcome would “reignite fears of prolonged political paralysis or snap elections, and could drive the spread toward 130 basis points on renewed fiscal-credibility concerns,” he said.
While Lescure described the bond turbulence as global, causing “a rise in the tide for everyone,” he acknowledged that France has “issues” and is trying to address them.
“It’s important for us to tell the markets: we are aware of those deficits,” Lescure said.

The French government said late Thursday that weaker growth and higher interest costs mean the budget gap will swell to 5.4% of economic output this year, while the finance law had targeted a slight reduction to 5%.
Read More: France Shouldn’t Throw Out 3% Budget Anchor, Lescure Says

The energy shock triggered by war in the Middle East is also weighing heavily on France’s bonds. The European Central Bank has hiked interest rates twice this year in an attempt to curb a fresh wave of inflation, which is driving up borrowing costs across the bloc.
ECB President Christine Lagarde, speaking at a press briefing after the eurogroup in Dublin, also pointed to the ructions on global bond markets when asked about the French spread.

“We monitor markets, we don’t see any disorderly movement, we don’t see any tension,” she said. “And we appreciate — as you do — that this is a global movement that affects all bonds and particularly at the long end of the curve, for multiple reasons, but no disorderly functioning.”

items.title: China's Fiscal Pullback Extends to August as Spending Slumps
body: China’s public expenditure declined at a quicker rate in August, indicating the government was still withdrawing fiscal support for the economy despite cooling growth momentum.

A measure of broad budget spending fell 6.7% last month from a year earlier, faster than its 4.4% drop in July, according to Bloomberg calculations based on Ministry of Finance data released on Friday. Broad revenue rose 2.9%.
As a result, the fiscal deficit shrank by a fifth in August, taking the shortfall in the first eight months of the year to 5.5 trillion yuan ($821 billion).

The deepening pullback in government spending partly explains the persistence of weak domestic demand in August, when consumption growth almost ground to a halt and investment continued to slump. Policymakers are likely keeping a close eye on how the economy fares in the next few weeks as they assess whether additional stimulus is needed to achieve their annual growth target of 4.5%-5%.

Officials have so far focused on the faster use of existing budget allocations instead of rolling out fresh supportive measures. In one such move, state-owned policy banks started deploying funding from a program that can unlock 800 billion yuan, mainly for infrastructure projects in 2026.

Government bonds slated to be issued during the rest of this year but still unsold were equivalent to around 1.1% of China’s gross domestic product, according to estimates by Miao Yanliang, chief economist at China International Capital Corp. Authorities should be able to meet this year’s growth target with spending financed by the borrowing, he said earlier this week.

items.title: Shapoorji Seeks Bond Payment Delay as Tata Listing Takes Shape
body: India’s Shapoorji Pallonji Group, the conglomerate behind the country’s biggest private credit deal, is in talks with lenders to one of its units to extend a bond payment due at the end of September, according to people familiar with the matter.

The group is seeking to delay by three to six months the repayment of 35 billion rupees ($365 million) due Sept. 30 on a zero-coupon bond issued by its financing arm Porteast Investment, said the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private matters.

The move comes as the debt-laden company continues to face repayment pressures. Proceeds from financing deals done in July were meant to help service Porteast’s bond, but the funds are now being kept for other purposes, the people said.
SP Group didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

An extension would buy SP Group more time to pay down Porteast’s debt just as the outlook for its biggest asset — a minority stake of 18.4% in Tata Sons — is improving, thanks to recent developments toward a potential listing of the Tata holding company. A listing could eventually give SP Group a way to unlock value from the stake it’s used as collateral for billions of dollars in borrowing.

On Thursday, Tata Sons decided to move ahead with the stock listing and extend its chairman’s term by five years, despite opposition from the founding family’s patriarch. SP Group said it’s ready to work with Tata Sons on the listing, a sign that years of tension between two of India’s oldest business families may be easing.

SP Group has held talks with investors in Singapore over the past week on the extension, in meetings arranged by Deutsche Bank, according to the people. Lenders would receive a consent fee for the extension, though details are still being worked out, they said. Deutsche Bank declined to comment.

Porteast raised $3.4 billion last year through three-year zero-coupon bonds at an annual yield of 19.75%, backed by SP Group’s stake in Tata Sons. It had initially raised the loan-to-value limit to 40% from 34% in early April, with the waiver running through July 15, before extending it to Sept. 30.

items.title: Hollywood Got Too Comfortable With Ryan Murphy's Monsters
body: Despite Ryan Murphy’s success as a writer, producer and director, there has always been sharp criticism of his style of mashing up sex and violence into an unsavory stew. Naysayers lament the corrosiveness of such content, referencing years of social science regarding the potentially numbing effects on those who marinate in grisly fare.

This month, however, there’s a nagging sense that fight is over, and critics of Murphy’s abundant output — waged on a two-service front between FX/Hulu and Netflix — have lost. Murphy’s monsters escaped into the mainstream. For Disney-Hulu bundle subscribers, his Hulu shows American Horror Story and The Shards are accessible through the same Disney+ ecosystem that houses Mickey Mouse, fairy-tale princesses and Marvel heroes.

Murphy and his collaborators have taken an axe to what once passed for TV standards. While the horror genre has consistently flourished in theaters — even weathering the roller coaster of post-Covid reopenings — television’s intimacy and accessibility, combined with Hollywood’s willingness to reward Murphy’s excesses, make his interpretation of the genre feel more problematic. Together, those forces have helped normalize sexualized violence, marking a cultural shift from which there may be no turning back.

When American Horror Story premiered in 2011, it was scheduled in the 10 p.m. timeslot on FX. The franchise returns later this month with its 13th edition in the watch-anytime streaming age. It follows closely behind The Shards, which premiered in August and concluded last week and unleashed a serial killer on rich prep-school teens in the 1980s. Then there’s Netflix’s debut this week of Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story, adding a feminine touch to a murderers’ row of Jeffrey Dahmer, the Menendez brothers and Ed Gein.

Although critics savaged the Gein installment of Monster, with a dismal 22% rating on Rotten Tomatoes, viewers tuned in, and the Television Academy blessed the series with seven Emmy nominations this year. The Lizzie Borden edition offers a much more sympathetic protagonist shackled by 19th-century misogyny and mores, but from the double homicide down to the last whack, the season still fits into Murphy’s pattern of combining sexy characters and violent situations — perhaps because that’s now expected.

His shows have become so ingrained in the culture there’s an “old man yells at cloud” quality to raising objections. The familiar rejoinder to critics is that these shows aren’t for you. Nobody’s forcing you to watch. Get over it. Still, those unnerved by the ooze of sexualized violence shouldn’t look away. Because even at the risk of coming across as a prude or scold, we cavalierly stumble down that path at our collective peril.

It’s not alarmism to contend we lose something by embracing distasteful themes or romanticizing heinous figures with thirsty headlines like “From Penn Badgley to Michael C. Hall: Why Are We Crushing on Hollywood’s Hot Serial Killers?” — that one courtesy of Us Magazine in 2025.
Employing a repertory company of high-profile talent, Murphy and his collaborators have settled into a commercially viable formula that consists of beautiful people, kinky sex and graphic violence.

As often happens, a replicable hit breeds imitators. American Horror Story and Monster have plenty of company to glamorize murderous subjects, never mind the true-crime docuseries devoted to homicidal “stars” like Gein, Ted Bundy, John Wayne Gacy and Charles Manson.

What consuming such fare says about “us” became part of Monster’s third installment. The series sought to have its sordid cake and eat it too by detouring to address the many movies inspired by Gein, including Psycho and The Texas Chain Saw Massacre, indicting the audience for its lurid appetites.

While Time critic Judy Berman said the show appeared to harbor “contempt” for its viewers, Murphy’s collaborator, Ian Brennan, told Netflix’s promotion site Tudum that the Gein storyline “turns the camera right on us,” and that people ought to be mindful of the “stories you consume.”

Yet that sounds like a familiar alibi employed by fans of these series and the people who make them: Any excesses are justified by the social problem they supposedly expose, so they’re really just shedding light on the problem, not exploiting it.

Murphy’s sci-fi-tinged The Beauty — which dealt with people transforming into model-pretty versions of themselves, only to go on blood-soaked rampages — deployed a similar defense. Although the show couched its sexualized violence as a device to explore our obsession with youth and beauty, much like the movie The Substance, it wound up feeling like its whole reason for being.

The trend of combining sex and violence, and its potential effects, has prompted concern among academics for some time. Researchers have linked consumption of violent pornography with sexual aggression and raised questions about the desensitizing impact of that kind of steady diet, particularly on younger viewers.

Discussing the topic with me in 2015, Neil Malamuth, a communications professor at UCLA who extensively researched mass media and sexual aggression, warned, “Gradually, the lines between pornography and mainstream entertainment are going to become fuzzy and blurred.”
Eight more seasons of American Horror Story later, such boundaries do indeed seem fuzzy, providing reason to wonder whether we have let ourselves become inured to that.

From that perspective, Brennan wasn’t wrong to point a finger at the audience, but that doesn’t absolve Murphy and his collaborators of responsibility for what they create. And as these shows’ popularity and industry accolades allow them to take a bit of a victory lap, the accountability doesn’t end with the people behind the camera. When it comes to television, we are what we eat.

items.title: Trump and Xi Jinping Face Off on AI as White House Meeting Nears
body: Welcome to Bloomberg’s AI Today newsletter. Every weekday we’ll break down artificial intelligence’s threats and opportunities for businesses, workers, finance and economies. Sign up now if you’re not already on the list.
The jockeying is underway before US President Donald Trump and Chinese premier Xi Jinping sit down at the White House together next week, with artificial intelligence high on the agenda.

The two superpowers are vying for the lead, with China’s best models fractionally behind the US competition on performance, and ahead on cost. Neither welcome calls from US industry leaders to slow down the technology’s development. “Whoever wins AI, wins,” Trump said. China’s foreign ministry described concerns about AI safety as “fearmongering,” clearly seeing the debate as a way to freeze out competition.

The US has been debating its views on the technology in public over the past week, between Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s doomy blogposts about AI posing a risk to humans, bipartisan lawmakers calling for greater regulation and Trump describing such concerns as a “hoax.”

China’s anxiety around AI is a little different, with governance influenced by Confucian values, which prioritizes societal order. Even as the country pushes forward to develop the technology, policymakers worry about the erosion of social stability, employment, internal security and everyday governance — ultimately, about any threat to party rule. Existential fear of the technology doesn’t have the same intensity that is dominating the AI conversation in the US.

Beijing has bet that sufficient regulation, technical standards and state oversight can manage these risks without having to completely slow AI’s march. Xi has proposed global AI cooperation and a centralized UN-style AI oversight body — ideas rejected by US experts.
Both sides view AI as entwined with their respective economic destinies. Neither quite trusts the other on how to prevent its dangers – or even agree upon the threats in the first place.
The following was produced with the assistance of Bloomberg Automation.

King Charles III hosted a summit at Dumfries House in Scotland on Thursday, bringing together AI industry leaders to discuss the risks and responsible development of artificial intelligence. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang called for rigorous testing of AI systems, stating that unsafe products should be held back. Attendees included OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar, Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis, and Anthropic’s public affairs chief Tino Cuéllar.

The Trump administration is weighing whether to update interagency antitrust guidance to address AI safety threats, according to Associate US Attorney General Stanley Woodward, who noted that existing guidelines allow companies to coordinate on cybersecurity risks without violating antitrust rules.

South Korea’s Deputy Prime Minister and Science Minister Kyunghoon Bae declared Wednesday that the country cannot afford to slow AI development, arguing there is a fundamental difference between leading nations choosing to decelerate and a country still catching up. His stance contrasts with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s calls for slower frontier AI development and stronger oversight, aligning more closely with the pro-acceleration positions of Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang.

AI pioneer Andrew Ng dismissed existential fears about artificial intelligence as “science fiction,” arguing that testing, safeguards, and engineering can make AI systems safer over time. He suggested the tech industry is stoking fears for publicity and regulatory influence, expressing dismay at what he called a renewed wave of PR around AI risks.

Nvidia has committed $2 billion to Brookfield Asset Management’s global AI infrastructure fund, confirming the size of a previously disclosed investment. Nvidia serves as an anchor investor alongside the Kuwait Investment Authority in the Brookfield Artificial Intelligence Infrastructure Fund, which targets AI factories, behind-the-meter power solutions, and compute infrastructure. Brookfield is raising $10 billion for the fund as part of a broader $50 billion infrastructure push.

Bitcoin miner CleanSpark is pivoting to AI infrastructure, seeking $2.23 billion in junk bonds to fund construction of a data center in Sandersville, Georgia, fully leased to Meta Platforms subsidiary Anviran LLC under a $6.6 billion, 20-year contract. The deal marks the first junk-bond offering tied to a Meta data center, with Meta guaranteeing rent and operating expenses. Data center developers have sold roughly $39 billion of high-yield bonds so far this year as demand for AI infrastructure surges.

French property services company Emeria SASU added €20 million in projected AI efficiency gains to its Ebitda figure, representing estimated cost savings from an agentic AI program over the next two years. At least ten investors, lawyers, and analysts told Bloomberg it was the first time they had seen potential future AI benefits used as an earnings adjustment. Credit analysts have criticized the move as inappropriate, arguing such savings should only be counted once they have been realized.

EssilorLuxottica received a rare sell rating from Kepler Cheuvreux, which slashed its target price, citing concerns that enthusiasm for AI-powered smart glasses has given way to worries over slower growth, structural margin dilution, governance issues, and the absence of a clear killer app. The Ray-Ban maker’s shares have lost 55% since November, hitting levels not seen since 2022.

UK AI startup Emulate, founded by former Google DeepMind researchers, is in talks to raise $700 million in a seed round at a $3 billion pre-money valuation. Index Ventures and Lightspeed Venture Partners are set to lead the round, with Creandum also participating. The company develops systems to simulate and predict physical world behavior, operating in the emerging “world models” AI space, which is seen as less competitive than the large language model sector.

Europe’s €5 billion Scaleup Europe Fund, managed by Swedish private equity firm EQT AB, is in talks to invest in AI voice startup ElevenLabs in a new funding round that could value the company at roughly $22 billion. ElevenLabs uses AI to generate realistic voices for applications including advertising, audiobooks, call centers, and sales training, and was previously valued at $11 billion in a Sequoia Capital-led round.

SpaceX has held internal discussions about purchasing customer and operational data from troubled or defunct startups to train its AI models at a lower cost, Bloomberg News exclusively reported. The talks within SpaceXAI, the company’s AI unit, are informal and may not result in a deal, with the firm targeting data to improve its Grok models. The approach mirrors Google’s $10 million bid to acquire business data from Spirit Airlines for AI training purposes, and represents a shift for SpaceXAI, which has previously relied on data from Musk’s social network X and in-house AI specialists.

San Francisco’s AI boom is generating enormous wealth ahead of anticipated IPOs from Anthropic and OpenAI, but many laid-off tech workers are being left behind. Former Google employee Basem Istanbouli has been organizing weekly hikes since December through a community called un(PTO), which has grown to over 1,700 unemployed tech workers navigating joblessness. While AI has created intense demand and record compensation for workers who can build the technology, it has simultaneously disrupted employment for many who previously powered the broader tech industry.

India’s outsourcing industry is adapting to AI rather than declining, with the country shifting toward higher-value services such as analytics, software development, and risk management, according to ING Bank. ING economist Deepali Bhargava argues that generative AI disruption fears are premature, noting that AI is reshaping what gets outsourced rather than shrinking demand, as growth moves away from repetitive tasks like data entry and customer support toward higher-complexity work.

Companies rolling out AI are encountering an unexpected human challenge: employee grief. Unlike past technological shifts such as fax machines or the internet, AI has triggered a far more emotionally charged response, with workers questioning their own value. As reported in the Management & Work newsletter, consultants are now advising CEOs to allow employees a formal grieving period as part of AI rollout strategies.

AI data centers are already causing significant environmental harm, with the 60 largest US facilities under construction projected to emit the equivalent of adding 24 million gas-powered cars to the road. As columnist Mark Gongloff writes, the Trump administration has compounded the issue by eliminating Biden-era EPA requirements for fossil-fuel power plants to cut carbon emissions and moving to officially dismiss the public health dangers of power-plant emissions. Critics argue these policy shifts, driven in part by surging energy demand from AI infrastructure, are accelerating climate damage.

Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned last week, citing concerns that AI developers believe the technology could cause mass casualties within the decade, with Anthropic’s alignment science lead Evan Hubinger placing the odds above 10% in the next 10 years. While AI existential risk is often associated with autonomous machines, writes columnist Gautam Mukunda, experts argue the greatest danger lies in AI-assisted bioweapon development.

Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez argues that while data centers are essential infrastructure for the AI revolution, their rapid expansion raises significant environmental, economic, and social concerns. In Ireland, data centers consumed 21% of electricity in 2023, potentially rising to 32%, while US demand is projected to triple to 12% by 2028; a Gallup poll found 71% of Americans oppose local data center construction.
