items.title: Bessent Got Ahead of Himself on Japan
body: It was always going to be a stretch for Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda to sound very hawkish. Given that officials have tightened cautiously the past two years, something major would have to change to hike interest rates at a faster pace.

There's little to suggest he’s eager to ditch the incremental approach. One of the most eagerly anticipated BOJ decisions in recent years risks satisfying nobody. Friday’s rate increase, by a quarter point to 1.25%, had looked like a slam-dunk. But even that relatively modest step ran into resistance from a couple of policymakers.

Traders wanting a more forthright signal that additional moves are in the works will be disappointed; the yen sold off as soon as the decision was announced. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who joined Tokyo in intervening to support the Japanese currency, had piled pressure on the BOJ to stem the yen’s steep decline. The sharp rally after the joint US-Japan effort in July needed an added extra to retain momentum. Bessent implied something special was in the works, asserting that he had information that the market didn't. If so, it didn’t come this week. He was bullish to a fault.

Chances that Ueda would disappoint were considerable; he has a history of being vague and rambling in his press conferences. Friday was no exception. The statement that preceded his briefing repeated a prior assessment that rates will need to keep climbing to ensure inflation doesn’t accelerate far beyond the 2% target. It was absent of any firm indication that multiple hikes will occur before year’s end. Short of drafting the communique himself, there’s not much Bessent can do to move an entire board. Still, it’s unlikely his scrutiny will come to an end any time soon.

Inflation isn’t about to run away in Japan and, while growth is decent, it’s not booming. While he declined to rule out future steps like a 50 basis point move or tightening at successive meetings, Ueda wasn’t going to be pushed further — or beyond what the board could support. Two officials, both appointed by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, dissented in favor of no change. That might signal that the premier’s team are ambivalent about higher borrowing costs, however much they appreciate Washington’s support.

Japan certainly has company when it comes to raising rates. Peers have either hiked or are likely to in the near future. The European Central Bank moved last week, and traders are counting on another step before year-end. The Federal Reserve nudged rates up on Wednesday and signaled the prospect of at least one further move. Higher energy prices may push the Bank of England to tighten.

The BOJ is now part of a Group of Seven cycle. That's an important shift and one that has eluded Japan for a long time. The mere suggestion that the nation might have something approaching normal policy settings is a victory for Ueda, who came to office three years ago with a distaste for the negative rates that his predecessor imposed in 2016. Consider this: When was the last time Japan didn’t have the lowest rate in Asia, a crown that now belongs to Thailand? Even in the unlikely event that Ueda makes no further moves during the remaining two years of his term, he can say that he's leaving the economy on firmer footing than he found it.

Ueda himself, in his most hawkish comments, signaled that the BOJ was now in a new “phase” of policy conduct, more focused on the need to prevent prices from rising too far above its 2% goal than seeking to boost prices toward it. That’s a big claim for a country that has still not officially declared itself out of deflation.

Bessent called for an end to the easy-money policy of Abenomics and Ueda’s predecessor, Haruhiko Kuroda, calling on Japan to “stop the reflation.” But browbeating the BOJ might miss the point of the nation’s current trajectory. “Reflationary policies that simply boost aggregate demand — like Abenomics — are already a thing of the past,” Takuji Aida, chief economist at Credit Agricole and a member of a panel advising the prime minister, said in a note.

BOJ chiefs frequently attend the Fed’s summer retreat in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, each August. Ueda wasn't able to make it last month, but had he been there, he would have heard Fed Chair Kevin Warsh joke about the natural beauty outside the venue. Some attendees prefer gentle strolls along a trail. Others are up for more vigorous hikes. Choose your path carefully, Warsh advised.
Ueda may yet pick up the pace, but a gravity-defying series of increases is out of character. There’s an argument for just being in the game.

items.title: Turkey Investment Funds: How Pusula, Tera Crisis Sparked Market Panic
body: Turkish citizens piled into some high-profile investment funds in recent years, lured by extraordinary gains that would make many finance professionals pause.

Some of these funds offered triple-digit percentage returns or more, fueling suspicion that they were being artificially inflated. In late 2025, regulators began to take a closer look. By mid-September, the concerns had morphed into a full-blown panic as investors rushed to withdraw their money.

Share prices plunged, forcing the firms to sell more assets to raise cash, threatening a cycle of further losses and withdrawals. More than 350,000 people’s savings were exposed to the liquidated funds, and regulators were trying to convince investors that the damage could be contained.

Finance executives in Turkey have long warned about the suspiciously high returns offered by some funds. The flagship fund of Tera Portfoy Yonetimi AS, for example, returned more than 66,000% in the three years to Sept. 16.

In November 2025, Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek acknowledged allegations of manipulation at some funds, without naming them, and pledged to act. The situation also caught the eye of global index providers including MSCI and FTSE, which warned that distorted share price movements were a threat to Turkey’s prized “emerging market” investment status.

In August, national markets regulator SPK moved into action, releasing a new set of guidelines aimed at easing investor concerns over the unusual stock moves. This triggered sharp outflows from some funds. One of these, Pusula Portfoy Yonetimi AS, saw the value of its share holdings crash and it subsequently defaulted, saying it was unable to meet redemption requests.
Read more: Turkey’s Markets Regulator Tightens Rules for Hedge Funds

Tera swiftly announced it would buy the investment firm, but questions continued to swirl over how it would honor redemption demands. Investors in Tera’s funds panicked, and on Sept. 16 the firm said it, too, would be unable to make payments to clients seeking an exit.

Investors pulled about 213 billion liras ($4.7 billion) from the nation’s investment funds between Aug. 31 and Sept. 16, according to fund tracker Fintables. Turkish stocks suffered their biggest slump in more than a year on Sept. 15.

Tera Chairman Emre Tezmen said the firm was facing an “extraordinary and unprecedented” speculative attack that risked spreading across the markets, in a post on X. In an effort to restore confidence and demonstrate that the weakness was confined to just a few firms, the SPK ordered the liquidation of 131 funds run by seven asset management firms.

On Sept. 17, government officials pledged to roll out measures to head off a liquidity crunch and said there was no risk to Turkey’s wider financial system. The benchmark Borsa Istanbul 100 stock index reversed losses. However, a majority of the stocks in the benchmark index continued to decline, with more than 100 falling by almost the regulatory daily limit of 10%.
Tera said it would cooperate fully with regulators to ensure the interests of its investors are protected. Some other companies issued statements saying they were not facing liquidity problems.

They concentrated their investments in illiquid, low-free-float stocks, where a limited supply of tradable shares made it easy to inflate the price. That meant relatively small purchases could drive the shares sharply higher, making their valuations easier to influence. They then used the inflated stock as collateral to take out short-term loans, which they reinvested in the same stocks, according to finance experts who’ve looked at the trading.
Read more: Behind the 40,000% Stock Surge That’s Mystifying Traders in Turkey

As word spread of the funds’ outlandish returns, more savers piled in, boosting their value further. When the regulator’s new guidelines prompted investors to offload some of the underlying stocks, prices tanked, leading to the wave of fund redemption requests.

More conventional money-market funds were also affected, as some of the firms in question were lending to those funds via so-called reverse repo transactions and taking in wildly inflated stocks as collateral. When the value of those stocks plunged, there was no longer enough money to pay back investors in the money-market funds. Funds also held some blue-chip stocks, and sold them for liquidity, leading to a drop in the wider market.

Istanbul-based OMG Capital Advisors Chief Executive Officer Murat Gulkan said losses were likely to continue in the smaller companies at the center of the crisis. “These assets would fetch pennies on the dollar in the event of an arms-length sale to a third party,” he said.
Top executives at the affected funds have not commented on the allegations since the crisis broke.

The SPK banned some market players from trading while it investigated allegations of share-price manipulation. The market regulator followed up with the order to liquidate funds, including at Pusula and Tera. It filed criminal complaints and issued two-year trading bans on some fund managers at the two firms.
The Financial Stability Committee, chaired by Simsek, said it would focus for now on averting a potential liquidity crunch, and said that the troubles were “temporary and manageable.”

The central bank also stepped in, increasing funding via its weekly repo auctions and raising lenders’ borrowing limits on the interbank money market. It began outright purchases of lira bonds, seeking to prevent a spike in yields amid the market volatility.
The funds due to be liquidated had total assets of more than $18 billion and some 350,000 investors.

On Sept. 18, the SPK said private Is Bankasi AS and state-run Ziraat Bankasi AS would oversee the liquidation, with the process to be completed within three months. The banks will sell assets held by the funds in stages and transfer the cash to investors in proportion to their holdings, according to the regulator.
Analysts said the contagion was largely limited for now to smaller stocks and the seven asset managers that were pumping them. The challenge ahead was to regain the trust of investors.
“Confidence in funds has been seriously damaged,” said Onur Duygu, founder of funds analysis platform Fon Turkey. “Bringing investors back into the fund ecosystem could take a long time.”

items.title: Turkey Fund Rout Erases $4 Billion From a Rapidly-Won Fortune
body: For a long time, it seemed little could stop Altunc Kumova, a discreet businessman who became one of Turkey’s richest people after a meteoric rise in his finance firm’s stock.

That all came to an abrupt end this week after the company Kumova owned was one of the worst hit by the nation’s market gyrations and he, along with other top fund executives, was detained as part of an investigation into mass fund outflows.

Kumova controls 74% of Destek Finans Faktoring AS, a finance company that’s lost almost one-third of its value in three days after defaults in some investment funds triggered a market rout and Turkey’s regulator began a widespread crackdown on the fund-management industry. The decline wiped almost $4 billion off Kumova’s paper fortune, which had stood at about $13.8 billion earlier this week.
Events then took an even more dramatic turn late Thursday when Kumova was detained along with several other figures from fund-management firms.
Read more: Turkey Detains Top Fund Executives, Imposes Travel Bans

Destek is one of multiple companies in the orbit of Tera Yatirim Menkul Degerler AS, an Istanbul-based brokerage and asset-management firm that came under intense scrutiny from regulators in recent months, spilling over this week. The Capital Markets Board moved to liquidate almost $20 billion of funds overseen by Tera and other firms while filing criminal complaints and trading bans against them, alleging price manipulation in shares including Destek.
Kumova didn’t respond to a phone call and WhatsApp message. Bloomberg didn’t receive a response to an email sent to Destek.

Destek shares tumbled 27% in three days, the biggest contributor to a 4% drop for the Borsa Istanbul 100 Index. The stock traded at 1,984 liras as of 10:36 a.m. in Istanbul for a market capitalization of 661 billion liras, valuing Kumova’s stake at about $10 billion.

Kumova wealth drop places him alongside Hamdi Ulukaya, the Turkey-born founder and chief executive officer of Greek yogurt company Chobani who’s worth $10.1 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

Destek operates in invoice factoring, a form of finance that involves buying the bills that are owed to companies and then securing payment from the parties they supplied. Founded in 1996, it’s part of a wider group of companies controlled by Kumova including a bank, according to its website.

The company generated net income of 2.6 billion lira for the first half of 2026, filings show. Destek’s price-to-earnings ratio, a metric comparing market value with reported profit, is about 132 times while JPMorgan Chase & Co., the biggest US bank, is at 15 times, Bloomberg data show.
Tera arranged Destek’s initial public offering in 2025. A Tera investment fund also became the company’s biggest shareholder after Kumova, data show.

Led by Chairman Emre Tezmen — who received a travel ban as part of the recent crackdown — Tera has been the talk of Istanbul’s financial circles for minting gains that seemed impossible by normal standards. Its flagship investment fund returned more than 66,000% over a three-year span, fueled by a strategy of pouring billions of lira into a tight circle of related companies and amplifying the bets with borrowed cash.
Read More: Turkey Turns to Two Big Banks to Liquidate Troubled Funds

In August, regulators tightened rules on investment funds holding concentrated bets in illiquid stocks. That forced funds to sell some of their positions and triggered a run to the exits. Funds at Tera Portfoy — Tera’s investment-fund subsidiary — and Pusula Portfoy Yonetimi AS announced in recent days that they’ve been unable to meet client redemptions.

items.title: BOE's Balance Sheet Move Eases Repo Pressure, Barclays Says
body: The Bank of England’s plans to slow the pace of its bond sales will ease pressure on repo operations as well as providing a tailwind for strained long-end gilts, according to a Barclays Plc strategist.

The move has “created a very positive environment for long-dated gilt spreads and the long end of the curve by creating a genuine shortage of paper that is unlikely to be alleviated any time soon,” Barclays’ Moyeen Islam wrote in a note. The BOE is also “implicitly taking some of the operational pressure off its repo operations.”
Read more: Bank of England Eases Bond-Market Pain With Gilt Sales Overhaul

The BOE’s short-term repo facility provides sterling in return for pledging gilts as collateral. Those operations had been expanding faster than reserves were being drained through the BOE’s asset purchase facility, which holds the bonds that were purchased during the BOE’s quantitative easing program.

Slowing the balance sheet runoff should allow both short- and long-term repo operations to grow more gradually, giving the BOE greater control over the banking system’s moves toward its equilibrium level of reserves.

Some gilts could become increasingly scarce. Of the seven bonds maturing between 2029 and 2034 that remain in the BOE’s legacy holdings, six have 30% to 50% of their outstanding stock held in the asset purchase facility, according to Barclays calculations. With little prospect of new supply, fewer may be available to trade or borrow over time, making them relatively more expensive and more sought-after in repo markets.

Some of the longer bond holdings in the asset purchase facilities could become candidates for the UK Debt Management Office’s tender program. This sells non benchmark bonds to ease dislocations and tap lower yields.

Islam said there are still kinks within this new system to be ironed out, including what the DMO will do with the gilts it receives. He said the September minutes “obliquely allude to the MPC discussing the DMO’s ‘ability to retire bonds,’ but this is something that would have to be done in consultation with the market.”
Read more: ‘Hurried’ QT Decision Suggests BOE Is Concerned About Gilts: BMO

items.title: FX Market Is Reliably Calm Even as the World Gets More Volatile
body: Currency volatility has been so low for so long that traders are starting to treat it as the new normal rather than a passing phase.

That subdued backdrop was among the major themes at an annual industry gathering in Amsterdam this week for a second year running, with investors describing a market where sharp changes in bonds, oil and geopolitics still struggle to generate lasting currency swings.

“What we are lamenting is a secular downtrend in currency volatility,” said Harish Neelakandan, co-chief investment officer at AlphaEngine Global Investment Solutions, a systematic trend-following fund. “That’s the hand we’ve been dealt. We have to learn to live with this.”

This lack of volatility in the $9.6 trillion-a-day foreign-exchange market is becoming a perennial problem for traders aiming to thrive on big swings. Yet the calmer environment is likely to be beneficial for asset managers and companies looking to hedge their exposure.

Neelakandan said greater coordination between central banks has helped contain currency moves, leaving geopolitical shocks to produce only brief bursts of volatility. Unless that backdrop changes fundamentally, traders are likely to keep treating such spikes as opportunities to short volatility once again.

“What we’re seeing is the ‘nothing ever happens’ trade, where people just keep selling volatility,” said Thomas Carreau, a currency portfolio manager at CN Investment Division, which manages Canadian National Railway’s pension fund.
Read more: Traders Blame ‘Insane’ Tech Advancements for Quiet FX Markets

Even recent yen moves have remained relatively contained, Carreau said. The currency has been in the spotlight in recent months after sliding to the weakest in four decades before joint US-Japanese intervention to support it caused a series of sharp rallies.

He added that carry trades, where investors borrow in low-yielding currencies to buy higher-yield assets, continue to perform well. He prefers to structure them to be dollar neutral because US President’s Donald Trump’s social media posts can still cause small day-to-day swings in the US currency. It’s a strategy that performs well when volatility is low.
“Carry is king,” he said.
Read more: Carry Traders Eye Franc, Krona as Yen’s Funding Appeal Ebbs

The prolonged calm does pose some risk. Harel Jacobson, associate portfolio manager at hedge fund Capstone Investment Advisors, said lower volatility forces traders to put on larger positions to generate the same returns, leaving portfolios more exposed when a rare big move hits.

“What you end up with is a ticking time bomb sitting on your portfolio,” said Jacobson. His fund routinely buys cheap hedges designed to protect against unusually large market moves, pointing to last year’s surge in the Taiwan dollar as the kind of event they are looking to cover.
Low volatility isn’t necessarily bad news for everyone. It can also reflect a liquid and efficient market that continues to absorb shocks in a volatile world.
“The world might not be reliable, but the FX market is,” said the conference chair Allan Guild, director of Hilltop Walk Consulting.

Companies are adapting their strategies. Georgios Velissariou, head of financial risk management at Hitachi Energy’s group treasury, said lower volatility had made options a more attractive way to hedge certain currency exposures.

Meanwhile for some banks, the environment is prompting a rethink of parts of their operations. Karel Sanders, head of FX product management at Rand Merchant Bank, said dollar-rand volatility at a two-decade low was forcing the South African lender to reconsider how it runs its options business.
“Do we stay principal market makers in FX volatility, or do we become an agency business? We’re leaning more towards an agency business,” he said.

There were also signs on the conference floor that traders were looking beyond traditional FX for action. At one stand, attendees were tempted by sweet Dutch waffles to vote on which currency pair would move the most over the main day. The winner was silver against the dollar.
A market increasingly built around low volatility may be poorly protected on the rare occasions when that calm breaks. Some see little incentive to prepare.
“The market finds itself in a situation where we don’t know what the catalyst will be for the next blow up and no one is positioned for it, because if you’re early you’re wrong,” said Carreau.

items.title: NSE's $2.4 Billion India IPO Fully Subscribed on Second Day
body: The $2.4 billion initial public offering of National Stock Exchange of India Ltd. was fully subscribed on the second day of bidding, bringing the world’s busiest derivatives exchange by volume closer to completing one of the biggest listings in the country’s history.

Bids exceeded the 88.6 million shares on offer, with the portions reserved for institutional and wealthy investors each covered 1.3 times, according to data on the BSE Ltd.’s website as of 2:45 p.m. local time. Retail investors bid for nearly 65% of the shares set aside for them.

Full subscription brings NSE to the brink of completing a long path to the IPO dating back to 2016, when the exchange first filed. The plan was delayed for years amid regulatory and governance issues.
Read More: NSE Slashes IPO Ambitions as World’s Biggest Options Boom Fades
NSE is offering shares at 1,700 rupees to 1,785 rupees apiece, with bidding scheduled to close on Sept. 21. The offering consists entirely of stock sold by existing shareholders.

At the top end of the range, the offering would raise about 226 billion rupees ($2.4 billion), making it India’s largest IPO after Hyundai Motor India Ltd.’s 279 billion-rupee share sale in 2024. The price would value NSE at about 42.9 times its earnings for the year ended March. While that’s a discount to domestic rival BSE Ltd., it’s well above the roughly 24 to 25 times earnings multiple for some of the world’s largest listed exchanges.

The exchange has the potential to emerge as a company that shows steady growth over the long term and could become a meaningful holding in investors’ portfolios, according to Thomas J. Priju, a portfolio manager at Karma Capital. In the near term, a resolution of the issues around the new closing auction mechanism could provide an additional catalyst, he said.

Still, one of the biggest risks is tighter regulatory scrutiny of speculative derivatives trading, a business central to NSE’s profitability. Options trading accounted for about 60% of operating revenue in the year ended March, leaving the exchange exposed to measures aimed at curbing activity in the segment.

Before opening its order book, NSE received the buy-in of anchor investors who committed 67.46 billion rupees. They included global funds like Goldman Sachs, HSBC, Fidelity, Eastspring, as well as sovereign wealth funds GIC Singapore and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority. Among local firms, Life Insurance Corp., SBI Funds Management Ltd and ICICI Prudential Asset Management Co. were some of the largest anchor investors in the offering.

items.title: The US Wants China to Know It Has Weapons in Space
body: In a surprising statement this week, Secretary of the Air Force Troy E. Meink revealed that the US has weapons in space. He said, “We are increasing readiness against existing threats, and the United States has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action.”

The surprise was less the substance than the decision to say it publicly. Military analysts have long assumed that the US possessed sophisticated counterspace capabilities, but the Pentagon had never acknowledged deploying weapons in orbit.

Meink, an Air Force veteran with a Ph.D. in aeronautical engineering, is an expert on space-based communications and intelligence systems. He did not discuss any details about what kinds of weapons are in orbit. There was no chance his remarks would go unnoticed: They came at the Air, Space & Cyber Conference, a high-profile annual gathering of military leaders and defense contractors in Maryland.
Why did he decide that this was an appropriate time to abandon Washington’s longstanding ambiguity about weapons in orbit?

First, as Meink said, talking about space weapons may serve as a deterrent against China and Russia. Both are likely moving ahead with systems that can put at risk America’s most valuable satellite constellations, which provide precise navigation, clear communications and high-grade intelligence-gathering.

Moscow and Beijing are testing or deploying maneuverable satellites, high-energy lasers and antisatellite missiles. Most alarming, Moscow may be developing a space-based nuclear weapon that could use electromagnetic pulses to disrupt or destroy US satellites across a wide area.
Given this rising threat, publicly signaling that the US can retaliate or protect its satellites will serve as a deterrent.

A second reason for the secretary’s revelation may be to build momentum for “Golden Dome,” President Donald Trump’s signature effort to build a missile shield around the entire US. It is a project of enormous scale and challenge, reminiscent of Ronald Reagan’s Strategic Defense Initiative, the never-realized “Star Wars” project.

Meink also highlighted the military’s progress on space-based interceptors that would be part of a national missile defense. Publicly acknowledging that the US has weapons in orbit may make Golden Dome seem more realistic. That’s important, because it has a whopping price tag: The Congressional Budget Office has estimated that a national missile-defense system like Golden Dome would cost $1.2 trillion over two decades; some think tanks such as the American Enterprise Institute have provided estimates of up to $3.6 trillion for more ambitious systems.

Third, the founding of the US Space Force and reestablishment of US Space Command during Trump’s first term has created momentum for space operations generally. The Space Force, the sixth branch of the US armed forces, organizes, trains and equips personnel for military space operations. But with only 15,000 active-duty members, it isn’t always taken as seriously as it should be.

Space Command was created in 1985 but in 2002 folded into US Strategic Command, which oversees the nuclear arsenal. The Trump administration revived Space Command as one of the 11 unified combatant commands, providing an operational center of gravity for the new Space Force. Counterintuitively and controversially, Space Command is considered a geographic command, with an “astrographic” area of responsibility extending from 62 miles above the earth (the Karman line) to the Moon and beyond.

In the late 1990s, while serving under the Joint Chiefs of Staff, I was present at arguments about whether Space Command should be considered geographic or functional like Strategic Command. Some said, “space is not a place like the surface of the earth, but rather a domain like cyber or the air.” I remember one general countered poetically that its area of responsibility should be “from the skies above the earth to the mind of God.” That’s a big AOR.

In publicly acknowledging the Pentagon’s orbital weaponry while revealing nothing about its scope or capabilities, Meink put America’s adversaries on notice. Ending years of strategic ambiguity about space will only increase deterrence here on Earth.
Stavridis is dean emeritus of the Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy at Tufts University. He is on the boards of Aon, Fortinet and Ankura Consulting Group.

items.title: Germany Gets First US Fighter Jet Amid Worry Over Dependency
body: Germany took delivery of its first F-35A fighter jet from US manufacturer Lockheed Martin Corp., part of Berlin’s unprecedented defense spending splurge at a time of simmering tensions with President Donald Trump.
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius lauded the capabilities of the fighter jet on Friday in a short speech during a rollout ceremony in Fort Worth, Texas.
“This aircraft ushers a new era of airpower for the German Luftwaffe,” Pistorius said. “It is an important step toward further strengthening the collective deterrence and defense.”

The ceremony was partly overshadowed by remarks from Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who told conservative party members on Thursday in Berlin that the era of “unconditional” ties between the US and Europe — built up since World War II — was done.

Amid the strain in the bilateral relationship, Pistorius defended the decision to buy the US jet. He argued it was the only fifth-generation stealth fighter jet capable of carrying US nuclear bombs as part of NATO’s nuclear sharing arrangement. Germany itself is not allowed to own nuclear weapons due to international treaties.

US officials have pushed back against rumors that the F-35 could be downed with a hidden kill switch. Critics also point to the frequent need for software updates that would make foreign clients of the jet dependent on future US cooperation.
Read more: Merz Says US Friendship Built Since War ‘Probably Over’ for Now
Germany decided to purchase 35 jets for €10 billion ($11.5 billion) in 2022 during former Chancellor Olaf Scholz’s administration, shortly after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Pistorius said the purchase of a US system would strengthen transatlantic defense cooperation, adding that Germany could trust the US administration and that mutual dependencies between the US and Europe were not a bad thing.

German Air Force Chief Holger Neumann pointed to the aircraft’s advanced sensors and communications systems, saying it would be an asset to every NATO ally, collecting and synthesizing large amounts of data. There are currently 19 nations that operate the F-35 globally.

The ceremony was also attended by Lockheed President Orlando Sanchez Jr., Texas Republican Rep. Craig Goldman and Dan Zimmerman from the US Defense Department, who called Germany a “model ally” given Berlin’s ramp-up in purchases of US military gear.

Lockheed Chief Operating Officer Frank St. John said that roughly 25% of each F-35 jet is manufactured in Europe, such as the center fuselage at a Rheinmetall factory in Germany. Other components are being built in the United Kingdom and Italy.

On Tuesday, Pistorius and his US counterpart Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth signed an agreement to deepen transatlantic defense industry cooperation and boost weapons production as both sides look to fill low stocks of air defense missiles and deep strike weapons.
Read more: Hegseth, Pistorius Ink Deal For Firms to License US Missiles
Germany’s F-35As will be stationed at Buechel Air Base in the western state of Rhineland-Palatinate.

Germany’s first eight aircraft will be handed over this year, followed by 10 units in 2027 and another 10 in 2028, with the remaining seven arriving in 2029. Some of the jets will remain in the US for training purposes.
The German Air Force is considering 15 additional jets, but Pistorius told reporters at the sidelines of the rollout that there was no final decision on the matter.

Germany this year buried a joint project to develop a sixth-generation fighter jet with France, in a program known as FCAS. Some lawmakers and military experts argue the future of modern warfare means certain capabilities could be covered more efficiently with precision deep-strike weapons and unmanned fighter jets or large drones.

items.title: Nestle India Faces Legal Action Over Infant Formula Claims
body: India’s food regulator said it has initiated legal action against Nestle India Ltd. for breaching infant nutrition marketing rules and for substandard manufacturing.

The company’s promotional material for Nan Excella Pro Stage 1 and Lactogen Pro Stage 1 claims to contain “whey Protein” and “5 HMOs” natural sugars, violating the rules that restrict such messaging to boost sales of baby food, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India said in an Instagram post Friday. It has sought clarification from the Gurugram-based unit of the Swiss foodmaker.

FSSAI also found a sample of the firm’s follow-up formula “sub-standard” for its Biotin content, it said, adding that legal action has been initiated against Nestle India “over several non-compliances pertaining to the Food Safety and Standards Act.”
Nestle shares reversed early gains to fall as much as 2.8% after the announcement compared to an advance in the benchmark Nifty 50 Index.

“Our products are fully compliant with all the applicable regulations,” a company spokesperson said, adding that the two infant formulas and their labels were approved by an expert committee at FSSAI.
Nestle has submitted a detailed response regarding statements appearing on the labels, “which are factual in nature, and supported by scientific literature,” the spokesperson said.

The probe against Nestle India highlights the nationwide crackdown on malpractices in the food industry in recent months. The national regulator has proposed warning labels indicating sugar, salt and fat content in packaged food for makers of soda to chocolate and chips.

items.title: SoftBank Boosts Credit Line to $6.5 Billion as AI Debts Mount
body: SoftBank Group Corp. secured an additional $450 million to increase the size of an existing credit line to $6.5 billion, people familiar with the matter said, giving the Japanese conglomerate more financial flexibility as it expands investments in artificial intelligence.

The previous facility equivalent to $6.05 billion was due to expire this month, and SoftBank will have another year to draw down on the expanded amount, according to the people who asked not to be identified because the information is private. It’s unclear whether SoftBank has tapped the new line or if it plans to do so.

SoftBank is at the epicenter of debates about the future of debt-fueled bets on AI, at a time when market volatility has increased amid safety warnings. One of the world’s biggest investors in the technology, the conglomerate has recently conducted a flurry of deals to finance its push that includes an expanded stake in AI giant OpenAI. In one of the latest examples, SoftBank increased its margin loan backed by shares of its chip unit Arm Holdings Plc by $5 billion to $25 billion.

There are currently more than 20 banks involved for the expanded credit line, the people said. The new deal carries an interest margin of 210 basis points over the benchmark Secured Overnight Financing Rate, they added.
A representative from SoftBank declined to comment.

Commitment or credit lines are revolving loan facilities that lenders make available for a set period. Companies often treat them as liquidity backstops and do not necessarily draw on the funds immediately.

The credit line adds to a wave of debt-raising activities tied to SoftBank’s bet on OpenAI and more broadly, on artificial intelligence. Recent financings include an $11.87 billion term loan and a $10 billion loan backed by its OpenAI stake, despite concerns about growing risks in the sector.
Founded and led by billionaire Masayoshi Son, SoftBank is slated to invest close to $65 billion in OpenAI by October.
SoftBank also signed a $40 billion bridge loan earlier this year to finance its OpenAI investments. The Japanese firm paid the entire outstanding balance of $25.9 billion on that borrowing this week.

The company has drawn down $30 billion from the bridge loan but it hasn’t given any guidance if it will take the remaining $10 billion. The next time it can do so is in early October, the people said.

The company has also been meeting with fixed-income investors in New York this week to test appetite for a possible junk bond offering that could total $10 billion to $20 billion, people familiar with those discussions have said. A deal could come to the market as early as next week, according to other people briefed on the matter.
“We have investor meetings to provide an update in New York on a non-deal basis. Nothing has been determined on bond issuance,” SoftBank said when asked about the meeting.

Separately, Apollo Global Management Inc. is in talks with SoftBank about boosting the size of a loan to $9 billion from $5.4 billion to help the Japanese firm finance its investment in OpenAI, people familiar with the deal said earlier this week.

Debate has been intensifying over the pace of AI development and the risks associated with increasingly powerful systems. Some executives are now voicing the need to slow the pace of development due to escalating risks from the technology. OpenAI Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman has said that his company wouldn’t proceed with a public offering this year as it addresses safety-related concerns.
The cost of insuring SoftBank’s debt against default has climbed this year, with credit-default swaps marking a three-year high earlier this week.

items.title: Is It Really AI End Times or Just 'Cognitive Surrender'?
body: Listen and subscribe to Everybody’s Business on Apple , Spotify, iHeart and the Bloomberg Terminal.

Senior tech executives spent the past few weeks loudly warning of the risks posed by artificial intelligence. Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei — who has been furiously racing to develop ever-more human-like chatbots ahead of a potential initial public offering — published an essay suggesting instead that the industry needs to slow down or risk eradicating all human beings. (Apparently some Anthropic employees put that possible outcome at around 10%.)

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he also favored a slowdown, and SpaceX’s Elon Musk concurred, sketching out a nightmare scenario. “If it were able to take control of military systems and, say, launch a nuke,” he said of AI, “that would be bad.”

Critics have pointed out there are aspects of these warnings — and previous warnings from the AI giants — that are potentially self-serving. For instance, they draw attention from more immediate risks, such as AI-generated scams, the proliferation of AI “slop” and the fact that college students are relying on chatbots to such an extent that administrators warn of “cognitive offloading” and “cognitive surrender.”

This week on Everybody’s Business, journalist Vauhini Vara joins to discuss a potential solution: software that promises to sort slop from the real thing. In the latest issue of Bloomberg Businessweek, Vara profiled Pangram, a startup whose founders contend we’ll eventually rely on detectors to avoid AI text in the same way we use spam filters to avoid junk email. Pangram is controversial, partly because it essentially offers an AI solution to AI problems, but also because critics have warned of the danger of false positives.

But Vara found that Pangram seems to offer an impressive level of reliability — or at least a low rate of false positives. It’s also, she says, somewhat different from the large language models it attempts to detect, in the sense that its own models are smaller and its founders have licensed the content they’ve scanned (in contrast to the main chatbot operators, which ingested huge quantities of copyright-protected text and video without initially paying licensing fees). Pangram has been popular on social media as a way to shame writers who may have  done a little bit of cognitive offloading, but it’s especially popular among college professors, who use it as a starting point to enforce a no-AI writing policy.

Also this week, we explore a possible fan backlash to the sudden influx of private equity cash into sports with Bloomberg reporter Randall Williams. As long as pro-football and other major sports continue to post huge ratings, and as long as franchise values soar, investors will look for sports investments. But there are hints of fan resistance in the National Basketball Association’s reaction to  alleged salary cap manipulation by the league’s wealthiest owner, and the swift demise of the plan to sell part of the World Cup to a   vehicle connected to the Kushner family.

Finally, we discuss Kevin Warsh’s decision to act like a conventional Federal Reserve chair, bucking pressure from Donald Trump, and Coyote vs. ACME, a David and Goliath story within a David and Goliath story that is also, maybe, the perfect movie for the current political moment.

About the show: every week, hosts Stacey Vanek Smith and Max Chafkin take a look at the week’s business news and break down what you need to know with the help of Bloomberg journalists, experts and the people and businesses trying to navigate the economy every day.

items.title: Iran War, Tariffs and Trump's Second-Term Quest to Be Consequential
body: Rarely has the post-World War II global order felt so messy. America’s six-month-long war against Iran has entrenched the Islamic regime, closed the Strait of Hormuz and sent oil prices  soaring. Despite Donald Trump’s promise that he’d end the conflict in Ukraine “on Day 1,” it rages unabated. Meanwhile, the president constantly swaps US enemies and allies, wooing North Korea’s Kim Jong Un while weakening ties with South Korea, making fresh threats to wrest control of Greenland from NATO member Denmark, and instigating a trade war and an absurd Great Lakes-naming tussle with America’s erstwhile friend to the north, Canada.

One of Trump’s favorite words these days to describe his own presidency is “consequential.” He wants to be seen as a historic leader who remapped the world and shifted the tectonic plates of history. At home, that’s meant erecting monuments, demolishing a wing of the White House to make way for a ballroom over a chorus of legal and practical objections, and renaming places for both himself and the US at a steady clip. Abroad, trying to preordain his own legacy has required waging economic warfare on an unprecedented scale and, in cases where that hasn’t worked on an acceptable timeline, such as Venezuela and Iran, using military force. But foreign countries and their leaders aren’t as easily coerced as US lawmakers. And Trump’s second-term quest to be consequential looks poorly conceived and, at least for now, nothing short of catastrophic.

The president’s crusade intensified on April 2, 2025, when he signed an executive order announcing sweeping tariffs on imports. China answered these so-called Liberation Day tariffs by rolling out its own levies and restrictions on US goods and withholding access to rare earths that are vital to manufacturing in aerospace, defense and other industries. At the same time, European nations, feeling jilted by a longtime partner, deepened their relationships in South America, Asia and the Middle East. Countries found they didn’t need America to the extent they once thought.

Instead, the primary victim of Trump’s tariffs wound up being America itself. US companies and their customers had to pay the levies, while business leaders were left to survey a more hostile landscape abroad, with long-standing allies searching for backups to America’s artificial intelligence models, cloud computing services and even the dollar. “You basically have the entire world eager now to build workarounds to the US financial system,” says Edward Fishman, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and the author of Chokepoints: American Power in the Age of Economic Warfare. “It’s not just problematic from an American power standpoint, it’s problematic for our businesses and for American economic dynamism.”

When economic pressure was ineffective, Trump’s quest to be consequential required a more forceful approach. That worked in Venezuela in January, when Special Forces neatly extracted President Nicolás Maduro and his wife from Caracas and installed a leader more inclined to give the US access to its prodigious oil reserves. Emboldened by their success, Trump and his advisers then tried to run the same playbook in Iran. Acting in concert with Israel, they killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, significantly set back the country’s nuclear program — and prodded Iran to use its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, the conduit for about 20% of the world’s oil shipments.

In trying to leave a lasting mark on the map in his second term, Trump has learned that coercion doesn’t always deliver the desired result. Sovereign countries aren’t easily steamrolled, and exerting pressure can be counterproductive — solidifying support for even unpopular leaders and hardening their resolve. Cuba, another country on Trump’s regime-change wish list, is a 70-year-old object lesson in the high pain tolerance of authoritarian nations bent on challenging American hegemony. Democracies, on the other hand, tend to have a comparatively low pain threshold. They wobble at the first sign of higher fuel prices, a slowing economy and, especially, wartime casualties.

One question the October issue of Bloomberg Businessweek poses is what kind of political price will be paid by Trump’s top foreign affairs advisers, primarily Marco Rubio, the secretary of state. As a senator, Rubio was an internationalist who seemed to have a good handle on the limits of economic statecraft and military intervention. But unlike his predecessors in Trump’s first term, who tried to counterbalance his impetuous whims, Rubio has ubjugated his expertise and sees his job as helping to execute the president’s “America First” vision of the world. If circumstances in the Middle East don’t improve by the US election in 2028, there will almost certainly be a backlash against anyone associated with that approach.

It’s always possible the wind could shift in Trump’s — and Rubio’s — favor. Iran’s economy is in shambles, its new leader hasn’t been seen in months, and its proxies in Gaza and Lebanon have been weakened. “If at the end of this we have a stronger NATO because the Europeans are finally doing their own part for defense, and we’ve got different regimes in Venezuela, Cuba and Iran, that is a different global map than when Trump came in,” says Matthew Kroenig, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Scowcroft Center for Strategy and Security and an adviser to Rubio’s 2016 presidential campaign. “But we’re not there yet. There’s still a lot of stuff that could go wrong.”

For now, Trump’s quixotic crusade to be considered one of history’s “great men” has awakened friends and foes alike to their own leverage over the US. It’s had consequences for sure. They’re just not the ones he imagined.Read next: Marco Rubio Remakes Himself as Trump’s MAGA Warrior

items.title: Diesel Is Coming for Trucking, Your Home - and the Midterms
body: US energy politics usually begin and end with gasoline prices. Those are at a seasonal record, but even $4.44 a gallon pales against diesel, now at an all-time high of $6.40. Most drivers’ eyes skim over that bit of the price sign — it’s called a gas station, after all — but America can’t afford to look away. Diesel isn’t just an immediate price (and politics) problem; it’s building up vulnerabilities for the US on several fronts that will play out through winter and into 2027.

A barrel of crude oil gets refined into different products such as gasoline, naphtha and so forth. One is “distillate fuel oil,” which consists of transportation diesel — about 75% of the total — along with fuel oil to heat homes and run generators and other industrial processes. The US uses about 3.9 million barrels of distillate a day, on average. That is far less than gasoline’s 8.8 million barrels. But diesel is the fuel of commerce, powering trucks, trains, tractors and more besides, meaning its price ripples into everything: logistics, manufacturing, agriculture, construction — even data centers.

This adds another sticky element to already stubborn inflation that, as my Bloomberg Opinion colleague  Jonathan Levin wrote recently, risks unmooring broad price expectations. Brief jumps in diesel can be passed on with temporary surcharges on freight contracts, but a sustained increase will ultimately get embedded in those contracts and hit kitchen tables as it flows down the supply chain.

The current increase has legs. Crude oil at $100-plus due to the Iran war is a big factor. JP Morgan Chase & Co.’s commodities analysts just threw their hands up on predicting where that goes, writing  “we simply don’t know how to model the endgame.”

But this clearly isn’t just about crude oil; it is also about refining, with diesel futures trading around $214 a barrel (retail equates to almost $269). The price difference between diesel and crude oil futures, or the “crack spread,” is now about $112 a barrel, higher than the price of crude itself — which is most unusual.

Alongside crude oil, the Iran war has also disrupted regional refinery production and fuel shipments. Ukraine’s drone attacks on Russian refineries have strengthened at the same time, to the point where President Donald Trump recently tried to shift the blame for expensive diesel to Kyiv (you may recall that Ukraine has reason to target Russia’s refineries). Russian and Middle Eastern diesel exports in August were together down 75%, year on year, the International Energy Agency estimates. Globally, refinery runs were down 4.2 million barrels a day.
When refineries aren’t running, stocks get drawn down. Things have been a little different in the US, though: Refineries are running flat out but stocks have still plunged.

The US had about 104 million barrels of distillate in storage at the end of August — the lowest level for that month since the early 1950s, when demand was a third of today’s level. Distillate demand rises from here to its winter peak, partly because of harvesting and households burning heating oil, primarily in northeastern states. New England, where stocks are around the lowest on record, best hope this winter isn’t like the last one.

Those huge crack spreads, though, mean US refineries are having a golden year; it is the leading S&P 500 sub-sector by far, up 141% to date. They are working harder, and for longer, than usual, with utilization running north of 95% all summer.

Diesel exports have risen, though, as other countries disrupted by geopolitical ructions bid for US barrels. There is a growing risk for oil companies that Trump, ally though he may be, panics about prices ahead of the midterm elections and bans fuel exports (see this). This week’s comment from Senate Majority Leader John Thune that he is “open to exploring” the idea won’t have gone down well in Houston.

The basic problem, however, is that there are only so many US refineries. Energy Secretary Chris Wright has mused about invoking the Defense Production Act to boost capacity. Federal funding conceivably might help reopen a recently closed refinery, such as Valero Corp.’s Benicia plant in California, analysts at ClearView Energy Partners point out, or even the “long-challenged” Limetree Bay facility in the US Virgin Islands. But none of that would be overnight. As for brand new refineries, any developer must weigh a multi-decade investment against flat US oil demand and federal energy policy that has swung from pro-fossil fuels to green energy and back again in the space of one decade.

Running refineries harder for longer, meanwhile, builds up a deficit of deferred maintenance. Utilization has been higher than average all year, and the fall maintenance season may be trumped by those high cracks. That risks teeing up disruptive unplanned outages next year, when the market might hope to rebuild depleted stocks.

By then, of course, the two wars underlying this crisis may be over. At least one of those is nominally under Trump’s control, and he is clearly aware of the political fallout from high energy prices as the midterms loom. Fuel oil may not be a blanket issue like gasoline, but it heats a lot of homes in several Senate battleground states such as Alaska, Maine and New Hampshire, and its use is more prevalent in rural areas that often skew Republican. Once the smoke clears after the Nov. 3 elections, however, America’s diesel problems will still be mounting.

items.title: Hungary Can Quit Russia Gas, Reviews Nuclear Deal, Minister Says
body: Hungary can meet European Union regulation to completely wean the country off Russian gas in a year’s time, the energy minister said, in a significant shift from the policies pursued under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban.

Hungary has enough pipeline connections to source gas from elsewhere at competitive prices, Economy Minister Istvan Kapitany said in a Telex interview published on Friday. The government is also reviewing the Russian-led expansion of its sole nuclear plant and is in talks with suppliers to diversify crude oil supplies away from Russia.

“If the situation develops the way it currently appears, Hungary’s gas supply can and will be secured from other sources” by October 2027, Kapitany said, citing the date when EU member states must stop natural gas imports from Russia.

The comments signal Prime Minister Peter Magyar’s readiness to break with Orban’s approach to Russia. During 16 years of rule that ended in April’s election, Orban had doubled down on Moscow for energy, even as EU peers moved to end their own reliance following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Orban had argued that landlocked Hungary had no other options to ensure its energy security. Critics had said the policy helped convert Budapest into a tool of the Kremlin, isolating Hungary as Orban sought to block sanctions against Moscow and worked to undermine Western aid for Kyiv in order to please Russia.
Read More: Hungary Expels 10 Russian Diplomats in Break from Orban Era

The Orban government’s decision to scrap an international tender for the expansion of the Paks nuclear plant and to hand the contract to Russia’s Rosatom Corp. in 2014 had been widely seen as the centerpiece of the country’s changing and ever closer ties to Russia.

Kapitany said the project, which is running years behind, is now also under review and that a decision would be made by the end of the year on whether the expansion of the 2,000 megawatt plant is needed at all.
He pointed to technological advances that may allow the country to extend the lifetime of the four current nuclear blocks — which would otherwise expire in 2032 — by another 20 years.

“The review is still ongoing, we’ll finish it by the end of the year and that’s when we’ll make a decision on whether Hungary needs the additional nuclear blocks in its energy mix,” Kapitany told Telex. He said the review was being conducted in an “open-minded and totally objective way.”
Read More: EU Court Puts Hungary’s Russia-Led Nuclear Project in Limbo (1)

Besides diversifying energy sources, Hungary is also aiming to reduce imports, particularly in electricity. Plans include to boost energy storage capacity and to open up the country to major wind power investments.

The country’s energy import reliance has for long been a key economic vulnerability, with global oil and gas price shocks having an outsized impact on the local currency. The forint swung this week as investors assessed whether energy supply concerns from the Middle East crisis may ease.

items.title: NYC's Flatiron Building Welcomes Buyers After Office-to-Residential Conversion
body: Bill Sofield refers to himself as an archaeologist. He is by profession, however, an interior designer, known for the stores he’s done for clients such as Tom Ford and Gucci. For the past 3½ years he’s been working inside the Flatiron Building, one of the most photographed structures in the world, turning it into 37 apartments.

When Sofield walked its first two floors, what he found was wreckage: severed cast-iron staircases that led nowhere, the bolted remains of a boiler, air handlers from another century. The building, one of New York City’s oldest surviving skyscrapers, had stood almost empty for years. His job was to turn the ruins into homes.

Designed by Daniel Burnham and built in 1902 as a construction company’s headquarters at the triangle where Fifth Avenue intersects Broadway, the Flatiron captured the popular imagination almost from the start. Alfred Stieglitz photographed the prow in the fog. Childe Hassam painted it in winter. Postcards from the first decades of the 20th century show women’s skirts lifting in the wind tunnel at the building’s base, an accident of air pressure that popularized one of the era’s more durable scraps of slang: “23 skidoo.” (That’s what police told the men loitering at the corner of 23rd Street for the view, or so it goes.) Andrew Dolkart, who teaches historic preservation at Columbia University and once worked at the city’s Landmarks Preservation Commission, calls the steel-framed Beaux Arts tower the first building to become a symbol of New York: “It became famous in both high culture and low.”

For 124 years the Flatiron has been celebrated by New Yorkers. Sometime late this fall, it will become home to a select few of them. Buyers have paid from $11 million to more than $50 million for units in the building, where the least expensive apartments are roughly the size of a suburban house. Sixteen of the 37 residences are under contract, according to Corcoran Sunshine Marketing Group, at an average price of $19 million. Over the years the office tower has housed the pulp magazine pioneer Frank Munsey, the puppeteer Tony Sarg, the Imperial Russian Consulate and, for a half-century, Macmillan Publishers. Never residents.

The Flatiron is now one of the crown jewels of a national office-to-residential movement, alongside the Chrysler Building, another similarly storied New York landmark whose owner has publicly proposed converting it into housing. Since the Covid-19 pandemic, tens of thousands of apartments have been carved out of distressed workspaces in American cities. Most of those buildings were bought for pennies on the dollar. Troubled office towers across the country are trading for fractions of their pre-pandemic value. As the Wall Street Journal reported in April, a 485,000-square-foot building in Chicago sold for $4 million. A complex in Denver that had traded for $176 million in 2013 changed hands recently for more than $5 million. The federal government sold an office building in Washington for $24 million, a sliver of its former worth.

But the Flatiron is something different. After a long and contested auction, it sold in 2023 for a little more than $160 million. The Brodsky Organization, one of New York’s established real estate families, is leading the conversion with the Sorgente Group. Dan Brodsky chaired the board of the Metropolitan Museum of Art for 12 years. “They consider this another way they’re giving back to New York,” says James Lansill, the Corcoran Sunshine Marketing Group executive who’s handling sales.

A permit for the Flatiron conversion listed as many as 100 units at nearly 2,000 square feet in size. To some of the building’s admirers, turning a publicly cherished landmark into just 37 private homes looks like a loss. But the choice was never between luxury housing and something more democratic. It was between luxury housing and vacancy. Office tenants had left; the building sat empty behind scaffolding while its terra-cotta was recast piece by piece. Only one kind of buyer was ever going to underwrite the cost of a project of this quality. Luxury residential conversion isn’t what happened to the Flatiron instead of preservation — it’s what saved the building.

Most office conversions strip down the building and start over. The Flatiron did the opposite. Sofield’s brief was to keep as much of the original as possible and to use the wreckage itself for the homes’ raw material. The balustrade spindles from the old staircases, for example, have been sandblasted and turned into the legs of bathroom basins. Fittings from the boilers have become decorations in the gym. In a crawl space, behind layers of plywood and drywall, Sofield found a 3-foot section of mirror and molding, the last surviving fragment of a 1,500-seat restaurant called Tavern Louie that vanished sometime in the 1920s. That scrap became the design source for the mirrored columns that will line the building’s new swimming pool in the basement, where the former restaurant’s enormous volume can still be felt.

“My parents were children of the Depression,” Sofield says. “Nothing ever got thrown out. It wasn’t because we needed to have it. It’s that it represented some kind of point in history, and it could always be used as something else. These things couldn’t just be tossed. They had to be remembered.”

The apartments themselves are modernist: Kitchens are Poliform Italian, dark metal cabinets, sleek appliances. The ceilings are high, and on the 21st floor, where the arched windows face west, late-afternoon light streams in over the Hudson River. Every window frame makes up a piece of the building’s ornament. The Flatiron’s exterior is loud and voluptuous, endowed with all the Beaux Arts flourish of 1902. The interiors are quiet. Above the residences sits a floor with no windows, only south-facing skylights, which will be folded into the penthouse when it goes to market this fall.

The case for converting the Flatiron runs deeper than sentiment: Every old building is a carbon debt already paid. The steel in the Flatiron was smelted in 1902, the terra-cotta fired and hauled and set by hand. To knock a sound building down is to throw that away and pay the debt over again for whatever replaces it. It also generates an extraordinary volume of waste. Construction and demolition debris accounts for more than half of New York City’s solid waste stream, the largest single source in the city. The greenest building, as the preservationists like to say, is the one already standing.

Frampton Tolbert, who runs the Historic Districts Council, the organization that protects the city’s historic neighborhoods, says he isn’t troubled by the Flatiron being turned into luxury housing. His organization supports conversions like this one as necessary for building housing at every level. “I don’t know that people will necessarily miss the interior,” Tolbert says. “Given that when it was commercial space, how much did people really engage with it?”

Dolkart agrees, and goes further. Adaptive reuse, he points out, has been a keystone of preservation since the movement began in New York in the late 1960s: A courthouse became the Jefferson Market Library; an immigrant aid society became the Public Theater. For most of us, Dolkart says, the Flatiron has always been an exterior object. Its public meaning is its silhouette. He guarantees that two years after the residents move in, there will be just as many tourist photographs of the building as there are now. “The Flatiron Building’s use has changed, but the meaning on the street will remain the same,” he says.

Three miles north, the Chrysler Building is a different case: Its lobby is a designated interior landmark, protected since 1978. Interior landmarks are rare in New York, with a little more than a hundred of them, and each must be publicly accessible to qualify. For decades, Dolkart brought his Columbia students into the Chrysler lobby to stand under the red marble and the painted ceiling, beside elevator doors inlaid with wood. No guard ever stopped them. Then, at some point after the Sept. 11 attacks, security tightened and the public lost the run of the space. The same thing happened at the Woolworth Building. In both cases the landmark designation remained in force. “These are great interiors,” Dolkart says. “They were meant to be public places. So that’s a loss.” Conversion isn’t what took the Chrysler lobby away from the public. Security did, while the building was still an office — and the landmark designation did nothing to prevent it.

New York has converted more office space than any other American city, and 2026 is on pace for its highest number yet. A 2024 zoning overhaul called City of Yes for Housing Opportunity widened the range of buildings eligible for conversion and stripped out barriers such as parking requirements. New York state’s tax incentive for conversions is, in Tolbert’s view, a good tool, though it reaches only certain kinds of affordable rental buildings. What the city hasn’t done, he argues, is give owners a reason to choose reuse over demolition. When the Midtown South rezoning passed last year, the city upzoned the district and allowed housing where it hadn’t been permitted before, with no incentives attached to conversion. His council supported the housing and wanted the incentives alongside it.

Tolbert has ideas about what those might look like. New York City Council Member Harvey Epstein has introduced legislation to create an Office of Conversion Assistance, which Tolbert reads as a signal that the city takes conversion seriously. He’d like to see a demolition fee, with the revenue directed toward preservation, so the waste a teardown generates is priced into the decision. And he wants a revolving fund for smaller projects, because adaptive reuse currently pencils out only for undertakings large enough to justify the cost. Which is to say, for projects like the Flatiron.

Several buyers have described the Flatiron to Corcoran Sunshine’s Lansill as their forever home. They raised their families somewhere else; the children are grown. Now these buyers are graduating, says Lansill, to what they intend to be the last home of their lives, in a tower that has stood at the corner of Fifth and Broadway since 1902.

The Flatiron was built to be looked at. It’s being remade to be lived in, and that’s what will keep it standing. The tourists will still gather in the park across 23rd Street and lift their phones, and the light will still come through the arched windows on clear afternoons, on the same diagonal it has traveled since the building was new.

items.title: Total, BlackRock Agree on $1.8 Billion Africa Asset Financing
body: TotalEnergies SE reached an agreement with BlackRock Inc.’s Global Infrastructure Partners for a $1.8 billion capital contribution toward some assets connected to oil and gas developments in Africa.

In return for the upfront investment, GIP will be paid a tariff based on the throughput at the assets for as long as 15 years, TotalEnergies said in a statement on Friday, without specifying which assets the deal will cover.

The French major has made significant investments in energy production across Africa. Notably, it is nearing completion of a multiyear project to develop oil fields in landlocked Uganda and transport it to the coast of Tanzania for export. This venture, called the East Africa Crude Oil Pipeline, was opposed by environmental groups that campaigned to discourage banks from getting involved in funding the $5.6 billion venture.

Financial institutions including the African Export Import Bank, the Standard Bank of South Africa Limited, Stanbic Bank Uganda Limited, KCB Bank Uganda and the Islamic Corporation for the Development of the Private Sector agreed to a first tranche of funding for the pipeline last year.
One major provider of financing for African infrastructure projects, Standard Chartered Plc, decided it would not finance EACOP.

items.title: JPMorgan, Santander Lead £1.1 Billion Loan for Drax Solar Deal
body: Banks including JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Banco Santander SA are leading a debt financing of more than £1 billion to fund Drax Group Plc’s purchase of renewable energy company Bluefield Solar Income Fund.
The two banks, along with NatWest Group Plc, have put £1.1 billion ($1.5 billion) in bridge funding in place for the acquisition, according to people familiar with the matter.

The banks will look to sell the debt to institutional investors either later this year or early 2027, said the people, who asked not to be identified because they’re not allowed to comment publicly. Drax may also consider refinancing outstanding debt, said the people.
Spokespeople for Drax, JPMorgan, Santander and NatWest declined to comment.

Long known as a biomass heavyweight, Drax is repositioning itself as a flexible power and storage operator amid sustained political and regulatory scrutiny of its wood-pellet imports. Drax’s purchase of Bluefield adds solar and wind assets to the company’s portfolio for the first time.

The financing is just one package in an already-packed pipeline of deals. Lenders are getting ready to offload more than $138 billion of buyout debt in the coming months, according to JPMorgan estimates. Volumes in the US have reached levels not seen since 2007, while those in Europe are at the highest since the pandemic.

items.title: Lagarde Says She'll Leave ECB in 2027, Won't Give Exact Date
body: Christine Lagarde reiterated that she’ll depart as European Central Bank president in 2027, declining to say whether she’ll remain until her term ends next October.
“I’ll leave in ‘27.” Lagarde told Ireland’s RTE Radio on Friday. Asked whether that means in October of that year, she said, “we’ll see.”
“What I can tell you at this point is that whatever the time it’ll be handled in the most professional way, as it should be,” Lagarde said.

In July, she told reporters that “you are not going to see the back of me before 2027.” Last week, she said that “when there is something to report about me personally, you’ll be the first one to know,” adding that “there is nothing to report.”

Lagarde recently boosted expectations of an early exit from the ECB by revealing that she’ll publish a memoir in January, with Bloomberg also reporting that the World Economic Forum, known for its annual gathering in Davos, is still courting her to take over and that she appears ready to accept the role.
Lagarde’s departure would open up one of the most powerful positions in global central-banking, with former monetary chiefs from the Netherlands and Spain among those competing for the job.
Speaking on Friday in Dublin , Spanish Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo said it’s time to start discussing the ECB’s future after Lagarde.

“It is up to her to decide whether or not she finishes her mandate and we will be supporting her no matter what,” he told Bloomberg Television on the sidelines of a meeting of finance ministers and central bankers in the Irish capital. “In any case, these discussions need to take place or to start taking place” because “it is not just the presidency, there are more vacant spots available and we need to engage these discussions.”
Asked after the gathering whether ministers questioned her about plans for a potential departure, she said “absolutely not.” There’s “nothing to report and nothing to be discussed,” she said.

In the radio interview, Lagarde said finding the right blend on the ECB’s key decision-making panels is key, with the terms of Chief Economist Philip Lane and Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel also ending next year.

“What matters is the skill-set that is at the table of the Executive Board, at the table of the Governing Council and having diversity of views actually helps,” she said. “Diversity of views because you have men and women, diversity of views because you have central-bank experimented economists and because you have other people with a different background, I think that is helpful.”

items.title: Dr. Reddy's to Roll Out Takeda's Dengue Jab in India Next Year
body: Indians will get the country’s first dengue vaccine Qdenga next year, a key milestone to control the infectious disease that is a major public health concern for the South Asian nation.

Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories Ltd. will start selling the shots — manufactured by Japan’s Takeda Pharmaceutical Co. — commercially in the first half of 2027, subject to completing applicable processes, it said in a statement Friday. Takeda’s long-term ambition includes getting the preventive treatment included in the country’s public immunization program, it said.
The companies did not disclose any upfront or milestone payments.
Read More: Takeda’s Dengue Vaccine Shows Long Lasting Protection

In July, the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation approved Qdenga for individuals aged four to 60 years in two doses three months apart. The World Health Organization lists India among the world’s 30 most highly endemic countries for the disease, with nearly 1.1 million people affected over the last five years.

Dr. Reddy’s and Takeda will promote and distribute the jabs in India, engage with healthcare professionals and boost disease awareness. The vaccine has been now approved in 43 countries, with more than 32 million doses distributed worldwide through public and private programs across Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, and Vietnam in Asia, as well as in Latin America and Europe.
